en: I bow to Hara, whose forehead is as beautiful as the moon, and who embraces the celestial river Ganges nestled within his matted locks bound upward.
Salutations forever to Kaṇāda and Bhavanātha, by whom I have indeed been properly instructed in the Vaiśeṣika system. (2)
"Just as one who moves through the supportless sky by relying solely on the thread [of a kite] proceeds playfully, so too shall my audacity here attain success. (3)

Those possessed of discernment, being afflicted by the threefold suffering, while investigating the cause for the cessation of that threefold suffering, perceived in the various Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas that the direct realization of the reality of the Self alone is the means thereto.

Desiring to know the path that serves as the cause for attaining that [liberation], they approached the sage Kaṇāda, who was supremely compassionate. Then the sage Kaṇāda—endowed with the knowledge of reality, dispassion, and sovereign power—reflected in his mind that the knowledge of the true nature of the six categories through their similarities and differences is indeed the supreme path for attaining the direct realization of the self. And since that [knowledge] will be accomplished without effort by means of dharma characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti*), he [proceeded to explain] dharma itself, both in terms of its definition and its essential nature.

Having resolved in his mind, "First I shall teach [the categories], and thereafter I shall teach all six categories through enumeration, definition, and examination," he makes a formal promise for their attention:
"Now, therefore, we shall explain Dharma. (1)

The word *atha* indicates the immediate succession following the disciple’s inquiry. The phrase *ataḥ* means that because the students—being capable of hearing [the teachings] and free from malice—approached [the teacher]. Alternatively, the word *atha* has the sense of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). As it has been said:
"The syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*—these two emerged from the throat of Brahmā in ancient times; therefore, both are auspicious."

And this is indeed appropriate; otherwise, how could one imagine that the Great Sage—who was engaged in composing the Vaiśeṣika treatise—failed to practice auspiciousness, which is a duty transmitted through the continuous tradition of the conduct of the virtuous?

Nor should it be argued that one should not perform [the rite] because its fruit is not seen even when auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) have been performed, while its fruit is seen even when they have not been performed—for a prudent person does not engage in what is fruitless. This is because, in the case of non-performance, one infers the existence of [merit] from another life, whereas in the case of performance, one infers a deficiency in the auxiliary factors (*aṅga-vaiguṇya*); thus, there is certainty regarding its fruitfulness. Indeed, there is not even a suspicion of its being causeless merely because its fruit is not immediately perceived, when its duty-to-be-performed status is enjoined by a Vedic injunction inferred from the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).

Nor does it follow that [the rite] has results pertaining only to this life, such that there would be no inference of results in another birth—as in the case of the *putreṣṭi* sacrifice—because here too, having results only in this life is untenable. In the case of the *kārīrī* sacrifice and others, however, because they are performed with the specific desire for rain and so forth, they have results only in this life. Here, moreover, the qualified performer (*adhikārī*) is one who desires completion, just as one who desires heaven is the qualified performer in a [standard] sacrifice; the distinction is that while the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is the instrument in the latter, here it is the destruction of obstacles. This is because the undertaking proceeds from the desire: "May what has been begun be completed without obstacles."

Nor should it be argued that the fruit is merely the destruction of obstacles while completion arises from its own causes; for that [destruction of obstacles] is not in itself a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), whereas completion is a human goal by virtue of being a means to happiness and because it is what is immediately present. Furthermore, the mere destruction of evil is not the fruit, because it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), as it can be accomplished through penance, the recitation of sacred texts, meritorious deeds, reaching the opposite shore, and so forth.

If the fruit [of auspiciousness] were defined as the destruction of the demerit that obstructs the completion of what has been commenced, then it would be more appropriate for the completion itself to be the fruit. Furthermore, since there is deviation—because completion can also be produced by acts such as giving gold or bathing at Prayāga—it would be reckless to designate those too as *maṅgala*. Moreover, the causality of *maṅgala* consists in the fact that when *maṅgala* is present, completion is necessary; as it has been said: "Because of the rule that from a Vedic rite performed with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), the fruit necessarily follows."

For this very reason, even a "doubtful" cause is indeed a cause, because its status as a Vedic cause consists precisely in the rule of its immediate succession to the result. As for the case of doubt, the postulation of a difference in kind (*vaijātya*) is itself the difference in kind; where the causality is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there the rule of the cause's existence prior to the result must be grasped. However, this does not apply even in the case of the Veda, because in that context the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not presented due to its complexity. Thus, since completion is necessarily contingent upon an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) performed with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Completion (*samāpti*), however, is the authoritative cognition that "this action is finished" once a certain thing has been performed. This [cognition] occurs at the writing of the final sentence at the beginning of a book, at the final oblation in a sacrifice, at the conjunction of the final thread in a cloth, or at the final step upon entering a village; it should be inferred accordingly in each respective case. Even if one postulates a distinct class (*vaijātya*) for completion produced by auspicious rites (*maṅgala*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in either case.

An auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) is an action whose fruit is completion by way of the destruction of obstacles; and that [rite] consists precisely of such forms as salutation to a deity. Even in a case where the absence of obstacles is self-evident, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), because the property of being the means to the destruction of obstacles—though grasped only in a general sense—is not lost, and because salutations and the like are understood to be the means to the destruction of obstacles precisely in that capacity. This is the direction of the argument. || 1 ||
Now he states the meaning of the proposition:
"Dharma is that from which the attainment of worldly prosperity and the supreme good results. (2)

Prosperity (*abhyudaya*) is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is the absolute cessation of suffering; that from which both of these arise is *dharma*. The compound "prosperity-gated-supreme-good" (*abhyudayadvārakaṃ niḥśreyasam*) is either a *madhyamapadalopa* (elliptical) compound or a *pañcamī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. Furthermore, that *dharma* will be described as characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti*). However, if *dharma* is that very unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) to be accomplished through yoga such as meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), then it is of the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*).

The authors of the *Vṛtti*, however, maintain that liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) is happiness consisting in the destruction of all specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self occurring at one and the same time. As for the proof regarding dharma, they say: "Devadatta’s body and so forth must have been preceded by the specific qualities of an enjoyer, because, while being an effect, they are the means for his enjoyment, just like a garland fashioned by him.
This explanation has been disregarded by later scholars because it is not comprehensive, whether taken individually or collectively.

In reality, when the disciple’s general inquiry arises as to what dharma is and what its characteristic is, the answer "that from which the attainment of worldly prosperity (abhyudaya) and the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) results" presents itself; and thus, that from which the attainment of prosperity results and that from which the attainment of the supreme good results—both of these constitute dharma.

Thus, while it should have been stated that dharma is the uncommon cause of the goals of human life (puruṣārtha), the expression "the attainment of prosperity and the highest good" (abhyudayaniḥśreyasasiddhi) was used for the sake of specifically acquainting [the reader] with the two ultimate goals of man: pleasure and the absence of suffering. This is because heaven and liberation alone possess the status of being the supreme goals of man, insofar as they are objects of desire independent of any other desire. Furthermore, the fact that the absence of suffering is also a goal of man will be established later. || 2 ||

Is it not the case that scripture (*śruti*) is the authority for the claim that dharma, characterized by cessation, is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) through the gateway of knowledge of reality? To this we reply: we disagree with the authority of scripture itself, due to the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and tautology.

Even when the *putreṣṭi* sacrifice has been performed, its falsehood arises from the non-production of a son; likewise, the injunctions "one should offer at sunrise," "one should offer before sunrise," and "one should offer at twilight" have their application already established, yet the performance of the oblation at those times—sunrise and so forth—is sublated by such texts as: "A dark dog devours the oblation of him who offers at sunrise; a brindled dog devours the oblation of him who offers before sunrise; both a dark and a brindled dog devour the oblation of him who offers at twilight."

Likewise, because the statement "he recites the first [verse] three times and he recites the last [verse] three times" prescribes the triple utterance of the first and last *sāmidhenī* verses, there is indeed redundancy. Furthermore, since there is no means of establishing the Veda as authoritative, its eternal and faultless nature is itself doubtful when its eternity is contested. If, however, it were of human origin, then its status as the word of a reliable authority (*āpta*) would also be doubtful due to the possibility of error, negligence, contradiction, or lack of proficiency in the instruments of cognition; thus, neither the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), nor the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) as its means, nor *dharma* itself would be established, and everything would be in confusion. To this, he says:
From his word, the authority of the sacred tradition [is established]. || 3 ||

The word *tat* refers to the Lord (*Īśvara*), even though He has not been previously introduced, by virtue of His being established through common renown (*prasiddhi*). This is just as in the sūtra of Gautama, "Its lack of authority [arises] from the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and tautology," where the word *tat* refers to the Veda, even though it has not been previously introduced. And thus, the authority of the *āmnāya*, that is, the Veda, follows from its being spoken—that is, composed—by Him, the Lord.

Alternatively, the phrase "that which" (*yad vā tad*) refers precisely to the proximate *dharma*; thus, the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the *āmnāya*—that is, the Veda—arises from its expression or presentation of *dharma*. The meaning is that whatever sentence presents an authoritative object is itself indeed a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the existence of God and His status as a reliable authority (*āpta*) will be established [later].

As for what was stated—"due to the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and tautology"—in that regard, if there were falsehood, one would have to assume either a result in another birth or a deficiency in the ritual action, the agent, or the means, because it is certain that a result must necessarily follow from a Vedic rite when performed with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*). Nor is it the case that the result is restricted to this life alone, as in the *Kārīrī* sacrifice; for in that case, the qualification belongs to one who desires the revival of withering crops, whereas in the *Putreṣṭi*, the qualification belongs to one who desires a son—this is the distinction.

Nor is there any contradiction, because having specifically promised the *udita* (post-sunrise) and other types of oblations, the performance of the oblation at a time other than that is presented as a censure in such passages as, "A dark [dog] devours his oblation.

Nor is there the fault of tautology, because the eleven *sāmidhenī* verses are recited in the archetype (*prakṛti*), and in the passage, "By means of the fifteenfold thunderbolt of speech, he strikes down this rival," the number fifteen of the *sāmidhenīs* is prescribed in such a way that it would be impossible to achieve without the triple recitation of the first and last *sāmidhenī* verses. || 3 ||

Having explained *dharma* according to its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in accordance with the student's inquiry, the following aphorism (*sūtra*) is presented to establish the subject matter and the relationship [between them]:

"From the knowledge of the true nature (*tattva-jñāna*) of the categories (*padārtha*)—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—produced by the specific [study of] *dharma*, through their similarities and differences, comes the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). (VS 1.1.4)

Since such knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) depends upon the Vaiśeṣika scripture, the latter's status as a cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) follows by the logic of "the stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpāyita*). [Objection: If the word *tattva* is taken in the sense of the scripture—based on the instrumental derivation meaning "that by which reality is known"—then there would be a lack of syntactic connection with the phrase "arising from a specific merit" (*dharmaviśeṣaprasūta*). [Response: Here, the compound is a copulative (*dvandva*) in which all members are equally principal, because the knowledge of the reality of all categories (*sarvapadārtha-tattvajñāna*) is the cause of the supreme good.

In this regard, the relationship between the treatise (*śāstra*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is that of cause and effect; between the treatise and the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), it is that of the instrument and the agent; between the supreme good and the knowledge of reality, it is that of effect and cause; and between the categories such as substance (*dravya*) and the treatise, it is that of the subject matter and the expositor. Through the knowledge of these relationships, those seeking the supreme good engage with this treatise. Furthermore, those desiring liberation engage with the treatise only after having accepted the sage’s status as an authoritative source (*āpta*).

The supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is the absolute cessation of suffering. The absoluteness of the cessation of suffering consists either in its not being contemporaneous with the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of any suffering that has a common locus [with it], or in its being contemporaneous with the destruction of all specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self that have arisen simultaneously [with it]. Alternatively, liberation (*mukti*) is the prior non-existence of suffering delimited by the destruction of all specific qualities. Nor is this a human goal because it is unattainable; for even a prior non-existence is attainable by way of the removal of its causes.

Nor is there any loss of its status as a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), because it retains that character by virtue of being the absence of that which produces the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Furthermore, "productivity" (*janakatva*) is merely a state of essential fitness (*svarūpayogyatā*); for a prior non-existence is not the final causal complex (*caramasāmagrī*), such that the effect would necessarily occur when it is present. If that were the case, it would follow that the effect itself is beginningless. Thus, just as it did not produce the effect for so long due to the absence of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), it will likewise not produce it later due to their continued absence; for even the statement, "the cessation of the cause occurs through human effort," has as its intended meaning merely the preservation of the prior non-existence.

For this very reason, in the second sūtra of Gautama’s work, the statement—"Upon the successive disappearance of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, through the disappearance of each subsequent member, there is the disappearance of the one immediately preceding it, which is liberation"—expresses the absence of the effect due to the absence of the cause, thereby confirming that liberation consists precisely in the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of suffering. For the "disappearance" mentioned here—namely, the disappearance of activity upon the disappearance of defects, the disappearance of birth upon the disappearance of activity, and the disappearance of suffering upon the disappearance of birth—is not destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), but rather non-origination; and that is nothing other than prior non-existence.

Nor is there a lack of establishment of the counter-positive (pratiyogin), because the counter-positive is established in a general sense simply as "suffering," just as in the case of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). For even in that case, what is required is precisely the non-arising of suffering by way of the destruction of transgression (*pratyavāya*). Furthermore, in the world, it is observed that the removal of things such as snake-bites results in the fruit of the non-arising of suffering; thus, the activity of discerning persons is directed solely toward the removal of the means of suffering.

Some, however, maintain that liberation is simply the absolute non-existence of suffering. Although this [non-existence] does not reside in the self (*ātman*), it is nevertheless established in the self by residing in clods of earth and other such things. Its establishment consists precisely in the destruction of suffering that does not coexist with the prior absence of suffering, because that [destruction] is accepted as being related to it; for when that [destruction] exists, the absolute non-existence of suffering is perceived therein. And this being so, they say that scriptural passages such as "he moves about completely liberated from suffering" are also rendered consistent.

That is not so, because the absolute non-existence of suffering cannot be achieved and is therefore not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). Furthermore, the destruction of suffering cannot have a relation to that [absolute non-existence], as it would result in a mere technical convention (*paribhāṣā*). This is because the scriptural passage, "He moves about completely liberated from suffering," intends to show that the prior non-existence of suffering itself takes on a form identical to absolute non-existence by way of the removal of its causes.

[Objection: But surely this [absence of suffering] is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), because it lacks the status of being the object of an unconditioned desire; for at the time of suffering, pleasure does not arise, and thus those who seek pleasure engage in activity precisely for the sake of the absence of suffering. [Reply: This is not so, because the opposite could equally well be asserted. Why might it not be the case that even the desire for pleasure is conditioned by the absence of suffering? For we observe that those overwhelmed by grief, even when indifferent to pleasure, engage in activities such as consuming poison or hanging themselves with the sole intention of attaining the absence of suffering.

[Objection: But surely this [liberation] is also a human goal only when it is known; however, for liberation as the absence of suffering, there is no such thing as being known, otherwise one would act even for the sake of states such as fainting. [Reply: This is not so, because it is impossible for that which is known through scripture and inference to be unknowable. For there is indeed scripture such as: "He moves about completely liberated from suffering," and "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death," and so forth.

There is also inference: "The continuum of suffering is absolutely severed, because it is a continuum, like the continuum of a lamp-flame," and so forth. Furthermore, the destruction of the final suffering is also cognizable through perception, because it is made an object for a moment by the direct intuition of suffering; and because it is admitted that for yogis, the destruction of future suffering is perceived through the power of the dharma born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*).

If it is argued that, despite this, it is not a human goal because gain and loss are equal—since there is a loss of pleasure just as there is of pain, as both are produced by the same causal complex—we reply: no, for generally those who are free from passion, who fear the storm-clouds of suffering, and who regard even a mere firefly of pleasure as sufficient, do engage in it.

[Objection: Even so, the cessation of suffering is not the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), because it is impossible to prevent future suffering, past suffering has already passed, and present suffering ceases even without human effort. [Response: This is not so, because human activity is directed toward the eradication of the cause, just as in the case of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). For instance, false knowledge accompanied by its latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); its eradication comes from the knowledge of the true nature of the self (*ātmatattvajñāna*); and that knowledge of reality is to be accomplished through the practice of yoga. Thus, engagement in such practice is logically justified for that purpose.

If it is argued that liberation is indeed the manifestation of eternal happiness and not merely the absence of suffering, we say no; for there is no evidence for such eternal happiness. Even if it existed, since its manifestation would be eternal, there would be no distinction between the liberated and the transmigrating soul. Furthermore, because this manifestation is something produced, once it ceases, the state of transmigration would necessarily recur.

If it is argued that liberation (*mukti*) is the merging of the individual self (*jīvātman*) into the Brahman-self, we say no; for if "merging" (*laya*) means becoming one, then it is untenable, since two things cannot become one. If it is argued that merging is the departure of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), and that the subtle body consists of the eleven organs along with their departure from the gross body—this is also not so, because by this much you have merely stated the absence of the causal complex of suffering (*duḥkhasāmagrī*). Thus, the conclusion remains that liberation is simply the non-existence of suffering.

By this, the doctrine of the Ekadaṇḍins—that liberation is the abiding of the solitary self upon the cessation of ignorance, and that the self consists of consciousness and bliss—is refuted; for there is no evidence for the self being either knowledge or bliss. Nor is the scripture, "Brahman is eternal consciousness and bliss," a proof [for this], as it establishes that Brahman possesses knowledge and possesses bliss. Indeed, the cognition occurs as "I know" and "I am happy," but not as "I am knowledge" or "I am happiness."

Furthermore, since Brahman exists even now, there would follow the consequence that there is no distinction between the liberated and those still transmigrating; moreover, the cessation of ignorance would not constitute a human goal (puruṣārtha) because Brahman is eternal and thus not something to be accomplished, and because its direct realization is not something to be accomplished since it is of the very nature of Brahman itself, and likewise, bliss also cannot be accomplished since it is of the very nature of Brahman—thus, any purposeful activity for that end is simply untenable.

If it is argued that liberation is a stream of consciousness free from affliction (*nirupaplava*), we say no. If "freedom from affliction" means the disappearance of afflictions such as suffering, then since that alone constitutes the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), there is no evidence for the continued persistence of the stream of consciousness. Furthermore, even if such persistence were to occur, it would necessarily entail the persistence of the body. Thus, it is established that the cessation of suffering in the manner described is itself the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

In the expression "knowledge of reality" (*tattvasya jñānam*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karma*). In the phrase "by means of similarity and dissimilarity" (*sādharmyavaidharmyābhyām*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of manner (*prakāra*). Here, "similarity" (*sādharmya*) is a common property (*anugato dharmaḥ*), and "dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya*) is a distinct property (*vyāvṛtto dharmaḥ*). Although in some cases what is a similarity for one thing may be a dissimilarity for another, and what is a dissimilarity for one may be a similarity for others, nevertheless, knowledge is intended here as being in accordance with that specific nature (*tādrūpyeṇa*). Furthermore, in this context, the mere enumeration (*uddeśa*) of the categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth results in their classification (*vibhāga*).

And that [definition] has as its result the exclusion of numbers both less than and greater than [six]; by means of it, the restriction "there are exactly six categories" is established. However, that is untenable: if another category (padārthāntara) to be excluded is apprehended, the restriction is untenable; if it is not apprehended, the exclusion is untenable.

Now, one might argue: "This is not an exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), but rather an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*); for among categories, the non-connection with the six characteristics is what is excluded. If this is said, we reply: no, because if the term "category" (*padārtha*) includes only those things already established as such, it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); furthermore, there is simply no perception of such a thing [as a category possessing all six characteristics]. Moreover, is the non-connection to be excluded that of the characteristics taken collectively or individually? In the first case, since the non-connection of the collective set exists everywhere, the exclusion is untenable.

If it is argued that even in the final case, since each pair of categories is mutually present everywhere, the exclusion [of others] is indeed untenable—this is not so. Regarding the categories accepted by others, such as potency (*śakti*), number (*saṅkhyā*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), and so forth, it is asserted by them that these do not possess the six characteristics; the purpose of that exclusion is for the sake of restriction. Thus, the meaning of "there are only six categories" is that among the six characteristics perceived, there is necessarily a connection with at least one of those characteristics, and not a lack thereof.

In this regard, it is understood that when connected with a substantive (*viśeṣya*), there is the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*); when connected with an adjective (*viśeṣaṇa*), the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*); and when connected with a verb (*kriyā*), the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*). Regarding this, some maintain that the particle *eva* possesses three powers; others hold that its power lies solely in the act of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), while the specific types of exclusion—such as the exclusion of non-connection or the exclusion of connection with another—are obtained through syntactic proximity (*samabhivyāhāra*).

The phrase "born from a specific merit" (*dharmaviśeṣaprasūtāt*) is an epithet of "knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñāna*). In this context, "specific merit" refers to merit characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti*). However, if "knowledge of reality" is defined as the scripture (*śāstra*)—in the sense that reality is known by means of it—then "specific merit" must be stated to consist of the command and grace of the Lord (*īśvara*). For it is heard that the great sage Kaṇāda composed his scripture after having obtained the command and grace of the Lord.

By "knowledge of reality" (tattvajñāna) is intended here the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of the truth of the Self, because only that is capable of uprooting false knowledge along with its latent impressions (savāsanā). This is because in such passages as "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey" and "Two Brahmans are to be known," the word "knowing" (vedana) refers to direct realization, and the same applies in the passage "He sees though he is sightless. Furthermore, that realization is attained through the sequence of scripture, reflection, and meditative concentration (nididhyāsana), as indicated by the ablative case used in the sense of cause (*hetu-pañcamī*). || 4 ||

Now, providing the classification and specific enumeration of the category of substance (*dravya*), which was mentioned first because it is the locus of all categories and the recipient of liberation, he says:
**The Determination of Qualities:** Earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind are the substances. (5)

The particle *iti* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). By this, the meaning is that there are exactly nine substances—neither more nor less. If it is asked: "Since the exclusion of a lesser or greater number is established by the very force of the enumeration itself, what is the purpose of the particle *iti*? [The answer is: Because even though the aphorism could have been possible as a mere statement of names (*uddeśa*), the particle *iti* is employed specifically to indicate that the primary intent (*tātparya*) of the aphorism lies in the enumeration.

Since gold and so forth, as well as Īśvara, are included within this very category, and since darkness—which might be suspected of being something additional—is demonstrated to be a non-entity (abhāva), this [definition] is to be understood as definitive. The reason for not employing a compound is to demonstrate that all these [categories] possess equal primacy. Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras himself will demonstrate their defining characteristics on the occasion of discussing their dissimilarities (vaidharmya).

Now, one might object: "Gold is not earth because it lacks odor; it is not water because it is devoid of natural fluidity (*sneha-sāṃsiddhika-dravatva*); it is not fire because it possesses weight (*gurutva*); for the same reason, it is neither air nor time and so forth; therefore, it is distinct from the nine [substances]. If this is argued, we reply: No. The first two [reasons] are non-apparent (*anābhāsa*). The third is self-contradictory (*svarūpa-asiddha*). Beyond that, there is the proving of what is already established (*siddha-sādhana*) and the non-establishment of the nature of the reason itself (*hetu-svarūpa-asiddhi*). Furthermore, the fiery nature (*taijasatva*) of gold will be established later. 5.

By virtue of their nature as qualities (*guṇatva*), qualities (*guṇa*) reside in all substances, are manifested by substances, and manifest substances. Thus, [the author] states another substance and provides the enumeration and classification of qualities:

"Color, taste, smell, touch, numbers, dimensions, separateness, conjunction and disjunction, priority and posteriority, cognitions, pleasure and pain, desire and aversion, and efforts—these are the qualities. (VS 1.1.6)

By the word "and" (ca), he includes heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, mental impression (*saṃskāra*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and sound; for these are already well-known as being qualities (*guṇa*), and thus they are not mentioned explicitly. Furthermore, the compound is used to indicate that their status as qualities will be established through their definitions at their respective places, so that there is no need to state their essential nature here. As for number (*saṅkhyā*) and dimension (*parimāṇa*), however, the lack of compounding and the use of the plural form are intended to indicate their co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with number and dimension existing at the same time.

Although there is no other oneness co-located with one oneness, nor any other largeness or length co-located with largeness or length, nevertheless, there is indeed mutual co-location among duality and the rest, as well as co-location between different kinds of dimensions such as largeness and length.

Although separateness (*pṛthaktva*) coexists with dual-separateness (*dvipṛthaktva*) and so forth, and thus—like number—it ought to be designated by a plural form, it is nevertheless expressed in the singular to indicate its distinction from number, characterized as it is by being manifested through a limit (*avadhi*). The dual number is used for conjunction and disjunction to indicate that both are produced by a single action, and also to indicate that priority and posteriority are alike in being marks of space and time, since they are defined by mutual dependence.

The plural number [in "buddhīnām"] is used to refute the Sāṅkhya-accepted view that there is only a single intellect (*buddhi*), by means of the distinction between various types of cognition such as knowledge (*vidyā*) and so forth. The dual number [in "sukhaduḥkhayoḥ"] is employed to indicate that both pleasure and pain are alike in producing the single effect delimited by the state of being an object of experience (*bhoga*), that they equally give rise to unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and to show that even pleasure is to be contemplated as suffering. The dual number [in "icchādveṣayoḥ"] serves to point out that both desire and aversion are causes with respect to purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).

It should be inferred that the plural number is used with reference to the fact that the ten types of efforts—those pertaining to what is enjoined and what is prohibited—are causes of merit, while another ten types are causes of demerit.

Alternatively, they are mentioned collectively in order to demonstrate that color, taste, smell, and touch are the causes for the arrangement of the elemental sense organs, or for the establishment of the process of transformation through heating (*pākaja*). Furthermore, since there is disagreement regarding number—such as whether it is dual or plural—the plural designation is employed to indicate the refutation of such misconceptions.

However, regarding distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), it is mentioned separately both to indicate that its plurality arises precisely from the plurality of number, and to indicate that its distinction from number lies in its being manifested by the cognition of limits (*avadhi*). Regarding dimension (*parimāṇa*), the plural number is used to dispel misconceptions such as length and shortness. Regarding conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*), the dual number is used to make known their mutual opposition.

Since distance (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) could be divided into spatial and temporal types, resulting in a distinct genus for each, there would be the contingency of having four qualities; thus, the classification of qualities would be deficient. Therefore, it should be inferred that even in those cases, they are designated by dual terms (*dvivacana*), and so forth. The definitions of these will be stated later. || 6 ||

Since actions (karma) are produced by substances and produced by qualities, and because they inhere in substances possessing color, they are perceptible. Therefore, immediately after the enumeration of substances and qualities, he states the mention and classification of action: "Action is defined as throwing upwards, throwing downwards, contraction, and locomotion; these are the actions. The word "iti" is for the purpose of restriction, since whirling and so forth are included within locomotion. In this context, there are five universals—throwing-upward-ness, throwing-downward-ness, contraction-ness, expansion-ness, and locomotion-ness—which are the direct subordinates of the universal of action (karmatva).

But is this not untenable? For "going" (*gamana*) is a synonym for "action" (*karman*), and the cognition "it goes everywhere" is observed; furthermore, since the four classes (*jāti*) such as throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇatva*) and so on—which are co-present with the absolute mutual absence of one another—are never experienced as being co-present [in a single locus], it might be argued that there are exactly four classes subsumed under "action-ness" (*karmatva*).

It is true that "going" (*gamana*) is merely a synonym for action (*karman*); however, its separate mention is for the purpose of subsuming under a single term those various actions—such as whirling, dispersing, flowing, upward flaming, bending, and straightening—which possess distinct cognitions and designations. Alternatively, "the nature of going" (*gamanatva*) is itself a fifth genus (*jāti*) subordinate to the genus "action-ness" (*karmatva*). Consequently, the application of the term "going" is primary (*mukhya*) only in the case of whirling, dispersing, and so forth; if the term "going" is applied to throwing upward (*utkṣepaṇa*), throwing downward (*avakṣepaṇa*), and the like, then it is secondary (*bhākta*).

The common characteristic, shared by both primary and secondary [motions], is precisely the state of being the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of conjunctions and disjunctions occurring in its own substratum. As for the universal *gamanatva* (the nature of going), its manifester is precisely the state of being the non-inherent cause of conjunctions and disjunctions with respect to various directions and locations; and since this [characteristic] exists in all cases such as whirling (*bhramaṇa*) and so forth, they are all included simply by the mention of "going."

However, "going out-ness" (*niṣkramaṇatva*) and "entering-ness" (*praveśanatva*), and so forth, are not [distinct] universals (*jāti*). For when a person goes from one house to another, to some observer there arises the cognition "he enters," while to another there arises the cognition "he goes out"; in that case, there would be a confusion of universals (*jātisaṅkara*). Likewise, in the case of a single water-channel where one turns around, exiting one [end] and entering the other, both cognitions—"he goes out" and "he enters"—are observed; therefore, one determines that this is merely a commonality of limiting conditions (*upādhisāmānya*). Thus, first there is upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*).

From the conjunction of the soul, which possesses the desire for throwing down (*avakṣepaṇa*), effort, and the impulse from the hand—acting as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) characterized by the upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*)—there simultaneously arises in both the hand and the pestle an action called throwing down, which is conducive to the falling of the mortar. Then, following that, from the conjunction of the soul with the hand—which possesses the desire for throwing down, knowledge, and effort—and from the impulse of the hand, there simultaneously occurs in both the hand and the pestle the action of throwing down, which is favorable to the falling of the mortar.

Then, when the upward motion of a pestle occurs due to the conjunction with a very firm substance, neither desire nor effort is the cause there; rather, the pestle’s leaping up arises from momentum (*saṃskāra*) alone. That is merely a form of motion and not true "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇa*); the conventional usage of the term "throwing upwards" in that case is figurative. Similarly, the conventional usage of "throwing upwards" regarding two winds colliding head-on or tail-to-tail, or regarding cotton and the like propelled by them, is also figurative.

Thus, even though water rises upward due to the impact of two streams meeting, the conventional usage of "lifting up" (*utkṣepaṇa*) and "throwing down" (*avakṣepaṇa*) is primarily applied only to the body, its parts, and objects connected to them—such as a pestle (*muṣala*) or a spear (*tomara*)—as in the expressions "he lifts up his hand," "he lifts up the pestle," or "he lifts up the spear," and likewise for "he throws it down."

Contraction (*ākuñcana*), however, is that action which, while the constituent conjunctions (*ārambhaka-saṃyoga*) of the parts still exist, produces non-constituent conjunctions (*anārambhaka-saṃyoga*) among those very parts, thereby producing the curvature of a composite substance such as a cloth; from this action arise the cognitions: "the lotus contracts," "the cloth contracts," and "the hide contracts."

Thus, there is an action called *prasāraṇa* (extension) which destroys the non-originative conjunctions of previously arisen parts; from this arises the cognition: "the cloth extends," "the hide extends," "the lotus opens," and so forth. Whatever collection of actions exists distinct from these four [types] is all a particular kind of motion (*gamanaviśeṣa*). Among those, *bhramaṇa* (revolution) is an action conducive to oblique conjunctions in a wheel or similar object, resulting from the conjunction of the hand with a self possessing effort, and from the impulse (*nodana*) and friction (*avaghaṭṭana*) caused by that hand which possesses the action.

The [processes] beginning with *recanā* (expulsion) are also to be explained. He will clarify this further ahead: it should be understood that these actions—such as the performance of enjoined sacrifices, ritual bathing, and giving—are produced by the conjunction of the self with an effort conducive to *dharma*, whereas prohibited acts such as traveling to forbidden places, violence, and eating *kalañja* are produced by the conjunction of the self with an effort conducive to *adharma*. || 7 ||

Immediately after the enumeration (*uddeśa*) of substance (*dravya*) and the other categories, he begins the section on the common properties (*sādharmya*) of three of them. Since the knowledge of the true nature (*tattvajñāna*) of the common properties of these three—substance, quality, and action—is conducive to liberation and is thus first desired by the student, he states their common properties even before the enumeration of the three categories beginning with generality (*sāmānya*): "The non-distinction of substance, quality, and action consists in their being existent, being non-eternal, having substance, being effects, being causes, and possessing generality and particularity. (VS 1.2.8) This is the non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*) among substance, quality, and action.

Even though there are distinctions, this term "non-distinction" (aviśeṣa) refers to similarity (sādharmya), namely, being the object of the cognition and designation "existent" (sat). This is because all three possess existence (*sattā*). Regarding "impermanent" (*anitya*): although being the counter-positive of destruction (*dhvaṃsa-pratiyogitva*) is not common to atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth, what is intended is the possession of a property that distinguishes categories of entities (*padārtha-vibhājaka-upādhi*) residing in that which is the counter-positive of destruction. Regarding "like substance" (*dravyavat*): [the same applies].

"Substantial" (*dravyavat*) means that which possesses substance by virtue of being its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); since this [quality] also does not exist in atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth, what is intended is the possession of a property that distinguishes categories (*padārthavibhājakopādhi*) residing in that which has substance as its inherent cause. "Effect" (*kārya*) means the possession of a property that distinguishes categories residing in that which is the counter-positive of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāvapratiyogin*). "Cause" (*kāraṇa*)... [is defined].

It is the state of possessing a category-distinguishing attribute (padārthavibhājakopādhi) that resides in a class of things which invariably precede their effects other than cognition. By this definition, there is no over-extension (*atiprasakti*) to "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like, which serve as causes by way of being objects (*viṣayatayā*) in the direct perception of themselves; nor is there non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of "sphericality" (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and the like, which are not productive causes. "Possessing generality and particularity" (*sāmānyaviśeṣavat*) means: generality (*sāmānya*) is existence (*sat*), while particularity (*viśeṣa*) refers to substancehood (*dravyatva*), qualityhood (*guṇatva*), actionhood (*karmatva*), and so forth, insofar as they mutually differentiate [their instances]; the meaning is "the state of possessing those."

If it is objected that causality is over-extensive because even a universal (jāti) generates merit and demerit—on account of Vedic injunctions such as "one should give a cow" and "a cow must not be touched with the foot"—we say no; for the universal is employed merely as a delimiting factor (avacchedaka). Furthermore, this is illustrative: one should also observe that being denotable by words whose meanings are inherent in themselves is a common characteristic (sādharmya) of the three [categories].

If, however, the common property established by the teacher Praśastadeva—namely, that "the state of being an effect," "impermanence," and "having a cause" belong only to those things that possess causes, while "the state of being a cause" belongs elsewhere—is what is being stated, then [the subject] should not be qualified by the possession of the attributes that differentiate the categories of entities (*padārtha*), according to the method stated in the Sūtra. For the three [categories] possess the quality of producing qualities and being produced by qualities, "elsewhere than eternal substances. (8)
He clarifies this very point by means of another aphorism:
"The common property (*sādharmya*) of substance and quality is their being the originators of things belonging to their own respective classes. (9)
Substances originate another substance, and qualities originate another quality. (10)

Excluding the ultimate composite substances and all-pervading substances, as well as the qualities of the ultimate composite—namely the qualities such as duality, double-separateness, priority, and posteriority—one should understand that the common property (*sādharmya*) consists in being the originator of its own kind (*sajātīyārambhakatva*). Alternatively, what is intended is the possession of a category-delimiting attribute (*padārthavibhājakopādhi*) that resides in things which originate their own kind; by this, even those individual substances that are not productive are included. || 10 ||
Now, one might ask: why do actions not initiate another action? To this he says:
"An action that is to be accomplished by another action does not exist. (11)

The term *vidira* has the meaning of "cognition" (*jñāna*) and does not denote "existence" (*sattā*). The meaning is that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for an action being accomplished by another action, as is the case with substances and qualities produced from their own kind. This is the underlying intention here: if an action were to produce another action, it would have to produce it immediately after its own arising, just like sound.

And thus, when a disjunction has been produced from all the substances in conjunction with which the prior action [occurred], what could a second action disjoin? For a disjunction must be preceded by a conjunction, and no other conjunction has arisen in that locus; furthermore, if it were not to produce a disjunction, the definition of action would be violated.

Nor should it be said that it will produce another action at a subsequent moment, because for that which is capable [of acting], delay is impossible, and because there is no other factor to be depended upon. Furthermore, if it were to produce [the effect] even at the moment of the destruction of the prior conjunction, its status as a producer of disjunction would be untenable; and if it were to produce it at the time of the arising of the subsequent conjunction, the same objection would apply. However, at the time immediately following the arising of the subsequent conjunction, the action itself is simply destroyed. Thus, it has been well said: "There exists nothing to be accomplished by action. (11)
He states the dissimilarity of substance from qualities and actions:
"Substance is neither an effect nor a cause. (12)

A substance does not destroy its own effect, nor does it destroy its own cause; the meaning is that there is no relationship of "slayer and slain" between two substances that have entered into a causal relation as effect and cause. The point is that the destruction of a substance occurs only through the destruction of its substratum or the destruction of the conjunctions that constitute its origin. The term *vadhāti* (he destroys) is a Vedic (Sūtra-style) usage. || 12 ||
He states that the group (gaṇa) is subject to destruction through cause and effect:
"In both ways, the qualities (guṇas). (13)

The meaning is that some are destroyed by their effects, while others are destroyed by their causes. Among the sounds beginning with the first (the second sound), destruction occurs through their effects; however, the last one is destroyed by its cause, because the penultimate sound destroys the final one. || 13 ||
Having stated that the qualities (guṇas) are opposed to both the cause and the effect, he now states that action (karman) is opposed to the effect:
"Action is opposed to the effect" (14).

The term *kāryavirodhi* (opposed by its own effect) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because action (*karman*) is destroyed by the subsequent conjunction produced by itself. It is an absolute rule that substances do not stand in opposition to their own effects or causes. However, there is no such fixed rule for qualities (*guṇa*) and actions, because it will be explained later that the destruction of these two occurs through the destruction of their substratum, the destruction of their non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), the destruction of their efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), or through opposing qualities. || 14 ||

Having established the commonality of the three [categories] in accordance with the student's desire, he now begins the definition of those three, saying: "Substance is that which possesses action and quality and is an inherent cause. (15)

It is "possessing action and qualities" (*kriyāguṇavat*) because actions and qualities exist within it. Here, the word *lakṣaṇa* signifies a mark (*cihna*); by the force of its etymological derivation—as that by which something is characterized—it denotes a specific distinguishing characteristic (*liṅgaviśeṣa*) that excludes both homogeneous and heterogeneous classes through its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Substance (*dravya*) is characterized by action (*kriyā*) and by the quality of possessing attributes (*guṇavattva*); thus, through its possession of qualities, substance is distinguished from both homogeneous and heterogeneous categories. In this context, the homogeneous categories consist of the five beginning with quality (*guṇa*), insofar as they share the nature of being existent (*bhāvatva*); the heterogeneous category, however, is non-existence (*abhāva*). Therefore, substance is distinct from qualities and the rest because it possesses qualities; for that which is not distinct from qualities and the rest does not possess qualities, just like qualities themselves.

Although possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*) does not exist in the composite whole (*avayavin*) at the first moment, nevertheless, what is intended is the state of possessing that which is opposed to the absolute non-existence of qualities (*guṇātyantābhāvavirodhimattva*), because even the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsa*) of a quality are opposed to the absolute non-existence of a quality. Likewise, being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) is also a definition of the category of substance (*dravyapadārtha*) that serves to differentiate it from the other six categories. Nor is there a lack of proof for the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*), because the difference [of substance] from qualities and so forth is established by perception in the case of a jar and the like.

Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) here; for although the exclusion of others is already established with respect to the delimitation of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is [intended] with respect to the delimitation of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*). Some maintain that there is no *siddhasādhana* when the delimitors of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) differ, as in the case of the argument "speech and mind are eternal. This is not correct; because even in such cases, the requirement remains indispensable: if the property to be proven is established anywhere within the locus delimited by the delimitor of the subject, the status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) is undermined.

The word "iti" follows "ityādi" (and so forth); by this, possession of number, possession of dimension, possession of distinctness, possession of conjunction, and possession of disjunction are also included as characteristics of substance. || 15 ||

Following the enumeration of substances, he states the definition of qualities (guṇas), because they are mentioned immediately after them: "That which resides in a substance, is devoid of qualities, and is not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions, being independent—this is the definition of a quality. (16)

That which has the nature of depending upon substance is "substance-dependent" (*dravyāśrayī*). Since this [definition] would also apply to substance itself, he says: "devoid of qualities" (*aguṇavān*). Even so, there would be over-extension to action (*karman*); therefore, he says: "not a cause of conjunctions and disjunctions. Even so, there would be a failure to include conjunction, disjunction, dharma, adharma, the knowledge of the Lord, and so forth; hence he says: "independent" (*anapekṣa*).

In this context, the word "quality" (*guṇa*) should be supplied immediately after the phrase "independent" (*anapekṣa*). The meaning is: that which, being independent with respect to conjunctions and disjunctions, does not function as their cause is a quality. This is because conjunctions, disjunctions, and so forth are dependent upon other conjunctions and disjunctions. The definition of a quality is: possessing a genus that is pervaded by existence (*sattā*) and resides eternally in eternal substances. That causality which belongs to something possessing generality, while lacking both inherent causality (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) and non-inherent causality (*asamavāyikāraṇatva*) with respect to both conjunction and disjunction taken together, is the indicator of the nature of a quality.

Conjunction and disjunction are each individually causes of conjunction and disjunction, not when combined. Dharma, adharma, the Lord’s knowledge, and so forth, possess merely the status of efficient causes (nimittakāraṇa) for both; they lack the status of inherent causes (samavāyikāraṇa) or non-inherent causes (asamavāyikāraṇa). This is their inclusion [in the category of substance]. Alternatively, the absence of being an inherent cause of conjunction and disjunction, while being devoid of the status of an inherent cause [of those], is the indicator of the common property of possessing qualities (guṇatva). Or rather, the definition of a quality (guṇa) is simply: being a possessor of qualities, while being a possessor of generality (sāmānyavat), and while being distinct from action (karma). || 16 ||
He states the definition of action (karman), which was mentioned immediately after the categories (gaṇa):
"Action has as its definition that which subsists in a single substance, is devoid of qualities, and is the independent cause of conjunctions and disjunctions. (17)

That which has only one substance as its substratum is "one-substance" (*ekadravya*); that in which no quality exists is "qualityless" (*aguṇa*). The phrase "the independent cause of conjunctions and disjunctions" means that it does not depend on any other entity that arises immediately after its own arising. Therefore, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhatva*) because of the dependence on an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) or the dependence on the prior absence of conjunction; for either [of these] is intended by the term "not depending on what arises immediately after its own arising," since even the destruction of a prior conjunction does not arise immediately after its own [cause], as it lacks a connection with the first moment due to being a non-entity (*abhāva*).

Action (*karmatva*) is the state of possessing a genus that is directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*) and is eternally recurring; or, it is the state of possessing a genus that delimits the causality of the unique cognition "it moves"; or, it is the state of possessing a genus that resides in what is other than qualities (*guṇa*) and in what is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*); or, it is the state of possessing a genus that delimits the causality of disjunction occurring in the moment immediately following its own production. Furthermore, this category, which is attested by the cognition "it moves," cannot be explained away as being merely the production [of an object] in contiguous locations and so forth, because momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) will be refuted later on. The manner in which a definition establishes the difference from others is exactly as stated previously. (17)
Now he begins the section on the common properties of the three [categories] by way of their causes:
"Substance is the common cause of substances, qualities, and actions. (18)

"Commonality" (*sāmānya*) means "the same," that is, "one," as in the expression "these two have the same mother. The meaning is that substance, quality, and action reside in one and the same substance which serves as their inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). The common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of these three is the possession of a genus (*jāti*) that resides in that which has a substance as its inherent cause. || 18 ||
He states the common property of the three [substances]—that they have qualities as their non-inherent causes:
"Likewise, [they possess] quality" (19).

The common characteristic of the three [categories] is the possession of a genus residing in that which has a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) as its cause. Conjunction is the non-inherent cause of substances; for the qualities of effects—such as color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, separateness, and so forth—their non-inherent causes are qualities belonging to the same class in their respective causes; for the qualities of the self, such as cognition and the rest, their non-inherent cause is conjunction with the mind; and for the qualities of the earthly atoms, their non-inherent cause is conjunction with fire.

Regarding action (*karman*), however, its having as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) the conjunction with a soul possessing impulsion, impact, gravity, fluidity, momentum, unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), or effort—just as in the case of fire and so forth—should be inferred by oneself accordingly. In some cases, even a single quality can be the originator of all three: substance, quality, and action. For example, the conjunction of a moving tuft of cotton with another tuft of cotton produces action in that other tuft, initiates the dual-substance (*dvitūlaka*) as a new substance, and also initiates its dimension (*parimāṇa*).

In some cases, a single quality initiates both a substance and a quality; for example, the conjunction of two tuft-masses alone—known as "accumulation" (pracaya) and independent of velocity—initiates the substance consisting of two tufts as well as its dimension. || 19 ||
In some cases, he states that a single action produces multiple effects:
"Action is common to conjunction, disjunction, and velocity. (20)

The word "cause" (kāraṇam) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence]. In whatever substance an action has arisen, having produced as many disjunctions as there were conjunctions with that same substance, it likewise produces that same number of conjunctions elsewhere; furthermore, velocity (vega) produces only one [conjunction] in its own substratum. The term "velocity" also implies "elasticity" (sthitisthāpaka). || 20 ||

[Objection: Surely, when a conjunction that initiates [a substance] is produced by a substance possessing action, and a substance is then initiated by that [conjunction], that [substance] must also be produced solely by action, because action precedes it; therefore, he says:
"Action is not [the cause] of substances. (21)
The meaning is that karma is not the cause of substances. || 21 ||
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of exclusion" (vyatirekāt). || 22 ||

"Because of exclusion" means because of cessation. Since the action ceases due to the subsequent conjunction, the substance is produced [at that point]; thus, action is not the cause of the substance. Furthermore, an action in a state of destruction is not the cause of a substance. Moreover, would action be the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the substance or the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*)? It cannot be the former; for since a substance is destroyed by the destruction of its non-inherent cause, it would follow that the substance is destroyed simply by the destruction of the action of the constituent parts.

Not the second [alternative], because when a large cloth is destroyed, a fragmentary cloth is produced from the very conjunctions that remained; thus, there is a deviation [from the rule] since we observe the commencement of a substance even from parts that are devoid of motion. || 22 ||
Having stated that many [substances] can initiate one [substance], he now states that many [substances] can initiate a single effect:
"The effect of substances is a substance; this is the general rule. (23)

The term "dravyāṇi" [in the compound] means "substances" (dravye) and "substances" (dravyāṇi); it refers to those substances. In that regard, a two-thread cloth is produced from two threads, and even by many threads, a single cloth is produced. Now, one might object: "Is not a single-thread cloth also seen, where the warp and weft are formed by a single thread alone? No; for in that case, due to the absence of conjunction in a single [thread], there is an absence of an inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), and thus no cloth is produced.

Nor can the conjunction of the swift threads be the non-inherent cause [of the cloth], because there is no conjunction between a part and its whole due to their being inseparable (*ayutasiddha*), since we do not admit the relation of "produced and producer" (*ārabhyārambhaka-bhāva*) between them; for it is a contradiction for corporeal entities to occupy the same location. If it is argued that this is indeed observed to be so, we say no: in that case, through the impact of the shuttle and other tools, the large whole—the single thread—is destroyed, and upon the production of several fragmentary wholes (the individual threads), the cloth arises from their mutual conjunction; it is only because of the mental superimposition (*abhimāna*) of unity upon those threads which are in fact distinct that such an appearance occurs.
Now, one might ask: "Just as substances have substances as their effects and qualities have qualities as their effects, why should actions not also have actions as their effects? To this he says:
"Because of its dissimilarity to qualities, action does not have action [as its effect]. (24)

The word "kāryam" (effect) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. It has been stated that the similarity between substance and quality is their capacity to originate what is of their own kind (*sajātīyārambhakatva*). In that regard, by the aphorism "action is not something to be accomplished by action," the production of action by action has already been prohibited; the sense here is that this [prohibition] is being restated in this context. || 24 ||

Now, demonstrating that qualities possessing the nature of *vyāsajya-vṛtti* (residing in multiple substrates) are composed of multiple substances, he says: "Numbers beginning with duality, as well as separateness, conjunction, and disjunction. (25)

The phrase "produced from multiple substances" (*anekadravyārabhyā*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Furthermore, the term *pṛthaktva* (separateness) when mentioned in conjunction with "duality" (*dvitva*) and so forth also refers to "twice-separateness" (*dvipṛthaktva*) and the like. Thus, numbers beginning with duality and ending with the highest number (*parārdha*), as well as "twice-separateness" and so forth, and conjunctions and disjunctions, are produced by two or many substances; this is their quality of residing in multiple substrata (*anekavṛttitva*). And that consists in their co-occurrence in the same locus (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with their respective inherent causes (*samavāyin*) and mutual absences (*anyonyābhāva*). || 25 ||

Now, one might ask: "Just as it has been stated that the wholes (avayavin) and their qualities (guṇa) exist by way of pervasion (vyāsajyavṛtti), why should action (karman) not be the same? To this, he says:
"Because it is not inherent (asamavāya), action does not constitute a common effect (sāmānyakārya). (26)

In the phrase "due to non-inherence" (*asamavāyāt*), it should be construed as "in two substances" or "in [many] substances. Thus, a single action does not inhere in two substances, nor does a single action inhere in many substances; therefore, there is no action that is the effect of a universal or of a collection. Here too, the verb *vid* means "to be known," not "to exist. If action were to have a distributive occurrence (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), then when one substance moves, there would be the cognition that "two substances move" or "many substances move"; but this is not the case. Therefore, the meaning is that action does not have a distributive occurrence.

[Objection: Surely the action of the body and its parts is indeed initiated by many bodies and their parts; otherwise, how could there be the cognition that when the body moves, the hands, feet, and so forth also move? And this applies similarly to other composite wholes (*avayavin*). [Reply: This is not so, because the causal complex for the action of the whole is pervaded by the causal complex for the action of the parts, as is observed in experience. It is not the reverse; for when a part moves, there is no cognition that the whole moves everywhere. Otherwise, from the conjunction of the cause and the non-cause [the whole would always move].
There would also be no conjunction between cause and effect, because the conjunction of the effect can be accounted for by the action of the cause alone. || 26 ||
Furthermore, he states that for many conjunctions, there is a single effect, namely substance (dravya). || 27 ||

The meaning is that a single substance is the effect of many conjunctions. This should be understood as excluding those conjunctions of intangible substances—namely, ultimate composite substances and heterogeneous substances. || 27 ||
Now he states a single effect of many qualities: "The form of forms. (28)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that "form" (*rūpa*) is the single effect. Both instances of the word "form" are used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*), and this indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is of the type where the primary sense is not abandoned (*ajahatsvārthā*). The property common to both the denoted (*śakya*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*) is the state of being the substratum of the relation of produced and producer through the proximity of inherence in the same object as the cause (*kāraṇaikārthasamavāyapratyāsatti*). By this, color, taste, smell, touch, viscidity, natural fluidity, unity, and individuality are included. For these, while residing in their causes, produce in their effects only a single quality of the same genus.

For there are two ways in which non-inherent causes (asamavāyikāraṇa) operate. Some produce their effects through proximity with the same object as the cause (*kāraṇaikārthapratyāsatti*). Here, "cause" refers to the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); and that [inherent cause], such as a jar, is the inherent cause of an effect characterized by color and so forth (*rūpa*) that is to be produced. Thus, color residing in a potsherd, by virtue of its inherence in the same object as that inherent cause—the jar—produces the color of the jar through the relation of inherence in the same object as the cause. The same applies to taste and the rest.

In some cases, however, there is the status of being a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) due to the proximity of being inherent in the same object as the effect (*kāryaikārthapratyāsatti*). For example, sound, though itself an effect, initiates another sound in the ether; likewise, color and other qualities are produced in an earth-atom by contact with fire through the proximity of being inherent in the same object as the effect, specifically in the ether itself. || 28 ||
He states that a single action can have multiple effects: "From gravity, effort, and conjunction, upward motion [arises]. (29)

The meaning is that throwing upward (*utkṣepaṇa*) is the single effect produced by these [causes]. Here, gravity residing in the hand, the clod of earth, and so forth, is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*); the contact of the self endowed with effort is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the upward motion residing in the hand; however, for the upward motion residing in the clod of earth, the impulsion (*nodana*) of the hand is the non-inherent cause. In this context as well, the term "upward motion" (*utkṣepaṇa*) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to include downward motion (*avakṣepaṇa*) and the others as well. || 29 ||

Now, it has been stated that the qualities of material effects are preceded by the qualities of their causes and are preceded by the qualities of their own substrates; furthermore, it has been stated that action is not the cause of substance or action. Consequently, it follows that action has no effect whatsoever. Thus, even the inference of supersensible motions such as those of the sun would be difficult to obtain due to the absence of a mark (liṅga). Therefore, reminding us of what is stated in the Sūtra—"Action is [inferred] from conjunction, disjunction, and velocity"—he says:
"And conjunctions and disjunctions [are the marks] of actions. (30)

The word "janyāḥ" (to be produced) is the ellipsis. The plural number is used with reference to individual instances; by this, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are also to be understood as included. || 30 ||

Now, it was previously stated that substance and action are not effects of action; however, conjunction and disjunction are indeed effects of conjunction and disjunction. If this is so, then the current assertion that action is a cause is contradictory. To this, he says:
"Regarding the general category of causes, it was stated that among substances and actions, action is not a cause [of another action]. (31)

By the term "commonality of cause" (*kāraṇasāmānyapada*), that specific context is indicated; thus, in that section, it was stated that action is not a cause with respect to substance and action, but it was not intended to mean that action is in every respect entirely non-causal—by which [intention] the sūtra "conjunctions and disjunctions are also [effects] of actions" would be contradicted. This is the sense. || 31 ||
Thus ends the first daily lesson of the first chapter in the *Śāṅkara-Vaiśeṣika-Sūtropaskāra*.
Now begins the second daily lesson of the first chapter.

Now, by this section, the common properties (*sādharmya*) of the three categories—substance (*dravya*) and so forth—consisting of the unity of effects and the unity of causes have been stated; however, that is untenable because the very relationship of cause and effect is unestablished. To this he says:
"From the absence of the cause, there is the absence of the effect" (1).

For it is observed that even when clay, the potter’s wheel, water, the potter, and the string are all present, the absence of the staff results in the absence of the jar; and even when earth, water, and so forth are present, the absence of the seed results in the absence of the sprout. And this [absence] would be inexplicable without a causal relationship between the staff and the jar, or between the seed and the sprout. Otherwise, there would be an absence of the jar even in the absence of the loom and other such factors, and an absence of the sprout even in the absence of fragments of stone and the like.

Furthermore, the occasional nature (*kādācitkatva*) of jars, cloths, and so forth is experienced; that too would be inexplicable without the relationship of cause and effect. For the occasional nature of entities—consisting in their existence at one time and non-existence at another—is not possible without dependence on a cause. In that case, an entity would either always exist or never exist at all, but it would not exist only occasionally. Indeed, an entity does not simply fail to exist, nor does it arise without a cause, nor does it arise by chance, nor does it arise from something indefinable such as a rabbit's horn.

However, since limits such as the staff, the loom, and so forth—which possess their own designations—are observed in effects such as jars and cloth, the limit is indeed the cause. Thus, in the absence of the causal relation between effect and cause, neither engagement nor withdrawal would occur; consequently, the world would become inert. For indeed, there can be no engagement without the cognition that something is a means to a desired end, nor can there be withdrawal without the cognition that something is a means to an undesired end. || 1 ||

If it is argued: "Surely only that which exists arises, not that which does not exist, because of the authority of such scriptural passages as 'In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone'; otherwise, since non-existence is uniform, there would be no restriction as to why a cloth arises from threads alone and not from potsherds," [we reply: even by the proponents of transformation (*pariṇāmavādin*), who accept a cause, this very restriction must be admitted; otherwise, how could it be that the manifestation of a jar occurs only in potsherds and not in threads?

Furthermore, if manifestation (*abhivyakti*) also existed previously, then since it too would be eternal, the statement that "production and destruction are merely appearance and disappearance" (*āvirbhāva-tirobhāva*) is empty. If, on the other hand, appearance and disappearance depend upon causes, then it follows that even for jars, cloths, and the like, their production—even though they were non-existent—depends solely upon causes. As for the objection raised regarding the impossibility of a restriction with respect to causes, the answer there is simply that such restriction is determined by the very nature of things (*svabhāva-niyama*).

And that restriction of essential nature is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka); for there is a universal experience witnessed by all that "without a staff there is no jar, but when the staff exists, the jar exists. Thus, causality consists either in being of a class that invariably precedes [the effect] without being otherwise established, or in possessing the absence of the effect due to a deficiency in auxiliary conditions.

Although in cases such as "one should sacrifice with barley or with rice," there is no fixed state of being a prior antecedent—since a sacrifice performed with rice is not a prior antecedent for the fruit produced by a sacrifice performed with barley—nevertheless, an optional prescribed cause is indeed a cause, because both are established as causes despite the unity of the genus of the result.

And thus, the nature of causality common to both worldly and Vedic contexts consists in possessing the absence of an effect due to the deficiency of auxiliary factors (*sahakārivaikalya*). However, the worldly nature of causality, which is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), consists in being invariably antecedent. For in injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," even the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not the object [of the injunction], since activity is established by the mere knowledge of positive concomitance alone. For this very reason, it is also consistent to say: "In the case of an option (*vikalpa*), both [positive and negative concomitances] are not the meaning of the scripture," because [the result] is of that same class [as other results].

Because [if the result were produced by one alone], the performance of the others would be useless; for this very reason, the statement that "there is a rule of the necessary occurrence of the fruit from a Vedic rite when performed with its auxiliary parts (sāṅga)" is also appropriate. Furthermore, the Master’s statement—"and since this matter is rooted in scripture, deviation is not a fault"—has precisely this straightforward meaning as its intended import. However, in the case of grass, fire-sticks, and a gem, a difference in the nature of the effect (kāryavaijātya) is necessary, because the causal capacity (kāraṇatā) there is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), and thus the absence [of the cause] must necessarily entail the absence [of the effect].
