However, in the case of alternative options (*vikalpa*), if one were to postulate a difference in the nature of the result (*phala-vaijātya*), then even in rites such as the *rājasūya* and the *vājapeya*, there would have to be optional causality; thus, while establishing the very rule of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva-niyama*), he says:
"But it is not that from the absence of the effect follows the absence of the cause. (2)

If the rule of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāvaniyama*) did not exist, then the absence of the cause would follow even from the absence of the effect. However, the absence of the effect is not necessarily dependent upon the absence of the cause, whereas the absence of the cause is necessarily dependent upon the absence of the effect. Therefore, for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), there is purposeful activity directed toward the cessation of false knowledge for the sake of the absence of defects; toward the absence of defects for the sake of the absence of activity; toward the absence of activity for the sake of the absence of birth; and toward the absence of birth for the sake of the absence of suffering. This is the purpose of this two-sūtra section, which serves as an introductory supplement (*aupodghātika*). || 2 ||
Immediately after the enumeration and definition of the three categories, he now states the definition of the category of generality (sāmānya), which was previously enumerated:
"Generality and particularity depend upon cognition" (NS 2.2.3).

Generality (sāmānya) is of two kinds: the higher (para) and the lower (apara). Among these, the higher is existence (sattā), while the lower consists of substanceness (dravyatva) and so forth, which are pervaded by existence. In this context, the definition of generality and its particularity is cognition alone: inclusive cognition (anuvṛttabuddhi) belongs to generality, and exclusive cognition (vyāvṛttabuddhi) belongs to particularity. By means of the particle "iti," both are delimited and referred to; therefore, the neuter gender is used in the expression "buddhyapekṣam" (dependent on cognition).

The author of the Vṛtti, however, states that there is a connection with a specific [gender]; but by means of the rule "the neuter [is used] with a non-neuter as a single [form], optionally," he says that there is a singular form and a neuter gender. That which has cognition (*buddhi*), dependence (*apekṣā*), gender (*liṅga*), or definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is "dependent on cognition" (*buddhyapekṣam*). Among these, a universal (*sāmānya*) is that which eternally resides in multiple individuals; or, while being eternal, it is the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of its own substrata.

There is both a higher generality (*para-sāmānya*) and likewise a lower generality (*apara-sāmānya*); however, the lower generality also receives the designation of "particular" (*viśeṣa*). For instance, while the inclusive cognition "this is a substance" exists, there arises the particular cognition "this is not a quality" and "this is not an action. Thus, even universals such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) possess the nature of being particulars.

Is it not the case that there is no positive universal at all, since the cognition of a commonality is accounted for solely through the exclusion of what is other (atad-vyāvṛtti)? For the cognition "this is a cow" has as its object "this is excluded from non-cows," since even the proponent of universals (jāti-vādin) must admit that the qualified cognition of "cowness" and so forth has that [exclusion] as its object; indeed, being qualified by something else is nothing other than the exclusion of what is other, and even the ground for the application of words such as "cow" is simply the exclusion of non-cows.

Furthermore, where does "cowness" (gotva) reside? It cannot reside in a cow, because cowness does not exist prior to its subsistence in the cow; nor can it reside in a non-cow, due to contradiction. As for the specific cow-individual in which it arises, from where could cowness come to reside there? It certainly was not already present in that very individual, for if it were, then that particular place would also incur the status of being a cow.

Nor can it be that the universal (*gotva*) itself is produced at that very moment, since its eternity is admitted; nor has it come from elsewhere, since its lack of action (*niṣkriyatva*) is admitted; nor does a single eternal entity reside in multiple individuals, because the dilemma of whether it exists in its entirety or in part (*kārtsnya-ekadeśa-vikalpa*) is untenable. For it cannot exist in its entirety in one place alone, as that would entail the impossibility of the cognition qualified by it arising in another; nor can it exist in part, since a universal has no parts. As it has been said: "It does not go there, nor was it there before, nor is it newly produced, nor does it have parts;
it does not abandon its former substratum—oh, what a succession of calamities!"*

There exists a universal, and that is manifested solely by configuration (*saṃsthāna*), like "cowness" (*gotva*) or "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), but it does not reside in qualities or actions; such is the internal dispute among our own school (*sagotra*).

To this it is replied: the universal (*sāmānya*) is eternal and all-pervading; and its pervasiveness consists in its being connected to all locations by its very nature (*svarūpataḥ*). Nor does it follow that the [individual] locations themselves would be subject to the linguistic usage "cow" (*gavyavahāra*), because such usage is admitted to apply to them only through inherence (*samavāya*), just as there is no cognition or linguistic usage of "time possesses color" even though time possesses color and other qualities. Nor should it be argued that time does not exist at all, on the grounds that it is merely a distinction in the designations for the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); for the existence of time will be established later.

And likewise, since it is accepted that "the universal 'cowness' (gotva) resides precisely where the individual body (piṇḍa) arises and becomes connected with it; thus, being born and being connected occur at one and the same time," by this [principle], the answer to the question "In what kind of substratum does it reside? is "Where it is perceived. To the question "Where is it perceived? the answer is "Where it resides. And to the question "What was that individual body like prior to the existence of cowness? the answer is simply "It did not exist."

And thus, expressions such as "it does not blow, nor was it there," and so forth, are merely lamentations. In the case of the statement that "cowness is simply the exclusion of what is not that," the subverting factor is precisely the positive cognition, "This is a cow. For even direct experience cannot be explained away; as it has been said: "This other cognition born of affirmation is incapable of supporting [the theory of] exclusion (vyatireka)."

Indeed, even the exclusion of the non-cow (*agovyāvṛtti*) does not appear in the cognition "This is a cow. How could the dilemma regarding the whole or the part (*kārtsnaikadeśavikalpa*) arise? It would arise only if a single universal possessed either a totality (*kārtsnya*) or a partiality (*ekadeśa*). For totality consists in being the entirety of many [individuals], and that is not possible in a single [entity]. Thus, the experience "This is a cow" and so forth has an unreal object and is incapable of establishing the reality of things. To this, the following answer will be given.

The Prābhākaras, however, maintain that a universal (*sāmānya*) is manifested solely by its configuration (*saṃsthāna*). If that [universal] is attested by a corresponding inclusive cognition (*anugatapratīti*), then what harm has been done to the universals residing in qualities and actions? For there indeed arises an inclusive cognition regarding color, taste, and so forth; and that [cognition] is precisely what establishes a genus (*jāti*), provided there is no subverting evidence. As for the universals such as "color-ness" (*rūpatva*), the fact that they do not differ from their individual instances (*vyakti*) is not a subverting factor, as it is in the case of "space-ness" (*ākāśatva*) and the like, because the individual instances of color and so forth are manifold.

Nor is there any sublation by parity [of status], as in the case of *buddhitva* and *jñānatva*, or like *ghaṭatva* and *kalasatva*. This [parity] consists in having neither fewer nor more individual instances (*vyakti*). [The property of being blue, etc.,] has fewer instances than *guṇatva*, and it has more instances than *nīlatva* (blueness), and so forth. For this very reason, there is no confusion (*saṅkara*), as in the case of *bhūtatva* (elementality) and *mūrtatva* (corporeality); for while there is co-occurrence with the absolute absence of one another, there is no co-occurrence with another universal (*jāti*).

Nor is there an infinite regress, because no further universal is admitted to reside in [the universal] "form-ness" and so forth. Nor is there a loss of its own nature, as is the case with the particular (*viśeṣa*); for if particulars were to possess a genus while being subsistent in substance, they would be either qualities or actions; and if they were to possess a genus while being subsistent in an all-pervading substance, they would be qualities—just as there is a loss of the essential nature of the category of "particular," such a loss does not occur in the present case.

Nor is it unrelated like the property of inherence (samavāyatva) itself; for while one might accept such a lack of relation in the case of inherence out of fear of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if another inherence were admitted, in the present case, inherence itself is accepted as the relation. Although the non-difference of the individual instances (*vyakti*) is indeed the subverter of the universal "inherence-ness" (*samavāyatva-jāti*), this point should nevertheless be understood with reference to the view of those who hold that there are many inherences subject to production and destruction. Alternatively, this serves as a subverter against the admission of universals such as "non-existence-ness" (*abhāvatva*).

The authors of the *Vṛtti* maintain that the proof for the universal (*jāti*) is as follows: "The cognition of a locus of dispute is produced by an underlying cause (*anugatanimitta*), because it is an uncontradicted, recurring cognition, like the cognition of a jasmine flower. This, however, is to be examined. (3)
Explaining the two-fold division stated as "the universal" and "the particular," he says:
"An entity is only a universal because it is the cause of inclusive cognition alone. (4)
Existence (*bhāva*), which is being (*sattā*), is the cause of inclusion alone, but not the cause of exclusion; and thus, it does not receive the designation "particular" (*viśeṣa*). || 4 ||
In response to the inquiry as to which universals (sāmānya) possess the designation of "particular" (viśeṣa), he says:
"Substance-ness (dravyatva), quality-ness (guṇatva), and action-ness (karmatva) are both universals and particulars. (5)

The word "ca" (and) includes the universals residing in substance, such as *pṛthivītva* (earthness) and so forth; the universals residing in qualities, such as *rūpatva* (colorness) and so forth; and the universals residing in actions, such as *utkṣepaṇatva* (upward motion-ness) and so forth. In expressions such as *dravyatvam* (substance-ness), the absence of a compound is intended to indicate that there is no mutual relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between them.

In the expression "universals and particulars" (*sāmānyāni viśeṣāśca*), the lack of compound (*asamāsa*) is for the purpose of making it known that [the entities] possess particularity precisely while possessing universality; otherwise, there would be the misconception of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) such as "universals-of-particulars," and in that case, the state of being a particular while possessing universality would not be understood. Now, one might object: "Substance-ness (*dravyatva*) is not something witnessed by a cognition that conforms to the form of substance, because even if it exists in some way in earth and so forth, it is impossible in air, ether, and so forth."

Nor can its existence be established by its being the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the inherent causality (*samavāyikāraṇatā*) for effects delimited by "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*), because quality-ness—since it subsists in both eternal and non-eternal things—is not a delimiting property of effecthood (*kāryyatā*). Furthermore, the objection would remain in force even regarding the establishment of quality-ness itself. This is not so; for substance-ness (*dravyatva*) is established as the delimiting property of the inherent causality for effects delimited by "conjunction-ness" (*saṃyogatva*). Indeed, that [inherent causality] cannot be delimited by earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth, because those are of narrower extension (*nyūnavṛttitva*); nor can it be delimited by existence (*sattā*), because that is of wider extension (*adhikavṛttitva*). For there must necessarily be a delimiting property, otherwise there would be the consequence of causelessness (*āka-smikatā*).

In this regard, [the existence of conjunction] is established in atoms by their being the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of dyads; in dyads, by their being the non-inherent cause of triads; and in the four all-pervading substances, simply by virtue of their being conjoined with all corporeal things. Furthermore, it is necessary to admit conjunction in space because it is the locus of the contact between sense organs and the mind, in air because it is the substratum for the movement of grass and so forth, and in perceptible substances simply by virtue of their perceptibility.

However, there is no such thing as "eternal conjunction" (aja-saṃyoga) by which [the property of] conjunctionness itself—since it subsists in both effects and non-effects—would fail to be a delimiting factor for effectness. Likewise, the existence of substancehood is easily established by its being the delimiting factor for the inherent causality of disjunction.

As for the nature of quality (*guṇatva*), it has been stated that it is established precisely as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of that causality which exists in things possessing generality (*sāmānyavat*), while being devoid of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) or a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of conjunction and disjunction. The nature of action (*karmatva*) is also evidenced by the perceptual cognition "it moves" in the case of perceptible substances. In other cases, however, it is inferable from conjunction and disjunction; for it is necessary to establish the nature of action as the delimiting factor of the non-inherent causality of both conjunction and disjunction.

For this very reason, the motion of the sun is inferred from its arrival at another location. In that case, even though other locations such as space (*ākāśa*) are beyond the senses, the conjunctions and disjunctions of its rays with those locations are perceived by means of its orb; it is from these alone that its motion is inferred. Master Uddyotakara states: "The sun possesses arrival at another location because, while being imperishable and a substance, it is recognized through re-cognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—being perceived by one facing west as the very same entity previously perceived by one facing east"—thus, the motion of the sun is inferred from the inferred arrival at another location. || 5 ||

Now, one might ask: "Is that very category of particularity (viśeṣa) which was previously mentioned being designated here as both a generality and a particularity? Anticipating this inquiry of the student, he says: "Except for the ultimate particulars. (6)

The meaning is that, excluding those "ultimate particulars" (*antyā viśeṣāḥ*) which have been described as residing in eternal substances, there is the designation of "general and particular" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*). The teachers (*ācāryāḥ*) maintain that they are called "ultimate" (*antya*) because they exist at the end (*ante*), that is, at the limit (*avasāne*), since there is no further differentiator beyond them. The author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) maintains that they are "ultimate" because they exist at the end of production and destruction—that is, in eternal substances—and thus they are "ultimate particulars. For these are indeed particulars alone, being the causes of the cognition of differentiation, and not also of the nature of generalities (*sāmānya*). || 6 ||
Regarding the universal of existence (*sattāsāmānya*), there are many conflicting views; therefore, he states the proof for it:
"That from which [the cognition] 'existent' arises with respect to substances, qualities, and actions is existence (*sattā*). (7)

By the word "iti" (thus), he teaches the manner in which both cognition and linguistic usage occur. Thus, existence (*sattā*) is that upon which depends the cognition of the form "existent, existent" regarding the three categories beginning with substance, as well as the employment of words in the form "this is existent, this is existent. (7)

[Objection: But surely, existence (*sattā*) is not experienced as distinct from substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*); therefore, existence is simply one or another of these—substance and so forth—because whatever is different from something else is experienced as distinct from it, just as a jar is [distinct] from a cloth; and since existence is not experienced as distinct from them, it must be identical with them. To this, he says: "Existence is a separate entity from substance, quality, and action. (8)

Substances and the like are non-pervasive (ananugata), whereas existence (sattā) is pervasive (anugata). Thus, because their difference from those [substances] is established through the imposition of contradictory properties characterized by pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness, that which is not perceived elsewhere than in them [the substances] exists by virtue of inseparable inherence (ayutasiddhi); however, in the case of a jar and a cloth, there is separable inherence (yutasiddhi). Nor is existence merely the individual nature of the manifest (vyakti), because individuals themselves are non-pervasive.

If "being its own nature" (*svarūpatva*) is what is pervasive, then that is simply existence (*sattā*). If, on the other hand, there is a pervasive linguistic usage even through natures that are themselves non-pervasive, then this [pervasiveness] is already accounted for by [universals] such as "cowness" (*gotva*). For this very reason, the argument that since the linguistic usage [of "existent"] is established by the substrata in which existence inheres, existence itself is redundant, is refuted. Therefore, it is incorrect to say that existence is either the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) or being epistemically warranted (*prāmāṇikatva*), because the cognition "it exists" (*san*) occurs even when one is not reflecting upon those [criteria]. (8)
He states another point of distinction:
"And because it exists in qualities and actions, it is neither an action nor a quality. (9)

While it should have been stated that "it is neither a quality nor an action," the expression is inverted to also indicate that "it is not a substance. For an action does not reside in actions, nor does a quality reside in qualities, nor does a substance reside in a quality or an action; however, existence (sattā) resides in both qualities and actions. Therefore, because of its difference from substance, quality, and action, existence is indeed distinct from them. || 9 ||
He states another ground for differentiation: "And by the absence of generalities and particulars" (sūtra 10).

If existence (*sattā*) were a substance, a quality, or an action, then it would possess generalities and particularities (*sāmānyaviśeṣavat*). However, generalities and particularities such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like are not perceived in existence; for there is no experience among anyone that "existence is a substance, a quality, or an action. (10)
Having thus stated that existence (*sattā*) is a distinct entity from substance, quality, and action, he states that substantiality (*dravyatva*) is a distinct entity from them:
"Substantiality is said to be [defined] by the possession of multiple substances. (11)

That which has multiple substances as its inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) is "possessing multiple substances" (anekadravyavat). Here, the word "multiple" (aneka) refers to all [substances]; by this, there is a distinction from earth-ness (pṛthivītva) and the like. Permanence, however, is already established by the definition of a universal (sāmānya); by this, there is a distinction from composite wholes (avayavin). Furthermore, "possessing multiple substances" means being inherent in only multiple substances; by this, there is a distinction from existence (sattā). Therefore, substance-ness (dravyatva) is permanent and inherent in only multiple substances. It was stated that eternal conjunction (aja-saṃyoga) is not accepted. And substance-ness has indeed been proven.
"Substantiality has been explained": the meaning is that substantiality, like existence itself, has already been defined. || 11 ||
Now, one might object: "Even *dravyatva* (substance-ness) would be a genus (*jāti*), and since it is non-different from its substratum, what fault is there? To this, he says:
"And because of the absence of specific universals (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*). (12)

The meaning is that if *dravyatva* (substance-ness) were a genus (*jāti*) whose very nature consisted of substance and so forth, then within it there would have to exist the specific genera (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) such as earth-ness, water-ness, fire-ness, and so on. For there does not arise in anyone the cognition that "substance-ness is earth," "water," or "fire. This is the meaning of verse 12.
He states its nature as a quality:
"Likewise, because it exists in the qualities, its status as a quality is declared. (13)

The meaning is that because it exists only in qualities through inherence (*samavāya*), "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) is said to be distinct from substances, qualities, and actions, just like existence (*sattā*). || 13 ||
He states another ground for differentiation: "And because of the absence of both generality and particularity. (14)

The meaning is that if the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*) were not distinct from substance, quality, and action, then it would be perceived as possessing the lower genera (*avāntarajāti*) of substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), or action-ness (*karmatva*). || 14 ||
He states the differentiator of *karmatva* from substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*):
"Because it exists in actions, *karmatva* is said [to be the universal of action]. (15)

The meaning is that because it exists only in actions and because of its inherence [in them], "action-ness" (karmatva) is also stated to be a distinct genus, different from substance, quality, and action, just like "existence" (sattā). || 15 ||
He states another point of distinction: "And by the absence of general and particular [properties]. (16)

The meaning is that if "action-ness" (*karmatva*) were of the nature of a substance (*dravya*) and so forth, then the generalities and particulars such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) would inhere in it. It should be noted that this single section consisting of four sūtras concerning existence (*sattā*), substance-ness, quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness—namely, these four universals—is stated together in one context for the purpose of demonstrating the distinctions among substances, qualities, and actions. || 16 ||

[Objection: Surely, existence (*sattā*), while subsisting in substances, qualities, and actions, must be distinct according to the differences in its delimiters such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth; why then should it not be manifold? To this he says:
"Because there is no difference in the mark [indicating it], and because there is an absence of any specific mark, Being (*bhāva*) is one. (17)

The cognition in the form "it exists" (*sad*) or the employment of the word "existent" is the mark (*liṅga*) of being (*sattā*). And that [mark] is common and undifferentiated across substances, qualities, and actions. Therefore, being (*bhāva*), which is existence (*sattā*), subsists as one and the same in them; otherwise, because they would have the same individual instances (*vyakti*) as [the universals] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), either existence itself would not exist, or those [substances, qualities, and actions] would not exist. Furthermore, "due to the absence of a specific mark" (*viśeṣaliṅgābhāvāt*): the meaning is that there is no difference [among them], because of the absence of any mark—that is, any inference—of distinction (*bheda*) therein.

For there is indeed a continuous recognition there, such as "this is that very same lamp"; however, while there is a specific mark of distinction there, namely the difference in dimension such as length and shortness, the point here is that no such specific mark of distinction exists. || 17 ||

Thus ends the second section of the first chapter in the *Śāṅkara* commentary on the *Bhagavat-kaṇāda-sūtra*. The subject matter of the first section of the second chapter is the definition of the nine substances (*dravya*). Among these, there are the sections on the definitions of earth, water, and fire; the proof of the existence of God (*Īśvara*); and the inference of space (*ākāśa*). Regarding that, he states the definition of earth, which was mentioned first:
Earth possesses color, taste, smell, and touch. || 1 ||

Form (*rūpa*) exists in earth alone in various types such as blue, yellow, and so forth; thus, the definition is: "the possession of a genus subordinate to substantiality (*dravyatva*) that coexists with blue form. Likewise, taste (*rasa*) exists in earth alone in various types such as pungent, astringent, and so forth; thus, the definition is: "the possession of a genus subordinate to substantiality that coexists with pungent taste. In this manner, other definitions should be inferred by inserting terms such as "astringent" and the like.

Odor is of two kinds: fragrant and non-fragrant. Thus, the definition [of substance] should be understood as: possessing a genus that is co-extensive with odor and is pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*); likewise, it is to be seen as: being a substance that is the locus of a genus which is co-extensive with odor, yet not co-extensive with odor, and not co-extensive with any quality other than odor.

Nor should it be argued that this [definition] is over-narrow (avyāpaka) regarding both [smell and taste] because smell and taste are not perceived in stones and the like; for although smell and taste are not initially perceived there, they are indeed found in the ashes of those very things, since the same atoms that constitute the stone are also the constituents of its ashes. Thus, there is no lack of pervasion.

If it is asked, "How then do we have the cognitions 'the breeze is fragrant' and 'the water of the *kāravella* is bitter'?", the answer is no; for those two—smell and taste—are contingent upon their respective substrates in earth. Furthermore, touch that is neither hot nor cold and produced by maturation (*pākaja*) exists in earth alone. Thus, the definition [of earth] is: possessing a genus subordinate to substantiality (*dravyatva*) which co-exists with touch produced by maturation.

Furthermore, the state of being produced by baking (*pākajatva*) is manifested only in the touch of earth through other specific qualities (*viśeṣāntara*); and these other specific qualities are most clearly evident in particular touches found in the *śirīṣa*, clove (*lavaṅgī*), and *kuṣṭha* plants, but not so in the touch of water and the like. Although touch and other qualities are not produced directly from the baking—that is, from the contact with fire—in a composite whole (*avayavin*), nevertheless, because they originate from that series [of transformations], a specific difference in kind (*vaijātyaviśeṣa*) must be recognized there as well.

Now, is this definition a negative reason (*vyatireki-liṅga*) that establishes the difference from others or establishes linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*)? In that regard: "Earth is different from others because it possesses smell; whatever is not different from others does not possess smell, as in the case of water and so forth; and this [earth] possesses smell, which is the counter-positive of the absence that pervades the absence of difference from others; therefore, it is different from others."

In that case, if the probandum—namely, the difference from others—is already established, then the reason would be either (a) *asādhāraṇa* (uniquely inconclusive), because it is excluded from both the similar (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar (*vipakṣa*) instances due to its absence from them; or (b) it would be a positive concomitant (*anvayin*), because it is not excluded from them. Furthermore, if [the probandum] is not established, the subject (*pakṣa*) has an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*). Consequently, in such a case, there is neither doubt, nor a desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), nor an inference consisting of a cognition qualified by that [probandum].

Furthermore, there is pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the two negative instances (*vyatireka*); thus, there is an asymmetry: that which possesses pervasion does not necessarily have the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), and that which is a feature of the subject does not necessarily possess pervasion. For this very reason, the uselessness of the application (*upanaya*) is also explained, but not because pervasion has not been grasped. As it has been said:
"The non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*), the asymmetry [of pervasion], and the uselessness of the application;
and establishment by positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone—these are the defects in the case of a negative-only inference (*vyatirekin*)."

The same applies to that which is to be established through linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*). In that case, although the convention consists in being denotable by the word "earth," and this [denotability] exists even in the universal "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*), where the reason "earth-ness" itself is absent—thus resulting in the fallacy of the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇya*)—nevertheless, since what is to be proven is "being denotable by the word 'earth' as having the universal 'earth-ness' as its ground for application," there is no such fallacy of the uncommon.

Alternatively, one might argue: "Earth-ness (pṛthivītva) is the occasional basis for the application of a word because it is a genus, like pot-ness (ghaṭatva). Once this is established in a general sense, the probandum (*sādhya*) is formulated as follows: "The word 'earth' has earth-ness as its basis of application, because while not having anything other than that as its basis of application, it does have a basis of application; for whatever is not so [is not thus]. If this is the case, then here too, the probandum remains unestablished (*sādhyāprasiddhi*). Thus [the opponent objects].

Do not say so; for the difference of other things such as water and the like is well-established in the jar itself. Even though air and the like are beyond the senses, their difference—namely, their mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)—is established in the jar and other objects through perception alone, because in the apprehension of mutual non-existence, the only necessary factor is the fitness of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-yogyatā*), as is seen in cases such as "the pillar is not a piśāca. And if this is so, let the jar itself be the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*); what is the use of a negative inference (*vyatirekin*)?
For who would establish by a circuitous path that which is being established by a direct path?

If it is to be said that a non-exclusive (*avyatirekin*) logical mark (*liṅga*) is not a fallacy (*anābhāsa*), then this path is likewise unimpeded for those of a crooked taste (*vakraruci*). For when the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) is refuted, the defects rooted therein are also refuted. There is no disparity [between the two types of inference], because through negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*) one grasps precisely the positive pervasion (*anvaya-vyāpti*), or because the positive pervasion is inferred from the negative pervasion. Nor is the application (*upanaya*) redundant, since it is the very reason whose pervasion has been grasped that is here subsumed under the subject (*pakṣa*). As it has been said: "The nature of being the regulated (*niyamya*) and the regulator (*niyantṛ*) between two entities is considered to be such [as follows]..."
"But those very [characteristics] are to be understood as reversed in the case of their absence.

Thus, conventional usage arises precisely from instruction, such as "earth is that which possesses odor," or "that which has a conch-like neck and so forth is denoted by the word 'jar'. Similarly, in certain instances—such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) or clay—the fact that "possessing odor" is the ground for applying the term "earth" to earth-ness is grasped through instruction. Consequently, the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) also applies here: "Everything possessing odor is denoted by the word 'earth' because of having odor as its ground for application; whatever does not possess this [odor] is not like that."

Now, one might object: in a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) that establishes difference, is that difference (1) dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), (2) essential difference (*svarūpa-bheda*), or (3) mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)? It cannot be the first two, because they are already apprehended through perception itself. Nor can it be the third, because since the difference between absences (*abhāva-bheda*) is itself yet to be proven, the mutual non-existence of those absences would not exist therein; furthermore, if one were to prove an essential difference with respect to that [mutual non-existence], the probandum would lack consistency (*ananugama*). If this is argued, we reply: no, for even the mutual non-existence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is an absence is what is to be proven. If that [mutual non-existence] is distinct [from its relata], then it certainly exists; if it is not distinct, then it culminates in their very essential nature (*svarūpa*). Thus, there is no fault.

In reality, it is indeed distinct, because its dissimilarity is pervaded by its mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*); nor is there an infinite regress, for one does not rest until the limit of experience, whereas elsewhere one rests simply due to the absence of experience.

As for the claim that thirteen mutual absences (anyonyābhāva), each well-known in thirteen [substances], are combined and then established in earth—that is false; for the individual establishment of each is not the requisite factor, and there is no such thing as a collective establishment. Rather, what is to be established is the mutual absence whose counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) is delimited by the property of being odorless (*nirgandhatva*). This is because a difference in absences is necessarily required due to the difference in the delimiters of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*), and it has already been stated that such an absence is perceptually established only in things like a jar.

If it is asked, "What is the status regarding space and so forth?"—[we reply: Space is different from others because it is the substratum of sound; that which is not so is not so. Although, in such cases, the probandum (*sādhya*) is not previously established in one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśa*), nevertheless, by the force of a general pervasion (*vyāpti*) operating as follows—"Whatever possesses a dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with X possesses mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) having X as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*)"—the mutual non-existence having as its counter-correlative that which possesses the absolute non-existence of being the substratum of sound is already established. It is merely now made known as residing in the subject, just like fire.

Our established doctrine is that [the reason] resides in the mountain because of its dissimilarity to that [dissimilar instance]; for that dissimilarity is pervaded by the mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) of that [property]. If it is argued that the presence of the absolute absence of being the substratum of sound has not been apprehended in the counter-example (vipakṣa), then "being the substratum of sound" can be neither a definition nor a logical mark (liṅga), as it is beset by the suspicion of straying into the counter-example. || 1 ||
He states the definition of these [elements] which were mentioned immediately after earth:
"Water possesses color, taste, and touch; it is liquid and viscous. (2)

The color, taste, and touch of water are exclusively white, sweet, and cold, respectively, as is its natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhika-sneha*). Its essential nature is indeed fluidity. Now, it may be objected that it is incorrect to say that the color of water is exclusively white, since blueness is perceived in the waters of the Yamunā and other such rivers. It is also incorrect to say that the taste is exclusively sweet, since acidity and pungency are perceived in the juices of the *jambīra* citron and the *karavīra* plant, and so forth. Furthermore, it is untenable to claim that the touch is exclusively cold, since heat is indeed perceived at midday.

Intrinsic fluidity (*sāṃsiddhika-dravatva*) is non-pervasive, as it is absent in snow, hail, and the like. As for viscidity (*sneha*), however, it is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*) and over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), because it is not experienced in water, yet is experienced in earthy substances such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Nor is "water-ness" (*jalatva*) itself the definition of water, since that is untenable due to the absence of anything that could establish it as a genus (*jāti*).

Nor can its establishment be achieved through its being the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for the inherent causality of viscidity (*sneha*), because the property of viscidity (*snehatva*)—subsisting in both effects and non-effects—is not a delimiting condition for effectness (*kāryatā*). Therefore, since there is no differentiator, water is not distinct [from other substances]. If this is argued, it is not so; for that which is merely non-luminous white color (*abhāsvara-śukla-mātra-rūpa*) is precisely what differentiates it, since the blackness observed in the waters of the Yamunā (*Kālindī*) and elsewhere is due to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of its substrate, as whiteness is perceived in the waters of the Yamunā when scattered in the sky.

Therefore, the definition of water (*ap*) is: possessing a genus that is directly pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*), which resides in that which possesses color, and which is not co-located with colors other than those that are luminous and white. Taste (*rasa*) is also exclusively sweet; for the sourness, pungency, and so forth found in the juices of the *jambīra* and *vīra* fruits are due to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of earth. If it is argued that sweetness is never experienced in water, we say no, because it is manifested immediately after consuming an astringent substance.

Nor is that sweetness of the *harītakī* itself manifested by water, because only an astringent taste (*kaṣāya-rasa*) is perceived there; for in the *harītakī*, just as in the *āmalakī*, the taste is indeed astringent, as that alone is experienced. Nor does the non-origination of tastes therein occur due to a contradiction between qualities, since even the constituent parts possess an astringent taste. As for the common report of it having six tastes, that is based on its capacity to produce the effects of those respective tastes.

The theory of variegated taste (*citrarasa*), however, is refuted precisely because there is no evidence for it; whereas in the case of variegated color (*citrarūpa*), the very perception of a multicolored cloth serves as proof. As for the production [of a smell] from parts that are both fragrant and foul-smelling, this is already refuted by the contradiction between qualities. Furthermore, there is no evidence for a variegated odor (*citragandha*). Therefore, the sweetness perceived immediately after eating a myrobalan fruit belongs to the water itself; its intensity, however, depends on the proximity of a particular substance, just as the intensity of coldness arises in water through contact with sandalwood.

As for the bitterness experienced immediately after eating a *karkaṭī* fruit, that belongs to the *karkaṭī* itself, since bitterness is perceived even in its parts without the drinking of water; or else, it is the bitterness of the *pitta* substance located at the tip of the tongue that is experienced there. Thus, the definition of water (*ap*) is: possessing a genus directly pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*) which coexists with a taste that is not coextensive with tastes other than sweet. Similarly, the definition of water is: possessing a genus pervaded by substanceness which coexists with a cold touch (*śītasparśa*).

As for the heat at midday, that belongs to fire alone, because it follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of fire. Thus, "intrinsic fluidity" (*sāṃsiddhika-dravatva*) is the definition [of water] by its very nature; or alternatively, the essence of water (*jalatva*) is the possession of a genus subordinate to substanceness (*dravyatva*) which resides in that which possesses intrinsic fluidity. Viscidity (*sneha*), however, is a specific quality (*guṇa-viśeṣa*) and not a specific universal (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) like "milkness" (*dugdhatva*), because we perceive a gradation such as "viscid," "more viscid," and "most viscid. And a gradation is not possible within a universal.

[Objection: Let it be granted that viscidity (*sneha*) is a quality; however, what is the proof for its existence in water? [Response: It is not so, because it is inferred from the cohesion (*saṅgraha*) of parched grain, sand, and the like by means of water. For cohesion is a specific kind of contact caused by both viscidity and fluidity (*dravatva*). Indeed, it is not dependent on fluidity alone, because cohesion would otherwise be impossible in the case of the fluidity of glass or gold. Nor is it caused by viscidity alone, because cohesion would be impossible in the case of solidified substances such as ghee. Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that cohesion is caused by both viscidity and fluidity.

And that water, being observed even in flour, sand, and so forth, strengthens the viscidity (*sneha*) in the fire; this reasoning serves as a support for perception, because viscidity itself is perceptible. In the case of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and the like, however, the supporting water resides in the viscidity through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), appearing as belonging to it [the butter]. The same applies to oil, sap, and so on. Furthermore, the supporting substance is indeed water possessing an excellence of viscidity; it is precisely due to this excess of viscidity that this water is not opposed to fire.

If moisture (*sneha*) were a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of earth, it would subsist in all earthly substances, just like odor. Furthermore, "water-ness" (*jalatva*) is a genus directly pervaded by "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), because such a genus—which serves as the delimiting property for the inherent causality (*samavāyikāraṇatā*) residing in conjunctions that subsist solely in things possessing moisture—is established as being common even to atoms. || 2 ||
In accordance with the order of enumeration, he states the definition of fire:
"Fire possesses color and touch. (3)

The meaning is that fire is that which possesses luminous color and hot touch. Now, an objection may be raised: "Luminosity is the quality of illuminating others, and such a color is not found in heat, nor in fire residing in gold, nor in fire residing in water; furthermore, white color is not present in any of those mentioned, and hot touch is not present in lunar fire or in gold—so how can this be? If this is asked, the answer is no, because in cases such as heat, the presence of luminous color is inferred from its being fire.

If it is argued that "fire-ness" (*tejastva*) itself is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*) therein, we say no; for it is inferred from the possession of hot touch (*uṣṇasparśavattva*). If it is asked, "How is this so in the case of gold?"—it is because, as will be explained later, fire-ness is inferred in gold by means of a negative inference (*vyatirekin*): namely, that it is the substratum of a produced liquidity which is not destroyed even by contact with an intense fire, despite the absence of a brilliant color (*bhāsvararūpa*) there. Furthermore, fire-ness is inferred in the frying pan and other such objects by virtue of their possessing hot touch.

For light is of four kinds: some has manifested color and manifested touch, such as that of gold; some has manifested color and unmanifested touch, such as lunar light; some has unmanifested color and unmanifested touch, such as ocular light; and some has unmanifested color and manifested touch, such as summer heat and the fire residing in a vessel for boiling water. Ocular light will be established further on. (3)
He states the definition of air, which follows in sequence:
Air possesses touch. (4)

1—The state of possessing a genus that is co-present with touch but not co-present with color (rūpa); 2—the state of possessing a genus that is co-present with touch that is neither hot nor cold, but not co-present with taste (rasa); 3—the state of possessing a genus that is co-present with touch that is neither hot nor cold, but not co-present with odor (gandha); or 4—the state of possessing a genus that is co-present with a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) which is co-present with a specific quality other than touch—this is the definition of air (vāyu). || 4 ||
Now, one might ask: why is the possession of color and other qualities not also a defining characteristic of space, time, direction, and the self? To this he says:
"These do not exist in space. (5)

In this context, the root *vid* signifies "perception. Since they are not perceived, it follows that those [qualities] such as color and so forth do not necessarily exist—either by way of aggregation (*samuccaya*) or by way of alternation (*vikalpa*)—within substances such as space; this is the meaning. If it is asked, "But how is there the cognition 'space is white like curd'?", the answer is no, because that is merely a misconception arising from the perception of the distinct forms of the rays of the sun.

If it is asked, "How then does the cognition 'the sky is blue' arise?", the answer is no; for it arises from the conceit of those who, having traveled toward the southern direction of Mount Sumeru, behold the radiance of its sapphire peaks. As for the view that the eye, traveling to a great distance and turning back, perceives its own pupil and thus generates such a conceit—that is incorrect, because even those with tawny eyes (piṅgala-sāra-nayana) have such a conceit.

If it is argued that space and time also possess the fourfold set of qualities beginning with color (rūpa) because of the cognition "here [is] now [this] color," etc., we say no; for the definition of earth and the other substances has been stated as possessing those qualities through inherence (samavāya), and not through any other relation. Furthermore, since there is also the cognition "here [is] now the absolute absence of color," space and time are indeed the substratum of all things. || 5 ||
Now, it might be argued that the definition of water as possessing fluidity is incorrect, because fluidity is also perceived in earth; to this, he says:
"The fluidity of clarified butter, lac, and beeswax, resulting from contact with fire, is a common property shared with water. (6)

The liquidity that exists in substances such as clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) is due to the instrumental cause of contact with fire, and is not innate (*sāṃsiddhika*); such [innate] liquidity is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of water. However, while mere liquidity is a commonality between earth and water, innate liquidity is not; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition to earth]. This is the meaning. || 6 ||
[Objection: Even so, since [fluidity] is present in tin, lead, iron, and the like—which are forms of fire—the over-extension remains exactly as it was. To this, he says:
"The fluidity of tin, lead, copper, silver, and gold, resulting from contact with fire, has water as its commonality. (7)

This is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicative illustration), and it includes bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), copper (*tāmra*), brass (*ārakūṭa*), mercury (*pārada*), and so forth. It is applicable to both the possible (*śakya*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*). The definition is simply: "being the substratum of a produced liquidity that is not destroyed even by intense contact with fire. Thus, the liquidity of gold and the like is indeed adventitious (*naimittika*), since the cause—contact with fire—is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). However, the distinction is this: in the previous sūtra, the word "fire" (*agni*) refers to light (*tejas*) characterized by an excellence of heat (*auṣṇya-prakarṣa*), whereas here it refers specifically to fire (*vahni*).

If it is argued that gold and other such substances must also be either earthy or distinct substances—because their yellowness, heaviness, and so forth establish their earthiness, and because their liquidity is not destroyed even by fire establishes a dissimilarity from earth, thereby establishing them as distinct substances—the answer is no. Gold is fiery (taijasa), because it is the substratum of a liquidity that is not destroyed even upon contact with intense fire; for whatever is not thus [fiery] is not thus, like earth. Thus, its nature as fire is established through a negative inference (*vyatirekin*).

Nor is there any contradiction regarding water-atoms, because fluidity must be qualified by non-eternality. Nor is there the fallacy of being "uncommon" (asādhāraṇya) due to the reason's exclusion from half of the similar instances (sapakṣa), such as lamps and the like, because the intended probandum is that gold is not earthy. Furthermore, there is no sublation (bādha) if the substratum of gravity is taken as the subject (pakṣa), nor is there a lack of locus (āśrayāsiddhi) if something other than that is the subject, because the subject is defined here as the locus of fluidity.

Nor is it difficult to state that [the fluidity] is not absolute, for what is intended is that it remains as the substratum of non-eternal fluidity even when in contact with fire until the end of the hour (*prahara*). Nor should it be argued that the destruction of fluidity must necessarily be admitted on account of the notions of "more" or "less" (*taratama*) and the destruction of its substratum; for the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is: "because it possesses fluidity which is a generality of fluidity residing in something that is not a counter-positive of a destruction produced by fire-contact that is not accompanied by the causal complex of fluidity residing in the same locus."

Alternatively, that which is the substratum of yellow weight is conjoined with a liquid substance that obstructs colors other than yellow, because—even when in conjunction with fire for as long as a *prahara*—it does not become a substratum for colors other than yellow, like a yellow cloth situated in the midst of water conjoined with fire.

[Objection: But surely, in the dark, there would be the apprehension of the form of gold, because at that time there is no suppression (*abhibhava*) of that form; for the meaning of the term "suppression" is non-apprehension caused by the apprehension of a stronger member of the same class. [Reply: This is not so, because in that case, by the force of the result (*phala*), the meaning of the term "suppression" is merely the connection with a stronger member of the same class. As it has been said: "And due to contact with the earth, another form does not manifest at all. This is the general direction. (7)

Having thus concluded the section on the characteristics of the four substances possessing touch, and wishing to avoid the objection that the definition of air (*vāyu*) is unestablished with respect to its substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*), he first presents inference as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Having established the validity of inference itself by following observed instances, he begins the section proving the existence of air: "Possessing horns, having a hump, having hair at the ends [of the tail], and having a dewlap—this is the mark seen for 'cowness' (*gotva*). (8)

The sense is that just as horns and other such marks are to be grasped as signs (*liṅga*) for the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) once their pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been apprehended, so too do the signs for the five substances beginning with air (*vāyu*), which are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), attain the status of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when they are observed through generalization (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

In this regard, although the mere state of having horns (*viṣāṇitvamātra*) is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) for [the presence of] cowness (*gotva*), because it deviates in the case of buffaloes and the like; nor is "having a dewlap and so forth" (*sāsnādimattva*) a qualifying attribute, because that would result in the qualifier (*viśeṣya*) being redundant—nevertheless, for those who perceive the distinctness of a cow's horn in comparison to the horns of buffaloes, rams, and others, various specific features indeed attain the status of a logical mark, just as smoke does. Among the horns themselves, these include straightness, curvature, hardness, softness, shortness, and length.

And those specific features (viśe�ṣas) certainly exist as objects to be known with even greater precision; thus, in the case of a cow-pen that is obstructed or distant, the inference—"This is a cow, because it possesses a particular set of horns, like a previously experienced cow-pen"—is indeed unimpeded. Likewise, the possession of humps is also a logical mark (liṅga) for cowness.

The state of being a tail at the end (*prāntebāladhitva*) is also an independent mark for [establishing] cowness (*gotva*). A "tail at the end" (*prāntebāladhi*) refers to a specific kind of tail, based on an *aluk* compound meaning "that in which tails are placed at the end. Thus, it is specifically the cow's tail that is called "tail at the end"; for the state of being a tail at the end does not exist in the tails of horses, rams, and so forth, because those are composed entirely of hair, and because there is a distinction in that the tails of buffaloes and others do not possess such length.

Even the possession of a tail-tip and so forth is considered a mark for "cowness" (gotva), by which a cow-individual is expressed through the elision of the possessive suffix -matup; thus, "this is a cow, because it possesses a tail-tip and so forth, like a previously experienced cow-individual. However, the possession of a dewlap is indeed the well-known mark for "cowness. || 8 ||

Having thus stated that inference, which carries out the entire course of worldly affairs, possesses validity in accordance with what is observed, the author, wishing to begin the section on the proof of air, says: "And touch belongs to air. (9)

The word "liṅga" (inferential mark) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. By the word "ca" (and), sound, support, and trembling are included. Now, one might object: "Could this perceived touch not belong to earth itself when its color is unmanifest? This is not so, because the touch of earth is invariably concomitant with manifest color.

And thus, this touch which is experienced must reside in something, because it is a touch, like the touch of earth and so forth; by means of this inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), the substratum of touch is established. Then, through the assistance of "exclusion of others" (*itarabādha*)—namely, that the substratum of touch cannot consist of the triad beginning with earth because it lacks color, nor can it consist of the five beginning with space because it possesses touch—the existence of a substance distinct from the eight [known] substances is established.

In this way, a particular sound is also an inferential mark (*liṅga*) for air (*vāyu*). For instance, when there is no impact from a substance possessing color (*rūpavat*), this series of sounds produced by leaves and the like must have its cause in an impact from a substance possessing touch and velocity (*sparśavad-vegavat*). This is because it is a series of sounds belonging to a substance whose parts are not being divided, just like the series of sounds produced in a gong by the impact of a stick. Furthermore, the absence of an impact from a substance possessing color is known through non-perception of a perceptible object (*yogyānupalabdhi*). And that substance possessing touch and velocity is indeed distinct from the eight [known] substances, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).

Thus, the specific support [of objects] is also a mark of air. For instance, the support in the sky of grass, cotton, clouds, and celestial chariots is produced by conjunction with a substance possessing touch and velocity, because it is the support of a substance not presided over by a conscious being, like the support of grass, wood, boats, and so forth in a current. Furthermore, in the case of the support of poison and the like produced by mere thought (abhidhyāna), there is indeed our own [human] presiding agency. The same applies to the support of birds, eggs, and so forth. Nor is the qualification of the reason unestablished due to the presiding agency of God, because by the word "conscious" (cetana), anything other than Him is intended.

Likewise, trembling (*kampa*) is also a mark (*liṅga*) for the existence of air (*vāyu*); for instance, this action (*karman*) in grass and the like occurs without the impact of a material substance possessing form (*rūpa*), and it is produced by the impact of a substance possessing touch and velocity (*vega*). It is not governed by gravity, effortful contact with the self, fluidity, or residual impressions (*saṃskāra*); therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is its being an action not produced by those [other causes].

If it is argued, "Is not air indeed perceptible? Why seek for a logical mark (*liṅga*) in this matter?"—we say no. Air is not perceptible, because it is an external substance devoid of color, like space; thus, its supersensuous nature is established by inference. If it is argued, "Air is perceptible because it is the substratum of touch, like a jar"—this inference for perceptibility is not valid, because "possessing manifested color" (*udbhūtarūpavattva*) serves as a limiting condition (*upādhi*) here. This condition is not non-pervasive with respect to color and so forth, or with respect to the self (*ātman*), because it pervades the probandum (*sādhya*) as delimited by the property of being an external substance (which is the locus-property, *pakṣadharma*), or as delimited by the probans (*sādhana*).

Nor should it be argued that visual perceptibility depends solely on that [color], because in that case alone do its presence and absence follow the presence and absence of the [visual object]; whereas tactile perceptibility depends merely on possessing a suitable touch. This is not tenable, because both the presence and absence of color are equally necessary factors in both cases; for the perceptibility of color is never observed through touch alone, without the apprehension of color. Furthermore, if air were perceptible, it would have to be a factor even in the perception of general qualities such as number and so forth.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of blowing with the mouth (*phūtkāra*) and the like, there is indeed the perceptibility of number, of dimension such as a cubit or a span, of the distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) of the two air-currents situated on either side, and of priority and posteriority; for even you do not maintain a rule that [these] must belong to a specific individual of the class "air," since they are not perceived in a cloth pressed against the back and so forth. [Reply: No, because the rule applies precisely to specific individuals, and because number and the other qualities are perceived in a cloth pressed against the back when it is in a straight position.

However, due to the defect of being in a state of non-straightness (*anārjava*), there is no perception of that [light]. According to the author of the *Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā*, in the case of the external perception of a substance, both color and touch must be manifest and combined; thus, light, the yellow substance within the eye, and moonlight are imperceptible because their touch is unmanifest. Similarly, the heat of summer and aqueous substances with separated parts are imperceptible because their color is unmanifest.

The experts of the tradition maintain that even when touch does not manifest, there is indeed perception of light and so forth; for this very reason, in moonlight within the sky, the conjunctions and disjunctions of birds, eggs, and the like are indeed perceived. Nor should it be said that possessing manifested touch is the general cause for the perception of external substances, for then the light of a sapphire would fail to be perceived. Nor is it the case that possessing a manifested specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) alone is the decisive factor, for then space (*ākāśa*) would also have to be perceived.

Nor is it the case that possessing a manifested specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) co-extensive with produced magnitude (mahattva) is the [necessary condition], because the bitter substance of bile located at the tip of the tongue is not perceived even when its bitterness is manifested. Therefore, possessing manifested color (rūpa) alone is the determinant for the perceptibility of substances other than the self; and since that [manifested color] does not exist in air, air is imperceptible. || 9 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that no mark (liṅga) is perceived here through direct perception? For, unlike fire and smoke, there is no apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti) here by means of perception. Furthermore, this touch might belong to one of the [elements] such as earth. To this he says: "And it is not the touch of those things seen"; thus, air has an unperceived mark. (10)

This touch which is made the subject (pakṣa) does not belong to the perceived [elements] of earth, water, and fire, because it does not coexist with color; likewise, this touch must be inferred to be supported by something, and thus its logical mark (liṅga) is unperceived. The meaning is that even though it is a case of inference from a general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa), it arrives through the force of the property of being a characteristic of the subject (pakṣadharmatā).

Although the fourfold set beginning with touch is indeed a perceived mark (*dṛṣṭa-liṅga*), nevertheless, because its invariable concomitance (*vyāpti*) has not been apprehended in relation to air, it is described as having the nature of an unperceived mark (*adṛṣṭa-liṅga*). For one cannot establish air by first asserting the subject (*dharmin*) as "this is air. Thus, the point is that the establishment of air occurs through the mark known as *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation), assisted by other [marks]. || 10 ||
Having established the whole (avayavin) as the substratum of the perceived touch, he states [the following] in order to establish air characterized as atoms:
"Substance [is established] by its being devoid of [other] substances. (11)

"Substantial" (*dravyavat*) means that which has substance as its substratum; "non-substantial" (*adravyavat*) means not having substance as its substratum, i.e., not dependent on substance. Thus, like space, air characterized by atoms (*paramāṇu*) is a substance, because other categories of entities are dependent on substances. Furthermore, since it is stated that dependence [on substance] applies everywhere except for eternal substances, and because the production of a large composite whole through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth—starting from two atoms—is to be established, [air is a substance]. || 11 ||
Combining two reasons that establish the substantiality of the air-atom (vāyuparamāṇu), he says: "Because it possesses motion and because it possesses qualities. (12)

The remainder [of the definition] is that "the wind-atom is a substance. Although it might be argued that there is a circular dependency—since once substantiality (*dravyatva*) is established, possession of action (*kriyāvattva*) and possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*) are established, and once those two are established, substantiality is established—nevertheless, the possession of action by the atom is established because otherwise the conjunction that serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for the composite whole (the air) which possesses the perceived touch could not be explained; and its possession of qualities is established because of the rule that the touch, color, and other qualities of a composite whole must be preceded by the qualities of their causes.

And because [the definition] consists of both of these, there is no fault. Among those [definitions], "possessing action" (*kriyāvattva*) occurs in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), while "possessing qualities" (*guṇavattva*) pervades all similar instances. By the word "and" (*ca*), he conjoins "being an inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) as a prover of substantiality (*dravyatva*). If it is objected: "There is no proof for atoms themselves; of what, then, is substantiality being proven?"—we reply: No. For when a gross effect is broken down by the logic of action, disjunction, and so forth, it reaches a state of being increasingly smaller and smaller. That which cannot be made smaller than that is the atom (*paramāṇu*).

If the regress of parts and wholes were without limit, then, since there would be no distinction in having infinite parts, there would follow the absurdity that things such as Mount Sumeru and a mustard seed would be identical in size; for apart from a difference in the number of causes, neither the number of constituent parts nor their aggregation can account for a difference in magnitude. Nor is this regress of parts and wholes terminated by destruction, because destruction is impossible for a final partless entity, and if it were to have parts, it would follow that the regress is without limit—a fault already stated.

If it is argued that "the atom (truṭi) itself is the limit, because it is perceived, and there is no evidence for postulating anything unperceived," we say no; for it is necessary [to admit] its status as a visual substance. Therefore, just as in the case of earth and the other elements, the atom is simply the part of a part of a *trasareṇu*—even in the case of air—and thus the air-atom is established. || 12 ||

Now, one might object that because it possesses action and because it possesses qualities, the impermanence of the atom should be inferred from its similarity to a jar and other such objects; therefore, he says:
"Its permanence is stated on account of its being a non-substance. (13)

The phrase "of the air characterized as atoms" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. For a substance perishes due to the destruction of either its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) or its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); however, since an atom lacks parts, neither of those two [causes] exists for it. Thus, in the absence of a cause of destruction, it does not perish. Furthermore, in the two reasons—"possessing action" and "possessing qualities"—the property of "having parts" (*sāvayavatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*). This [condition] pervades the probandum as delimited by the property of being a subject-attribute (*pakṣadharma*)—namely, substantiality (*dravyatva*)—whereas the counter-correlativity of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāvapratiyogitva*) is the limiting condition that pervades the probandum simpliciter. || 13 ||

Since the production [of gross objects] through the sequence beginning with dyads has been established, and although the plurality of air is already proven, he states the following to establish it by another method as well:
"The mingling of air with air is a mark of its plurality. (14)

Regarding "the convergence of winds" (*vāyusaṃmūrcchanam*): it is the specific conjunction of two winds or of multiple winds. This is a collision between two [winds] possessing equal velocity and moving in opposite directions. It is inferred by the upward movement of grass, cotton-wool, and the like, because the upward movement of the two winds and their collision are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). However, since the upward movement of grass and other such objects is perceptible, it is inferred that this action, characterized by upward motion, is produced by either the impact or the push of a substance possessing touch and velocity.

For instance, the upward movement of wind, which by nature moves horizontally, is impossible without mutual resistance; thus, it establishes the existence of such resistance, as this is observed in the case of two currents of river water. Furthermore, that upward movement of the wind is to be inferred from the upward movement of grass and other objects, for the upward movement of grass and the like does not occur without either the impact or the push of a substance possessing touch and velocity. || 14 ||
Now, it has been stated that air has an unperceived mark; how then is this so? To this he says:
"Because there is no perception upon contact with air, a perceived mark does not exist. (15)

For a mark (*liṅga*) is said to be "seen" where the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is grasped through perception, as in the case of smoke [as a mark] for fire. However, in the case of contact with air, there is no perception of an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) with air; for it is not the perception of anyone that "whatever possesses touch, vibration, and so forth, that is air," because air itself is imperceptible. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no such mark whose pervasion is grasped by perception. || 15 ||
If that is so, how then is there inference of air? To this, he says the following in order to reinforce what has already been stated:
"And there is no distinction from the 'generally observed' (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa) [type of inference]. (16)

Inference is indeed threefold: *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*. Thus, this perceived touch, being a touch or a quality, must reside in something; by means of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* inference alone, assisted by the exclusion of other possibilities (*itarabādha*), it is established that it resides in a substance distinct from the eight [known] substances—this is the meaning.

If it is argued that [the proof] then belongs solely to the purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) inference, we say no. For where a general inference (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa) operates after the exclusion of other possibilities, there the qualification of the subject—namely, "not being supported by the eight substances"—is already established. Thus, the meaning of the proposition, "this touch, which is not supported by the eight substances, must be supported by something," does not reach its final conclusion without implying support by a substance distinct from the eight; therefore, its establishment occurs through a positive (anvayin) inference alone, as the meaning would otherwise remain incomplete.

However, in cases where the general-corroborative inference (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) has already been sublated by the onset of a contradiction, the [inference] results in the cognition of the object itself; therefore, it is accepted as being purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*). The claim that "the purely negative inference is for the sake of providing a specific attribute (*prakāra*)" is utterly trivial, because in the aforementioned instance, the attribute presented is necessarily one that is positively concomitant (*anvayin*). Furthermore, the restrictive rule that "inference must always have a specific attribute as its determinant of pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka-prakārikā*)" lacks any authoritative basis, since it is possible for an inference to possess a different attribute due to the assistance of a particular causal complex (*sāmagrī*). || 16 ||

Now, if it is intended that there is no distinction such that the inference of space does not take the form "this is air," but rather occurs only in the manner of being "residing in a substance other than the eight substances," then what is the proof for the designation "air" for that substance? To this, he says:
"Therefore, it is based on scripture. (17)

Since there is no inference [of air] in its specific form, the name "air" (*vāyu*) is derived from scripture (*āgamika*); the meaning is that it is established from the *āgama*, which is the Veda. The designation "air" is understood solely from the *arthavāda* passages that serve as supplements to injunctions, such as: "Air is indeed the swiftest deity," and "One should sacrifice a white goat dedicated to Air. This is just as the designation "heaven" (*svarga*) is understood from the *arthavāda*: "That which is not mixed with pain, nor followed by anything else... and so forth.
In spring, the shedding of leaves occurs for all crops;
yet the barley stalks stand rejoicing, adorned with ears of grain.

Thus, from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the name *yava* [barley], from the explanatory passage "the *vetasa* grows in water" regarding the name *vetasa*, and from the explanatory passage "cows run after the boar" regarding the name *varāha*.

Otherwise, in cases such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," if a specific pleasure were not presented, those seeking heaven would not engage in sacrifices and the like; nor would there be a failure to determine the course of action in cases such as "the sacrificial oblation consists of *yava*," "he offers the *prājāpatya* on a mat of *vetasa*," or "boar-leather for sandals," by following the usage established among the Mlecchas.

For the Mlecchas indeed employ the words *yava*, *varāha*, and *vetasa* to denote *kaṅgu* (millet), crow, and *jambu* (blackberry) respectively; thus, in the absence of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), there would be doubt. Therefore, the meaning of each specific term is understood solely through traditional scripture (*āgama*). This is the intended sense. The name alone is derived from scripture, whereas the establishment of the substance [of the object] results from inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). || 17 ||

Having thus concluded the section on air (*vāyu*), [the author], wishing to establish that the scripture is composed by an omniscient being—arguing that the designation "air" is not like the names "Ḍittha" or "Ḍavittha" uttered by the insane—and desiring to begin the introductory section on God (*īśvara*), says:
"The naming [of things] is a mark of those superior to us. (18)

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of excluding [the inference from] marks such as touch. "Designation" means a name; "action" means an effect, such as the earth and so forth. Both of these are marks of the existence of those superior to us—the Lord and the great sages—even though they too exist. || 18 ||
To the question "How is this so?", he says:
"Because the act of naming proceeds from direct perception. (19)

Here too, the compound "saṃjñā ca karma ca" (name and action) is treated as a singular collective (ekavadbhāva) in order to indicate the non-difference between the creator of names and the creator of the world. For instance, only one who has direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of heaven, the unseen potency (*apūrva*), and so forth, is capable of establishing the names "heaven," "unseen potency," and so on for them—just as a father assigns the names "Caitra," "Maitra," and so forth to physical bodies such as Caitra and Maitra that he perceives directly, or just as one assigns the names "pot," "cloth," and so forth.

And thus, even the application of designations such as "pot" or "cloth" is dependent solely upon the convention of God; whatever word has been designated by God for a particular object is correct in that regard. For example, the designation that "any medicinal herb touched by the fang of a mongoose destroys the venom of a snake" serves as an inferential mark (*liṅga*) for those superior to ourselves [such as God]. Furthermore, even the name given by a father to a son, such as "Maitra," is established by injunctions such as, "On the twelfth day, the father shall give him a name."

Surely [the name] must be employed by God; thus, it is established that the name is a mark (liṅga) of God. Likewise, action (karman)—that is, an effect—is also a mark of God. For instance: "The earth and so forth have an agent, because they are effects, like a jar."

In this context, although what is intended by "earth and so forth" (*kṣityādi*)—as the subject of the inference—is not restricted to that which is non-produced by a body, or produced [but] not produced by an effort that is itself produced, or that which is the object of dispute regarding having an agent or not having an agent, or that whose having an agent is doubted; for even earth and so forth are produced by an effort that is itself produced via the medium of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), and because dispute and doubt would be over-extensive (*atiprasakta*), they cannot serve as the delimitors of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, if "having an agent" (*sakartṛkatva*) means being produced by one possessing volition (*kṛtimat*), then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of [the agency of] Śiva and others.

Since even the action of beings such as ourselves produces the earth and so forth by way of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), [the reason] would fail even if it were "produced by an action whose object is the material cause," because our own actions likewise have some material cause as their object.
