Furthermore, if "being an effect" (*kāryyatva*) means being the counter-positive of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva-pratiyogitva*), then there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). Nevertheless, the earth has an agent (*sakartṛkā*) because it is an effect. And here, "having an agent" means being produced by an action that does not operate through the unseen force, while "being an effect" means being the counter-positive of existence delimited by prior non-existence.

Nor is there the fallacy of "doubtful inconclusiveness" (*sandigdhānaikāntikatva*) regarding the sprout and so forth; for doubtfulness constitutes a flaw only when there is uncertainty as to whether the reason exists or not while the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is certain—otherwise, it would follow that all inference would be abolished. Nor should it be said that this flaw applies only outside the subject (*pakṣa*), for that would be a mere royal decree; for it is not the prerogative of a logical flaw that it should not affect the subject.

Therefore, since the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) in that [subject] is unimpeded by means of a reason whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been ascertained during the state when the sprout manifests, how could there be any "inconclusiveness due to doubt" (*sandigdhānaikāntikatā*)? It is even more so during the state when it does not manifest; such is the summary. || 19 ||
Having thus concluded the section on Īśvara with these two sūtras, and being about to commence the section on Ākāśa, he says:
"Going out and entering are the marks of Ākāśa. (20)

The word "iti" (thus) signifies "manner" or "kind," and it includes actions such as upward throwing (utkṣepaṇa) and others. The Sāṅkhyas maintain that movement—namely, exiting and entering—is the inferential mark (liṅga) of space (ākāśa), which is otherwise not an effect [of other elements] but possesses the quality of touch through its association with substances that do. || 20 ||
To refute this, he says:
"That [shadow] is not a mark [of motion], because action resides in a single substance. (21)

Action, such as going out or entering, does not infer the existence of space by way of being its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because action inheres in a single substance; that is, it has as its inherent cause only one corporeal substance. Furthermore, it has been stated that action does not subsist in multiple substances, nor does it subsist in incorporeal things. || 21 ||
But will it not infer the existence of space precisely as its non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) for actions such as going out and entering? To this he says:
"And because of the difference [of this case] from the postulation of other causes. (22)

"Anuklṛpti" (conformity) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), based on the etymological derivation that it is "that by which another [cause] is made known or indicated. The meaning is: because of the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) to that conformity which is the characteristic of another cause, namely the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). To begin with, a substance (*dravya*) is never a non-inherent cause. Furthermore, the state of being a non-inherent cause occurs through proximity with the cause in a single object (*kāraṇaikārthapratyāsatti*) and through proximity with the effect in a single object (*kāryaikārthapratyāsatti*).

The first [type of non-inherent causality] is that of the threads' forms with respect to the form of the cloth; this non-inherent causality receives the designation "great" because it is difficult to comprehend. The second is, for example, that of the contact between the self and the mind with respect to cognition and so forth; this non-inherent causality receives the designation "small" because it is easy to comprehend. However, in the case of ether, there is neither inherent nor non-inherent causality with respect to actions such as exiting and entering. Thus, action is not a mark for the existence of ether. || 22 ||
[Objection: Let space be the efficient cause for action, for the movement of birds, eggs, and so forth is observed in space; to this he says:
"Due to conjunction, there is the absence of action. (23)

Due to the obstruction of the causes of action—such as velocity, gravity, and so forth—by contact with a corporeal substance (*mūrta*), there is the non-existence or non-production of action; this is not, however, due to the absence of space (*ākāśa*), because space is all-pervading (*vyāpaka*). Therefore, the concomitance (*anvaya*) with space is merely established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*); it does not prove that space is the efficient cause (*nimitta*). This is the meaning. || 23 ||
Thus, having refuted the Sāṅkhya view, and wishing to establish sound as a mark [of the existence] of space, he sets the stage for a *pariśeṣa* (residual) inference, saying:
"The quality of an effect is observed to be preceded by the qualities of its cause. (24)

In effects characterized by earth and the other elements, those specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) such as color and so forth are observed to be preceded by the qualities of their causes. Sound, too, is a specific quality, because—while possessing a genus—it is perceptible solely by a single external sense organ, just like color and the rest. Thus, the meaning is that no such effect is perceived wherein sound would not be preceded by the qualities of its cause. (24)
[Objection: But surely sound is perceived in effects such as the lute, flute, drum, conch, and kettledrum; and thus it should be preceded by the qualities of its causes. To this, he says:
"And because no other effect [of touch] appears, sound is not a quality of things possessing touch. (25)

It might be argued that just as color, taste, and so forth are perceived in threads, potsherds, and the like, and another color or taste of the same genus is observed in cloth, jars, and so on; likewise, if the sound perceived in the parts of a lute, flute, drum, and so forth were of the same genus as the sound perceived in the whole—the lute, flute, drum, etc.—then it would be so. But this is not the case. On the contrary, we observe that the lute and other instruments are produced from parts that are themselves devoid of sound, whereas we never observe cloth, jars, and the like being produced from threads, potsherds, and so forth, which are themselves devoid of color.

Furthermore, if sound were a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of tangible substances, then the states of being loud, louder, soft, or softer would not be experienced therein; for qualities such as color and so forth, which reside in a single composite whole (*avayavin*), are not experienced with such variety. Therefore, sound is not a specific quality of tangible substances. || 25 ||
Now, one might argue that sound could be a quality of the self or a quality of the mind; therefore, he says:
"Because it inheres in something other [than the self or mind], and because it is perceptible, it is neither a quality of the self nor a quality of the mind. (26)

If sound were a quality of the self (*ātman*), then there would arise such cognitions as "I am filling [the conch]," "I am playing the instrument," or "I possess sound," just as one has the cognitions "I am happy," "I know," or "I desire. However, this is not the case; rather, people in the world perceive it as "the conch is being filled" or "the lute is being played," and they do not perceive it in the manner described above.

Furthermore, sound is not a quality of the self because it is perceivable by an external sense organ, like color and so forth. Moreover, if sound were a specific quality of the self suitable for the self, it would be perceived even by a deaf person, just like pain and other such qualities. Therefore, it has been well stated [in the Sūtra] that "because it inheres in another. He states the reason why it is not a quality of the mind: "because it is perceptible. By the fact that the compound *nātmamanasoḥ* (not a quality of the self or the mind) was not formed when it could have been, it is indicated—by the same logical principle—that the status of sound as a quality is also denied to space and time by this very reason of its being perceptible. || 26 ||
He states what remains for that purpose: "The inferential mark of space is established by elimination. (27)

The word "sound" is to be understood as the subject [of the inference]. Here too, sound is supported by something, because it is a quality, like color and so forth; thus, from a general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), there is the establishment of a substance distinct from the eight [known] substances. Furthermore, this [sound] is a quality because it belongs to a class perceivable by a single external sense organ, like color and so forth; and, being non-eternal while inhering in an omnipresent [substance], it is like cognition and so forth. Its non-eternality will be established later. Since there is no evidence for postulating parts for the substance established by elimination, it is eternal; and since sound is perceived everywhere, it is omnipresent. (27)
Establishing by means of extended application that the substance which is the mark of sound possesses both substantiality and eternity, he says:
"Substantiality and eternity are explained by [the case of] air. (28)

The meaning is: just as space possesses eternality because it lacks constituent parts (*adravyavattva*), like wind; and just as space possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*) because it possesses qualities (*guṇavattva*), like wind. || 28 ||
Is it then that there are many spaces, or is it only one? To this he says:
"By way of its true nature" (tattvambhāvena). || 29 ||

The word "explained" (vyākhyātam) is to be construed with the term "transformed" (vipariṇatena). The meaning is that existence (bhāva), which is being (sattā), is one, and just as it is one, so too is space (ākāśa) one. || 29 ||

[Objection: Surely, the oneness of existence (*sattā*) is established by the power of the inclusive cognition (*anugata-pratyaya*); how then can its oneness be established by the example of space? To this, he says:
"Because there is no distinction in the mark [of sound] and because there is an absence of any specific mark. (30)

The meaning is that the existence of space (*ākāśa*) is established as a reality (*tattva*). Since all sounds can be accounted for by having that [space] alone as their substratum when its vastness (*vaibhava*) is admitted, there would be the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) in postulating another substratum. Furthermore, whatever other space might be postulated, sound alone would be its mark (*liṅga*), and that is no different [from the first]. Nor is there any other distinct mark that establishes a difference or proves a division [between spaces]. Although the mark for the selves (*ātman*), such as cognition and so forth, is likewise non-distinct, it will be stated later that the plurality of selves is established through a different mark, namely, the principle of systematic distribution (*vyavasthā*). || 30 ||

Now, let it be granted that space possesses oneness; let it also possess supreme magnitude due to its pervasiveness; and let it possess both conjunction and disjunction because they are its non-inherent causes of sound. But how can there be numerical separateness (*ekapṛthaktva*)? To this he says: "And numerical separateness [is established] because it conforms to that" (sūtra 31).

Since unity invariably conforms to individuality (*ekapṛthaktva*), the existence of individuality is established. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the chapter; the subject matter of this chapter is the definition of a substance as that which possesses specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) not within the scope of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*). By this [definition], earth possesses fourteen qualities; and those qualities are color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, individuality, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, and momentum (*saṃskāra*). Water possesses exactly those same [qualities] as earth, with the addition of viscidity (*sneha*) in place of smell.

Excluding taste, smell, viscidity, and weight, these [qualities] belong to fire. Excluding smell, taste, color, weight, viscidity, and fluidity, these belong to air. Together with sound, the possession of the five qualities beginning with number belongs to ether. The mere five beginning with number belong to space and time. The five beginning with number, together with priority, posteriority, and velocity, belong to the mind. The five beginning with number, along with knowledge, desire, and effort, belong to the Lord. || 31 ||
Thus ends the first daily lesson of the second chapter in the Śrī Śāṅkara Vaiśeṣika Sūtra Upaskāra.
In the second chapter, the second section (Ahnika):

Now, desiring to examine the characteristics of the elements, such as odor and the rest, and establishing whether these odors and other qualities are inherent or adventitious, [the author] says: "Since there is no production of another quality when a flower and a cloth are in contact, the absence of odor in the cloth is the mark of the non-existence [of that odor]. (VS 2.1.1)

Where color, taste, smell, and touch arise through the sequence of the qualities of their causes, they function as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) only when they are inherent; not otherwise. Indeed, the fragrance perceived in the wind, the coolness perceived on a stone slab, or the heat perceived in water do not constitute defining characteristics [of those substances]. This is what he expresses by saying "in the case of the flower and the cloth. For the fragrance of the *kanakaketakī* flower is not a characteristic of the cloth when it is not perceived in the cloth that is in close proximity to that flower.

For that [fragrance] is not produced in the cloth by way of a sequence of causal qualities; rather, it is adventitious (*aupādhika*), arising from proximity to a *kanaka-ketakī* flower. Indeed, the absence of fragrance in the cloth is not the logical mark (*liṅga*) for the absence of the *ketakī* fragrance. What, then, is the logical mark? Therefore, it is said: "the non-appearance of other qualities."

"Non-appearance" means non-origination from a different quality, that is, from a quality of the cause. For if the fragrance perceived in the cloth were inherent to it, then it would have been perceived in its constituent parts, the threads, even prior to contact with the *ketakī* flower; yet this is not the case. Thus, the meaning is as follows: the fragrance under dispute is not inherent in the cloth, because it is a specific quality not produced by the qualities of its constituent parts, just like cold or hot touch. || 1 ||
He states the natural characteristic of earth as its smell:
"Smell is established in earth. (2)

The meaning is that smell (*gandha*), being established in earth and distinguished by its connection with it alone and its non-connection with anything else, serves as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) because it excludes [earth] from both homogeneous and heterogeneous classes. For earth is indeed possessed of smell; earth alone is possessed of smell; and earth is the only thing possessed of smell. Thus, it is established that smell is the natural property of earth, which distinguishes it from the eight homogeneous substances such as water and the five heterogeneous categories beginning with quality (*guṇa*). || 2 ||
Extending the method for establishing the intrinsic nature of odor to the case of heat as a characteristic of fire, he says:
"By this, heat is explained. (3)
This extended application (atideśa) should also be understood to apply to the coldness and other qualities that characterize earth and the other elements. || 3 ||
The characteristic of fire is perceived as follows:
heat is the property of fire. (4)
The meaning is that natural heat is the characteristic of fire; its form is also observed to be white and radiant. || 4 ||
He examines the characteristic of water: coldness in water. (5)

The meaning is that inherent coldness is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of water. Thus, the intention is that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of this definition to stone slabs, sandalwood, and the like. By means of "coldness," the author also indicates that color and taste possess the aforementioned characteristics, as well as viscidity (*sneha*) and natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhikadravatva*).

If it is asked, "Why is there a violation of the order of enumeration and definition?", we reply: No; for the examination of fire (*tejas*) is stated between [the examinations of] earth and water in order to indicate that the touch of fire overcomes the touches of earth and water, or else to indicate the examination of air (*vāyu*). Thus, the intended meaning is that the touch of air—which is neither produced by heating (*apākaja*) nor hot or cold—is its natural characteristic (*svābhāvika-lakṣaṇa*); this is how it should be inferred. || 5 ||

Thus, it has been stated that the specific qualities of substances possessing touch, such as odor and the rest, are preceded by the qualities of their causes and serve as the defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa) of earth and the other elements. Now, commencing the section on the definition of time which follows in the sequence, he says: "The marks of time are 'prior,' 'posterior,' 'simultaneous,' 'long,' and 'quick. (VS 2.2.6)

The particle *iti* refers to the various modes of cognition and is connected to each [term] individually; thus, the meaning is that the notion of "not yet," the notion of "simultaneously," the notion of "after a long time," and the notion of "quickly" are indicators of time.

By the phrase "the remote in relation to the proximate," one should also understand "the proximate in relation to the remote. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: when an elder person has been born with an interval of many more solar movements [than a youth], "remoteness" (paratva) arises in that elder, taking the youth as the limit. And that remoteness depends upon a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa). Neither color and so forth can be the non-inherent cause, because of deviation; for while there is the production of remoteness in the three—smell and so forth—in the air, it is not produced there from color and the rest. Nor can touch be the cause, because even touch, being divided into types such as hot and so on, deviates individually [from the production of remoteness].

Nor can it be a substance of limited dimension, because such a substance cannot originate a heterogeneous effect, and because the solar vibrations would be located in a different substratum. Consequently, by elimination, the non-inherent cause must be the conjunction with a substance delimited by that [sun]; and that substance, being conjoined with both the mass [of earth] and the sun, must be all-pervading (*vibhu*). If one were to postulate that space possesses this inherent nature, then from the striking of a drum anywhere, there would be the undesirable consequence of sound arising in all drums. Therefore, time alone is the bringer of the solar action [to the object].

Furthermore, for the qualities of one substance to be delimited by another substance, the self requires a sense-contact other than its own proximity; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that a crystal gem in Pāṭaliputra would appear red due to the crimson color of saffron in Vārāṇasī. However, since time is postulated as having that very nature [of transmitting qualities], this fault does not apply. If it is asked, "Why is the transmission of color not also effected by time?", the answer is that time is established precisely as the factor that brings about specific actions.

In this manner, having taken the elder as the limit, the production of "posteriority" (aparatva) in the younger person is to be examined. Regarding the term "simultaneously" (*yugapad*): the cognitions such as "they are born simultaneously," "they stand simultaneously," and "they act simultaneously" mean [occurrence] at one time, that is, at one solar movement, or at a time delimited by one solar movement.

Now, these solar movements do not become qualifiers merely by being unobtained (*aprāpta*), nor are they [qualifiers] merely by being proximate in their own nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, since such qualified cognitions would otherwise be inexplicable, that substance which brings about the qualifiers is Time (*kāla*). 6.
Granted that time is established, yet there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to determine whether it is eternal or a substance; therefore, he says:
"Its status as a substance and its eternity are explained by [the case of] air. (7)
The meaning is that, just as the air-atom possesses substantiality because it has qualities and possesses eternity because it is not composed of other substances, so too is it with time. || 7 ||

Nevertheless, [one might ask] whether there may be many [units of] time; to this he says: "By way of its nature as reality" (tattvambhāvena) [verse 8]. The word "explained" (vyākhyātam) is to be construed with the term transposed [from the previous verse]. The meaning is that although time appears to be manifold because the marks of time—such as the notions of "long" and so forth—are observed everywhere without distinction, yet, like the self (*ātman*), time possesses unity because there is no mark of specific differentiation, just as there is none for existence (*sattā*). If it is objected: "In this case, since there are many times distinguished by moments (*kṣaṇa*), instants (*lava*), hours (*muhūrta*), watches (*yāma*), days, nights, fortnights, months, seasons (*ṛtu*), solstices (*ayana*), years, and so on, how can time be one?", we reply: No, because the appearance of such distinctions is based upon limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Just as a single crystal gem appears as if divided due to the coloring of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as blue or yellow, so too time, though one, appears as if divided by the distinctions of delimitations such as the movement of the sun and by the distinctions of the non-interruption of its various effects; for this is the accepted position. And thus, a moment (*kṣaṇa*) is a temporal adjunct that does not pervade other temporal adjuncts, or rather, it is time which is not the locus of an occasional absence that has its own substratum as its counter-positive; this is to be determined because at every moment something arises and something perishes.

Two *kṣaṇas* constitute a *lava*, and so forth, as established by traditional scripture (*āgama*). Now, one might object: "Even so, let there be three divisions of time—past, future, and present—for it is heard in such passages as 'the non-establishment of the three times' (*traikālyāsiddhi*)"; but this is not so.

Because the linguistic usage of the three times occurs through the delimitation by the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsa*) of a thing: for whatever time is delimited by a given thing, that is its present; whatever time is delimited by the prior non-existence of something, that is its future time; and whatever time is delimited by both the prior non-existence and the posterior non-existence of something, that is its past time. Thus, the linguistic usage of the three times is dependent upon the triad of delimiters. (8)
Now he states that time is the cause of all things that possess origination:
"Because it exists in eternal things and because it exists in non-eternal things, the cause is called 'time'. (9)

The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*). For this reason—that is, for this cause—the name "Time" (*kāla*) is given to that which is the cause of all things that possess origination. He states the reason: "because of its absence in eternal things and its presence in non-eternal things. This means that in eternal things such as space (*ākāśa*), there is an absence of such cognitions as "born simultaneously," "born after a long time," "born quickly," "born now," "born by day," or "born at night"; whereas in non-eternal things such as jars and cloth, there is the presence of such cognitions as simultaneity and so forth. Thus, by both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), Time is established as the cause.

Not only on the strength of cognitions such as simultaneity is time established as the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) of all produced things; rather, this is also to be determined from the designations "winter," "spring," "rainy season," and so forth, applied to flowers, fruits, and the like. || 9 ||
Having completed the section on the indicative marks of time, he now begins the section on the indicative marks of direction, saying:
"That from which [one perceives] 'this is from here' is the indicative mark of direction. (10)

The meaning is as follows: "This is the direction" (diśyam) refers to that which indicates direction. From the fact that one object is the substratum of more numerous conjoined-conjunctions than another object which is the substratum of fewer conjoined-conjunctions, it is designated as "further" (param); and from the fact that one object is the substratum of fewer conjoined-conjunctions than another object which is the substratum of more numerous conjoined-conjunctions, it is designated as "nearer" (aparam). That substance by virtue of which this occurs between two objects existing at the same time in fixed directions and locations is "direction" (dik).

For there is no other entity besides such a substance that can bring about the conjunctions of many or few contacts between two masses; nor is there a cognition of those specific qualities without that bringing together; nor is there the production of priority and posteriority without that cognition; nor are there the conceptualization and linguistic usage based on those qualities without their production. Nor should it be argued that time itself may be the bringer of the conjunction, rendering a separate substance unnecessary; for time is established as the bringer of conjunctions only insofar as it brings about specific, restricted actions.

If one were to imagine that space causes the transfer of non-fixed properties from one thing to another, then it would follow that it would transfer the saffron-paste from Kashmir to the jar-like breasts of a beautiful woman from Karṇāṭaka. If space were likewise a transmitter of properties from one thing to another, the same undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) would apply.

However, since direction (dik) is established as a transmitter of fixed properties from one thing to another, there is no such over-extension (atiprasaṅga). And thus, direction, which brings about conjunction, is indeed distinct from time, which brings about action.

Furthermore, these notions—“this is to the east of that,” “this is to the west of that,” “this is to the south-east of that,” “this is to the south-west of that,” “this is to the north-west of that,” “this is to the north-east of that,” “this is below that,” and “this is above that”—are subsumed under the notion "from this, this [is]," because no other cause for these notions is possible. Moreover, time is the indicator of fixed limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), whereas direction is the indicator of non-fixed limiting adjuncts.

For that which is present in relation to something remains present in relation to that very thing; however, such a rule does not apply to spatial adjuncts (*dig-upādhi*), because that which is the east for one person may at some time be the west for that same person. The same should be said for the north and so forth. That direction which is proximate to the mountain of sunrise (*sūryodayācala*) in relation to a certain point is the west in relation to that same point.

Proximity (*sannidhāna*), however, consists in the minimal number of conjunctions with the sun; and those conjunctions with the sun, whether few or many, are to be determined by direction (*diś*). Thus, for a person facing east, the direction delimited by the region to his left is the north (*udīcī*); the direction delimited by the right side of such a person is the south (*dakṣiṇā*). "Leftness" and "rightness," moreover, are specific universals (*jāti*) residing in the limbs of the body. Downward direction (*adhaḥ*) is that which is the substratum of a conjunction produced by an action whose non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is gravity (*gurutva*).

Space (dika) is that which is the substratum of conjunction produced by the action of fire generated by the conjunction of the self with the unseen force (adṛṣṭa). Thus, there is another designation for space—namely, the ten directions—as characterized by the presiding deities Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, Īśāna, Nāga, and Brahmā, distinct from the designations such as "east" and so forth. 10.
He states that space possesses substantiality and eternity, just like an atom of air:
"Substantiality and eternity are explained by [the case of] air. (11)
The meaning is that it possesses the nature of a substance because it is endowed with qualities, and it is eternal because it is non-dependent. || 11 ||
Extending the same principle, he says:
"By way of its true nature. (12)

Because there is no distinction in their directional marks and because there is an absence of specific marks, there is oneness of existence; and because they conform to that, there is oneness of separateness. || 12 ||
Now, if there is indeed only one direction, how then do the cognition and conventional usage of "ten directions" arise? To this he says:
"Their multiplicity is due to specific effects. (13)
The meaning is that "difference of effect" refers to a specific distinction in effects, and by means of that, there is a figurative designation of manifoldness. || 13 ||
Demonstrating that very distinction of effects, he says:
"The 'east' [is determined] from the conjunction with the sun, whether it has occurred in the past, will occur in the future, or is occurring in the present. (14)

It is called "prācī" (eastern) because the sun moves toward it first; thus, that direction in which there has been, will be, or is occurring the first conjunction of the sun as it revolves around Meru in a clockwise direction is the eastern direction.

In this context, the description of the three times is based on the difference in the intentions of persons: for some, the conventional usage "this is the East" occurs because they intend that "the first conjunction with the sun occurred in this direction yesterday morning"; for others, the conventional usage "East" occurs because they intend that "the first conjunction with the sun will occur in this direction tomorrow"; and for others, the conventional usage "East" occurs because they intend that "the conjunction with the sun is currently occurring in this direction."

The suffix *kta* in the word *bhūtāt* denotes the inception of an action (*ādikarman*). Consequently, since there is no fixed rule regarding the intention [of the speaker], the application of the conventional term "east" is established even at night or at midday and other times when there is no conjunction with the sun; this is the intended meaning. || 14 ||
Extending this same principle even to the conventional usage of the intermediate directions, he says: "In the same way, [there are] the south, the west, and the north. (15)

In the same way, the conventional usage of "south" arises from the conjunction of the sun with a mountain situated in the southern direction—whether that conjunction has occurred in the past, will occur in the future, or is occurring in the present. The conventional usages of "west" and "north" are to be inferred in the same manner. The meanings of "leftness" (*vāmatva*) and "rightness" (*dakṣiṇatva*) have already been explained. || 15 ||
Extending this very same method to the conventional usage of the intermediate directions, he says:
"By this, the intermediate directions are explained. (16)

Due to the overlapping of the characteristics of the eastern and southern directions, there is the conventional usage "the south-eastern direction. In the same way, one should infer the terms "south-western," "north-western," and "north-eastern. Furthermore, that all-pervading substance by which these conjunctions with the sun are brought about is "direction" (dik); this has been explained in detail in the *Kaṇādarahasya*. 16.

It has already been established that the characteristics of the four elements, such as color and so forth, are real because they are preceded by the qualities of their causes; otherwise, they would be merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). Furthermore, it was stated that the mark of the all-pervading [space] is its being devoid of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*). Now, sound must be examined as the mark of space (*ākāśa*). Regarding this, there are conflicting views among the experts of the system (*tāntrika*): some declare sound to be a substance (*dravya*), while others call it a quality (*guṇa*); and even among those who accept it as a quality, some say it is eternal (*nitya*) and others say it is non-eternal (*anitya*).

Others, however, maintain that even in the case of sound (śabda), there is another distinct entity called *sphoṭa*. Now, beginning this investigation, the author first establishes doubt—the very first limb of inquiry—by means of its definition and its causes, stating: "Doubt arises from the perception of a commonality, the non-perception of specific qualities, and the recollection of specific qualities. (NS 2.1.17)

"From the perception of the universal" means from the apprehension of the substratum (dharmin) which possesses the universal, through the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*. "From the non-perception of the particular" means from the non-apprehension of the particular property that distinguishes [the object] from others, such as the curvature, hollows, and so forth, or the head, hands, and so forth. "From the recollection of the particular" means from the memory of the two alternatives (koṭi), namely the characteristics of being a post or being a person.

Even remembrance (*smaraṇa*) is included under "apprehension" (*grahaṇa*), because in some cases it possesses the status of a "term" (*koṭi*) regarding two properties being experienced; by the word "and" (*ca*), causes of doubt such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) are also subsumed. A unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is not mentioned [as a cause of doubt] because it does not produce knowledge that is non-conceptual in nature (*anadhyavasāyātmaka*). Alternatively, although a unique property is indeed a cause by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), it was not mentioned because exclusion from both similar and dissimilar instances (*sapakṣa-vipakṣa-vyāvṛtti*) is nothing other than a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*).

Misapprehension (*vipratipatti*) is also not mentioned separately because it does not produce doubt through the combination of two contradictory propositions; rather, it consists of two sentences such as "Sound is eternal" and another [sentence] such as "It is non-eternal. Since these two cognitions produced by them do not occur simultaneously, they cannot together cause doubt. Therefore, in that case, properties such as "being sound-ness" (*śabdatva*), which are uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), or properties such as "existence" (*sattva*) and "knowability" (*prameyatva*), which are common (*sādhāraṇa*), are the doubtful factors (*saṃśāyaka*). Thus, misapprehension is not stated as a distinct category.

In the *Gautamīya-samānatantra*, because knowledge characterized by indecision (*anadhyavasāya*) is not accepted, the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) property is stated to be the cause of doubt. Regarding "conflict of opinions" (*vipratipatti*), which consists of two contradictory statements, its status as a cause of doubt is stated on the grounds that it possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Furthermore, in the *Nyāyabhāṣya*, that which is stated as a cause of doubt—namely, "perceptibility"—is such that both what exists and what does not exist are perceived; thus, one wonders whether this perceived object is existent or non-existent. Likewise, "imperceptibility" applies to both: things like the root of a tree, a wooden peg, or water are not perceived despite being existent, while things like a sky-lotus are not perceived despite being non-existent. Consequently, it is argued that doubt is fivefold. However, this [perceptibility] is merely a form of generality (*sāmānya*), and its meaning is already covered by the statement "due to the perception of generality" (*sāmānyapratyakṣāt*).

Furthermore, as for the statement in the *Nyāyavārttika* that there are three types of doubt based on a distinction in their causes, that too is untenable; for it is impossible for the three—namely, the common property (*samānadharma*) and so forth—to function as causes due to their overlapping (vyabhicāra). Indeed, one should not postulate a specific difference in kind (*vaijātya*) here, as one does in the case of fire produced from grass, flint, or a gem; rather, the causality with respect to the effect delimited by the nature of doubt (*saṃśayatva*) is to be postulated solely on the basis of being a common property.

Furthermore, as for the heterogeneity mentioned—such as being a category of positive injunction (*pradhāna-vidhi*) or a category of negative prohibition (*pradhāna-niṣedha*)—that cannot serve as a defining characteristic (*avacchedaka*) because it lacks pervasiveness (*ananugatatva*). Consequently, doubt is neither threefold nor fivefold, but rather of only one kind; however, the author of the Sūtras himself clarifies its twofold nature according to another classification.

If it is argued that "doubt" cannot be defined as "a cognition that generates a desire to know," because this definition overextends to indeterminate cognition (*anadhyavasāya*); nor can it be defined as "a cognition that does not generate a mental impression (*saṃskāra*)," because this applies equally to indeterminate perception, since doubt—being a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*)—also generates a mental impression; and furthermore, even the universal (*jāti*) "doubt-ness" cannot serve as a definition, because the substratum (*dharmin*) lacks doubt-ness in its own part, and thus that universal would be absent from that part, and it is not admitted that a universal can have non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛtti*)—then [the answer is]: Doubt is defined as "a cognition possessing multiple contradictory modes (*prakāra*) with respect to a single substratum. (17)

Doubt is of two kinds: that which has an external object and that which has an internal object. That which has an external object is further divided into that which concerns a perceptible property and that which concerns an imperceptible property. Among these, an example of that concerning a perceptible property is: upon seeing a subject characterized by height, one wonders, "Is this a post or a person? An example of that concerning an imperceptible property is: in a forest, when a mass such as a cow or a gavaya is hidden by shrubs and the like, one wonders, "Is this a cow or a gavaya? upon seeing only its horns.

In reality, even in that case, the doubt concerns the subject (dharmin) which is the horn itself: "Is this horn related to a cow, or is it related to a gavaya? The mention of two types [of causes of doubt] is merely for the sake of the author's intention (*vivakṣāmātra*). Regarding the statement that the generality (*sāmānya*) which is the cause of doubt is either observed in multiple places and thus causes doubt, or observed in a single locus (*dharmī*) and thus causes doubt—the author states the first variety:
"And what is seen is like what was seen" (1.1.23).

The observed height is a cause of doubt. The suffix *vati* in the word *dṛṣṭavat* [indicates similarity]; thus, the meaning is that the height present in the object before one, which exists similarly to the two observed things—the post and the person—is the observed cause of doubt. || 18 ||
He illustrates that which has been observed as having a single characteristic:
"Because it is either as it was observed or not as it was observed. (19)

The phrase "the cause of doubt" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of a conjunction with what was previously stated. Because the reason (*hetu*) is not observed as it was [previously] observed, even that which was observed as such becomes a cause of doubt—for example, Caitra was previously seen to have hair; at another time, he is seen not as previously observed, being devoid of hair. This is the meaning. Subsequently, when that very same Caitra is seen with his head covered by a cloth, a doubt arises: "Is this Caitra with hair or without hair?

For in that case, the common property (*samāno dharma*), namely *caitratva* (the state of being Caitra), is the cause of doubt; and that [property], having been observed in one instance [alone], serves as the cause of doubt. || 19 ||

Regarding "vidyā" (knowledge): internal doubt arises from both knowledge and ignorance. For example, an astrologer may correctly predict an eclipse of the moon and so forth, or he may do so incorrectly. In that case, a doubt arises within him regarding his own cognition: "Has it been correctly predicted, or has it not? Alternatively, since knowledge is sometimes true (vidyā) and sometimes false (avidyā), being invalid (apramā), a doubt arises because it is an object of cognition: "Is this existent, or is it non-existent?"

The repetition of the term "doubt" (*saṃśaya*) here is for the purpose of indicating that even in this case, doubt arises solely from the perception of a common property (*sāmānya-pratyakṣa*) and not from any other cause. Thus, regarding the definition in the system of Gautama—"Doubt is a deliberation requiring specific characteristics, arising from the occurrence of common or multiple properties, from conflicting testimony, and from the lack of determination regarding perception and non-perception"—the claim made by some that "the lack of determination regarding perception and non-perception" (*upalabdhyanupalabdhy-avyavasthā*) is a distinct cause of doubt is thereby refuted. || 20 ||

Having thus explained doubt—the first limb of inquiry—by way of its definition and essential nature, [the author] now states, showing the word as the subject (*dharmin*) which is the object of inquiry:
"That object which is apprehended by the sense of hearing is sound" (VS 2.2.21).

That which has the ear as its apprehension and the instrument of apprehension is "audible by the ear" (*śrotragrahaṇa*); "object" (*artha*) means the substratum (*dharmin*). Thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to properties residing in sound that are audible by the ear—such as "sound-ness," "high pitch," "quality-ness," or "existence"—because the word "object" is intended to refer to the substratum, thereby indicating that there is no such thing as a sound called *sphoṭa* inherent in other sounds.

Indeed, on the strength of the common experience that "a word is one" or "a sentence is one," the *sphoṭa* must necessarily be admitted; for in a word consisting of many phonemes, or in a sentence consisting of many phonemes, there does not arise a cognition of unity. Furthermore, the designation "*sphoṭa*" is based on its function of making the meaning manifest (*arthasphuṭīkaraṇa*).

Each individual phoneme, for its part, is incapable of producing the cognition of meaning; yet a simultaneous conjunction of phonemes uttered by a single speaker is impossible because they perish so rapidly. Therefore, the cognition of meaning arises from the *sphoṭa* alone, since the manifestation of the meaning cannot occur without the knowledge of that *sphoṭa*. And although this *sphoṭa* exists potentially within all the phonemes as they abide in the form of words, it becomes manifest only upon the final phoneme. This is not so.

The state of being a word (*padatva*) consists in having a color-form (*varṇatva*) that possesses a convention (*saṅketa*). Thus, since the meaning is understood from a word solely through the power of convention, what is the use of *sphoṭa*? Although many letters (*varṇa*) possess the single property of conveying a single meaning, the figurative usage "one word" is employed with reference to that [property]. The same applies to a sentence (*vākya*). If some essence of a word distinct from the letters were perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then *sphoṭa* might indeed be accepted; however, this doctrine of *sphoṭa* has been disregarded by the author of the Sūtras because of its triviality. (21)

Thus, when sound is established as the subject (dharmin), it serves as an inferential mark (liṅga) for space only if it possesses the property of being a quality (guṇatva). Therefore, in order to establish that quality-status, [the author] sets forth a threefold doubt, saying:
"Because a specific feature is observed in both ways—among things of the same class and among things belonging to other classes. (22)

The remainder [of the sentence] is "there is doubt regarding sound. In sound, both "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) and audibility (*śrotragrāhyatva*) are perceived; and because these are seen in two ways—in both [classes]—due to the exclusion of the specific [characteristics] from twenty-three qualities of the same genus, from substances which are different entities, and from motions, they give rise to the doubt: "Is sound a quality, a substance, or an action? However, it does not fall under the categories of generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), or inherence (*samavāya*), because of the observation of its difference [from them], such as its possession of existence (*sattva*) and causality (*kāraṇavattva*).

If it is objected that because an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) does not produce a determinate cognition (*anadhyavasāya*), its capacity to produce doubt is prohibited—and since "soundness" (*śabdatva*) and "audibility" (*śrotragrāhyatva*) are indeed uncommon properties, how could they produce doubt?—this is true. However, the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of this [property] from both its own class and other classes is common; thus, it has been stated that only a common property, by virtue of its exclusion, produces doubt.

Exclusion having sound-ness (*śabdatva*) as its counter-correlative is a common property (*samāno dharma*); and sound-ness, being the counter-correlative of the exclusions residing in both [the similar and the dissimilar], is an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇo dharma*). This has been stated: "Because the particularity (*viśeṣa*) is observed in two ways. For here, the observation of the particularity—that is, of the exclusion—is presented as a cause of doubt because it occurs in both cases, namely among the similar (*sajātīya*) and the dissimilar (*vijātīya*); and that [particularity] is indeed a common property (*samāna eva dharma*). || 22 ||
Having thus demonstrated the doubt, he says—in order to exclude the possibility of its being a substance—the following:
"Because it consists of a single substance, it is not a substance. (23)

That which has a single substance as its inherent cause is "one-substance" (*ekadravya*). Since no substance whatsoever has a single substance as its inherent cause, sound is not a substance because it possesses the property of being unlike substances (*dravyavaidharmya*); this is the meaning. || 23 ||
Now, one might object: "But action is indeed a single substance, and thus sound would be an action"; to this he says:
"Nor is it action, because it is not visible to the eye. (24)

The meaning is that the cognition (pratyaya) whose object is sound is non-visual (*acākṣuṣa*), because it is produced by an external sense organ other than the eye. Thus, the intention is: "Sound-ness (*śabdatva*) does not reside in action (*karma*), because it is a genus (*jāti*) that does not reside in visual perception (*cākṣuṣapratyakṣa*), like taste-ness (*rasatva*) and so forth. || 24 ||
If it is argued that sound is an action because it perishes very quickly, like upward throwing and so forth, the author says in response:
"The cessation of that which exists as a quality is its similarity to actions. (25)

Apavarga (liberation) is rapid destruction; and although it possesses the nature of a quality, it is dependent upon the occurrence of a cause for its immediate destruction—just like duality and so forth—and thus it shares only a similarity with karma, but does not possess the very nature of karma. The point is that the reason you have stated, "being subject to extremely rapid destruction," is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of [the existence of] the cognition of duality, pleasure, pain, and so on. || 25 ||

Now, let it be granted that sound is a quality; nevertheless, it is not a mark (liṅga) for the existence of space. For space would only be inferred if sound were its effect. However, since this [sound] is indeed eternal, its occasional non-perception must be due to the absence of a manifestor. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because there is no mark for that which exists" (sato liṅgābhāvāt). || 26 ||

For if sound were existent prior to or after its utterance, then there would be another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) as a mark for that which already exists. However, there is no proof for the existence of sound during the state when it is not being heard; therefore, this [sound] is strictly an effect (kārya) and not something manifested (vyaṅgya).
|| 26 || For the following reason as well, he says that it is not manifested:
"Because of its dissimilarity with eternal things" (nityavaidharmyāt) || 27 ||

A difference in nature (vaidharmya) is perceived between this sound and that which is eternal; for in the case of "Caitra speaks," Caitra, Maitra, and others—even if they are not directly perceived—are inferred by means of the speech. Furthermore, a manifestor such as a lamp is never inferred from its manifested object such as a jar. Therefore, the sense is that this [sound] is produced (janya) alone, and not manifested (vyaṅgya). || 27 ||
Having stated the refutation against its being something manifested (*vyaṅgya*), he now states the reason for its impermanence:
"And this [sound] is impermanent because of its cause" (28).

The remainder [of the argument] is: "because arising from a cause is observed. For sound is indeed perceived as manifesting from the conjunction of a drum and a stick, and so forth; thus, because it possesses origination, it is impermanent. Alternatively, the term "from a cause" (kāraṇataḥ) indicates the logical reason of "having a cause" (kāraṇavattva). || 28 ||
But is it not the case that the fact of sound having a cause is unestablished with respect to its own nature? To this he says:
"And it is not unestablished, because of modification" (sūtra 29).

It should not be argued that sound possesses a cause [i.e., is produced] because this is unestablished; for its modification is observed through states such as intensity and dullness, since a sound is perceived as intense when there is a forceful impact of the drum and stick, and as dull when that impact is dull. Indeed, the intensity and so forth of the manifested object do not depend upon the intensity and so forth of the manifestor. Thus, because it undergoes modification due to its cause, it is inferred that this sound is produced (janya) and not merely manifested (abhivyaṅgya). || 29 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that this is merely the power of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), such that it manifests [the sound] through states of intensity, dullness, and so forth? Indeed, it is simply the air struck by the drumstick and the like that becomes intense or dull and thus produces the corresponding cognition. To this, he says: "Because of the fault in manifestation" (sūtra 30).

In the theory of the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of sound, it would be a defect that things occupying the same location and perceivable by the same sense organ are manifested by specific manifestors (*vyañjaka*). Furthermore, such specific manifestation by specific manifestors is never observed among things of that kind. If this were not accepted here, then upon the manifestation of the letter *ka*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the manifestation of all letters.

If it is argued that even for those [qualities] residing in the same location—such as being a sentient being (*sattva*), being a human (*naratva*), and being a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇatva*)—a difference in their own nature is indeed observed, and that they are manifested by specific manifestors such as configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and birth (*yoni*), we say no; because they do not occupy the same location. For the space occupied by "sentient being-ness" is not the very same as that occupied by "human-ness" or "Brahmin-ness. (30)
For this reason as well, he states that [sound] is not something manifested:
"The production of sound results from conjunction, disjunction, and [another] sound. (31)

From conjunction, such as the conjunction of a drum and a stick; from disjunction, as when a bamboo is being split. In that regard, conjunction is not the cause of the first sound because it is absent [in the case of splitting]; therefore, the disjunction between the two halves of the bamboo is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), and the disjunction between the half and space is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*).

Furthermore, where a sound is produced at a distance, such as in a lute (*vīṇā*), the sound produced there arises through a process of succession (*santāna*) until it reaches the portion of space delimited by the ear-canal (*karṇa-śaṣkulī*); thus, sound is produced even from sound. || 31 ||
He adds another reason for impermanence:
"And because of its indicative mark (liṅga), sound is impermanent. (32)

The meaning is: sound consisting of phonemes (varṇa) is impermanent, because while possessing a genus (jāti), it is perceptible by the sense of hearing, like the sound of a lute and so forth. || 32 ||
Now, in order to refute the reasons stated by the proponent regarding permanence, he says:
"But because of the absence of two types of activity" (33).

The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude what was previously stated and is intended to clarify the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). It is observed that both the teacher and the student are engaged in teaching and studying; [if the Veda were momentary], such engagement would be impossible, leading to the undesirable consequence of its non-existence. For teaching is indeed a formal transmission (*sampradāna*); the Veda is transmitted by the teacher to the disciple, and this transmission is only possible if it remains stable.

If it is argued that teaching is not a formal gift (*sampradāna*) because an object such as a cow being given is perceived in the interval between the giver and the receiver, whereas the Veda and so forth are not perceived in the interval between the teacher and the pupil, [we reply: even in the case of the latter, it is perceived by the ear of a person standing in that interval.

Furthermore, the eternity of sound is established through repetition (*abhyāsa*). Just as the repetition of a stable form is observed in such expressions as "one sees the form five times," so too the repetition expressed in "the verse has been recited ten times" or "it has been recited twenty times" serves as proof for the stability of sound. Once its stability is established, since no cause of destruction is perceived, the sense is that—"It remains stable for such a duration; who then will destroy it later?"—and thus its nature culminates in eternity. || 33 ||
He states another reason for the eternity of sound:
"from the first sound" (prathamācchabdāt) || 34 ||

The meaning is that the triple recitation of the first and the last *sāmidhenī* verses—expressed in the injunction, "He recites the first three times and the last three times"—is impossible without stability. || 34 ||
He states another reason for the eternity of sound:
"And because there is agreement [on this point]. (35)

*Sampratipattiḥ* means recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); the meaning is "because of its existence" (*tadbhāvāt*), that is, because of the existence of that [recognition]. Since the specific type [of cognition], namely recognition, is already obtained from the word *pratipatti* itself, the prefix *sam-* indicates its truthfulness (*satyatva*). Thus, one utters that very same verse which was uttered by Maitra; one recites that very same *śloka* again and again; you state the very same words over and over; you speak now that very same sentence which was spoken by you last year or last month. By the force of such recognitions as "this is that very same letter *ga*," the permanence (*sthairyya*) of sound is established. || 35 ||
Refuting all these reasons, he says: "If there were multiplicity, [the reasons] would be doubtful. (36)

The meaning is that they are doubtful and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). As it has been said: "Kāśyapa declared that the contradictory, the unestablished, and the doubtful are not valid logical marks (*aliṅga*). And likewise, since study, practice, and recognition are observed even where there is multiplicity and diversity, the reasons are inconclusive.

For instance, one says: "He studies dance," "he practices dance," "he danced twice," "the very same dance that you performed last year, you are performing now," or "this man is doing the same dance that was performed by a single dancer"—because this is observed in the case of dance, and because you yourself do not admit the permanence of that specific action (karman). || 36 ||

[Objection: But how can there be such enumerations as "the mantra consists of fifteen syllables," "the mantra has eight syllables," "the mantra has three syllables," or "the *anuṣṭubh* has eight syllables," if syllables were impermanent, since their infinity would be possible due to the differences in pronunciation? To this he says:
"The absence of number [is established] in general. (37)

The meaning is as follows: "the state" (*sadbhāva*) of a number such as fifty refers generally to the universal (*jāti*) of *katva*, *gatva*, and so forth. Even though there is an infinity of *ka*-sounds and the like, those delimited by the universal of *katva* and *gatva* constitute the number fifty, three, or eight; the point is that this is just as the number nine, twenty-four, and so on, applies to substances, qualities, and the rest, despite their internal subdivisions being infinite.

Is it not the case that recognition itself—namely, "this is that very same letter *ga*"—is the proof of its stability? Nor is this recognition sublated by the cognition "this *ga* is intense" or "this *ga* is weak," which apprehends contradictory properties, because intensity and so forth are merely adventitious (*aupādhika*) in that case.

Nor should it be argued that there is no difference [in the sound] even due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); for then, would not a crystal gem—which appears as blue, yellow, and so on through contact with indigo, turmeric, and the like—also be manifold? Or would not a face, appearing in the form of long and so on in a sword, a jewel, or a mirror, also fail to appear as manifold? If you ask, "To what does this property of intensity belong? Is it a property of the *ākāśa* limited by the adjunct? we say no; it will be a property of the air (*vāyu*), a property of the sound-vibration (*nāda*), or a property of the resonance (*dhvani*). What is the point of such inquiry here? For you too must admit that properties such as high pitch (*tāratva*) are inherent, because the relationship of priority and posteriority (or higher and lower degree) cannot be established between them if they were merely adventitious properties like the *ka*-ness or *ga*-ness of phonemes.

It is not so. For even when there are contradictory cognitions such as "the letter *ga* has arisen," "the letter *ga* has perished," "the previously heard letter *ga* no longer exists," or "the clamor has ceased," this recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) does not cease; therefore, one must assume that its object is the genus (*jāti*). Otherwise, if this recognition were to grasp the stability of the individual (*vyakti*), the aforementioned contradictory cognitions would simply not arise. Furthermore, this [recognition] does not have the air (*vāyu*) as its object, because the properties of air are not within the range of the auditory organ.

Nor is it a property of *nāda*, for if *nāda* were simply air (*vāyu*), then the aforementioned defect would apply, as nothing else could be defined [to serve as its substrate]. Nor is it a property of *dhvani*, because even when the sound of a conch or similar object is not perceived, there is still the cognition of pitch (*tāratva*) and so forth in the letter *ga*. If, however, this [property] were inherent, there would be no confusion of universals (*jāti-sāṅkarya*), since it is admitted that this [property], which is pervaded by *gatva* and the like, is manifold.

Furthermore, in the case of sounds such as the letter *ga* produced by parrots, mainas, or humans, there exists a very clear manifestation of a difference in form; the same applies to those produced by women or men, and even to those produced by the distinction between female and male, since parrots and others can be inferred even when concealed behind a screen or curtain. This [difference] is not based on an experienced limiting condition (*upādhi*), as in the case of a woman appearing red because she is smeared with saffron. Nor is its being conditioned [by something else] established through reasoning, because there is no such evidence for such reasoning. This is the summary. || 37 ||
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the second chapter in the Śāṅkara commentary on the Vaiśeṣika Sūtras.
This second chapter is also completed.

Thus, having conducted an examination of external substances in the second chapter, [the author] now says the following to prepare the foundation for the examination of the self (ātman), following the order of the enumeration:
The objects of the senses are well-known. || 1 ||

The objects of the sense organs—smell, taste, form, touch, and sound—are each apprehended by a single external sense organ. In this context, the meaning is that once the definition of sound has been established by the statement, "Sound is that object which is apprehended by the ear," the definitions of the other objects, from smell up to touch, are established by implication.

For instance, that object which is apprehended by the sense of smell is odor (*gandha*); that object which is apprehended by the sense of taste is flavor (*rasa*); that object which is apprehended by the eye alone is color-and-form (*rūpa*); and that object which is apprehended by the sense of touch alone is tangibility (*sparśa*). In all these cases, the word "object" (*artha*) denotes the substratum (*dharmin*) as an existing entity; therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the universal of odor-ness (*gandhatva*) or to the absence of odor. Thus, the definition of odor is: being a member of a sub-class of quality (*guṇatva*) that resides in what is apprehended by the sense of smell.
The same should be stated for flavor and the others; consequently, there is no failure to include supersensuous odors and so forth. (1)
He states the utility of the examination of the self (*ātmaparīkṣā*) for the sake of establishing the existence of the sense organs and their objects:
"The establishment of the sense organs and their objects is the reason [for inferring] something other than the sense organs and their objects. (2)

"The cause is the mark (*liṅga*) of the distinct entity that is the self (*ātman*): [it is] 'that which is dependent upon the sense organs and the objects. This means that the mark of the self—which is a distinct entity from the sense organs, from the objects such as color-form (*rūpa*), and from those [objects] possessing such qualities—is [the cognition]. Although it is precisely cognition (*jñāna*) that is intended here as the mark, nevertheless, because the direct perception of color-form and so forth is more well-known than the [inference of] the sense organs and objects, its status as a mark is stated in that very form.

For instance, [the self] is established as being dependent upon something, because it is an effect, like a jar; or because it is a quality, or because it is an action. And that establishment is produced by an instrument, because it is an action, like the act of cutting. That which is the instrument of this establishment is the sense organ. And that [instrument] is employed by an agent, because it is an instrument, like an axe or similar tools. Thus, he upon whom this establishment depends—that which employs the instruments such as the olfactory organ and so forth—is the Self. (2)

[Objection: Surely the body or the sense organs may be the substratum [of consciousness], because their positive and negative concomitance with respect to consciousness is far more evident; what is the use of postulating another substratum? For instance, consciousness is a quality of the body, because it is an effect of that [body], just like its color and other qualities. The same should be said regarding its being a quality of the sense organs. Anticipating this objection, he says: "That is not a valid reason" (so 'napadeśaḥ). || 3 ||

An *apadeśa* is a logical reason (*hetu*), while that which appears to be such but is not is a fallacious reason (*tadābhāsa*). Thus, the meaning is that "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is a non-reason (*anapadeśa*) because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to cognitions produced by lamps and the like. || 3 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that what is intended by 'being an effect' is simply being an effect of that which is delimited by consciousness? And since in the case of lamps and the like, consciousness as a whole is not an effect, there is no deviation [from the rule]. Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Because of ignorance regarding the cause" (sūtra 4).

The meaning is that [the body] is devoid of knowledge because of the ignorance—meaning the absence of knowledge—of the hands, feet, and so forth, which are the causes of the body, or rather its constituent parts. For it is observed that the specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) of earth and the other elements are preceded by the qualities of their causes; thus, if there were knowledge in the causes of the body, it might be possible for it to exist in the body as well, but this is not the case. Now, one might object: "Let there be consciousness even in the causes of the body. This is not so, because it would entail the consequence of a lack of consensus (aikamatya).

For it is not observed that many conscious beings possess a single consensus; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that what was experienced by one hand would not be remembered when that hand is severed, because "one person does not remember what was seen by another. Furthermore, upon the destruction of the body, there would be the undesirable consequence that one would not experience the fruits of violence and other acts committed by it; for Maitra does not experience the fruit of a sin committed by Caitra. Consequently, there would be the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāni*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). || 4 ||

Now, one might object: "Since there is a manifestation [of the qualities] in a subtle form within the causes of the body, but in a manifest form within the body itself, it follows that the qualities of the effect are not preceded by those of the cause, nor is there any impossibility of their being of a single nature. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because of the cognition [of the qualities] in the effects" (sūtra 5).

For if consciousness were present in the atoms, which are the primary causes of the body, then it would also be present in the effects produced from them, such as jars and the like. Furthermore, since the specific qualities of earth are pervaded by their presence in all earthly things, consciousness would likewise exist in the effects, such as jars; yet consciousness is not perceived therein. This is the meaning. || 5 ||
Anticipating the objection that consciousness indeed exists even in objects such as a jar, albeit in a subtle measure, he says: "And because of ignorance" (6).

The meaning is that consciousness does not exist in jars and the like because it is unknown by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If one were to accept something that is beyond the scope of all means of valid cognition, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of having to accept even things such as a rabbit's horn; for indeed, consciousness is not known in jars and the like by any means of valid cognition whatsoever. || 6 ||

Now, it was argued that the presiding agent is inferred by means of the instruments such as the sense of hearing; however, that is incorrect. For there is neither identity nor origination from those [instruments] on the part of the self, and without these two, the establishment of an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) is impossible; and without invariable concomitance, there can be no inference. Therefore, he says: "That which is other than the cause is not a probans. (7)

The reason (*hetu*) must be something other than the probandum (*sādhya*), and not identical with the probandum, because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of its being indistinguishable from the probandum. Therefore, the meaning is that a reason not constituted by identity with the probandum is a non-reason (*ahetu*), i.e., a non-indication (*anapadeśa*). || 7 ||

Now, one might object: "Just as the self has no identity (*tādātmya*) with the sense organs such as the ear, so too there is no origination from them (*tadutpatti*), for it is not possible for the ear and other instruments to arise from the self in the manner that smoke arises from fire. To this, he says:
"For one thing is not the probans (*anapadeśa*) for another thing" (NS 3.1.8).

For, just as an effect such as smoke is a distinct entity from something like a donkey, it is likewise a distinct entity from its cause, such as fire. Thus, since there is no difference in their being distinct entities, the fact that smoke does not indicate a donkey but indicates fire alone is governed solely by a specific nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*). If that specific nature belongs to something other than the effect as well, then that too would indeed be a non-indicator (*anapadeśa*). Consequently, an effect whose specific nature is not intended [to be relevant] is a non-indicator.

And thus, the meaning is that [the opponent’s position] is merely a technical definition intended to delude their own disciples; for it is only identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) that constitute inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), as the latter finds its ultimate limit in those two alone, or because they share the same means [of proof], or because the apprehension of both depends solely upon the apprehension of those two. || 8 ||

Now, in order to clarify precisely the deviation of both [types of inseparable connection] from that [invariable concomitance], he says: "The non-conjoined, the inherent, the inherent-in-the-same-object, and the contradictory. (9)

The reason "skin is like the body because it is a body" is a case of conjunction (*saṃyogin*). For skin is defined as that which is co-nascent with a substance subject to growth and decay and serves as its covering; it is neither an effect nor a cause of the body, but merely arises simultaneously with it, like a fixed conjunction. Similarly, [the reason] "space is an inherent cause (*samavāyin*) because it is a substance possessing dimension, like a jar," is an example of inherence.

In this context, dimension (*parimāṇa*) is the property to be proven; it is established by means of a property inherent in space (*ākāśa-samavāyin*), namely its substantiality (*dravyatva*). Alternatively, the gradation of dimension must terminate somewhere, and by this fact, a specific dimension—atomicity (*aṇutva*)—is established. By means of that [atomicity], the atom (*paramāṇu*), which is its substratum, is inferred. However, the inference of space from sound and so forth, or of the self (*ātman*) from cognition and so forth, involves the inference of a cause through its effect alone, and thus has not been cited as an example here. || 9 ||
The author of the Sūtras provides an example of that which inheres in the same object: "An effect [is the mark] of another effect. (10)

An effect is the mark of another effect, namely touch; this is an illustrative example, for even that which is not an effect—such as the oneness of space—is a mark of the singular separateness of space. The same applies to its supreme magnitude. || 10 ||
He provides an example of a contradictory mark: "The non-existent [is the mark] of the existent. (11)

Rain that has not yet occurred is the mark (liṅga) of the actual conjunction of wind and clouds; likewise, the recitation of a mantra is the adversary of [the occurrence of] a thunderclap and the like. Thus, the non-existent and unarisen thunderclap and so forth are the mark of the actual recitation of the mantra. || 11 ||
He states another example of a contradictory mark: "The real [is the mark] of the unreal" (sūtra 12).

An existing phenomenon, such as a crackling sound, is the mark of a non-existent mantra recitation; likewise, an existing conjunction of wind and clouds is the mark of non-existent rain; similarly, an existing fire is the mark of the non-existent proximity of a magnet and so forth; in this manner, other cases are also to be inferred. || 12 ||
He cites another indicative mark:
"The past [is the cause] of the past. (13)

In some cases, there is an inference of an existing contradictory by means of an existing contradictory, as when, having seen a hissing snake, one infers a mongoose hidden in the thicket. For here, the hissing snake is an actual, existing entity, and the mongoose hidden in the thicket is likewise actually existing; thus, the meaning is that an existing thing serves as the mark (liṅga) for another existing thing. However, rain, wind, and the conjunction with clouds do not exist at the same time [as the lightning], nor do the cracking sound and the recitation of a mantra. || 13 ||
Now he states the purpose of the enumeration: "Because an instruction is preceded by what is well-known. (14)

"Established fact" (*prasiddhi*) refers to the pervasion (*vyāpti*) as it is being recollected; "indication" (*apadeśa*) is the statement of the reason (*hetu*). Thus, the reason—characterized by the pervasion being recollected—is expressed either by the reason-member (*hetvavayava*) or the application-member (*upanayāvayava*), and so there is the rule that "the indication is preceded by established fact. The implication is this: in the case of the inference previously stated regarding the existence of a presiding agent (the Self) through the instrument of hearing and so forth, or through the quality of cognition and so forth residing in its substratum, pervasion exists in every such instance. However, in the case where you have sought to prove that cognition is a quality of the body by using the reason "because it is an effect of the body," there is no pervasion.

Now, what is this pervasion (*vyāpti*)? It cannot be a relation that is non-deviant, because non-deviation—defined as the state of not being the locus of co-occurrence with the absolute absence of the probandum (*sādhyātyantābhāva*)—is unestablished in the case of purely positive inference (*kevalānvayin*), since even smoke and the like reside in the locus of some non-locus of the probandum. Nor can it be the state of not being the locus of the probandum, because that is impossible in the case of a purely positive inference; for even smoke resides in something that is a non-locus of a particular probandum.

Nor can it be "inseparability" (avinābhāva). For is that the non-existence of the reason in the absence of the probandum, or its existence when there is a concomitance with the probandum? If you argue that—in the case of smoke as well—because it is absent where there is no donkey and present where there is a donkey, a restricted negative concomitance and a restricted positive concomitance are intended; we reply: no, because the very nature of such a restriction is what remains to be defined.

Nor is there a relation in its entirety; for if that were a relation of the entire probandum with the probans, it would not exist even in cases such as smoke, which has an uneven pervasion (viṣamavyāpti). Alternatively, if it were a relation of the entire probans with the probandum, that too is untenable, because a single probandum cannot have a relation with the entirety of the probans.

Now, as for the claim that there is a relationship between the entire probandum and the entire probans, this too is untenable; for a relationship between the entire probandum and the entire probans is not possible anywhere, because the relationship exists only between individual instances of the probandum and the probans, and because [the probans] would fail to pervade in cases of unequal pervasion (*viṣamavyāpti*).

Nor is the relation intrinsic (*svābhāvika*). For an intrinsic relation would mean either its own state (*svasya bhāva*) or its very nature (*svam eva bhāva*). In that regard, if the meaning of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) were "being produced by that" (*tajjanyatva*), then there would be an under-extension (*avyāpti*) in the case of pervasion (*vyāpti*) characterized as inherence (*samavāya*). If the meaning of the secondary suffix were "residing in that" (*tadāśritatva*), even then there would be an under-extension regarding inherence, for inherence does not reside anywhere; furthermore, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is also not produced by the property of being a cause, such as smoke, and so forth.

Nor is the relation one that is non-contingent (anaupādhika), because the contingency (upādhi) itself is difficult to state; even if it were easy to state, it would be difficult to apprehend; and even if it were easy to apprehend, there would be the fallacy of circularity (anyonyāśraya). Furthermore, the property of being a pervader of the probandum while not being a pervader of the probans, and so forth, can only be apprehended through the apprehension of pervasion itself. Nor is mere relation pervasion. For although the relation of a deviant (vyabhicārin) instance may take the form of pervasion when it is qualified by specific places and times, knowledge of such a relation is not a necessary factor for inference; rather, it is the pervasion that is the object of the knowledge which serves as the cause of inference that must be defined.

Nor is pervasion (*vyāpti*) the co-presence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the probandum (*sādhya*) of that which is not the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in the locus of the probans (*sādhanavanniṣṭhātyantābhāvāpratiyogi*).
