For even fire is the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in the locus of smoke; indeed, there is no absolute absence of the fire on the mountain in the kitchen (*mahānas*) which possesses smoke. Furthermore, in cases such as "this is conjunct (*saṃyogi*), because it is a substance (*dravyatvāt*)," there would follow the fault of under-extension (*avyāpakatā*), since the absolute absence of conjunction is co-present with the probans.

If it is argued that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is "the co-existence with the probandum (*sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya*) of that which is not the counter-positive of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that is both contradictory to its own counter-positive and resides in the same locus as itself," [we reply: no, because the absolute absence of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) lacks contradiction with its own counter-positive. This is not so, for even the absolute absence of conjunction is indeed contradictory to its own counter-positive; otherwise, the postulation of a distinction between delimiters (*avacchedabheda*) would be useless. Indeed, a distinction between delimiters is not postulated for the sake of the subsistence of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*). Nor is pervasion "the state of not being the non-locus of that which is non-co-located with the probandum."

In the case of a purely positive (kevalānvayin) inference, the property of being non-locus of the locus of the probandum (sādhyavaiyadhikaraṇya) is unestablished, for that [property] consists in being the locus of what is not the locus of the probandum. Nor is pervasion (vyāpti) the state of possessing a nature that delimits the relation of something to another, because even "fire-possessingness" (vahnivattva) would then serve as the delimiter of the relation to smoke.

If it is argued that this [smoke-ness] is not such [a pervader] because it exists in a larger locus, we reply that even the delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka*) is admitted to exist in a larger locus; for smoke-ness (*dhūmatva*) also exists in a larger locus, as it resides in smoke hanging from the surface of the sky. If it is further argued that a qualification is therefore necessary to exclude that, then one must intend that only what is the delimitor of being-pervaded (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*) is intended as the desired delimitor of relatedness (*sambandhitāvacchedaka*); and in that case, there is the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

If it is argued that the definition—"the state of possessing a nature that delimits co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) for whatever [subject] has it" is also beset by the aforementioned defects, we reply: pervasion (vyāpti) is a relation that is non-contingent (anaupādhika). Non-contingency, however, is either (1) the co-occurrence with the probandum (sādhya) of everything that does not deviate from that which deviates from the [subject], or (2) the co-occurrence with the probandum of that which co-occurs with the absolute absence whose counter-positive is an absolute absence co-occurring with the [subject] itself.

The meaning of the two definitions is: "the co-presence with the probandum (sādhya) of that which is not pervaded by whatever pervades the probans (sādhana)," and "the co-presence with the probandum of that which is not pervaded by whatever pervades the probandum. Alternatively, it is the state of being a pervader of the pervader of the probandum; however, this is difficult to grasp through a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Precisely for this reason, there is a requirement for repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) and for logical reasoning (*tarka*) in that context. Or rather, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the co-presence with the probandum of that which is not the counter-positive of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that is co-present with the probans.

And the absolute absence intended here is one whose counter-positiveness is delimited by a generality such as "fire-ness" (vahnitva). Therefore, even though there is co-existence with the absolute absence of a fire belonging to a mountain in smoke belonging to a kitchen, there is no fault; for the cognition "there is no fire in that which possesses smoke" does not arise.

Substantiality (*dravyatva*), however, is indeed not co-located with the absolute absence of being a possessor of conjunction (*saṃyogitva*); for there is no such cognition as "a substance is not a possessor of conjunction. Even though individual conjunctions are non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), the universal property of being a possessor of conjunction (*saṃyogitvasāmānya*) is pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*), and it is precisely that which constitutes the pervader (*vyāpaka*). If it is objected: "But 'absence of conditionality' (*anaupādhikatva*) is the absence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), and a limiting condition itself is difficult to define," we say no; for a limiting condition is defined as that which, while pervading the probandum (*sādhya*), does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*). As it has been said: "When the probans possesses a limiting condition, that which lacks the limiting condition [in relation to the probandum] is the limiting condition."

[Objection: But surely this [reason] is not non-pervaded by an upādhi that pervades the probandum (sādhya) alone. For example, in the case "Air is perceptible because it is the locus of perceptible touch," the upādhi is "possessing manifested color" (*udbhūtarūpavattva*); and in the case "He is dark-complexioned because he is the son of Mitrā," the upādhi is "being produced from the cooking of vegetables" (*śākapākajatva*). For "possessing manifested color" does not pervade perceptibility, since it is absent in the self (*ātman*) and in perceptible qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karma*); nor does "being produced from the cooking of vegetables" pervade dark complexion, since it is absent in things that are dark—such as crows, cuckoos, clouds, and jambu fruits. [Reply: This is not so.

This is because what is intended [by the definition of an upādhi] is the state of not pervading the probans while pervading the established conclusion (sādhya) as it is finally determined (*paryavasita*). And the "finally determined" probandum is that which is delimited by a particular property such that the pervasion of the upādhi with respect to it remains unbroken; in the present case, being possessed of manifest color (*udbhūtarūpavattva*) pervades perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*) as delimited by the property of being an external substance, and this is grasped through positive and negative concomitance. [Furthermore, in the case of the argument regarding] the innate darkness of human beings, [the upādhi is shown] in the *Caraka*, *Suśruta*, and other texts with respect to the probandum as delimited by that [property].

This should be inferred in other cases as well, precisely because the state of being produced from the cooking of vegetables (*śākapākajatva*) has been determined to be the pervader (*vyāpaka*). Now, one might object: "This [state of being produced from the cooking of vegetables] is not what is denoted by the term 'limiting condition' (*upādhi*), for a limiting condition is a property that appears elsewhere [than its own locus], such as a hibiscus flower appearing in a crystal. Furthermore, in the case of a limiting condition with unequal pervasion (*viṣamavyāpta*), the property of that condition does not appear in what is intended as the probans (*sādhana*), because it lacks the state of being pervaded (*vyāpyatvābhāva*). True. The primary usage of the term 'limiting condition' applies only to those with equal pervasion (*samavyāpta*), such as the possession of fire produced from damp fuel; in other cases, however, the usage is secondary (*gauṇa*).

And its function (*guṇa*) is the indication of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). For whatever deviates from the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of something necessarily deviates from that [thing] itself; and since the probans (*sādhana*) deviates from the adjunct (*upādhi*), which is the pervader of the probandum (*sādhya*), it therefore deviates from the probandum. Alternatively, its function is the indication of the "unestablishedness of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*), because that which is not pervaded by the pervader of something is itself not pervaded by that [thing]. Or, its function is the raising of a counter-inference (*satpratipakṣa*), because the absence of the adjunct—which is the pervader of the probandum—from the subject (*pakṣa*) establishes the absence of the probandum. As it has been said: "Even if it falls away from the restriction of the probandum stated by the proponent, the adjunct must still be pointed out by the debaters."
[The definition] concludes by restricting [the scope] due to the equality of the grounds for being a defeater (*dūṣakatābīja*).

This [definition] is further elucidated by the absence of a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*) against sublation (*bādha*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*), as well as by unfavorable arguments (*pratikūlatarka*). As for the statement: "That [property] by whose deviation the probans (*sādhana*) deviates from the probandum (*sādhya*) is the *upādhi*," in that case, the instrumental suffix (*tṛtīyā*) does not denote the instrument (*karaṇa*), nor the cause (*hetu*), nor the manner (*prakāra*), nor the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Nor should it be supplemented with the phrase "by whose deviation, when known, the deviation of the probans from the probandum is known," because this would fail to include an *upādhi* that is unknown, and would fail to include an *upādhi* in cases where deviation is manifest.

However, [the property] consisting of "fitness" (*yogyatā*) is difficult to define, because it is impossible to point out a limiting condition (*upādhi*) without first establishing the presence of a deviation (*vyabhicāra*). As for "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*), although it is indeed covered by the definition of a limiting condition, it is not a true limiting condition because it is self-contradictory—just as "doubtful inconclusiveness" (*sandigdhānaikāntikatva*) is not a fault in the subject. For if there were no doubt in that case, there would be no status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*); and if there is the status of being a subject, then doubt is necessary, since doubtful inconclusiveness is thereby certain. The remainder should be sought in the *Mayūkha*. || 14 ||

Now, beginning the section on fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) for the purpose of distinguishing them from valid reasons (*hetu*)—both those already discussed and those yet to be discussed—he says: "That which is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), that which is non-existent (*asan*), and that which is doubtful (*sandigdha*) are non-indicative (*anapadeśa*). (NS 1.2.15)

"Unestablished" (*aprasiddha*) means that which is non-pervasive (*avyāpta*), whose pervasion is not grasped, or whose pervasion is inverted (*viruddha*). By this, the "unestablished due to lack of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*) and the "contradictory" (*viruddha*) are included. "Non-existent" (*asan*) means non-existent in the subject (*pakṣa*), that is, not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*). This occurs sometimes because of the absence of its own nature (*svarūpa*), and sometimes because of the absence of doubt or the desire to prove. "In the case of proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*). "Doubtful" (*sandigdha*) means that which generates a doubt regarding the two alternatives of the existence or non-existence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject.

And that doubt arises from the perception of a common property in some cases, from the perception of an uncommon property in others, and from the perception of the concomitance of the probans with both the probandum and its absence in the subject itself in yet others. The first is the common inconclusive (sādhāraṇānaikāntika); the second is the uncommon inconclusive (asādhāraṇānaikāntika); and the third is the non-exclusive (anupasaṃhārī). || 15 ||

In that regard, he states an example of the unestablished due to lack of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*): "Because it has horns, therefore it is a horse. (16)

In this case, having taken the body of a donkey as the subject (*pakṣa*), one who is deluded by the observation of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*)—thinking "this [donkey] is necessarily a horse because it has horns; for whatever is not a horse does not have horns, such as a hare, a jackal, a human, a monkey, and so forth"—employs the following argument. This is an example of the fallacies of unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*), unestablished nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), and contradiction (*viruddha*). || 16 ||
He illustrates the inconclusive [reason]:
"Because it has horns, therefore it is a cow"—this is an example of the inconclusive. || 17 ||

Where one establishes "this is a cow because it has horns" by taking a buffalo as the example, there the reason is inconclusive due to being common (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*). However, when one establishes "space is eternal because it is the substratum of sound," then this very reason is inconclusive due to being uncommon (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*). Likewise, [the reason] "sound is non-eternal because it is sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) is also exclusively inconclusive due to being uncommon during the stage when [the presence of the reason in the similar class] is not apprehended; but when the probandum is established in the subject itself through the application of a subverting argument (*bādhaka-tarka*) against the counter-example, then, at the stage of knowing its occurrence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), [it becomes a valid reason].

Since the subject (*pakṣa*) itself is indeed a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), it possesses a valid reason (*saddhetu*). Among these, that which is not established by way of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) while being pervaded (*vyāpta*) is the unestablished (*asiddha*). It is of three kinds: unestablished due to lack of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*), unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), and unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). Among these, the unestablished due to lack of pervasion is that whose pervasion has not been grasped; this occurs in two ways: because the pervasion exists but is not grasped, or because the pervasion is absent. Therefore, the absence of a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*) and so forth are varieties of the unestablished.

And this very [fallacy] is divided a thousandfold through the expansion of its varieties: the unestablished qualifier (*asamartha-viśeṣaṇa*), the unestablished qualified (*asamartha-viśeṣya*), the unestablished both (*asamartha-ubhaya*), the doubtful unestablished qualifier (*sandigdha-asamartha-viśeṣaṇa*), the doubtful unestablished qualified (*sandigdha-asamartha-viśeṣya*), and the doubtful unestablished both (*sandigdha-asamartha-ubhaya*). In all these cases, it is precisely the absence of proof (*siddhi-viraha*) that must be pointed out.

Herein lies the essential point: the probans (*hetu*) is of three kinds, distinguished as purely positive (*kevalānvayin*), positive-negative (*anvayavyatirekin*), and purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*). Among these, a property that resides in every possible subject (*dharmī*) is purely positive; for example, cognisability (*prameyatva*), nameability (*abhidheyatva*), being the object of a substantive (*viśeṣyatva*), being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*), and the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of eternal substances, perishable qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth. Indeed, there is no such thing where these properties are not found.

And thus, being coextensive with existence (*savargatva*) or not being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence constitutes "exclusive pervasion" (*kevalānvayitva*). There is no fault even if these [properties] reside in their own selves; as it has been said:
"In the case of occurrence, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the refuge, since neither difference nor non-difference [is the criterion]."

A reason whose probandum possesses only positive concomitance (kevalānvayin) is itself called *kevalānvayin*. For this [type of reason], there are four characteristics conducive to its capacity for proof (*gamakatva*): presence in the subject (*pakṣasattva*), presence in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*), non-sublation (*abādhitatva*), and absence of a counter-balanced reason (*asatpratipakṣitatva*). In the case of a reason possessing both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*), there are five [characteristics] including the absence from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣāsattva*); whereas for a purely negative reason (*kevalavyatirekin*), there are four, excluding the requirement of presence in similar instances. Thus, a reason that lacks even one of those characteristics which are conducive to its capacity for proof is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

Thus, the state of being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) consists in the absence of at least one of the two forms necessary for being a prover. Consequently, just as the certainty of the absence of one of these two forms obstructs inference, even doubt regarding it does so; furthermore, it establishes the lack of probative power in the proponent's reason. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that reasons which are purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) or purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) would become fallacious due to the absence of one of these two forms; for in the case of a purely positive reason, the absence from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), and in the case of a purely negative reason, existence in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), are not required as being useful for proving.

And thus, the fallaciousness of the unestablished-in-the-substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*), the unestablished-in-its-own-nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), and the partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*) arises from their lack of the property of existence in the subject (*pakṣasattva*). The fallaciousness of the unestablished-in-pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the common inconclusive (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) arises from the deficiency of the property of non-existence in the counter-subject (*vipakṣāsattva*). The fallaciousness of the uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) and the non-conclusive due to lack of co-presence (*anupasamhārī*) arises from the deficiency of existence in the similar instance (*sapakṣasattva*). The fallaciousness of the sublated (*bādhita*) and the countered-by-an-equal-force (*satpratipakṣita*) arises from their lack of being unsublated and lacking a counter-prover, respectively. Likewise, the incapacity of the reason to produce knowledge in the cases of being "possessed of a condition" (*sopādhika*) and being "unproven" (*aprayojaka*) also results from the absence of certainty regarding its non-existence in the counter-subject.

If fallacious examples—namely, those lacking favorable means of proof, those lacking both [favorable and unfavorable means], and those that are deficient—are considered defects by way of being fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), then it is because there is no certainty regarding their presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*). Even if they are considered fallacious examples independently, the gateway for that remains the very lack of certainty regarding the reason's presence in the similar class.

However, those [reasons] in which the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not shown, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not shown, the positive concomitance is shown in a contrary manner, or the negative concomitance is shown in a contrary manner, are deficient; they result in nothing other than the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "inopportune timing" (*prāptakāla*). Furthermore, self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), circularity (*cakraka*), and infinite regress (*anavasthā*), by undermining the ascertainment of pervasion (*vyāpti*), attain the status of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) precisely because they lack one of the two required forms: presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*) or absence from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣāsattva*).

In that system, the *savyabhicāra* (inconclusive) fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is that which generates a doubt regarding the two alternatives of the presence or absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*pakṣa*). The *viruddha* (contradictory) fallacious reason is that which results in the certain determination of the absence of the probandum in the subject. The *asiddha* (unestablished) fallacious reason is the lack of valid cognition regarding either the pervasion (*vyāpti*) or the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). As for *bādha* (sublation) and *satpratipakṣa* (counter-balanced), in the system of the followers of Kaśyapa (the Vaiśeṣikas), they are not independent [fallacies]. In that regard, *bādha* ultimately reduces to either an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) or an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*). Thus it has been said: "In the case of sublation, the reason is either not a property of the subject or it is inconclusive."

The *satpratipakṣa* (counter-balanced) reason also results in nothing other than the *anaikāntika* (inconclusive) and so forth, as it merely induces doubt regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other criteria in one of the two cases. However, the author of the *Vṛtti* states that the word "and" (*ca*) in the Sūtra—"That which is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), non-indicative (*anapadeśa*), non-existent (*asan*), or doubtful (*sandigdha*) is a non-indicative [reason]"—is intended to include both *bādha* (sublation) and *satpratipakṣa*. By this, he follows the very opinion of Gautama, namely: "The fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) are fivefold: the deviant (*savyabhicāra*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the counter-balanced (*prakaraṇasama*), the identical-to-the-probandum (*sādhyasama*), and the mistimed (*atītakāla*)."

However, because of statements such as "Kāśyapa declared that the non-reason (aliṅga) is the contradictory, the unestablished, and the doubtful," the true intent of the author of the Sūtras is that there are three types of fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa); the word "ca" (and), moreover, serves to include those already mentioned—this is the essential point. For fear of making the book too voluminous, I have not elaborated here; the detailed discussion should be sought in the *Mayūkha*. || 17 ||

Now he states the result of the analysis of fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa): "That which is produced from the contact of the self, the senses, and the objects is [the means of valid cognition] other than that. (18)

First, knowledge arises from the contact of the self, the sense organs, and their objects; and that [knowledge] is a mark (*liṅga*) of the self, being distinct from the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), meaning it is not fallacious (*anābhāsa*). For instance, knowledge is a mark of the self in two ways: either by the inference "knowledge must reside in something [as its substratum], because it is an effect, like color and so forth," or by way of recognition, such as "I, who saw [it], am the same I who touch [it]. In this regard, the fact that knowledge is an effect is not unestablished (*asiddha*), since it is designated as that which is produced.

It is not contradictory, because there is no contradiction here in the case of the "inference from general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). Nor is it inconclusive for that very same reason. Thus, by means of the properties of being an effect and being a quality residing in itself, cognition itself is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the self through the inference from general observation. Furthermore, recognition, by excluding those acts performed by different agents, culminates in the state of having a single agent. Moreover, even if consciousness were a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), the unification of cognitions would not be based solely on the relation of cause and effect; for otherwise, it would follow that the cognitions of a disciple and a teacher would also be unified.

If it is argued that the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādāna-upādeya-bhāva*) does not exist there [in the intellect], and yet it is that which effects the linking of cognitions (*pratisandhāna*), we reply: this is because being a material cause (*upādānatva*) is a property of substances (*dravyadharma*), and thus cannot possibly reside in a cognition; or, even if it were possible, since cognitions are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), the linking of what was previously experienced would be untenable. For no latent impression (*saṃskāra*) can be deposited by a preceding cognition into subsequent cognitions, since you do not admit the existence of any stable entity.

Furthermore, that which consists of a stream of momentary cognitions lacks the capacity for recollection at a later time or for the act of recognition (*pratisandhāna*). If it is argued that the continuum of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna-santāna*) is indeed distinct from the continuum of the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna-santāna*) and is the one who remembers and recognizes, then if that [continuum] is stable, our desired conclusion is proven. If, however, it consists of a stream of momentary cognitions, then the aforementioned fault remains unavoidable; for even there, no stable impression (*saṃskāra*) exists. Moreover, there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence apart from the active consciousnesses.

If it is argued that the very cognition "I" is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), let it be so; however, if the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṭtivijñāna*) were to appropriate only the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), then, in the absence of appropriation by the evolving consciousnesses, they would lack even the status of being a causal condition (*nimittatā*), because the status of being a causal condition is pervaded by the status of being an appropriating cause (*upādānatā*). If it is argued that let there be no status as a causal condition either, then their existence (*sattva*) is also lost, since the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*) is the defining characteristic of existence.

If it is argued that two streams are acquired together—one being the stream of active functioning (*pravṛtti-santāna*) and the other the stream of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*)—then what fault has been committed by the whole (*avayavin*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and so forth? For you yourself must admit their existence as subsisting in multiple loci (*vyāsajyavṛttitā*). Therefore, there is nothing inconsistent in the claim that the self, inferred as the substratum (*āśraya*) by means of cognition, establishes itself as stable through the process of recognition (*pratisandhāna*).

Alternatively, this sūtra—"That which is produced from the contact of the self, the senses, and the objects is distinct [from them]"—is presented in order to refute the Sāṅkhya position that eternal cognition cannot establish the self as its cause. The meaning is as follows: that principle of cognition (*buddhi-tattva*) which you speak of is indeed knowledge (*jñāna*); for *buddhi*, *upalabdhi*, and *jñāna* are synonymous terms. And since that [knowledge] arises from the contact of the self and so forth, it is indeed distinct from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as you have postulated.
Thus, the sense is that it serves as a mark (*liṅga*) of the self. || 18 ||

Having explained the inference regarding one's own self, he now states the inference regarding another's self: "And activity and cessation, being observed in one's own inner self, are the inferential mark for another. (19)

"In the inner self" (pratyagātmani) means in one's own self. Effort (pravṛtti) and cessation (nivṛtti), produced by desire and aversion, are specific types of volition; and from these two, bodily actions characterized as movement—which have the results of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful—are generated. Thus, having observed movement in another's body, [one infers]: "This movement is produced by volition, because it is movement, like my own movement. And that volition is produced by a self, or resides in a self, because it is volition, like my own volition. This is the inference for a supreme self (paramātman). || 19 ||
Thus ends the first daily lesson of the third chapter in the *Śāṅkara-vaiśeṣika-sūtropaskāra*.

The subject matter of the second daily lesson of the third chapter is the discrimination between valid reasons (*hetu*) and fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). Now, intending to proceed with the examination of the self (*ātman*), which is beyond direct perception, [the author], bypassing the order of enumeration, introduces the examination of the mind (*manas*), saying:
The occurrence and non-occurrence of cognition when there is contact between the self, the sense organs, and their objects, is the mark of the mind. 1.1.16.

He will state that the mind (*manas*) is the mark (*liṅga*) of the self (*ātman*). If the mind has already been examined as an instrument of cognition and as being corporeal (*mūrta*), then it is established that the self is that which impels the mind so that it connects with a sense organ capable of grasping a desired object from among the various organs; this is the purpose of skipping the [usual] sequence. The meaning is: when there is contact between the self, the sense organ, and the object, that sense organ with which the mind is conjoined results in the existence—that is, the production—of cognition, whereas when it is not conjoined, there is the non-existence—that is, the non-production—of cognition; that is the mind.

If it is argued that even in the case of the all-pervasiveness (*vaibhava*) of the mind, there is proof for its pervasiveness—such as "because it possesses the nature of being an instrument," "because it is the substratum of the conjunction that is the non-inherent cause of cognition (just like the self)," or "because it is entirely devoid of touch (just like space)"—it is not so. For if the mind were all-pervasive, then since it would be in contact with all the sense organs simultaneously, there would result only a single cognition produced by all the senses at once.

If it is argued that this is not so because of a contradiction with the effect, we say no; for the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) does not itself apprehend contradiction or non-contradiction, such that it would fear a contradiction between visuality and the state of being tasted. [Rather,] it would simply result in a variegated form, like a variegated color (*citrarūpa*). If it is argued that this indeed occurs in the case of eating a long *śaṣkulī* (a type of fried cake), we say no; for even there, a distracted perception (*vyāsaṅga*) is observed.

If it is asked, "In that case, how can there be the subsequent reflective cognition (anuvyavasāya) that 'I simultaneously perceive color, taste, smell, and touch'?"—it is not so, because this is merely an illusion of simultaneity regarding the five cognitions produced by the mind moving rapidly, which are actually presented through memory. If it is argued that "inattention (vyāsaṅga) also depends on the nature of the instruments," we say no, for the answer has already been given. If it is argued that "inattention is dependent on the desire to know (bubhutsā)," we say no, because if every desire to know were to depend on it, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of all objects being perceived at once when there is a desire to know everything.

Since even the desire to know (bubhutsā) has as its sole fruit the mere connection between the sense organ and the mind which apprehends the intended object, the mind is established as being atomic (aṇu) because otherwise the non-simultaneity of cognitions would be inexplicable. Consequently, the arguments for its all-pervasiveness (vaibhava) are sublated by the very means of knowledge that establish its nature as a subject. Furthermore, if the mind were all-pervasive, the localized nature of pleasure and the like—such as "there is pleasure in my foot" or "there is pain in my head"—would not occur; for it is a rule that pervasive effects arise only in the space delimited by their non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa).

If it is argued that pleasure and the like would nevertheless occupy the same location as the atom, we say no; for there is a rule that an omnipresent effect produced by a non-inherent cause must arise in the very location of that cause. And thus, since the cause—such as sandalwood paste—is delimited, there is no contradiction in its production occurring in a larger space. If you argue that even for me (the opponent), there must be conformity with the presence of the efficient cause, we say no; for that would entail the violation of the aforementioned rule. Furthermore, how could there be a conjunction of the mind with the omnipresent self? If you claim that this [conjunction] is unproduced (*aja*), we say no; for then it would follow that disjunction (*vibhāga*) is likewise unproduced.

If it is argued that both [conjunction and disjunction] are non-contradictory with respect to a difference in delimitation, we say no; for while the difference in delimitation of conjunction and disjunction depends upon their own causes, such a difference does not exist for those two which are unproduced (*aja*). This is the general direction of the argument. || 1 ||

Now, one might object: "The perception of pleasure and so forth is accomplished by an instrument because it is an action, like the perception of form"—by such inferences, or by the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions, the mind (manas) is established as an instrument; and since it is thus an instrument, how can its status as a substance and its eternity be established?
To this, he says: "Its status as a substance and its eternity are explained by [the case of] air. (2)

Just as a wind atom, inferred from its being a composite substance, is a substance because it possesses qualities and because it possesses motion, so too the mind, inferred from the non-simultaneous production of cognitions, is a substance because it possesses qualities; for it does not produce cognition without conjunction with a sense organ, such that it would lack the possession of qualities. Furthermore, the direct perception of pleasure and so forth has a sense organ as its instrument because it is a direct perception, like the direct perception of color and so forth; thus, the mind is established as being beyond the reach of the senses.

And since the nature of being a sense organ (*indriyatva*) consists in being the substratum of the conjunction of the mind (*manas*) with the internal organ that is the instrument of cognition, the substantiality (*dravyatva*) of the mind is established without effort. Furthermore, its eternality follows from its being non-dependent (*anāśritatva*); for there is no evidence for its being conceived as dependent upon anything else, and thus it is non-dependent. || 2 ||

Regarding the doubt as to whether [the internal organ] is one or many in each body, he states the decisive factor: "Because of the non-simultaneity of effort and the non-simultaneity of cognition, it is one. (Sūtra 3)

The phrase "to each body" is the ellipsis for "the mind. If there were many minds even in a single body, then there would be a simultaneity of cognitions and volitions. As for the view that many volitions arise simultaneously because one observes simultaneous actions in the hands, feet, and fingers of a dancer—that is incorrect, since such an occurrence is explained simply by the rapid movement of the mind; for it is not admitted that the qualities of the self (such as cognition) can exist simultaneously while in a state of non-destruction.

By this, the view that even in a single body there are five minds, and that when two, three, four, or five of them are in contact with their respective sense organs, two, three, four, or five cognitions are simultaneously produced, is refuted due to the consequence of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*). However, the appearance of simultaneity has already been established. Furthermore, the occurrence of two simultaneous cognitions—such as "the sugar is bitter"—due to the mind's connection with the tactile organ while being delimited by the gustatory organ, does not arise either, precisely because [simultaneous cognition] is a property of the instruments [of perception].

Even in the case of a lizard, a snake, or similar creatures whose hindquarters have been cut into two or three parts, the movement occurs in both portions either due to the blow of a sword or the like, or due to the rapid movement of the mind, or because at that very moment the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) causes the internal organs to be grasped [by the mind]. As for the claim that the mind is indeed a composite whole (*avayavin*), like a leech, and that the simultaneity or non-simultaneity of perceptions arises from its contraction and expansion—that is refuted by the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating such constituent parts. This is the general direction [of the argument]. || 3 ||
Now, demonstrating the purpose of skipping over [the intermediate topics] in order while continuing the remainder of the examination of the self (ātman), he says:

"Exhalation, inhalation, closing and opening of the eyes, life, the movement of the mind, the modifications of the other sense organs, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are the marks of the self. (4)

It should not be thought that consciousness alone is the mark (*liṅga*) of the self; for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and others are also marks of the self. To explain: the upward and downward movements—namely, inhalation and exhalation—of the wind moving within the body are impossible without effort, just like the lifting and lowering of a pestle or similar object. That whose effort these movements arise from is certainly the self. For it is not possible for the wind, which has the nature of moving horizontally, to undergo a reversal of its natural state without [the application of] effort.

Nor should it be argued that two winds moving in opposite directions would result in an upward motion like that of water; for if that were the case, there would only be upward movement and never downward movement, nor lateral movement in the case of a loud shout or the like. Furthermore, there exists someone who, through effort, impels the wind upward or downward. If it is asked how there can be upward and downward movements of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* during deep sleep, the answer is no; because even in the absence of the effort currently under consideration, another effort exists. That very effort is called the "life-source" (*jīvanayoni*) effort.

In this way, even the closing and opening of the eyes lead to the inference of a controller of the body. Thus it is said: first, blinking (*nimeṣa*) is the action that produces the conjunction of the two eyelashes; opening (*unmeṣa*) is the action that produces their disjunction. These two actions, occurring continuously without any visible cause such as a push or a blow, do not arise without effort (*prayatna*).
Just as the dancing of a wooden puppet occurs through the effort of someone, so too does the dancing of the eyelashes; therefore, one possessing effort is inferred.

In this way, vitality (*jīvana*) also serves as a mark of the Self. To explain: by the term "vitality," one indicates through secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*) the effects of vitality, such as the healing of growths, wounds, and fractures. Thus, just as a householder repairs a broken house or enlarges a small one, so too the presiding agent of the body—standing in the place of a house—effects growth and nourishment through food and the like, heals wounds with medicine and the like, and restores broken limbs such as hands and feet. And so, like a householder, the presiding agent of the body is established.

Likewise, the movement of the mind (*manogatir*) is also a mark of the self (*ātma-liṅga*). For it has been established in the preceding section that the mind is indeed corporeal and atomic. Furthermore, its application to a sense organ capable of grasping a desired object depends upon the direction of desire (*icchā-praṇidhāna*). Thus, one from whose desire and direction the mind is impelled is inferred to be the self, just as a child situated in a corner of a house moves a ball or a lac-ball back and forth within the interior of the house itself.

Now, one might object: the householder or child who causes a wooden puppet to dance is not something other than the body; what then is the example [for a self distinct from the body]? Furthermore, the body itself is the substratum of consciousness, because it is the locus of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). For there occurs a cognition in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the ego-sense, such as "I am fair" or "I am stout. As for the fact that one remembers what was experienced in childhood during youth or old age—if the body were different [at each stage], then memory would not occur, just as Caitra does not remember what Maitra experienced, according to the principle: "One person does not remember what another has seen."

In that case, let there be no recognition between Caitra and Maitra because they belong to different continua (*santāna*); however, even though there is a difference between childhood and youth, recognition will be established through the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) since the continuum is one. To this we reply: it would follow that a son could also remember what was experienced by his father.

If you argue that the perception of a difference in bodies is the subverting factor (*bādhaka*), then recognition would be impossible, because an adult perceives his own body precisely as distinct from the body of his childhood. Furthermore, in the case of a child who has not perceived a father, there is likewise an absence of the perception of a difference in bodies.

If it is argued that, because the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) appears through the commonality of the possessive sense (*mamakāra*) as "my body," the same must apply to the expression "my self" (*mama ātmā*), we say no; for in that case, the possessive sense is merely figurative. Just as in the phrase "the head of Rāhu," the genitive case is justified even when there is no actual difference [between the whole and its part]. Furthermore, the fruit of violence and other such acts would not accrue to the agent, since the body is something else [than the self]. Thus, for the materialist (*bhūtacaitanika*) who desires sin, there would be the fault of the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāna*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). This is the general direction of the argument.

Because of the transformation of another sense organ. For indeed, it is observed that after experiencing a particular taste accompanied by a particular form—such as that of a nāgaraṅga or a ciravilva fruit—a person who encounters such a fruit again experiences a flooding of saliva in the mouth, impelled by a longing for that taste.

And that [cognition of sourness] does not occur without an inference regarding the sour taste; that inference does not occur without the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*); that recollection does not occur without a mental impression (*saṃskāra*); that impression does not occur without the experience of pervasion; and that experience does not occur without repeated observation. Thus, this succession of cognitions, existing as cause and effect, is not possible without a single agent who traverses them. And so says the Sūtra of Gautama: "Because of the modification of another sense organ."

Pleasure and the rest should be regarded as indicators of the self (*ātman*), just like cognition itself. For instance, pleasure and so forth must reside in something; they must reside in a substance, because they are effects or because they are qualities, like color and other such properties. This inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), when assisted by the exclusion of other possibilities (*itarabādha*), establishes that they reside in a substance distinct from the eight [known] substances. Indeed, the proposition "desire is not resident in the eight [substances] beginning with earth, yet it resides in a substance" cannot be finalized without adopting the specific mode of being resident in a substance distinct from those eight.

However, where there is no initial application of sublation (*bādhāvatāra*), the probandum (*sādhya*) for the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) is "residing in a substance other than the eight substances"; such is the distinction. The claim that an inference must necessarily have the delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka*) as its qualifier is trivial; for only that which, without which the cognition would not be complete, serves as the qualifier in that context. Otherwise, in an inference such as "the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), being non-resident in an effect, must reside somewhere because it is a whole (*avayavin*)," an inference qualified by "not residing in an effect" would not arise. || 4 ||
Now, let it be granted that the self is stable; but on what grounds is it eternal, and on what grounds is it a substance? To this he says:
"Its status as a substance and its eternity are explained by [the case of] air. (5)

Just as there is no means of valid cognition for the conceptualization of parts in the case of an atom of air, and therefore its eternity [is established], so it is with the self as well. Just as an atom of air is a substance because it possesses qualities, so too is the self; this is the meaning. || 5 ||
He states the prima facie view: "In the case of [the cognition] 'Yajñadatta,' because there is no perception due to proximity, no perceived mark (liṅga) exists. (6)

If it is argued that when there is proximity, "this is Yajñadatta" is a matter of perception, [we reply] that in that case, there is no observed mark (liṅga) whose invariable concomitance (vyāpti) has been grasped through perception. Just as smoke, which is grasped as accompanying fire through perception, is an observed mark for fire, so too there is no observed mark that establishes the self; this is the meaning. || 6 ||

Now, one might object: "Even in the absence of a visible mark whose pervasion has been perceived through direct observation, there will still be an inference based on a mark known by general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*); for it is not the case that no inference arises from such a mark. Anticipating this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says again:
"And there would be no distinction [between your case] and that which is known by general observation. (Sūtra 7)

Even a mark perceived through general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*) exists, yet from that there can be no proof of the self (*ātman*) either as a self in itself or as a substance distinct from the eight substances; rather, by it only the fact that desire and so forth must have some substratum would be established, and that is not useful for the contemplation of the self. This is what he says: "Because of the lack of distinction" (7).

Anticipating the objection that, if so, scriptural passages such as "That which is free from evil is the Self" would be entirely purposeless, he himself says: "Therefore, [the Self] is known through scripture. (8)

The self (ātman) is established solely through scripture (āgama) and is not inferable, because there is an absence of any mark (liṅga) belonging to either the class of perceived objects (dṛṣṭasāmānya) or the class of objects known through inference from the general (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa). Therefore, the direct realization of reality (tattvasākṣātkāra) arises from the correct hearing of the Upaniṣads, and not through the mediation of reflection (manana). Thus, this system (tantra), which has reflection as its purpose, is not essential. For it is observed that in cases such as crossing a river infested with crocodiles, knowledge that brings about direct realization arises from mere instruction alone. Thus, having presented the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of these three sūtras, the proponent of the final conclusion (siddhāntin) says: "Because of the distinction [of the word] 'I', [the self] is not [known] through scripture alone. (Sūtra 9)

The self is established not only by the authority of mere names, but also through the following inference: the word "I" or the word "self" possesses a denotable object (*sābhidheya*), because it is a word, like the word "pot" and so forth. Now, one might object that its denotable object could simply be earth and the other elements; to this he says, "because of exclusion" (*vyatirekāt*). This means that the word "I" is excluded from, or differentiated from, earth and the other elements. This is the sense.

For there is neither designation nor cognition such as "I am earth," "I am water," "I am fire," "I am air," "I am ether," "I am time," "I am direction," or "I am mind. If it is argued that [such cognition] occurs with respect to the body, no; for that would entail its occurrence even with respect to another's body. If it is argued that it occurs with respect to one's own body, no; for "one's own" cannot be defined as distinct from the self, and because there is the cognition "my body," which indicates a relation of different substrates (vaiyadhikaraṇya).

[Objection: Is this not also merely an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), and since that does not terminate in a specific [object], it is indeed subject to the same refutation? [Reply: No; for in the word "I" (*aham*), the qualifier (*prakāra*) is simply "I-ness" (*ahantva*), which is identical to selfhood (*ātmatva*). Thus, by the force of the property residing in the subject (*pakṣadharmatābalāt*), "I-ness" terminates in its etymological ground (*pravṛttinimitta*); and since that is unique and not shared by anything else, the specific [self] is established. In this way, even from an inference based on general observation, the specific object is established when assisted by the absence of sublation (*bādhā*).

As for what was said—that "realization occurs from hearing alone; what is the use of this [other stage]?"—that is incorrect. For without reflection (*manana*), there can be no cleansing of the stain of lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) in that which has been heard; and without that, one lacks the qualification for meditative cultivation (*nididhyāsana*) regarding it; and without meditative cultivation, there can be no direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*) capable of uprooting false knowledge along with its latent impressions (*savāsanā*). Indeed, it is only through practice that a man tormented by desire suddenly attains a direct vision of his beloved.

The point is that neither verbal nor inferential knowledge has been observed to be capable of uprooting false cognition, as seen in cases such as the confusion regarding directions. Now, one might ask: "Even so, how can there be a grasp of convention (*saṃketa*) regarding the self, which is beyond the senses? For the grasp of convention—such as 'this is denoted by the word "pot"'—is observed only in relation to perceptible objects. Who says that the self is not perceptible? Rather, the self is grasped through the mind by means of the proximity of conjunction (*saṃyoga-pratyāsatti*). Otherwise, how could there be such cognitions as "I am happy," "I know," "I desire," "I exert myself," or "I am miserable"?

This [cognition] is not devoid of an object, nor is its object doubtful, because—unlike the cognition of "blue" and so forth—it possesses a determined object. Nor is it inferential, because it arises even without the knowledge of a logical mark (*liṅga*). Nor is it verbal, because it does not conform to the recollection of words. If it is argued that this is a semblance of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*), then [we reply]: in some cases, even an object that is not a semblance [of perception] may be [the content], for it will be explained that what is not cognized cannot be superimposed. || 9 ||
If this is so, what is the use of inference? Thus says the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī):
"If it is directly perceived that 'I am Devadatta,' 'I am Yajñadatta,'" [then there is no need for inference]. || 10 ||

The word "iti" expresses the mode of cognition. "Dṛṣṭam" (seen) ends in the suffix *kta* used in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*), and "anvakṣam" means direct perception (*adhyakṣam*). Therefore, the meaning is this: if there is already a direct perception consisting of the observation of the specific mode—"This is Devadatta," "This is Yajñadatta"—then what is the use of the effort of inference? For when an elephant is seen, people do not infer it by its trumpeting. || 10 ||
On this point, the proponent of the established view says:
"In the case of a mark (liṅga) that is perceived as being identical with the self, there is only a single cognition, because of its firmness, just like perception. (11)

When the self is seen—that is, when it has been apprehended by direct perception—and the causal complex for the inferential mark (*liṅga*) has arisen, there arises only a single cognition, one whose object is singular. By the term "cognition" (*pratyaya*), he indicates that all suspicion of error has been eliminated. Why is this so? He says: "Because of its firmness," meaning because its sharpness is established through the convergence of means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇasaṃplava*), which eliminates any doubt of its being otherwise. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Like direct perception. Just as, even when water is directly perceived from a distance, one may still infer it by the mark of cranes in order to confirm it.

As it has been said: "Those who delight in reasoning (*tarkarasika*) desire to know through inference even that which has already been determined by perception. The underlying intention here is as follows: even if the self (*ātman*) does indeed manifest at some time in perceptual consciousness, nevertheless, being eclipsed by other contradictory cognitions such as "I am fair" or "I am thin," it does not attain stability, like a cognition produced by a flash of lightning. In that case, another cognition arising from an unerring mark (*liṅga*) takes as its very object the same [self] that was the object of the previous cognition.

[The author] confirms this. Furthermore, the meaning is as follows: since the inquiry into the Self (*ātma-manana*)—enjoined by injunctions such as "it is to be heard and reflected upon" (*śrotavyo mantavyaḥ*)—is understood to be a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), one must necessarily engage in the inference of the Self out of a desire for such inference (*anumitsā*). This is because, in the absence of that [inference], meditative cultivation (*nididhyāsana*) would be impossible; and in the absence of meditative cultivation, there would be no direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), and consequently, no liberation (*apavarga*). The mention of the two cognitions, "I am Devadatta" and "I am Yajñadatta," is intended to indicate that the Self is something to be personally experienced (*pratyātmavedanīya*) by each individual. || 11 ||

Now, if the cognition "I am Yajñadatta" refers to the self, then the appearance of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the expression "Yajñadatta goes" would be untenable; therefore, he says:
"The cognition [of 'I'] with respect to the body occurs through metaphorical usage, as in 'Devadatta goes' or 'Yajñadatta goes'. (12)

For there exists the cognition "I am fair" or "I am stout," and there also exists the cognition of difference, "This is my body. In that regard, the experience and the linguistic usage of "Devadatta goes"—which involve a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with motion—are figurative, because the cognition "my [body]" is in accordance with reality.

Although Devadatta-ness is a genus residing in the body, and thus the expression "Devadatta goes" is primary and the cognition is indeed real, nevertheless, if the word "Devadatta" is applied to the self as delimited by that [body], it must be understood as figurative. || 12 ||
Here an objection is raised: "But the metaphorical application is doubtful. (13)

The word "tu" (but) indicates the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Since the cognition "I" is observed to apply to both the self and the body, there arises a doubt as to where it is primary (*mukhya*) and where it is figurative (*aupacārika*). || 13 ||

He provides the formal argument: "Because [the notion] 'I' exists with respect to the internal self (pratyagātman) and does not exist with respect to anything else, it is a perception of a distinct entity. (14)

The nature of being a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) consists in having as its object something other [than the self]. That cognition in which this occurs is a "direct perception of another object" (*arthāntara-pratyakṣa*). The meaning is this: because the cognition "I" exists with respect to the inner self (*pratyagātman*), one's own self, and does not exist with respect to another, i.e., another self, it is appropriate to conceive of it as primarily referring to one's own self, which is the "other object. If, however, it were primary with respect to the body, it would have to be produced by the external sense organs.

The body is certainly not an object of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), for this mental cognition "I" arises even without the operation of the external senses; since one cognizes "I am happy," "I know," "I act," or "I desire," the self, as qualified by its specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), is made an object of the mind. Nor is this [cognition] inferential (*laiṅgika*), because it arises even without the consideration of a logical mark (*liṅga*). Nor is it verbal (*śabda*), because it arises even without the apprehension of words.

Therefore, it is purely mental; the sense is that since the mind lacks independence with respect to external objects, it does not function in relation to the body and so forth. Furthermore, if it were present in one's own body, it would have to be present in another's body; and if it were present in one's own self, it would likewise have to be present in another's self. If this is objected, we say no, because another's self is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and its specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) are unperceivable, whereas [the self] is perceivable only by virtue of being assisted by specific qualities that are themselves perceptible.

This quality of being perceptible belongs not only to the self, but to substance in general; for a substance becomes perceptible only through the apprehension of its specific, suitable qualities. If it is argued that space would then likewise possess color upon the apprehension of sound, [we reply] that the same applies to the self, since the possession of color is the necessary condition for perceptibility only with respect to external substances. The word "pratyak" (internal/perceptible) denotes that which is excluded from others. || 14 ||
Again, he raises an objection:
"The notion of 'I' with regard to the perception of the body in the statement 'Devadatta goes' is merely due to metaphorical usage or self-identification. (15)

Egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) is the notion "I am. And that [notion] is "perceptible with respect to the body" (*śarīrapratyakṣa*), meaning that in which the body is the perceptible object. You have perhaps maintained that the usage or the notion—such as "Devadatta goes"—is merely figurative (*upacāra*). However, that figurative usage is based on false identification (*ābhimānika*); for this reason, notions and usages such as "I am fair," "I am thin," "I am fortunate," or "I am born again" cannot be reconciled with such figurative interpretation. This is the meaning. || 15 ||
He states the established conclusion:
"But metaphorical usage is subject to doubt. (16)

The word "tu" (but) indicates the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). The meaning is that although this [usage of "I"] is metaphorical (*aupacārika*) and based on identification (*ābhimānika*), there remains doubt even regarding the statement that the notion of "I" pertains only to the body. Thus, since the cognition (*pratyaya*) serves as a neutral witness (*kūṭasākṣin*) in both cases, one must strive to determine the distinction. When such an effort is made, because the notion of "I" is observed even by one with eyes closed, it must be understood to refer to an entity distinct from the body and beyond the range of the external senses.

If [the self] existed in one's own body, it would also exist in another's body; furthermore, it would not exist independently of the eyes. If it is asked how there can be grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in such expressions as "I am thin," "I am fat," or "I am happy," the answer is no, because the body can appear therein even as a delimiting adjunct (avacchedaka) of pleasure and so forth—just as in the expression "this thicket [resounds with] the roar of a lion. The mere sense of "I-ness" (ahantva), which is presented by the mind, is superimposed upon the body, just as in the expression "the body is hot" where the heat is conveyed by the tactile organ (tvagindriya). || 16 ||
Strengthening his established conclusion, he says:
"But knowledge is not the object [of cognition] due to a specific body, as in the case of Yajñadatta and Viṣṇumitra. (17)

The term "knowledge" (jñāna) indicates the quality of the self (ātmaguṇa), such as pleasure, pain, and so forth, which is fit [to be so designated]. Just as the bodies of Yajñadatta and Viṣṇumitra are mutually distinct, so too are knowledge, pleasure, and the rest distinct.

And thus, just as "this is Yajñadatta’s body," so too, when knowledge, pleasure, or the like has not arisen in Yajñadatta, [the cognition] "I am happy" or "I have a desire" takes that knowledge and so forth as its object. Since it is possible for his knowledge and the rest to be perceptible—just like his color and other qualities—by virtue of having his specific body as their object, [it follows that] such perception does not actually occur. Therefore, the point is that one must assert that the substratum of knowledge, pleasure, and so forth is indeed something other than the body. "Due to the distinction of the body" means due to the difference of the body.

And thus, having attained a different body, [the soul possesses] knowledge, but not [knowledge of] the object; here, the ablative case is used in the sense of "having reached" (lyablope pañcamī). || 17 ||

Surely the self is not perceptible, because it is a formless substance or a partless substance, like space. Thus, it must be said that the object of the cognition "I am thin" or "I am fair" is the body itself. Even though there are instances such as "I am happy," nevertheless, since pleasure and so forth appear without a [separate] substratum, it is more reasonable to assume their superimposition upon the body, just as heat and fragrance are perceived in water despite having no other substratum.

[This is] a superimposition (*samāropa*). However, one should not—on account of this [superimposition]—conclude that even the cognition of water has a different object than the well-known water; likewise, "I-ness" (*ahantva*) is real only in the body, while pleasure and so forth are sometimes superimposed upon it. Therefore, there is no cognition at all in the form of a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the self. To the objection that what must be postulated as the substratum of pleasure and so forth may be established by scripture (*āgama*), but there is no apprehension of it even there, he says: "Because of the non-deviation [of the term 'I'] from its primary and secondary [referents], like the word ['fire'], and because of the establishment of a distinction, [the self] is not [known] through scripture. (18) [This means: Just as the word "fire" applies primarily to the element of fire and secondarily to a person who cooks with fire, the term "I" applies primarily to the self and secondarily to the body. Since the term "I" does not deviate from these two referents, and since a specific [substratum] is thereby established, the self is not known merely through scripture.

This is the meaning: the cognition "I am happy" or "I am unhappy" is neither derived from scripture (*āgamika*), nor verbal (*śābda*), nor inferential (*laiṅgika*), because it persists even without the application of words or logical marks (*liṅga*). As for its being perceptual (*pratyakṣa*), the objections raised regarding its being formless (*nīrūpatva*) and partless (*niravayavatva*) apply only to external sensory perception, since in that case possession of color (*rūpavattva*) and existence in multiple substances (*anekadravyasattva*) are the necessary conditions; however, mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣatā*) occurs even without those.

Now, this might be so if there were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the self; however, that very thing does not exist. To this he says: "Because, as in the case of sound, a specific [substratum] is established through the non-deviation of its absence. Just as in the case of substances such as earth and the rest, the absence of sound is invariably restricted, and by that, a specific substratum consisting of ether (*ākāśa*), which is distinct from the eight substances, is established; likewise, because the absence of desire (*icchā*) from earth and the other [substances] is non-deviant, its substratum must also be something distinct from the eight substances.

But surely, even by this much, the self remains merely inferential and not perceptual; to this he says: "I" (*aham iti*). Regarding the phrase "by the primary and the fit": by the particle *iti* in "I," he indicates the form of the cognition. Thus, the cognition "I," which arises for one with eyes closed without any recourse to words or logical marks, must be accounted for by that which is primary—the possessor of "I-ness"—which is fit and established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not by the body and so forth, because desire is invariably concomitant with its absence [in the case of the body].

The phrase "upapādanīyam" (to be established) is to be supplied immediately after "mukhyayogyābhyām" (by means of the primary and the secondary). Regarding the many proofs for the Self, those that would have burdened the text have been omitted by me; they are to be sought in the Mayūkha. || 18 ||

Having concluded the chapter on the examination of the self (*ātmaparīkṣāprakaraṇa*), he now begins the chapter on the plurality of selves (*ātmanānātvaprakaraṇa*). In this regard, the sūtra of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣasūtra*) is as follows:
"There is a single self (*aikātmya*) because there is no distinction in the production of pleasure, pain, and cognition. (19)

The self is indeed one, even though there is a difference in bodies such as those of Caitra and others. Why? Because there is no distinction in the production—that is, the arising—of pleasure, pain, and cognition; for the arising of pleasure, pain, and cognition is precisely the same across the limitation of all bodies.

If there were another inferential mark (*liṅga*) that established a difference between selves, then the plurality of selves would be proven; however, such a mark does not exist. For example, although sound is produced in various specific locations, space is one and the same because there is no difference in the inferential mark of sound; time is one and the same because there is no difference in the inferential marks of cognitions such as simultaneity; and direction is one and the same because there is no difference in the inferential marks of cognitions such as "east" and "west. || 19 ||
He states the established conclusion:
"They are manifold because of their distinct arrangements. (20)

The selves are manifold. Why? Because of their distinct distribution (*vyavasthā*). Distribution means specific determination; for example, "one is wealthy, another is poor; one is happy, another is miserable; one is of high birth, another is of low birth; one is learned, another is a fool. This distribution, being untenable without a difference among the selves, establishes the plurality of selves.

Nor should it be argued that just as there is a fixed state for a single self despite the differences of birth, childhood, youth, and old age, so too would it be in the case of different bodies such as those of Caitra and Maitra; for in the case of different times, the superimposition of contradictory attributes is possible. || 20 ||
He states another means of valid cognition: "And by the power of scripture" (sūtra 21).

The scripture (*śāstra*) is the *śruti*, for it also establishes the difference between the [individual] self and the [Supreme] Self. Indeed, it is heard [in the scriptures]: "Two Brahmans are to be known," and likewise, "Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree," and so forth. (21)
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the third chapter in the *Upaskāra* commentary on the *Kaṇāda-sūtra* by Śrī Śaṅkara Miśra.
And so, this third chapter is completed.

Having established the enumeration (*uddeśa*), definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and examination (*parīkṣā*) of the nine categories beginning with earth, and desiring to refute the Sāṅkhya position that primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is the root cause, [the author], wishing to prove that atoms (*paramāṇu*) are the root cause and that they are included within the category of earth and the others, first states the general definition of eternity (*nityatva*).
That which has the nature of having no cause is eternal. || 1 ||

It is not [defined] as "having a cause" or "not having a cause," because that would merely be a grammatical refinement of the term. Thus, there is the exclusion of jars and the like. Nevertheless, since this definition would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), he says: "existent" (*sat*). This means "that which is connected with existence" (*sattāyogin*). The connection with existence for the categories of inherence (*samavāya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*) consists precisely in their inhering in the same object as existence (*sattaikārthasamavāya*). For other universals (*sāmānya*) and for existence itself, the connection with existence is simply being the object of the cognition "existent" (*sat-pratyaya*); and that cognition is based solely on the intrinsic nature of the thing itself—this is another matter.

Nor should it be said that the same should apply elsewhere as well, rendering existence (sattā) redundant; for it has already been stated that its establishment follows from the cognition of a commonality. || 1 ||
Having explained eternal generality, he now speaks with reference to the atom: "Its effect is the mark [of its existence]. (2)

The effect of that atom, such as a jar and so forth, is the *liṅga* (inferential mark). Accordingly, this is the Sūtra of Gautama: "The production of the manifest from the manifest follows from the authority of perception. Indeed, the process of parts and wholes is experienced; if it were without limit, then there would be no difference in magnitude between Mount Meru and a mustard seed, since both would be equally composed of infinite parts.

Nor should it be argued that the specific difference [in size] would depend on a specific accumulation of dimensions, because since there is no specific number [of parts], those two [dimension and accumulation] are also untenable. If it is argued that the limit [of the process] would be the dissolution (*pralaya*), that is not so; for if anything final were partless, dissolution itself would be impossible, since only the separation of parts and the destruction of parts cause the destruction of a substance. Furthermore, separation cannot be the limit, because it is impossible for it to have a single substratum. Therefore, the partless substance is the limit; that alone is the atom (*paramāṇu*).

Nor is the *trasareṇu* itself the ultimate limit [of division], because it is a visible substance (*cākṣuṣadravya*) by virtue of its possessing magnitude (*mahattva*) and being composed of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*). Furthermore, magnitude is the cause for visual perception only by means of its being composed of multiple substances; otherwise, magnitude itself would not exist, and what could then be the cause? Nor are the parts of the *trasareṇu* themselves atoms (*paramāṇu*), because they too must be inferred to possess parts due to their being the originators of a large substance, just like threads or potsherds.

Therefore, whatever is an effect-substance (kāryadravya) possesses parts (sāvayava), and whatever possesses parts is an effect-substance. Thus, since the state of being an effect ceases where it does from a certain part, the state of possessing parts also ceases there; hence, the existence of partless atoms (niravayavaparamāṇu) is established. This has been stated by the teacher Praśastadeva: "And that [substance] is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. || 2 ||
Now, he states the proof for the existence of form and other qualities in the atom:
"The existence of the effect follows from the existence of the cause. (3)

The meaning is that because the qualities of form and so forth exist in the cause, they exist in the effect; for the qualities of an effect are preceded by the qualities of the cause, as is observed in the case of jars, cloths, and the like. || 3 ||
Now, in order to refute those who maintain that everything is impermanent, he says:
"The term 'impermanent' constitutes a specific negation. (4)

The suffix *tasi* is used here after a word ending in the genitive case (*viśeṣataḥ*). (And thus: There would be a negation of a permanent particular only if there were no such cognition as "impermanent" and no use of the word "impermanent," because the negative particle (*nañ*) has the function of negating the meaning of the following word. Therefore, how could there be the term "impermanent" in the absence of the permanent? Yet it does exist; hence, it is established that the permanent exists. Alternatively, by the expression "the impermanent is not permanent," you must negate the permanent atom in this manner.

In this manner, negation is not established, because it is obstructed by the contradiction between proof and non-proof. Furthermore, the Sūtra should be interpreted thus: the letter *a* alone is a word expressing negation, according to the rule "the particles *a*, *mā*, *na*, and *no* are words expressing negation. Thus, "impermanent" means "not permanent. Negation is the very nature of the absence of affirmation; therefore, "not permanent" is the nature of the negation of the specific quality of permanence, and that [negation] is not possible—this is the remainder of the sense. || 4 ||

Is it not the case that the atom is not eternal because it possesses form, like a jar? In this way, the reasons such as possessing color and possessing taste should each be inferred. Furthermore, because of its simultaneous conjunction with six [other atoms], the atom must have six parts; and thus, because it has parts and because it is the locus of a non-pervasive conjunction. Moreover, if there is space within the atom, then it would possess parts by virtue of having cavities; if there is no space, then it follows that space is not omnipresent.

Furthermore, because it possesses shadow and because it possesses obstruction; moreover, the impermanence of the atom follows from the inference proving momentariness, such as "whatever exists is momentary," and so forth. If there is such a succession of inferences, how can it be said that the atom is permanent? To this he says:
"Ignorance" (avidyā). || 5 ||

Every inference concerning the impermanence of the atom is ignorance in the form of an error, because it originates from a fallacious appearance (*ābhāsa*). At first glance, there is sublation by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādha*); furthermore, due to the absence of any proof that sublates the contrary (*vipakṣabādhakapramāṇa*) in all cases, there is the fallacy of the unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*), and in some instances, the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the reason itself (*svarūpāsiddhi*). These and other points should be investigated in the *Samānatantra*. || 5 ||

Now, one might object: "If the atom exists, why is it not perceived by the sense organs? For you yourself have established that possessing color and possessing tangibility are the conditions for being perceptible by the senses. To this, he says: "Perception [occurs] because of largeness, because of having multiple constituent substances, and because of color" (VS 4.1.6).

In the case of a large substance—that is, one possessing largeness—the suffix *matup* denoting a quality is elided after the word "large" (*mahat*), which here denotes a dimension (*parimāṇa*). Regarding the phrase "because of having multiple substances": that which has many substances as its substratum is "multiple-substance-possessing" (*anekadravyavat*); the state of being such is "having multiple substances," and it is because of this that [the substance is perceptible]. If this were the case, then air too would be perceptible; therefore, it is said "and because of color" (*rūpāt*). It will be stated later that this refers to color that is manifested and not overpowered. The term "perceived" (*upalabdhi*) implies "by means of an external sense organ."

Thus, it is stated that the atom is not perceived because it lacks magnitude (*mahattva*). Furthermore, "possessing multiple substances" (*anekadravyavattva*) means either being dependent upon multiple substances or being the substratum of a magnitude that is contingent upon a plurality of constituent parts. Nor should it be argued that "possessing multiple substances" is already established by "magnitude" alone; for the reverse could also be possible.

If it is argued that the producer (*janaka*) is established as otherwise-accomplished (*anyathāsiddhi*) by the produced (*janya*), but not vice versa, we say no; for when the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the producer and the produced are apprehended simultaneously, there is no lack of proof [for the latter's status]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the staff and other such instruments are established as otherwise-accomplished by the act of rotating and so forth. If it is argued that the excellence of perceptibility at a distance is due to the excellence of magnitude (*mahattva*), we say no; for since the excellence of possessing multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*) is also possible there, there is a lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*).
