Furthermore, in the case of a spider’s web consisting of threads woven by insects, which measures four cubits or more and is not perceptible from a distance, the fact that it is perceived only by a monkey depends solely on the excellence (*utkarṣa*) of its possession of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*), because an excellence of magnitude (*mahattva*) resides in the web. Likewise, in the case of cloth and other objects composed of fine threads, even when there is an excellence of magnitude at a distance, one should observe that small-sized objects such as hammers and the like remain imperceptible. || 6 ||
There would also be the perception of that which is large and possesses color-inherence; therefore, he says:
"Even though air possesses substantiality and magnitude, it is not perceived due to the absence of the manifestation of color. (7)

By the term "color-constitution" (*rūpa-saṃskāra*), the inherence of color (*rūpa-samavāya*), the manifestation of color (*rūpa-udbhava*), and the non-overpowering of color (*rūpa-anabhibhava*) are intended. Therefore, although in the case of air the very same inherence of touch is the inherence of color, nevertheless, there is no [perception] defined by color there, because of the existence of the absolute absence of color (*rūpa-atyantābhāva*). Furthermore, in the visual ray (*raśmi*), there is no manifestation of color; and in the light of a torch at midday, there is no non-overpowering of color despite the presence of color-constitution; thus, these are not perceptible. In the same way, the absence of color-constitution should be inferred in the case of summer heat, baking earthenware, fire, gold, and so forth.

The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, states that "form and the formation of form" (*rūpaṃ ca rūpasaṃskāraśca*) is a case of eliding one of the identical words *rūpa*; thus, they say that because of the absence of form, air is not perceived, and because of the absence of the formation of form, the eyes and other [senses] are not perceived. || 7 ||

Thus, immediately after the section on the eternity of atoms, having concluded the section on the perceptibility of external substances through the introductory connection of the atom as a mark, and intending to proceed with the section on the perceptibility of qualities by way of that same introduction, he says:
"The perception of color arises from its inherence in multiple substances and from a specific quality of color. (VS 4.1.8)

A specific quality belonging to color is "color-specification" (*rūpaviśeṣa*); this consists of its being manifest, its being unoverpowered, and its being color-ness (*rūpatva*). From that, there is the perception of color. [Objection: But in that case, the color of an atom (*paramāṇu*) and a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) would also be perceived. To this, it is said: "because of inherence in multiple substances" (*anekadravyasamavāyāt*).

The term *aneka* (many) means "more than one," and *bhūyas* (many) means "numerous. Thus, that which has numerous substances as its substratum (*āśraya*) is called *anekadravya* (composed of many substances), such as a mote of dust (*trasareṇu*) and so forth. Due to inherence (*samavāya*) in such [substances], even jars and other objects—which are composed of two or more parts—are, by way of a traditional succession, indeed dependent upon many substances. Regarding taste, touch, and so on, the specific universal (*jāti*) residing in the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) such as color is precisely that which is subsumed under [the universals] such as "color-ness" (*rūpatva*).

[Objection: But in this way, the relation of priority and posteriority would likewise be untenable for whiteness, fragrance, coldness, pungency, and so forth; moreover, if one were to postulate a multiplicity of those [qualities] as being pervaded by that [property], there would be the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*), and the term *udbhava* (manifestation) would possess multiple meanings. [Reply: This is not so, because "manifestation" (*udbhava*) is simply the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of being a quality capable of being grasped by each of the external sense organs individually; and "non-manifestation" (*anudbhava*) is simply the absence of that limiting adjunct. Some maintain that manifestation is merely the absence of non-manifestation.

That [definition] is to be reconsidered, because it is impossible to establish "non-manifestation" (anudbhava) in this manner. If it is argued that non-manifestation is the state of being a specific quality beyond the senses (atīndriya-viśeṣaguṇatva), then it would follow that manifestation (udbhavatva) is simply the state of being a specific quality within the range of the senses (aindriyaka-viśeṣaguṇatva). If one asks what constitutes the delimitor of being within the range of the senses, the answer is the same. Furthermore, some maintain that there is only one universal (jāti) called "manifestness" (udbhūtatva) among specific qualities, and they argue that the impossibility of a hierarchical relationship (parāparabhāva) between universals residing in qualities does not constitute a fault. || 8 ||

Since for those [qualities] other than touch, being apprehended by an external sense-organ is conditioned solely by their co-referentiality with color (*rūpa*), he states—after having described the causal complex for the perception of color—that this same [complex] is extended to other cases:
"By this, knowledge regarding taste, smell, and touch is explained. (9)

"By that" means by the perceptual cognition of color (*rūpa*). Just as there is the apprehension of color due to a specific quality of color characterized by its not being overwhelmed and its being manifest (*udbhūta*), so too is there the apprehension of taste due to a specific quality of taste characterized by its not being overwhelmed and its being manifest; this should be applied similarly to the other [senses]. Furthermore, the inherence in multiple substances (*anekadravyasamavāya*) is to be extended [to all cases] by analogy.

Due to the non-manifestation of the sense organs of smell, taste, and touch, there is no perception of odor, flavor, or tangibility; for instance, odor and flavor do not manifest in stones and the like, since those two are perceived only in their ashes. Some maintain that while odor and flavor are indeed present in stones and such, they are simply not clearly perceived. Others hold that these are not perceived because of the non-manifestation of the form of the water-substance (āpyadravya) whose parts are divided. The same applies to flavor as well.

In hot water, color (*rūpa*) does not manifest because it is of the nature of fire (*tejas*), and its touch (*sparśa*) is suppressed. In expanded camphor, campaka flowers, and the like, there is non-perception because color, taste, and touch do not manifest. In gold and similar substances, color is indeed manifested, though its whiteness and brilliance are suppressed. Some maintain that even the color itself is suppressed; however, the mention of "gold" is used because of its association with other colors.

Furthermore, "overpowering" (*abhibhava*) is a non-apprehension caused by the apprehension of a stronger object of the same class, and not merely a connection with a stronger object of the same class; for since even a connection with a stronger object of the same class is itself defined by non-apprehension, it is non-apprehension alone that serves as the foundational condition (*upajīvya*). Nor is the stronger object of the same class the foundational condition simply by virtue of being the cause of non-apprehension, because non-apprehension—whether understood as the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of apprehension or its absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*)—is not caused by that [connection], and because the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of apprehension is absent therein.

If it is argued that, for you as well, non-perception caused by the perception of a stronger member of the same class is likewise untenable, let it be so; nevertheless, whether the member of the same class is strong or weak, or whether such a relationship exists, it is precisely perception and non-perception that are the determining factors. Thus, that alone is the meaning of the term "overpowering" (abhibhava). || 9 ||
[Objection: But surely gravity (*gurutva*) is also inherent in multiple substances and co-occurs with color (*rūpa*) and magnitude (*mahattva*); so why is it not perceived? [The author] replies:
"Because of its absence, there is no deviation" (sūtra 10).

Since that universal, such as *rūpatva* (the nature of color), lacks gravity (*gurutva*), gravity is not perceptible. [Objection: Even if *rūpatva* and the like were absent there, it might still be perceptible; therefore, he says "non-deviation" (*avyabhicāra*). This means that for each of the five universals, such as *rūpatva*, there is a non-deviation—that is, an absolute rule—regarding their being perceivable by a single external sense organ. The meaning is that wherever any one of the five [universals] beginning with *rūpatva* exists, there alone is the state of being perceivable by a single external sense organ, and this is due to the absence of anything other than those.

However, because the nature of gravity and the like is not clearly defined in the Sūtra, although Praśastadeva included it among the supersensible qualities, Vallabhācārya has stated that gravity is perceptible by touch.
Having thus described those [qualities] perceivable by each single sense-organ individually, he now states those perceivable by two sense-organs:
"Number, dimensions, separateness, conjunction and disjunction, priority and posteriority, and action—because of their inherence in substances possessing color—are visible. (11)

The absence of a compound (asamāsa) in these cases indicates their mutual independence, whether they are visible (cākṣuṣa) or tangible (spārśana). Although there is a dependence on magnitude (mahattva), it is not by way of dimensionality (parimāṇatva). The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of including viscidity (sneha), fluidity (dravatva), and velocity (vega). The term "visible" (cākṣuṣāṇi) also implies tangibility. Alternatively, the word "ca" itself may be construed with the phrase "and [they are] visible. Regarding "number" (saṅkhyā)—the plural number includes all numbers, beginning with unity (ekatva).

If it is argued that oneness is merely a generality (*sāmānya*) and not a quality (*guṇa*), then if it subsists only in substances, it would have a distribution neither less nor more than that of substantiality (*dravyatva*). If, however, it also subsists in qualities and actions, then it would have a distribution neither less nor more than that of existence (*sattā*).

If it is asked, "How then is there a cognition of unity and so forth even with respect to qualities and the like? [The answer is: It is by means of a superimposed unity; or rather, through the proximity of inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), there arises a correct cognition of unity. This very unity is eternal in eternal substances, while in non-eternal [substances], its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is the unity of the cause. However, duality and so forth are produced by a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). And this relative cognition consists in the apprehension of a collection of multiple unities upon the visual contact of two substances—whether of the same or different classes. || 11 ||
Intending only these as the limits of action, he says:
"In the case of formless things, they are not perceptible by the eye. (12)

It should also be understood that number and the other qualities, up to action, which reside in substance-devoid [substances], are not visible to the eye, nor are they tangible. They are not described as "imperceptible," for if that were the case, even the oneness of the self would not be perceptible. || 12 ||

Color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest are each perceivable by a single sense-organ; number (*saṅkhyā*) and the rest are perceivable by two sense-organs; pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest are mental (*mānasa*); and thus it follows that the two universals (*sāmānya*), existence (*sattā*) and quality-ness (*guṇatva*), are perceivable by all the sense-organs. To this he says:
"By this, [the perception] of quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and existence (*bhāva*) by all the sense-organs is explained. (13)

The very capacity for the apprehension of the individual is itself the capacity for the apprehension of the genus (jāti). The meaning is that if all individuals are apprehended by their respective sense organs, then it follows as a logical conclusion that the two genera—namely "quality-ness" (guṇatva) and "existence" (sattā)—are also apprehended by all the sense organs. || 13 ||

Thus ends the first daily lesson of the fourth chapter in the *Śāṅkara-Vaiśeṣika-sūtropaskāra*. In the second daily lesson of the fourth chapter, for the purpose of examining substances possessing touch, the author—having already examined the ultimate atoms which are the root causes—now speaks, desiring to examine those very substances possessing touch by way of their effects: [The sūtra: "Earth is that which possesses smell. (VS 4.1.1) [Commentary: Following the examination of the ultimate atoms, which are the primary causes, the author now intends to examine the substances possessing touch through their effects. He says: "Earth is that which possesses smell. By this, he establishes the definition of earth. Since smell is a quality unique to earth, its presence serves as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of earth. Thus, that substance in which smell resides is earth. This definition excludes other substances, such as water and the rest, from being classified as earth. Therefore, it is established that earth is the substratum of smell. Furthermore, since smell is observed to be of two kinds—agreeable and disagreeable—it follows that earth is also twofold: eternal and non-eternal. It is eternal in the form of atoms (*paramāṇu*), and non-eternal in the form of products (*kārya*). Among these, the eternal earth consists of atoms, while the non-eternal consists of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), triads (*tryaṇuka*), and so forth, up to the great earth. The production and destruction of these are explained by the same principles as those of the body and sense organs. Thus, the examination of earth is concluded. Now, the author proceeds to examine water. [The sūtra: "Water is that which possesses cold touch. (VS 4.1.2) By this, he provides the definition of water. Cold touch is the specific quality of water; therefore, that substance in which cold touch resides is water. This definition excludes fire and other substances from being classified as water. Thus, water is established as the substratum of cold touch. Furthermore, since cold touch is observed to be of three kinds—cold, warmer than cold, and extremely warm—it follows that water is also threefold: eternal, non-eternal, and mixed. It is eternal in the form of atoms, non-eternal in the form of products, and mixed in the form of bodies and sense organs. The production and destruction of these are explained by the same principles as those of the body and sense organs. Thus, the examination of water is concluded. Now, the author proceeds to examine fire. [The sūtra: "Fire is that which possesses hot touch. (VS 4.1.3) By this, he provides the definition of fire. Hot touch is the specific quality of fire; therefore, that substance in which hot touch resides is fire. This definition excludes earth and other substances from being classified as fire. Thus, fire is established as the substratum of hot touch. Furthermore, since hot touch is observed to be of two kinds—intense and mild—it follows that fire is also twofold: eternal and non-eternal. It is eternal in the form of atoms, and non-eternal in the form of products. Among these, the eternal fire consists of atoms, while the non-eternal consists of dyads, triads, and so forth, up to the great fire. The production and destruction of these are explained by the same principles as those of the body and sense organs. Thus, the examination of fire is concluded. Now, the author proceeds to examine air. [The sūtra: "Air is that which possesses touch not belonging to others. (VS 4.1.4) By this, he provides the definition of air. Touch not belonging to others means a touch distinct from the touches of earth, water, and fire. That substance in which such a touch resides is air. This definition excludes earth and other substances from being classified as air. Thus, air is established as the substratum of a touch distinct from the touches of earth, water, and fire. Furthermore, since such a touch is observed to be of two kinds—agreeable and disagreeable—it follows that air is also twofold: eternal and non-eternal. It is eternal in the form of atoms, and non-eternal in the form of products. Among these, the eternal air consists of atoms, while the non-eternal consists of dyads, triads, and so forth, up to the great air. The production and destruction of these are explained by the same principles as those of the body and sense organs. Thus, the examination of air is concluded. Now, the author proceeds to examine ether. [The sūtra: "Ether is that which possesses sound as its quality. (VS 4.1.5) By this, he provides the definition of ether. Sound is the specific quality of ether; therefore, that substance in which sound resides is ether. This definition excludes earth and other substances from being classified as ether. Thus, ether is established as the substratum of sound. Furthermore, since sound is observed to be of two kinds—articulate and inarticulate—it follows that ether is also twofold: eternal and non-eternal. It is eternal in the form of atoms, and non-eternal in the form of products. Among these, the eternal ether consists of atoms, while the non-eternal consists of dyads, triads, and so forth, up to the great ether. The production and destruction of these are explained by the same principles as those of the body and sense organs. Thus, the examination of ether is concluded. Now, the author proceeds to examine time. [The sūtra: "Time is that which possesses the qualities of priority and posteriority, simultaneity, and duration. (VS 4.1.6) By this, he provides the definition of time. Priority and posteriority, simultaneity, and duration are the specific qualities of time; therefore, that substance in which these qualities reside is time. This definition excludes space and other substances from being classified as time. Thus, time is established as the substratum of priority, posteriority, simultaneity, and duration. Furthermore, since these qualities are observed to be of two kinds—eternal and non-eternal—it follows that time is also twofold: eternal and non-eternal. It is eternal in the form of atoms, and non-eternal in the form of products. Among these, the eternal time consists of atoms, while the non-eternal consists of dyads, triads, and so forth, up to the great time. The production and destruction of these are explained by the same principles as those of the body and sense organs. Thus, the examination of time is concluded. Now, the author proceeds to examine space. [The sūtra: "Space is that which possesses the qualities of priority and posteriority, simultaneity, and duration, as well as distance and proximity. (VS 4.1.7) By this, he provides the definition of space. Priority and posteriority, simultaneity, duration, distance, and proximity are the specific qualities of space; therefore, that substance in which these qualities reside is space. This definition excludes time and other substances from being classified as space. Thus, space is established as the substratum of priority, posteriority, simultaneity, duration, distance, and proximity. Furthermore, since these qualities are observed to be of two kinds—eternal and non-eternal—it follows that space is also twofold: eternal and non-eternal. It is eternal in the form of atoms, and non-eternal in the form of products. Among these, the eternal space consists of atoms, while the non-eternal consists of dyads, triads, and so forth, up to the great space. The production and destruction of these are explained by the same principles as those of the body and sense organs. Thus, the examination of space is concluded. Now, the author proceeds to examine self. [The sūtra: "Self is that which possesses desire and aversion. (VS 4.1.8) By this, he provides the definition of self. Desire and aversion are the specific qualities of self; therefore, that substance in which desire and aversion reside is self. This definition excludes earth and other substances from being classified as self. Thus, self is established as the substratum of desire and aversion. Furthermore, since desire and aversion are observed to be of two kinds—eternal and non-eternal—it follows that self is also twofold: eternal and non-eternal. It is eternal in the form of atoms, and non-eternal in the form of products. Among these, the eternal self consists of atoms, while the non-eternal consists of dyads, triads, and so forth, up to the great self. The production and destruction of these are explained by the same principles as those of the body and sense organs. Thus, the examination of self is concluded. Now, the author proceeds to examine mind. [The sūtra: "Mind is that which possesses the qualities of desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition. (VS 4.1.9) By this, he provides the definition of mind. Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the specific qualities of mind; therefore, that substance in which these qualities reside is mind. This definition excludes self and other substances from being classified as mind. Thus, mind is established as the substratum of desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition. Furthermore, since these qualities are observed
Furthermore, that effect-substance consisting of earth and the other elements is threefold, being designated as body, sense-organ, and object. (1)

In this context, "body-ness" (*śarīratva*) is a specific limiting adjunct (*upādhi-bheda*) consisting in being a final composite whole possessing motion, which has as its non-inherent cause a conjunction with a self endowed with effort; it is not a universal (*jāti*), because the relationship of higher and lower universals (*parāpara-bhāva*) is untenable with respect to "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and other such categories. "Sense-organ-ness" (*indriyatva*) is the state of being the substratum of a mind-conjunction that is the cause of a cognition which does not produce memory; or alternatively, it is the state of being the substratum of a mind-conjunction that is the cause of cognition, while not being the substratum of manifested specific qualities other than sound. As for the ray of light from the eyes of nocturnal creatures, it is simply another kind of luminous matter (*tejas*).

Regarding the nature of the eye (*cakṣus*), however, one must add the qualification: "while not being the substratum of specific qualities produced by anything other than sound and color. But *indriyatva* (the state of being a sense organ) is not a genus (*jāti*), because the relationship of higher and lower generality (*parāparabhāva*) cannot be established with respect to [genuses] such as "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*). Furthermore, although "object-ness" (*viṣayatva*) consists in being a means of experience by virtue of being perceived—and that indeed consists simply in being the object of ordinary direct perception (*laukikasākṣātkāra*), which is common to substances, qualities, actions, universals, and absences—nevertheless, in accordance with the Sūtra, it should be understood as "being a substance that is an effect and the object of ordinary direct perception.
For the Sūtra states, "It is threefold," and thus object-ness is likewise not a genus. || 1 ||
Now, in order to refute the doctrine that the body consists of three or four elements, he says:
"Because the conjunction of perceptible and imperceptible [elements] is itself imperceptible, there exists no [body] composed of five [elements]. (2)

"Because of [the presence of] fragrance, moisture, digestion, structural arrangement, and the provision of space, [the body] consists of the five elements" (A.3.1.3). If the body were [composed of all five elements], it would be imperceptible; just as the conjunction of wind and trees—which are respectively imperceptible and perceptible—is itself imperceptible, so too the body would be imperceptible. This is the sūtra by way of an illustration. "That which consists of five [elements] does not exist"—the word "body" is to be supplied. However, moisture, digestion, and so forth belong only to the water and fire that serve as supporting factors (*upaṣṭambhaka*). The same applies to [the view that the body] consists of four elements.

[Objection: Let it be that [the body] consists of the three elements (*traibhautika*), because the three elements are perceptible. [Reply: No, because the production of something from heterogeneous elements has been refuted. This is because a single quality does not produce qualities in a composite whole (*avayavin*). Thus, if its production were from earth and water, then what is produced from them would be devoid of smell and taste; likewise, if from earth and fire, it would be devoid of smell, color, and taste; if from earth and air, it would be devoid of smell, taste, color, and touch—and so on, as should be inferred. || 2 ||
He states this very point:
"And because no other qualities manifest, it is not composed of three natures. (3)

Even if a body were composed of earth, water, and fire—which are themselves perceptible—it might still be perceptible provided that some other quality (guṇāntara) appeared therein as preceded by the qualities of its causes; however, this is not the case, because it has been stated that a single quality such as odor cannot be a producer [of another]. Thus, the meaning is that the body is neither composed of three elements, nor is it even possessed of color, as it is not produced from the three elements [air, ether, and mind] which lack that property. || 3 ||
How then is there the perception of cooking and so forth within a single body? To this he says: "But the conjunction of atoms is not prohibited. (4)

The conjunction of the five elements with one another as mutual supporters is not denied; however, the conjunction of two atoms of different species is not accepted as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of a substance. Thus, it is through their support that cooking and other processes are perceived in the body. If so, what is the material cause (*prakṛti*) of this human body? On this point, the sūtra of Gautama applies: "It is earthy, because its specific qualities are perceived" (Nyāya Sūtra 3.1.31).

Odor, which is a specific quality of earth, is observed in the human body to persist until death; however, qualities such as heat from digestion are not perceived in a dried-up body. Thus, while those qualities are adventitious, odor is natural; this establishes the earthly nature [of the body]. || 4 ||
He analyzes the body:
"In that regard, the body is of two kinds: born from a womb and not born from a womb. (5)

Among those bodies composed of earth, water, and so forth, the earthly body is of two kinds. To the question "What are these two kinds?", he says: "born from a womb (yonija) and not born from a womb (ayonija). Bodies composed of water, fire, and air—which are well-known in the worlds of Varuṇa, Āditya, and Vāyu—possess exclusively the quality of being not born from a womb. Not being born from a womb means not depending on the union of semen and blood. And [bodies] not born from a womb belong to the gods and the sages; for it is heard in scripture: "Manu and others were the mind-born sons of Brahmā."

If it is asked how there can be an effect in the absence of a cause, [we reply that] the womb is not the cause with respect to the delimitation of being a body, because of the deviation in the case of bodies produced from heat, such as worms and mosquitoes, and because the possession of a specific configuration is unestablished, since the bodies of those like us are of a different nature than the bodies of celestial sages. Furthermore, that which is born from a womb is of two kinds: viviparous and oviparous.

The viviparous (*jarāyuja*) consists of humans, domestic animals, and wild beasts, because their womb is covered by a placenta (*jarāyu*); the oviparous (*aṇḍaja*) consists of birds and reptiles, because they have the habit of crawling all around; snakes, insects, fish, and so forth are indeed also reptiles. Although trees and the like are also distinct types of bodies because they serve as the locus for experience, for certainly, without being a locus for experience, there cannot occur life, death, dreaming, waking, the application of medicine, the persistence of similar seeds, or the encounter with favorable and unfavorable circumstances.
The healing of growths, wounds, and fractures, as well as the attainment of enjoyment, are indeed manifest; there is also a scriptural tradition (āgama):
"The *sarala* and *arjuna* trees growing on the banks of the Narmadā attain the supreme goal through contact with the waters of the Narmadā."
And so forth;

"In a cremation ground grows a tree frequented by jackals, vultures, and the like," and so on. Nevertheless, because the possession of movement and the possession of sense organs are not clearly evident in trees (*udbhijja*), they do not receive the designation of a "body. || 5 ||
He states the cause for the production of a body not born from a womb:
"Because it does not have a specific direction or location as its antecedent. (Sūtra 6)
Atoms, whose directions and locations are not fixed, perform actions produced by a specific quality (dharma); because they are preceded by those [actions], non-maternal bodies come into existence.

Now, one might ask: how can there be a conjunction of atoms—which is the non-inherent cause of a substance—without action? Or, how can the production of a substance occur without conjunction? To this, he says: "And from a particular dharma."

The meaning is that at the beginning of creation, motion arises in the atoms solely from the conjunction of the Self with the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); by means of that motion, the atoms, having come together through the process of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, originate the non-womb-born bodies of gods and sages. This is also an illustration; it should be understood that from a particular kind of demerit (*adharma*), the agonizing bodies of small creatures born from heat, such as mosquitoes and the like, are produced. || 7 ||
Regarding the bodies of the divine sages (*devarṣi*), which are not born from a womb, he states another means of valid cognition: "And because of the existence of traditional designation" (Sūtra 8).

The designation is etymologically significant and is well-known in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, Purāṇas, and other texts. For instance: "Durvāsas and others were mind-born; from the ego-principles (ahaṃkārāḥ) Aṅgiras was born," and so forth. Thus, it is understood that there are bodies for gods and sages that are not born from a womb. || 8 ||
He states another means of valid cognition: "Because of the primacy of naming" (sūtra 9).

The meaning is that at the beginning of creation, by that primary and initial designation "Brahmā" and so forth, it is known that there exists a body not born from a womb; for at that time, Brahmā has no mother or father by whom the designation "Brahmā" and so forth could have been made. || 9 ||
It is established that there are beings not born from a womb. || 10 ||
The ellipsis is "specific types of bodies. || 10 ||
To provide further corroboration for what has been established and to ensure its extreme firmness, he states another means of valid cognition: "And from the indicative mark of the Veda" (sūtra 11).

The Veda is the *mantra*, and that which is characterized by the Veda—meaning that by which [the truth] is indicated or made known—is the *Brāhmaṇa*; the meaning is that from that [Brāhmaṇa] one attains a body not born from a womb (*ayonija*). For instance, the Brāhmaṇa says: "Prajāpati created many offspring; he performed austerity, thinking, 'May I create offspring. He created the Brāhmaṇa from his mouth, the Rājanya from his arms, the Vaiśya from his thighs, and the Śūdra from his feet. The Veda also says: "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya was made from his arms."

"From his thighs the Vaiśya was born, and from his feet the Śūdra arose," and so forth. Thus, the earthly body has been described as being both womb-born (*yonija*) and not womb-born (*ayonija*). However, the watery, fiery, and airy bodies are exclusively not womb-born, because semen and blood are invariably earthly in nature, and because that which belongs to the water-element cannot originate [directly] from what is earthly.

The olfactory sense-organ (*ghrāṇa*), however, is earthen; it is common to all living beings and is composed of earthy constituents that are not overwhelmed by water and the other elements. The nose is earthen because, while not manifesting taste and so forth, it manifests odor, just like the cry of a cock which manifests the scent of musk. Similarly, the gustatory organ (*rasana*) is watery because, while not manifesting color and so forth, it manifests only taste, just like water which manifests the taste of flour-paste.

Thus, the eye is composed of light (*taijasa*), because, while not manifesting taste and so forth, it manifests only color, just like a lamp. Or, the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*) is composed of air (*vāyavīya*), because, while not manifesting odor and so forth, it manifests only tactile sensation, just like the breeze from a fan that manifests the coldness of water clinging to the body.

The object of the earth element (*pārthiva*) is characterized by clay, stone, and immobile things (*sthāvara*). Among these, the regions of the earth, walls, bricks, and the like are modifications of clay; mountains, gems, diamonds, red ochre, and so forth are stones; and grasses, medicinal herbs, trees, shrubs, creepers, spreading plants, and forest giants are the immobile things. The objects of the water element (*āpya*) consist of rivers, oceans, snow, hailstones, and so forth. The object of the fire element (*taijasa*), however, is fourfold, distinguished as terrestrial, celestial, digestive, and mineral. Terrestrial fire originates from wood fuel; celestial fire has no fuel and includes lightning and the like.

The internal [fire] is that which resides in the stomach and is capable of digesting food and other substances; the mineral [fire] is gold and the like. The objective domain of air (vāyu), however, is air itself, which is the substratum of the perceived touch. The fourth effect of air is that which is called *prāṇa*; though it is one, it receives the designations of *apāna* and so forth due to differences in its functions, being the cause of the propulsion of the bodily fluids, waste products, and constituent elements within the body. || 11 ||
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the fourth chapter in the venerable Śāṅkara’s Vaiśeṣikasūtropaskāra.
And this fourth chapter is completed.

The examination of action (*karmaparīkṣā*) is the subject matter of the fifth chapter. The examination of action accomplished through effort (*prayatna*) is the subject matter of the first daily lesson (*āhnika*). Within that, there are: the section on upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), the section on upward throwing accomplished without effort, the section on action caused by merit (*puṇya*), and the section on action that is neutral with respect to merit and demerit (*apuṇyapāpa*). With reference to a specific type of movement (*ceṣṭā*), he says:
"Action in the hand [arises] from conjunction with the self and from effort" (VS 5.1.1).

Conjunction and effort constitute "conjunction-effort. From the conjunction of the self and effort, action arises in the hand, which is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). For that action, the conjunction of the self possessing effort is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and effort is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). This alone is "volitional action" (*ceṣṭā*), because it is an action whose non-inherent cause is the conjunction of the self possessing effort; or alternatively, it is an action produced by an effort belonging to another who possesses a touch distinct from one's own and not inherent in oneself. || 1 ||
Having described the upward motion of the hand, he now states that the upward motion of the pestle depends upon it:
"And from the conjunction with the hand, there is motion in the pestle. (2)

By the word "ca" (and), he includes gravity (*gurutva*) as another efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). "In that manner" (*tathā*) means of the same nature as throwing upward (*utkṣepaṇa*). Alternatively, it means "from the conjunction with the hand," just as there was a throwing upward from the conjunction with the hand. In this case, the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) is the conjunction of the pestle with the hand, which is itself conjoined with the self possessing effort; the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) is the pestle; and effort and gravity are the efficient causes. || 2 ||
Regarding the sudden upward flight of a pestle that has been struck by a mortar, he states the cause:
"In the case of motion produced by impact, such as in a pestle and the like, the conjunction with the hand is not the cause, because it is absent [in that specific instance]. (3)

In this case, although there is indeed a conjunction of the hand with the pestle as it flies upward, that conjunction is "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha); rather, the impact against the mortar (*udūkhala*) alone is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of the negative concomitance" (*vyatirekāt*). This means because of the deviation from effort (*prayatna*). The sense is: if there were effort at that time, the pestle would not fly up spontaneously; rather, the pestle would either be held up by a counteracting effort or its upward flight would be dependent upon volitional action (*ceṣṭā*). || 3 ||
In order to refute that conjunction is a non-inherent cause, he says: "Likewise, conjunction with the self [is not the cause] in the action of the hand. (4)

The meaning is that, regarding the action of the hand as it flies up together with the pestle, its conjunction with the self is likewise not the cause—meaning it is not the cause because it is a conjunction with the self that possesses effort. The term "not the cause" from the preceding sūtra is extended here by the word "likewise. || 4 ||
From what, then, does that upward motion in the hand arise? To this he says:
"From the impact, [that is] from the conjunction with the pestle, there is action in the hand. (5)

Just as when the pestle rises, the iron [weight] situated at the mouth of the pestle rises, so too does the hand rise at that time. Here, by the term "impact" (abhighāta), the impression (saṃskāra) produced by the impact is expressed through figurative usage (upacāra).

By the extremely intense action of the rising mace, assisted by the impact, a momentum (*saṃskāra*) is produced in its own substratum, the mace. Depending upon that momentum produced therein, and taking the conjunction between the hand and the mace as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), an upward motion occurs in the hand as well. However, that upward motion of the hand is not caused by a conjunction with the self possessed of effort (*prayatnavad-ātman*) as its non-inherent cause; for the point is that the hand rises involuntarily along with the mace. || 5 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that when an action arises in the body or in a limb of the body, the cause is the contact of the self with something possessing effort (*prayatnavadātmasaṃyoga*)? Why is it not so in the present instance? To this, he says:
"From an action of the self and from contact with the hand" (6).

The word "self" (*ātman*) refers here to a limb of the body by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). The impossibility of [the literal] connection (*anvayānupapatti*) is itself the seed for this metaphorical usage. Thus, the action of the self—which is also a limb of the body, namely the hand—arises from the conjunction of the hand and the pestle; the word "and" (*ca*) serves to include velocity (*vega*). In the case of the action of the hand, the conjunction of the hand [with the self] is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), so there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that regard. Furthermore, in some cases, it is the conjunction of the self, which possesses volition (*prayatnavat*), with the hand; in other cases, it is the conjunction of the hand with a pestle or similar object, which possesses velocity (*vegavat*), as in the case of the action of a limb belonging to one who is possessed by a spirit (*vātula*). This is the intended meaning. || 6 ||
He begins the section on actions not dependent on effort:
"In the absence of conjunction, falling occurs due to gravity. (7)

By the term "conjunction" (saṃyoga), he indicates merely an obstructing factor. Therefore, in the absence of such an obstruction, falling—a motion resulting in downward conjunction—arises from gravity as its non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa). In that regard, in the case of fruits and the like which possess gravity, the obstructing factor is conjunction; in the case of birds and the like, however, the counteracting effort (vidhāraka-prayatna) is the obstructor of falling; and in the case of a discharged arrow and the like, momentum (saṃskāra) itself is the obstructor of falling. The meaning is that in the absence of these [obstructors], falling occurs due to gravity and so forth.

When poison and the like are suspended in the atmosphere through intense meditation and other means, the cause of obstruction is either the contact of the self with unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) or the mantra itself; these too are included under the term "contact" (saṃyoga). || 7 ||
Now, if falling occurs due to gravity, then how could a clod of earth or similar object, when thrown, move upwards in some cases and sideways in others? To this, he says:
"Due to the absence of a specific impulse, there is neither upward nor sideways motion. (8)

Furthermore, the upward or oblique motion of a clod of earth, a stick, and so forth, even though they possess weight, is due to a specific impulse—that is, from a more intense impulse. Thus, in the case of a fruit, a bird, an arrow, or the like, where there is falling in the absence of conjunction, effort, and momentum, there is no specific impulse; therefore, the point is that there is neither oblique nor upward motion. || 8 ||
Now, one might ask: from what does this particular impulse arise? To this he says:
"A particular impulse arises from a particular effort. (9)
From a specific kind of impelling, there arises a specific kind of upward throwing. || 10 ||

The specific effort caused by the desire "let me throw [it] obliquely, upwards, far, or near" produces a specific impulse (*nodana*). From that, the upward and oblique motion of a heavy substance such as a clod of earth is established. Throwing upwards (*udasanam*) is the act of tossing something to a distance. || 9 || 10 ||

The action that arises in the hand together with the pestle due to the striking of the mortar is not preceded by conscious effort (*prayatna*), nor is it a cause of merit or demerit; therefore, he extends this same principle to the movement of a child’s hands, feet, and so forth in play—“By the action of the hand, the action of the child is explained. (11)

The meaning of this extended application (atideśa) is that although a child’s movement of hands, feet, and so forth is indeed preceded by effort, it does not result in the attainment of what is beneficial or harmful, nor is it a cause of merit or demerit. || 11 ||
Now, extending by analogy the similarity to the actions of a child even in the case of an action preceded by conscious effort where there is no causality for merit or demerit, he says:
"Likewise, in the bursting of a blister. (12)

When a house is being set on fire by some assassin (*ātatāyin*), and a person therein is burnt and suffers an eruption caused by the fire, the action produced in the hand or other limbs through an effort conducive to the killing of that assassin is neither a cause of merit nor a cause of sin. As they say: "In the slaying of an assassin, no fault whatsoever accrues to the killer; whether done openly or in secret, it is fury that meets fury."
The incendiary, the poisoner, the one with a weapon in hand, the thief of wealth, and the robber of land or wife—these six are assassins (ātatāyin). 12.
Now he states those actions which occur without effort:
"In the absence of effort, there is movement of one who is asleep. (13)

The phrase "of one who is asleep" indicates a state characterized by the absence of consciousness; therefore, in this context, one should observe that even for one who is unconscious yet alive—such as one who has fainted—there is movement caused by the vital air (vāyu). || 13 ||
Having explained the actions pertaining to the body, he states the others: "The action of grass [is] from conjunction with air. (14)
By the word "grass," he indicates everything including trees, shrubs, creepers, and spreading vines. || 14 ||
Enumerating action as dependent upon the unseen (adṛṣṭa), he says:
"The movement of a jewel and the gliding of a needle are caused by the unseen. (15)

By the word "jewel" (*maṇi*), he indicates [objects such as] bronze (*kāṃsya*) and so forth. When that consecrated jewel, bronze, or other object moves toward a thief, in that movement the jewel and so forth are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); the conjunction of the thief’s self with the jewel, characterized by the presence of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭavat*), is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); and the thief’s demerit (*pāpa*) is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Regarding "the needle's gliding": by the word "needle," he indicates iron in general as well as grass.

Likewise, regarding the movement of a needle or similar object toward a magnet, the needle and so forth are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). The contact of that [needle] with the soul possessing unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭavat-ātman*), due to which that grass, needle, or other object moves, is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). That very unseen merit or demerit is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Other cases should be inferred in the same way. For example: the upward flaming of fire, the horizontal movement of air, and the action of atoms at the beginning of creation. || 15 ||

Now, regarding the doubt as to whether the action in an arrow, a bird, a row of firebrands, a wheel, and so forth, remains one and the same until its cessation or whether it is multiple, he states the reason for the determination:
"The specific conjunctions occurring at non-simultaneous intervals are the cause for the difference in action" (1.1.6).

In the word *iṣau*, the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhy-arthe*). This is the underlying intention here: for arrows and the like moving with velocity, it is observed that the cessation of motion occurs immediately after contact with a wall or similar object, even while the arrow itself still exists. In this case, the destruction of the substratum cannot be the cause of that [motion's] destruction, because the substratum is still present. Furthermore, no other opposing quality (*guṇa*) is perceived; therefore, it is inferred that the conjunction produced by the action itself is what destroys the action. And that conjunction, having arisen in the fourth moment, destroys the action in the fifth moment.

For instance, there is first the arising of action, then the separation, then the destruction of the prior conjunction, then the subsequent conjunction, and finally the destruction of the action. Therefore, the meaning is that these specific conjunctions occurring at non-simultaneous moments serve as indicators of the diversity of actions. Regarding the phrase "specific conjunctions" (*saṃyogaviśeṣāḥ*): the "specificity" (*viśeṣa*) in conjunction consists precisely in its being produced by the action itself; otherwise, if every conjunction in general were the destroyer of action, no action would ever persist anywhere. || 16 ||
Immediately following the section on actions produced by impulse (*nodana*), he begins the section on actions produced by latent impressions (*saṃskāra*):
"The first action of an arrow is due to impulse; from that action is produced a latent impression, and from that [impression] subsequent actions follow, each after the other. (17)

When an arrow is impelled by a *patañjikā* (bowstring) drawn by human effort, its initial action (*karma*) arises; in this case, the impulsion (*nodana*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), the arrow is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), and effort and gravity are the instrumental causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). By means of that initial action, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) called velocity (*vega*) is produced, which resides in the same substratum as the action. That it moves by means of that velocity is indeed established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). By that latent impression, further action is produced in that arrow; here, the latent impression is the non-inherent cause, the arrow is the inherent cause, and the instrumental cause is a specific, intense impulsion.

And thus, as long as the momentum (*saṃskāra*) continues, a successive series of actions (*karmasantāna*) is produced; when an action is destroyed by its own resulting subsequent conjunction, another action is generated by that momentum. Therefore, it is shown that a single momentum is the generator of the series of actions, but a series of momenta—like a series of actions—is not fit to be admitted because of its complexity (*gaurava*). To demonstrate this, he says: "and so each subsequent [action]," and uses the singular number in the phrase "from that momentum which causes those actions."

In the Nyāya system, however, there is the burden of accepting a continuum of impressions (saṃskāra) as being like a continuum of karma. As for the case where two arrows are shot simultaneously, one having a swift velocity and the other a slow one, the cause therein is the intensity or mildness of the initial propulsion (nodana). || 17 ||

Now, if there were only a single formative impression (*saṃskāra*) that generates the continuum of action, then the fall of an arrow would never occur, because the formative impression that generates the action would still exist. To this, he says:
"The absence of formative impressions results in falling due to gravity. (18)

Weight, first of all, is that which persists as the cause of falling. And that weight, being obstructed by momentum (*saṃskāra*), did not produce falling. Now, the meaning is that in the absence of the obstructing factor, that very same weight produces falling. 18.
Thus ends the first daily lesson of the fifth chapter in the *Vaiśeṣikasūtropaskāra* by the venerable Śaṅkara.
The second daily lesson of the fifth chapter.
The section on the examination of action produced by impulsion and so forth. Regarding this, he says:
"Action in earth arises from impulsion, impact, and conjunction with that which is conjoined. (VS 1.1.30)

Impulsion (*nodana*) is a specific type of conjunction—that conjunction by which the action produced does not become the cause of mutual disjunction between the two conjoined objects, or that conjunction which is not the efficient cause of sound. That conjunction which is the efficient cause of sound and for which the action produced becomes the cause of mutual disjunction between the two conjoined objects is the specific conjunction called impact (*abhighāta*). By each of these two [impulsion and impact] as well, action is produced individually.

In the case of mud known as *paṅka*, action arises from the pushing and the striking of the foot upon the earth; therein, the mud is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the pushing and the striking are the non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) according to their respective roles, and gravity, momentum, and effort are the efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*) as applicable. [This occurs] "through conjunction with that which is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasaṃyogāt*); for when action arises in the mud due to pushing or striking, action is observed in the pot or other objects situated in that mud at the very same time. || 1 ||
Now, one might ask: in the case of earthquakes and the like, which arise without any prior impulse or impact, what is the non-inherent cause? To this, he says:
"That [earthquake] is produced by a specific [type of] unseen merit or demerit (adṛṣṭa). (2)

The word "tat" (that) refers to the action of the earth. If an action occurs specifically or intentionally upon the earth itself, then it is caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). In that case, regarding an earthquake, the conjunction of the unseen force with the self of the person who experiences pain or pleasure therein is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); the earth is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); and the unseen force is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Alternatively, "tat" refers to the exclusion of impulsion and impact (*nodanābhighāta*). "Specifically" (*viśeṣeṇa*) means "by way of distinction. Thus, the meaning is: that action which occurs in the earth in the absence of impulsion and impact is caused by the unseen force. || 2 ||
Now begins the section on the examination of action inherent in liquid substances. Regarding this, he says:
"In the absence of conjunction [with another], falling occurs due to gravity. (3)

The falling of water in the form of rain has gravity as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). That [falling] occurs when there is an absence of conjunction—namely, the conjunction with a cloud; therefore, the meaning is that the absence of conjunction is its efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). || 3 ||
How is it that those very raindrops produce an action resulting from their mutual conjunction? To this he says: "From fluidity, there is flowing" (4).

When drops of water fall upon the earth, through their mutual conjunction there arises a large form consisting of a stream of water-parts; the flowing or distant movement of that [stream] is produced from fluidity as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) and from gravity as its efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), within the waters which serve as the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*). || 4 ||
Now, one might object: if water situated on the earth moves upwards, then, due to its weight, it would be expected to fall down; why then does it rain? To this he says:
"The ascent [of water] occurs through the connection with the vital air (vāyu). (5)

The word "kārayanti" (they cause to rise) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The meaning is that those rays of the sun which are the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) cause the waters to ascend upwards. In some readings, the text says "nāḍyavāyusaṃyogāt"; this is to be explained as the conjunction of the wind with the channels—that is, the wind associated with the channels. || 5 ||
Now, one might ask: how can this be the greatness of the sun's rays, that they carry water situated on the earth upwards? To this, he says:
"Because of pushing, squeezing, and from conjunction with what is conjoined. (6)

By "impelling," that is, by the impulsion of a powerful wind, the rays conjoined with the wind and the waters conjoined with those rays rush upwards due to the pressure or the impact, just as water situated in a pot, when being boiled, is led upwards by the rays of fire driven by the wind. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "iva" (as if); in that context, the water situated in the pot is to be understood as the point of comparison. || 6 ||
Or rather, the solar rays do not prevail against obstacles; how then is that so? To this he says:
"The climbing of trees is caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa). (7)

*Abhisarpaṇa* (flowing toward) means moving toward; that *abhisarpaṇa* [is the action] of the waters poured at the root of a tree. That action, caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), produces the growth of leaves, stalks, fruits, flowers, and so forth. For those selves who possess pleasure or pain produced by that [growth], due to the conjunction with those selves—which serves as the non-inherent cause—and having the unseen force as the efficient cause, that action occurs in the waters, which serve as the inherent cause. By means of that action, the waters move upward and cause the tree to grow; such is the meaning. || 7 ||

Now, it might be objected: "The natural fluidity of water has been stated as its defining characteristic, and the upward, downward, and lateral movement of such waters has been established. Furthermore, the fact that snow, hail, and the like are water due to their coldness is established beyond dispute; so how can there be a solidification (*saṃghāta*) of them, and how can there be their melting? To this, he says: "Solidification and melting of water result from conjunction with fire. (8)

Due to the obstruction by divine power (*divya-tejas*), water-atoms (*āpya-paramāṇu*) initiating a binary compound (*dvy-aṇuka*) do not initiate fluidity (*dravatva*) within those binary compounds. Consequently, through a process beginning with binary compounds, snow, hailstones, and the like are produced from constituent parts devoid of fluidity; therefore, their solidity (*kāṭhinya*) is perceived. Now, one might ask: what is the proof for the watery nature (*āpyatva*) of snow, hailstones, and so forth? To this it is said: "And their melting occurs due to contact with fire."

Through conjunction with a powerful fire, an action arises in the atoms that constitute the snowflake; from that action comes disjunction, and from that, through a series of destructions of the originating conjunctions, there is the destruction of the large composite whole such as the snowflake. In that state, due to the cessation of the conjunction with the fire that was obstructing its fluidity, those very same atoms initiate fluidity within the dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). Thereafter, the melting of the snowflakes and other such things—which now possess fluidity—occurs, and in this process, the penetration of powerful fire is the efficient cause (*nimitta*). || 8 ||
Now, one might ask: what is the proof that there is an entry of powerful divine splendor (*divyatejas*) therein? To this, he says:
"In that case, thunder is the sign. (9)

In that context, regarding the divine waters, the "thunder" (*visphūrjathu*) is the sign of the entry of divine fires; the meaning is that the roar of the thunderbolt itself is the sign. An extreme flash of lightning is indeed directly perceived, and immediately following it, the thunder is also directly perceived. By this, it is inferred that the divine fire in the form of lightning has entered into the cloud from which hailstones emerge; through its support, there is an obstruction of the fluidity of the waters that constitute the hailstones.
Right here he states another means of valid cognition: "And that which is Vedic" (sūtra 10).

The meaning is that the entry of fire (*tejas*) into the midst of the waters is indeed established by scripture (*āgama*). For instance: "May the waters receive Agni as their embryo," and "Those waters which have received Agni as their golden embryo," and so forth. || 10 ||
Now, one might ask: how does a thunderclap arise, given that conjunction and disjunction are the sources of sound, and yet these two are not perceived? To this, he says:
"From the conjunction and disjunction of the waters of the rain-cloud. (11)

The word "visphūrjatha" (thunder) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Through water, the conjunctions and disjunctions of the thunderbolt (*stanayitnu*) act as the efficient causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), and from the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*)—which is the conjunction of that very thunderbolt with space (*ākāśa*)—they produce sound, namely the roar (*garjita*), in space, which serves as the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*). In some cases, however, the conjunctions and disjunctions of wind and clouds (*balāhaka*) are the efficient causes, while the conjunctions and disjunctions of the cloud and space are the non-inherent causes. Although this was introduced under the section concerning action as a cause, it has been stated here incidentally (*prāsaṅgika*).

Alternatively, it is indicated that in the case of the conjunction or disjunction of a cloud with space—which serve as the non-inherent causes of sound—the cause is simply the action produced by the impulsion or impact of water; for it is action alone that has attained the status of being the primary factor here. || 11 ||
By means of the action of earth, the action of fire and the action of air have been explained.

Regarding an earthquake, it has been stated that the conjunction of the self with the unseen force (*adṛṣṭavat-ātma-saṃyoga*) is the cause; likewise, in the case of a sudden conflagration of the quarters, the action that arises from fire as its cause, and the action of a wind-storm that causes the sudden agitation of trees and so forth—there too, the conjunction of the self with the unseen force is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), while air and fire are the inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), and the unseen force is the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). This is the meaning. The repetition of the word "action" (*karman*) is for the purpose of indicating the actions of great meteors and the like. || 12 ||
He states another type of action, which has as its non-inherent cause the conjunction of the self with the unseen (adṛṣṭa):
"The upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of air, and the initial actions of atoms and of the mind are caused by the unseen. (13)

"Initial" (ādyam) means occurring at the time of the beginning of creation. Since there is an absence of pushing, striking, and so forth at that time, the conjunction of the self with the soul possessing unseen merit (*adṛṣṭavat*) alone is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) therein. "Initial upward flaming" and "initial horizontal blowing"—it is appropriate to consider other actions of flaming and blowing as having speed (*vega*) as their non-inherent cause, because when a visible cause exists, there is no room for the postulation of an unseen one. || 13 ||
Concerning the beginningless mind (*manas*), he says: "The action of the mind is explained by [the analogy of] the action of the hand. (14)

Just as the action of the hand in raising a pestle and so forth has the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) of the conjunction of the self with that which possesses effort, so too the action of the mind directed toward the sense organ for the sake of contact with the intended object must likewise have the non-inherent cause of the conjunction of the self with that which possesses effort. Although the sense organ—the mind—is not the direct object of effort, the production of action in the mind should nevertheless be understood to result from effort directed toward the channel through which the mind flows.

Furthermore, it must be admitted that the channels (nāḍī) are perceptible by the sense of touch; otherwise, even the intake of food, drink, and so forth, through the movement within the life-sustaining channels, would not be possible. || 14 ||
Is it not the case that there is no proof for the claim that action arises in the mind? To this he says:
"Pleasure and pain arise from the contact of the self, the sense organs, the mind, and the objects. (NS 3.2.15)

"Pleasure and pain" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa); knowledge, effort, and so forth should also be understood [as implied]. The all-pervasiveness of the mind has already been refuted, and its atomic nature (aṇutva) has been established; furthermore, it was stated that the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the inferential mark (liṅga) of the mind. Therefore, if there were no action (karma) in the mind, pleasure and pain would not occur at all without the mind’s conjunction with the respective locations of the sense organs. Consequently, there would be no such experience as "pleasure in my foot" or "pain in my head," and so forth—this is the meaning.

Although every specific quality of the self is dependent upon contact with the mind, pleasure and pain are mentioned [specifically] because they are extremely clear due to their intense velocity. || 15 ||

Now, if the mind is thus flickering, then because there would be no cessation of the mind (*cittanirodha*), there could be no realization of the Self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*) without yoga, nor liberation (*mokṣa*) without that; therefore, the commencement of the treatise would be futile. To this, he says:
"In the absence of its [the mind's] activity, when the mind is situated within the Self, the body's lack of suffering is conjunction. (16)

When the mind of one who is indifferent and has attained the conviction that sense-objects are insufficient turns away from the external senses and becomes established in the Self—resting solely upon the Self—then, due to the absence of effort corresponding to such activity, no action arises in the mind; the mind becomes exceedingly steady, and that indeed is Yoga, because Yoga is characterized by the cessation of the mind. "The non-commencement thereof" means the non-commencement of the mind's activity. Alternatively, by the word "that," pleasure and pain themselves are denoted, as they have been the subject under discussion.

Regarding the phrase "the absence of suffering": because it is the means for achieving the absence of suffering, yoga itself is the absence of suffering, just as in the expression "food is indeed life. Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is an absence of suffering," referring to the self as delimited by the body; since that [state] is established by common renown as yoga, the word "that" refers to it—this is that yoga. Or else, by the word "self" (*ātman*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is expressed here figuratively, because the self is inferred through the vital breath. And thus, through action upon the channel that carries the vital breath, the activity of the vital breath is also produced.

Alternatively, the action of the vital breath (prāṇakarma) has as its non-inherent cause the conjunction of the self and the vital breath, which is accompanied by the effort that is the source of life. This effort, which is the source of life, is supersensible and is inferred from the movement of the vital breaths; for otherwise, how could there be the coming and going of inhalation and exhalation even during the state of deep sleep? Such is the sense. || 16 ||

Now, if the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*) is caused by effort (*prayatna*), then when the vital breath and the mind withdraw from the body at the time of death—meaning they exit the body—and subsequently approach and enter it again upon the production of another body, both of those [processes] would be untenable due to the absence of effort. Furthermore, how could there be the arising of that activity which produces the conjunction that causes the growth of the body's parts through what is eaten and drunk, such as food and water, nor the activity that produces conjunction and disjunction during the state of dwelling in the womb? To this, he says:
Receding, approaching, the conjunctions resulting from eating and drinking, and the conjunctions resulting from other actions—these are caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa). || 17 ||

In this context, the neuter designation [in the rule] "napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyānyatarasyām" and the term "saṃyoga" are used figuratively (lākṣaṇika) to refer to the action that is the cause of that [conjunction].

Departure (*apasarpaṇa*) is the exiting of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind from the very body upon the exhaustion of the karma that initiated that body; arrival (*upasarpaṇa*) is the entry of the vital breath and the mind into another body when another body is produced; and the karma that is the cause of the conjunction with what is eaten, drunk, and so forth, as well as the other effect—the embryonic body—and the karma that is the cause of its conjunction—all these have the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) consisting of the conjunction of the self with the unseen force (*adṛṣṭavat-ātma-saṃyoga*). By the word "iti," [the author] indicates that even the processes of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), waste products (*mala*), and actions likewise have the conjunction of the self with the unseen force as their non-inherent cause.
17 | Now, if the necessity of the arising of another body is indeed required, then how can there be liberation? To this he says:
"In the absence of that [desire], there is the absence of conjunction and the non-manifestation [of a new body]; this is liberation. 18 |

The intended meaning here is as follows: when the direct realization of the reality of the self occurs through the power of yoga, and by that [realization] the ignorance along with its latent impressions (*savāsanā-avidyā*) is destroyed, then—due to the removal of the defects of passion, aversion, and delusion which are rooted in that [ignorance]—there is the cessation of activity; due to the cessation of activity, there is the cessation of birth which is rooted in it; and due to the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of suffering which is rooted in it. Such is the course of things.

In that regard, by the power of the dharma born of yoga, the yogin perceives the collection of dharmas which are the uncommon causes of pleasure and pain experienced through various bodies—such as those of horses, elephants, birds, and so forth—in specific places and times. Having manifested an array of such bodies, there occurs the exhaustion of previously arisen dharma and adharma through experience. For one whose defects have ceased, since no further dharma or adharma arises, no new body arises; the absence of the self's conjunction with the former body is itself liberation (*mokṣa*). Thus it is called "the absence of that [conjunction]."

The meaning is that there is an absence of conjunction due to the non-arising of future bodies. Now, one might object that this state is common to the dissolution of the universe (*pralaya*); therefore, he says: "non-manifestation. The meaning is that liberation (*mokṣa*) is that state after which there is no further manifestation of the body and so forth. The meaning is that liberation is the destruction of suffering that occurs in that state. || 18 ||

[Objection: But surely action is also observed in the substance darkness, since there is the cognition "the shadow moves. In that case, there is neither effort, nor impact or percussion, nor gravity or fluidity, nor momentum; thus another cause must be stated, yet it is not experienced. To this, he says: "Darkness is a non-existence (abhāva), because its properties are those of the production of substances, qualities, and actions. (VS 5.2.19)

By this, the restriction that there are exactly nine substances is also established. To begin with, the production of a substance depends upon a substance possessing touch; yet, no touch is perceived in darkness. Nor is it the case that the touch is merely unmanifest, because when color is manifest, the manifestation of touch is necessarily present.

If it is argued that there is this restriction regarding earth, and that darkness (*tamas*) is the tenth substance (*dravya*), we say no; for another substance cannot have blue color as its property, and blue color is invariably concomitant with weight (*gurutva*) and with taste and smell. If it is argued that just as space has sound alone as its specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*), so too darkness would have blue color alone as its specific quality, we say no; because that would contradict its being perceived by the eye (*cākṣuṣatva*).
For if darkness were blue color, or if it were merely a blue-colored object, it could not be grasped by the eye without the assistance of external light. || 19 ||
If that is so, what is the basis for the perception of motion? To this he says:
"And because light is obstructed by another substance. (20)

The meaning is that when light is covered by a moving substance, because the previous location of the light is no longer perceived and its subsequent location is perceived, this notion regarding the light is an error (*matibhrama*) due to its similarity to a moving object, and not a real cognition on your part; for such is the understanding established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Darkness (*tamas*) is the absence of contact with as much light as possesses manifested color (*udbhūta-rūpa*). 20.
Having thus concluded this incidental section on darkness consisting of two sūtras, he states the section on the emptiness of action:
"Space, time, and ether are devoid of action because they possess properties contrary to that which possesses action. (21)
By the word "and" (ca), self-inclusion [of time] is indicated. Space and the other [directions] possess the property of being actionless, as they are formless; for action conforms to form. || 21 ||
He states that qualities and actions are devoid of activity:
"By this, actions and qualities are explained. (22)

"By this" means by way of the dissimilarity with that which possesses action (*kriyāvat*). The meaning is that since formlessness (*amūrtatva*)—the dissimilarity with that which possesses action—is present in both qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*), those two as well are explained as being devoid of action (*niṣkriya*). || 22 ||

Now, if qualities and actions are devoid of motion, then how can there be a connection between them and substance? One might suppose the connection to be conjunction (*saṃyoga*), but that depends entirely upon action; therefore, he says:
"For things devoid of motion, inherence (*samavāya*) is precluded by [the analysis of] actions. (23)

The relation of qualities and actions, which are themselves devoid of activity, is merely inherence (samavāya); and that [inherence] is negated by [the absence of] action. The meaning is that for such a relation, there is no origination at all, let alone its dependence upon action. || 23 ||

Now, if qualities, being formless, do not constitute the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of qualities and actions, then how are qualities and actions produced by means of qualities? For causality is not possible even in the form of being distinct from the inherent cause; to this, he says:
"But qualities are the non-inherent causes (*asamavāyin*). (24)

Qualities are non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), but not inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*)—which would otherwise make them the substrata of action. And this status as a non-inherent cause arises, in some cases, from inherence in the same object as the effect, as in the case of the conjunction of the self with respect to the specific qualities of the self, or in the case of conjunction, disjunction, and sound with respect to sound. In other cases, it arises from inherence in the same object as the cause, as in the case of the conjunction of the self and the mind with respect to the specific qualities of the self, or in the case of conjunction, disjunction, and sound with respect to sound. In yet other cases, it arises from inherence in the same object as the cause, as in the case of the color and other qualities of the potsherds with respect to the color and other qualities of the jar. || 24 ||

Now, one might object: on the strength of such cognitions as "here action arises" or "now action arises," space and time must also be the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of action; otherwise, how could they serve as its substratum? To this he says:
"Space is explained by [the discussion of] qualities. (25)

The meaning is this: just as qualities such as gravity (*gurutva*) are not the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of action because they are formless (*amūrtatva*), so too space (*dik*) is not the inherent cause of action precisely because it is formless. The point is that the status of being a substratum (*ādhāratā*) is possible even without inherent causality, as in the cases of "jujube fruits in a bowl," "curd in a bowl," or "the roar of a lion in the forest. || 25 ||
With the same intention as previously stated, he says:
"Time [is established] by its cause. (26)

The phrase "is explained as being devoid of action" is to be supplied by transposition. The term "by the cause" (kāraṇena) is an indication where the abstract state is primary; thus, the meaning is that time is merely the substratum of the action by way of being a non-inherent cause (nimittakāraṇa), and not its inherent cause (samavāyin). || 26 ||
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the fifth chapter in the *Śāṅkara-Vaiśeṣika-sūtra-upaskāra*.
This fifth chapter is now complete.

The subject matter of the sixth chapter is the examination of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are the root causes of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Merit and demerit are to be postulated through the force of injunctions and prohibitions, such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" and "one should not eat *kalañja*," provided that the authority of these injunctive and prohibitive statements is established.

And its validity is established because it is preceded by a quality (guṇa) in the speaker characterized by knowledge of the sentence-meaning as it truly is, since intrinsic validity has been refuted; therefore, he first begins the proof of the quality that serves as the cause for the validity of the Veda:
"The composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by intelligence" (Sūtra 1).

The composition of sentences—that is, the arrangement of sentences—is preceded by the intelligence of a speaker, being preceded by the speaker’s knowledge of the true meaning of the sentence, because it is an arrangement of sentences, like the arrangement of sentences such as "There are five fruits on the riverbank" made by people like us. By "Veda," the meaning is a collection of sentences. In this context, the subject (*pakṣa*) is the composition of the individual sentences within that collection. Nor is there a proof-by-alternative (*anyathāsiddhi*) based on its being preceded by the intelligence of people like us; for in cases such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," the status of being a means to a desired end or the status of being a task to be accomplished does not fall within the scope of the intelligence of people like us.

By this, it is established that the Veda has a self-dependent person as its source. And the nature of being a Veda (*vedatva*) consists in being a word that produces knowledge of its sentence-meaning not produced by another word, while having as its object a thing that is not the object of a valid cognition produced by any means of knowledge other than words or those dependent upon them. (1)
