Because the destruction of the substratum necessitates the destruction of what is contained therein—it is neither logical nor accepted that when a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is destroyed due to the cessation of the conjunction of two atoms, the triad (*trasareṇu*) supported by it, or the powder and sugar-candy supported by that, would not also be destroyed. If it is asked, "How then is there recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)?"—it is because it is an error, like the recognition that "this is the same flame of the lamp.

If it is argued that even the recognition of a lamp is indeed valid knowledge (*pramā*), and that while its shortness or length is subject to production and destruction [the substance remains], we say no; for it has already been stated that such destruction is impossible without the destruction of the substratum. (18)

In that case, does atomicity residing in atoms perish—just as the color and other qualities of earthly atoms do—or does magnitude residing in ether and so forth also perish—just as sound, cognition, and the like do? To this he says:
"In the eternal, it is eternal. (19)
The dimension that belongs to eternal things such as space and to atoms is itself eternal, because there is no cause for its destruction. || 19 ||
He states the name established by the Vaiśeṣikas for the dimension of the atom: "The eternal spherical. (20)
Sphericity (*pārimāṇḍalya*) is simply that which is spherical (*parimaṇḍala*); as it has been said: "Except for sphericity and the like. || 20 ||

Now, if the smallness or shortness conventionally attributed to things such as the *kuvala* fruit, the *āmalaka* fruit, sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), and sugar-cane (*ikṣu*) is not ultimately real, then what is the proof for those two [dimensions] that are ultimately real?
He says: "And ignorance is the mark of knowledge. (21)

Knowledge is the mark of ignorance; this is the meaning. The cognition of minuteness in things such as the *kuvala* fruit or the *āmalaka* fruit, and the cognition of shortness in things such as sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) or sugarcane (*ikṣu*), is indeed ignorance, because absolute minuteness and shortness are absent therein. This is because those who maintain the theory of "misapprehension" (*anyathākhyāti*) accept that every invalid cognition (*apramā*) must be preceded by a valid cognition (*pramā*). Thus, the meaning is that a true cognition of minuteness and a true cognition of shortness are to be inferred.
And since figurative application of a word does not occur without a primary sense, the primary [senses] of minuteness and shortness must necessarily be admitted in some cases. || 21 ||
He states the nature of dimension (parimāṇa) as it is inferred for ether and the rest by the reason of their being substances:
"Ether is great because of its pervasiveness; and so too is the self. (22)

Pervasion (*vibhava*) is the state of being conjoined with all corporeal objects; since this is untenable without supreme magnitude (*paramamahattva*), it leads to the inference of supreme magnitude. Furthermore, the simultaneous production of sound is observed here in both Vārāṇasī and Pāṭaliputra, and since space (*ākāśa*) is the single inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) in those instances, the all-pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) of space is established. All-pervasiveness consists precisely in the possession of supreme magnitude; for the postulation of multiple spaces would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Thus, one should accept that space is indeed one.

The designation "a region of space" (*ākāśasya pradeśaḥ*), however, is figurative (*bhākta*) and based on its conjunction with objects such as jars that possess regions. And this figurative usage consists in being conjoined with substances that possess regions. So too is the case with the self (*ātman*). Just as space is "supremely great" (*paramamahat*) because of its all-pervasiveness—that is, because of its conjunction with all corporeal things—so too is the self supremely great.

If the self were not in conjunction with all corporeal objects, then action would not arise in those various corporeal things due to the conjunction of the self with the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), because an unseen merit/demerit located in a different substratum produces action only when it depends upon a specific proximity. And that proximity is precisely the conjunction of the self with the possessor of the unseen merit/demerit. Thus, since the production of cognition, pleasure, and so forth in a moving body at various locations would be inexplicable without the omnipresence of the self, the self is also all-pervading.

The sense is that it has already been stated that this [dimension] is not a single entity like space, because we observe its various arrangements. Furthermore, that magnitude is gradated and eternal, just as atomic minuteness is in atoms. In the same way, one should infer supreme length in space and so forth, and supreme shortness in atoms. || 22 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that the mind (*manas*) is all-pervading (*vibhu*), because it is a substance devoid of touch, like space (*ākāśa*), and because it is the substratum of the conjunction that serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of cognition and so forth, like the self (*ātman*); thus, why is the mind not also stated to be like space and the self? To this, he says:
"Because of the absence of that [conjunction], the mind is atomic (*aṇu*). (23)

The mind is atomic because that all-pervasive nature, which consists of conjunction with every corporeal object, is absent in it. If, however, the mind were conjoined with all corporeal objects simultaneously, there would be a simultaneity of cognitions through the simultaneous conjunction with multiple sense organs; and in that case, there would be no lack of attention (vyāsaṅga). As for inference, as long as the mind is not yet established, the reason suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi); but at the stage when the mind is established, [the reason] is sublated by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (dharmigrāhakamānabādhita).

If it is argued that "atomicity (aṇutva) is not established because of the very absence of omnipresence (vibhava), since there is a deviation in the case of objects such as a jar," we say no; for by the absence of omnipresence, non-pervasiveness (avyāpakatva) is established. Thus, in a single body, the mind is indeed one, because the assumption of multiplicity would entail the fault of unnecessary complexity (kalpanā-gaurava). Furthermore, even if one were to assume parts for that single [mind], there is no [need] due to the complexity of such a hypothesis, and because [the mind] does not originate [matter] by virtue of being a tangible (sparśatva), and so forth—this is the sense in which atomicity is established through reasoning. || 23 ||
He states the reasoning for the supreme magnitude of space:
"Space is explained by [the same] qualities. (24)

The meaning is that space (*dik*) is also explained as being all-pervasive by means of qualities consisting of notions such as "east," "west," and so forth—which are common to all persons residing in every continent—and which are characterized as "remoteness" (*paratva*) and "proximity" (*aparatva*) residing in all corporeal things. This is because it will be stated later that the cause for the production of remoteness and proximity is the "cognitive judgment" (*apekṣābuddhi*) regarding the greater or lesser number of conjunctions with something conjoined; and because the postulation of multiple spaces is obstructed by the logical fault of excessive complexity (*kalpanāgaurava*).

If it is asked, "How then do the cognition and designation 'the ten directions' arise?", we reply: no, because it has already been stated that they are based upon their respective limiting adjuncts (upādhi). || 24 ||
He states the pervasiveness of time: "Time [is present] in the cause. (25)

The designation "time" (*kāla*) refers to that substance which is the cause of the notions of priority and posteriority, simultaneity and non-simultaneity, and slowness and quickness. Furthermore, such a notion—being common to all persons in all places—is not possible without the pervasiveness of time; thus, its pervasiveness means its possession of supreme magnitude (*paramamahattva*).

Alternatively, by the force of cognitions such as "born now," time is perceived to be the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) of all things that arise; this too depends upon pervasiveness, because there is a rule that an efficient cause must be in proximity to the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

Alternatively, since the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of past, future, and present is universal, time (*kāla*) must indeed be omnipresent (*sarvagata*). Or rather, because the linguistic usage of the term "time" is universal with respect to that substance which is the cause of the linguistic usages of moments (*kṣaṇa*), instants (*lava*), hours (*muhūrta*), watches (*yāma*), days, nights, fortnights, months, seasons (*ṛtu*), half-years (*ayana*), years, and so forth, time is omnipresent and thus infinitely great; furthermore, it has been stated that the postulation of its manifoldness is obstructed by the fallacy of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*). || 25 ||
Thus ends the first daily lesson of the seventh chapter in the venerable Śāṅkara’s Vaiśeṣikasūtropaskāra.
The second daily lesson of the seventh chapter.

In the second chapter (*ahnika*), there are the following sections: the section on the examination of qualities residing in one or many; the section on the examination of qualities residing in more than one; the section on the examination of the relationship between word and meaning by way of incidental discussion; the section on the examination of qualities residing in a single [substance] which have as their non-inherent cause the conjunction with an all-pervading substance devoid of specific qualities; and the section on the examination of inherence (*samavāya*). Regarding these, since the perceptibility of number and the other [qualities] also depends upon inherence in the same object as magnitude (*mahattva*), [the author], having set aside the order of enumeration, states the following after the definition of dimension (*parimāṇa*) in order to examine number and distinctness (*pṛthaktva*):
Unity is a distinct entity, because it is different from color, taste, smell, and touch. (1)

"Color, taste, smell, and touch"—this is an indication of the qualities distinct from the pentad beginning with number. "Due to exclusion" means due to deviation. This is the meaning: the qualified cognition "one jar" is produced by a qualifier; and that qualifier is not color and so forth, because it arises even in their absence. Nor is "jar-ness" (ghaṭatva) and the like the cause, because it arises even in the case of a cloth. Nor is oneness a universal like existence (sattā), because it does not subsist in a manner that is neither less nor more than existence.

Nor is that [existence] a mere generality of substance, because it occupies a space no smaller and no larger than that of "substanceness" (*dravyatva*). Nor can there be a difference [between them] based on a difference in cognition even when the space occupied is identical; for if the difference in cognition were caused by their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), then even "Being" (*sattā*) would have to be divided. If, however, it were caused by a difference in the object, a difference in the object has already been shown to be untenable; otherwise, a distinction between "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and "jar-ness" (*kalasatva*) would also result.

Furthermore, the view of the Bhūṣaṇakāra that oneness consists in the non-difference of essential nature (*svarūpābheda*) is not tenable; for if oneness were the non-difference of the essential nature of a jar, then the cognition of oneness would not occur in relation to a cloth or other objects. Likewise, the Bhūṣaṇakāra’s position that duality and so forth consist in the difference of essential nature is untenable, because since the difference of essential nature is common to three, four, and more, it would follow that the diversity of linguistic usage could not be accounted for—this is the intended meaning. || 1 ||
In order to establish "oneness-in-separateness" (ekapṛthaktva) by means of the equality of oneness, he says: "Likewise, separateness [is established]. (2)

There indeed exists the conventional usage of "extraction" (*apoddhāra*), which takes the form: "this is separate from that, another, a different object. Extraction is that determination (*nirdhāraṇa*) made by setting aside a limit (*avadhi*); it is this very process that constitutes extraction. In this context, color and other such qualities are not the governing factor (*tantra*), because they are subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and because [separateness] must be defined in relation to a limit. Now, one might argue that separateness is simply mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), since the cognition "it is distinct"—as in the expression "this is separate from that, another, a different object"—has mutual non-existence as its objective basis.

No; for although words such as *pṛthak* (separate) and so forth are synonyms, they do not have "mutual non-existence" (*anyonyābhāva*) as their meaning, because the use of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) would be untenable there. This is because the cognitions "this is separate from that" and "this is not this" have different objects. Nor is the object possessing mutual non-existence what is meant by "separateness," for then the use of the ablative case would result even in cases such as "the cloth is not a jar. If it is argued that since the cognitions "it is separate" and "it is qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) have the same form, separateness is simply qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*), we say no. For then, at a time when Maitra possesses a staff, the cognition "this Maitra is separate from Maitra" would also result.

For this very reason, even difference (*vaidharmya*) is not distinctness (*pṛthaktva*). For if it were, there would arise the undesirable consequence of the conventional usage: "This pot [now] red from baking is distinct from the pot [formerly] dark. Indeed, its difference from that consists simply in its possessing a property opposed to it; and that [possession of an opposing property] exists even at the stage of redness immediately following the dark state. Nor is generality itself distinctness, because a generality cannot be defined by reference to a limit (*avadhi*). Furthermore, there would be the consequence of a confusion of universals (*jātisaṅkara*): if it subsisted in pure existence (*sanmātra*), it would be coextensive with existence (*sattā*); if it subsisted in substance alone, it would be coextensive with substantiality (*dravyatva*), resulting in neither being less nor more extensive than the other. || 2 ||

But surely, since there are conventional usages such as "oneness is distinct from form and so forth" and "distinctness," there must be oneness even in oneness, and distinctness even in distinctness; and thus it would be the same in those cases as well. To this he says:
"The absence of oneness and distinctness in oneness and distinctness is explained by [the analysis of] atomicity and magnitude. (3)

The meaning is as follows: just as minuteness and magnitude do not possess [the qualities of] minuteness and magnitude, and thus the linguistic usage of those terms regarding them is figurative (*bhākta*), so too the linguistic usage of unity and separateness regarding [substance] is figurative, because substance does not possess unity and separateness. The two illustrative sūtras, "actions by actions" and "qualities by qualities," also appear here as forming a single syntactical unit with the preceding illustrative sūtra; the meaning is that just as actions do not possess actions and qualities do not possess qualities, so too the eight [categories] do not possess unity and separateness. || 3 ||

Now, an objection is raised: "Is not the linguistic usage of 'oneness' indeed common to both qualities (guṇas) and actions (karmans)? What here is the determining factor that oneness exists only in substances and not in qualities and so forth? To this, he says:
"Because qualities and actions are devoid of number, universal oneness does not exist [in them]. (4)

The state of being one for all things is "the oneness of all" (*sarvaikatva*); that does not exist. To this, he says: "Because actions and qualities are beyond number" (*niḥsaṃkhyatvāt karmaguṇānām*). Those which have gone beyond number (*saṃkhyā*) are "beyond number" (*niḥsaṃkhyā*); their state is "being beyond number" (*niḥsaṃkhyatvam*). Thus, actions and qualities are beyond number. Since number is a quality (*guṇa*), there is no such thing as number among the [nine] categories (*guṇa*), nor is it found among actions, because qualities are excluded from actions—otherwise, they would result in being substances (*dravya*).
And it has been established that number is a quality and that oneness is a type of number; such is the meaning. || 4 ||
If so, how is it that there is such cognition as "one form," "one taste," and so forth? To this he says:
"That is erroneous. (5)

The meaning is that the cognition of oneness regarding qualities and actions is erroneous. In the Sūtra, the word "cognition" (jñāna) is to be supplied as a remainder, because the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) has been previously implied. Furthermore, the application [of the term] is figurative; and even the non-difference of essential nature is merely figurative, for that very oneness has already been refuted in the preceding discussion. || 5 ||
[Objection: "But surely, even regarding substances, this usage of 'oneness' may be figurative, and the cognition therein may be erroneous; what is the use of actual oneness? To this, he says:
"Because oneness is absent, there can be no figurative usage. (Verse 6)

If ultimate unity were not to be admitted anywhere, then metaphorical usage would be impossible—since metaphor is preceded by a primary sense—and cognition would not be erroneous—since error is preceded by a valid means of knowledge (pramā). For that which has been cognized through valid means is what is superimposed, not that which has not been so cognized; this is because the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (asatkhyāti) has been refuted and the theory of the manifestation of something else (anyathākhyāti) has been established. This is the underlying point. || 6 ||

The cause and the effect—the thread and the cloth—possess both identity and numerical distinctness. Precisely because there is identity, there is also numerical distinctness; for it is not possible for something to be distinct from itself. Indeed, when a cloth is being torn and each thread is pulled out, no cloth distinct from those threads is perceived. If the cloth were distinct from the threads, it would be perceived as such, like a jar. Likewise, when a jar is broken, since nothing distinct from the two shards is perceived, the jar too [is not distinct].
It consists of nothing other than the two halves themselves. As it has been said: "The whole is not something other than its parts. Desiring to refute this Sāṅkhya position incidentally, he says:
"Because there is neither identity nor difference between cause and effect, neither identity nor difference exists [in the whole]. (7)

The effect and the cause are not one and the same; why is this so? He says: because of the absence of oneness, that is, because of the absence of non-difference. If it were the case that the effect is the very same as the cause—as in "the threads are the cloth"—then the co-referential application (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of plurality and singularity would be untenable. If it is argued that such co-referentiality does indeed exist, since we employ the term "water" (*āpaḥ*) even for a single drop of water, and the term "wife" (*dārāḥ*) even for a single woman, we reply: no, for in those cases the usage is justified by taking into account the plurality of parts.

Some maintain that the plural form [in "atoms"] is used by taking into account the multiplicity of color and other qualities inherent in the constituent parts. Others hold that this is simply the natural character of the word and is not to be questioned. Furthermore, threads situated within a basket do not receive the designation of "cloth," nor are individual threads capable of performing the functions of holding or pulling; moreover, neither the effect nor the cause can both reside in a single unit of separateness (*ekatva-pṛthaktva*), because they are perceived as being mutually relative.

Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of the absence of oneness and separateness. Oneness and separateness constitute non-difference; because of their absence, there is the experience of mutual difference between cause and effect. This is because the distinct cognitions and designations of "thread-ness" and "cloth-ness," as well as "pot-ness" and "sherd-ness," are universally recognized. [Objection: How then is there no perception of difference among color, taste, smell, and touch? [Reply: Because of extreme similarity (*atyantasārūpya*). However, in some cases, such as a variegated cloth (*citrapaṭa*), there is indeed perception of difference, as the distinction in number, dimension, and so forth, is extremely clear. || 7 ||
He states that for the two impermanent qualities, unity and separateness, there is the property of being preceded by the qualities of their causes:
"This has been explained regarding the two impermanent [qualities]. (8)

The statement that number and separateness (*saṅkhyā-pṛthaktva*) in their impermanent forms are preceded by the qualities of their causes should be understood as applying only to the impermanent unity (*ekatva*) and singularity of separateness (*eka-pṛthaktva*), because other numbers and separatenesses are produced by relative cognition (*apekṣā-buddhi*). Just as the impermanent color and touch of fire are preceded by the qualities of their causes, so too is the enumeration of unity and singularity of separateness; and there is another supplementary rule: "And [separateness] co-inheres with that [substance], ranging from duality of separateness (*dvi-pṛthaktva*) up to the limit of the highest number of separateness (*parārdha-pṛthaktva*)."

Thus, this is the sequence for the production and destruction of duality and so forth: when there is sensory contact with two substances—whether of the same or different classes—the universal "oneness" belonging to the two unities residing in them arises; immediately after the indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), there arises a cognition of the quality as qualified by that [universal]. This very cognition is the "relational cognition" (*apekṣābuddhi*), and by it duality is produced in those two substances. Furthermore, the universal "duality-ness" belonging to the produced duality is perceived; by that perception, the relational cognition is destroyed.

A cognition qualified by duality and a cognition whose object is the quality of duality arise simultaneously; in the subsequent moment, due to the destruction of the enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi), the quality of duality is destroyed, and at the same time, the knowledge of the substance as qualified by duality—namely, "two substances"—arises. From that knowledge of the substance as qualified by duality, a mental impression (saṃskāra) is produced.

Thus, this is the summary: first, there is the sense-organ contact with the substratum of the duality about to arise; from that, the cognition of the universal residing in the quality of unity; from that, the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) which takes as its object the collection of the quality of unity as qualified by the universal "unity-ness"; from that, the production of the quality of duality; from that, the cognition of the universal residing in that [duality]; from that, the cognition of the quality of duality as qualified by that universal; from that, the cognition of the substance as qualified by the quality of duality; and from that, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*). Thus, beginning from the sense-organ contact and ending with the mental impression, there are eight moments.

Regarding the sequence of destruction: the destruction of the cognition of the generality "oneness" results from the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*); the destruction of the enumerative cognition results from the cognition of the generality "duality"; the destruction of the cognition of the generality "duality" results from the cognition of the quality "duality"; the destruction of the cognition of the quality "duality" results from the cognition of the substance qualified by duality; and the destruction of that [cognition of the substance] results from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) or from the cognition of another object.

[Objection: Surely, why does the cognition of the substance qualified by that [number] not arise from the cognition of oneness, since its causal complex is present? For there is no delay in the cognition of the substance once the cognition of the quality has occurred; and thus, when the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is destroyed by that very [cognition], the number two would be destroyed in the very next moment. Consequently, since the destruction of the number two would occur in the moment preceding the qualified cognition "two substances," the cognition of the substance qualified by the number two could never arise. [Reply: This is not so, because the causal complex for the production of duality and so forth is not overcome [by the cognition of oneness].

This is because it is a rule that enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) produces a cognition qualified by a substance, and such a postulation is made on the strength of the resulting effect. Now, one might object: "Even so, if enumerative cognition is destroyed by the very mental impression (*saṃskāra*) it itself produces, then that same fault remains as before; for the destruction of duality would be possible at the very moment preceding the cognition qualified by duality. This is not so, because a cognition of a quality alone does not produce a mental impression. Indeed, a quality is never remembered in isolation, since the remembrance of a quality always occurs through its connection with a substance.

[Objection: "Granted that this may be so, nevertheless, even at the time of the cognition of the qualified [object], if the duality has perished, the non-arising of the cognition of the qualified remains exactly as it was; for a cognition of the qualified appearing as present cannot occur at the time of the destruction of the qualifier, since such is not observed. [Reply: No, because the causal complex for the cognition of the qualified—which consists of the cognition of the qualifier, the sensory contact with the qualificand, and the non-apprehension of the non-existence of a relation between the two—is possible in the present case as well.

If, however, contact with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is also required, then since that too exists in the preceding moment—and because it is accepted that only the contact existing in the preceding moment is the cause—it is possible for the qualifier to not be an object of the qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*). For in being a qualifier, the only essential factor is merely being an object of the qualified cognition; it is not necessary that it be an object of the qualified cognition at the very time [the cognition arises].

If it is argued that this would result in the accidental characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) becoming a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), we say no; for being a qualifier depends on having the same locus (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the object to be conveyed, whereas an accidental characteristic does not share that locus. Thus, when there is a crow in Devadatta’s house, the crow is a qualifier; but when it is absent, hovering above, it is an accidental characteristic. If this were so, one might argue that in expressions such as "there is taste in what possesses color," color and the like would also become qualifiers; but this is not a fault, for it is accepted.

If it is argued that taste must therefore also reside there [in the substance], we say no; for the occurrence of a qualified entity does not necessarily entail the occurrence of its qualifier, since the qualifier and the qualified are not one and the same reality. If it is asked how there can be a cognition of the qualified when the relation with the qualifier is absent at the time of the destruction of duality, we say no; because "qualifiedness" (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is simply the exclusion of what is other than that [qualifier]. Since that [exclusion] exists there as well, nothing is untenable—so say the Teachers (*Ācāryāḥ*). In this way, the production and destruction of triad-ness (*tritva*) should also be inferred to be like those of duality.

Duality is destructible by the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), because—as long as there is no destruction of its substratum and no other opposing quality—there is no destruction of an existing quality, just like the final cognition; for the final cognition is destructible by the destruction of unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).

In some cases, it [the number] is destroyed even by the destruction of its substrate, where the cognition of the universal "oneness" occurs at the same time as the action in the parts that serve as the substratum for duality. For example, when there is the action in the parts and the cognition of the universal, there is the production of disjunction and the production of a quality [duality] based on the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). Then, upon the destruction of the substance and the cognition of the universal "duality," the destruction of duality results from the destruction of the substance, while the destruction of the relative cognition results from the cognition of the universal; this is because the destruction of the relative cognition is simultaneous with the destruction of duality, since there is no coexistence between cause and effect.

When, however, there is simultaneity between the action in the constituent parts that serves as the substratum for duality and the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), then the destruction of duality occurs through two causes: the destruction of its substratum and the destruction of the enumerative cognition. For example: [simultaneously with] the action in the parts and the enumerative cognition, there arise disjunction and the production of duality; [subsequently] there arise the destruction of conjunction and the cognition of the universal "duality"; [and finally] the destruction of the substance and the destruction of the enumerative cognition. From these two, the destruction of duality follows, because the causal capacity of each has been established individually. And this process is most appropriately explained under the view that cognitions are mutually obstructive (*badhyabādhaka*); and that very view is the one supported by authoritative evidence (*prāmāṇika*).

Now, one might ask: if the causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) for duality, triad, and so forth are identical, how can there be a difference in their effects? If it is argued that duality arises from two unities and triad from three unities, this is not tenable, because duality and the like do not exist within a single unity.

If it is argued that the duality, triad, and so forth residing in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) alone is the governing factor, we say no; for prior to the production of duality and the rest, duality and so forth do not exist therein, and thus the inquiry into their cause remains unavoidable. Furthermore, such a specific distinction is not perceived in the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) or in the unities themselves. If one were to postulate it on the strength of the effect, then let the linguistic usage of "duality" and so forth proceed from that very [enumerative cognition]—what is the use of duality and the rest as separate entities? If it is argued that the distinction arises from a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*), then, this being the case, even by the causal complex that produces duality, triad or tetrad might sometimes be produced, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of lack of regularity (*aniyama*).

To this it is replied: the distinction [in the effects] is established by the distinction in their prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), just as in the case of color, taste, smell, and touch produced by cooking from an identical causal complex. If it is argued that prior non-existence is likewise common [to all], we say no, because it is determined that each thing's own specific prior non-existence is the cause for its respective effect. Or else, it is not the case that duality arises from a pure enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) and that trinity arises from a cognition accompanied by duality.

In cases such as "A hundred ants have been killed by me," duality (dvitva) cannot arise in the absence of an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa); thus, the linguistic usage of number there must be regarded as figurative (gauṇa). Regarding armies, forests, and the like, Śrīdhara Ācārya maintains that because of the absence of a determinate enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi), only "plurality" (bahutva) arises, but not specific numbers such as "hundred" or "thousand. Udayana Ācārya, however, argues that if this were so, there would be no doubt regarding whether [the army] consists of hundreds, thousands, or tens of millions, nor could one distinguish between a "large" or "larger" army; therefore, he holds that it is not so.

In this regard, the following must be considered: Is "plurality" (*bahutva*) simply the number itself, beginning from three and extending up to the highest possible number (*parārdha*), or is it a different number distinct from that? It cannot be the first, because even in cases such as an army or a forest, there is a rule that numbers such as one hundred or one thousand arise [as specific instances]. Nor can it be the second, because we do not experience a plurality that is distinct from "three-ness" (*tritva*) and so forth. Thus, plurality is simply the number of one hundred and so on, produced by a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) that does not rely upon restricted singularities; however, the manifestation of "one hundred" and so on does not occur therein due to the absence of such a manifestor (*vyañjaka*).

We, however, say this: plurality (*bahutva*) is indeed another number co-located with three and so forth, produced by the same enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) that produces three and so forth; its existence is due precisely to the difference in its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Otherwise, how could one say: "There are many, though we do not know specifically whether there are a hundred or a thousand"? Just as largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*) exist in a single substance, so too do three and so forth and plurality exist in one and the same substratum.

For instance, in response to the question, "Shall I bring one hundred or one thousand mangoes?", the reply is often, "Let many be brought; what is the need for a desire to know the specific number? And thus, while a triad arises from a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) accompanied by duality, and a tetrad from a relative cognition accompanied by a triad, and so on for the production of higher numbers, there is no fixed rule that the relative cognition must be qualified by each preceding number in the sequence.

For this very reason, in cases such as an army or a forest, only plurality (*bahutva*) arises, and not another number; however, doubt may indeed occur even regarding a non-existent alternative. Furthermore, "separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is co-located with that [number]"; thus, just as there is duality (*dvitva*), so too is there dual-separateness (*dvipṛthaktva*), and so forth.

If it is objected: "Since the linguistic usage [of 'two', 'three', etc. can be accounted for by means of single instances of separateness (*pṛthaktva*) that are co-located with duality, triadity, and so forth, what is the purpose of dual-separateness (*dvipṛthaktva*) and the rest?", we say no. For there is a difference: in the cognition "the cloth and the clod are separate from the pot," one does not perceive a mutual non-obstruction of dual-separateness, whereas such a cognition is perceived in each individual instance of separateness. Nor does this lead to the consequence of [having to postulate] dual-distance (*dviparatva*), because that usage is accounted for by two instances of distance (*paratva*) that are co-located with duality.

Just as there is a contradiction regarding mutual relativity in the case of "separateness" (pṛthaktva), such is not the case for "remoteness" (paratva). This is because it is logically consistent to say "these two are remote," just as one says "these two are blue"; for even when two objects situated in the same place are equal in terms of the multiplicity of conjunctions with other conjoined things, the production of distinct effects is possible due to the difference in the non-inherent cause, namely the conjunction between the spatial direction and the object.

Just as two conjoined unities possess the status of being non-inherent causes (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) with respect to duality, so too it is possible for two conjoined singular separations (*eka-pṛthaktva*) to be non-inherent causes with respect to dual separation (*dvi-pṛthaktva*). This is because we do not observe multiple conjunctions acting together to produce a single effect that is distinct from its substance, except through the proximity of "inherence in the same object as the effect" (*kāryaikārtha-samavāya*). However, by means of the proximity of "inherence in the same object as the cause" (*kāraṇaikārtha-pratyāsatti*), many conjunctions between threads and a shuttle do indeed initiate a single conjunction between the cloth and the shuttle; such is the general direction of the argument. Furthermore, the destruction of dual separation and the like should be inferred in the same manner as the destruction of duality and the like. || 8 ||
He begins another section:
Conjunction is produced by the action of one [of two things], produced by the action of both, and innate conjunction. (9)

In the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), the uncontradicted cognition of things being conjoined is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), as are its effects: from the conjunctions of parts arises a substance; from conjunction with fire arise qualities such as color produced by cooking (*pākaja*); from accumulation (*pracaya*) arises a particular dimension (*parimāṇa-viśeṣa*); and from the conjunction of a drum and space arises sound—such instances are to be inferred. Nor is conjunction merely the production of things in close proximity, since the theories of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhanga*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*) have already been refuted.

Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the attainment (*prāpti*) of what was previously unattained. It is produced by the action of one of two things—such as the conjunction of a moving hawk with a stationary post (which lacks action directed toward it), or the conjunction of a running man with another running man behind him (who also possesses action). It is produced by the action of both—as in the case of two rams or two wrestlers, since that conjunction is generated by both of them, each possessing the requisite capacity. The third type is the conjunction of the hand with a tree resulting from the conjunction of a finger with the tree.

And that [conjunction] arises even from a single [conjunction], as for instance, from the conjunction of a thread and a *vīraṇa* grass, there arises the conjunction of a cloth and a *vīraṇa* grass. Sometimes a single conjunction arises from two conjunctions, as for instance, from two threads there are two conjunctions with space; from those two, there arises only one conjunction of the two-threaded cloth with space.

And sometimes a single conjunction is produced even by many conjunctions, as for instance, ten conjunctions of ten threads with space produce only one conjunction of the ten-threaded cloth with space.

In some cases, however, two conjunctions arise from even a single non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) which is itself a conjunction. For example, when an initial non-productive conjunction has arisen between an earth atom and a water atom, two conjunctions that initiate two dyads (dvyaṇuka) are produced: one between the earth atom and another earth atom, and one between the water atom and another water atom. From those two conjunctions, which reside in homogeneous [substances], two dyads are simultaneously initiated. In that case, whichever...

A non-productive conjunction having arisen between an earth atom and a water atom, two further conjunctions are produced simultaneously with the arising of color and other qualities in the dyads: one conjunction between that single earth atom and the water dyad, and another conjunction between the water atom and the earth dyad; for by means of the conjunction of the cause and the non-cause, the conjunctions of the effect and the non-effect must necessarily be produced.

The conjunction of corporeal substances with all-pervading ones arises solely from the action of one of the two. However, there is no conjunction between two all-pervading substances due to the absence of its cause; for action does not exist therein, nor is there any other cause. Consequently, the conjunction of effect and non-effect—which results from the conjunction of cause and non-cause—is also absent. Furthermore, an eternal conjunction is impossible, because conjunction is defined as the attainment of what was previously unattained, and this definition would be contradicted by eternality. If that were the case, then disjunction would also have to be non-produced in that instance.

Nor can this be accepted as a desired consequence, because it is impossible for conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*), which are contradictory, to coexist in a single locus while both remain in a state of non-destruction. Furthermore, separateness-in-existence (*yutasiddhi*) is the necessary condition for conjunction; however, that is not possible between two all-pervading (*vibhu*) entities. For such separateness consists either merely in the separate motion of two things or of one of them, or in their having separate substrates.

The destruction of conjunction, however, occurs sometimes from a disjunction residing in the same locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*) and sometimes from the destruction of the substratum (*āśrayanāśa*). For example, immediately after the conjunction of two threads, an action arises in a part (*aṃśu*) of one thread; by that [action], a disjunction from the other part is produced. From that disjunction comes the destruction of the originating conjunction, then the destruction of the thread, and from the destruction of the thread comes the destruction of the conjunction—in cases where two threads have been conjoined for a long time and no action has arisen [in them].

Some, however, say that when the destruction of the conjunction initiating the thread is produced by the action of a constituent part of the thread, then—due to the consideration of an action in another thread—the conjunction is destroyed simultaneously by both the destruction of its substratum and by disjunction, which have arisen at the same time.

But that is untenable, because disjunction does not arise at the moment of the destruction of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), since there is a rule that an inherent cause must persist until the same time as its effect. Furthermore, this conjunction is independent in the production of a substance, but dependent in the production of qualities and actions; it is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence co-located with itself, because it is experienced as such. For instance, even when a monkey's conjunction exists on a large banyan tree only as delimited by a single branch, there is the experience: "There is a conjunction of a monkey on the banyan tree."

If [the non-pervasive nature of conjunction] were established merely by way of limitation (*avaccheda*), it would follow that [conjunction] resides in atoms; and if that were so, it would not be perceived. Even for all-pervading entities (*vibhu*), a "location" is nothing but a distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); thus, the non-pervasive occurrence of a conjunction existing through such a limitation must be understood. Furthermore, one should consider that even for a conjunction residing in an atom, the directions and so forth serve as its limiting adjuncts. || 9 ||
Extending by analogy the manner in which conjunction arises [from disjunction], he says:
"By this, disjunction is explained" (10).

Disjunction, like conjunction, is produced by the action of one [of two things], by the action of both, and by disjunction. The disjunction between a post and a hawk arises from the action of the hawk; the disjunction between those two [wrestlers or rams] who were previously in contact arises from the actions of both. Furthermore, this [disjunction] arises in the moment immediately following the production of the action, because there is no other factor to be awaited. As it has been said: "Action is the independent cause of conjunction and disjunction."

If it is argued that [the action] is not independent, we say no, because the action is independent in its lack of dependence on any other entity for its own production or the production of something else. However, disjunction produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*) is of two kinds: distinguished as that produced from the disjunction of two causes (*kāraṇa-mātra-vibhāga*) and that produced from the disjunction of cause and non-cause (*kāraṇa-akāraṇa-vibhāga*); and further distinguished as that produced from the disjunction of cause and non-cause and that produced from the disjunction of effect and non-effect (*kārya-akārya-vibhāga*). Among these, the disjunction of cause and non-cause arises from the disjunction of two causes, as for example, the disjunction between the potsherd and space arising from the disjunction between the two potsherds.

And from the division of the cause and the non-cause, there follows the division of the effect and the non-effect; for example, from the division of the finger and the tree comes the division of the hand and the tree, and from that, the division of the body and the tree.

If it is argued that disjunction (*vibhāga*) itself is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the conventional usage of "disjunction" is merely the absence of conjunction (*saṃyoga-abhāva*), we say no; for if this absence of conjunction were an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), then the conventional usage of "disjunction" would follow even in the case of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*). If it is argued that the absolute non-existence of conjunction existing between two substances (*dravya*) is the cause of the cognition of being "separated," we say no, because this would then follow even in the case of parts (*avayava*) and the whole (*avayavin*). If it is argued that it must be between two substances that do not stand in the relation of cause and effect, then it would also apply to the Vindhya and Himalaya mountains.

If it is argued that [disjunction] exists there [in the case of the destruction of conjunction], we say no, because even qualities and actions exist for one who is deluded; and since our investigation concerns conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) with respect to one who is not deluded. If it is argued that disjunction is the destruction of conjunction, [we reply: this would entail the application of the term "disjunction" when a conjunction has been destroyed by the destruction of one of the two conjoined things. If it is argued that [disjunction occurs] only when both conjoined things still exist, [we reply: then even during the state of conjunction of a *kuvala* and an *āmalaka* fruit which have been conjoined again immediately after the destruction of a previous conjunction, there would be the erroneous application of the cognition of "disjunction," because in that case the [required] object does not exist.
Therefore, disjunction exists as a distinct entity (*arthāntara*).

And that quality is destroyed by another opposing quality, because it is impossible for a quality to perish while its substrate remains without another opposing quality existing in the same locus. If it is argued that action might be the destroyer of conjunction, we say no; for it is a quality that destroys a quality, as they are opposites.

Furthermore, in a case where there is contact with a tree by means of the respective actions of the finger, hand, arm, and body, although it is possible for the contact between the finger and the tree to be destroyed by the action produced in the finger alone, it would follow that the contacts between the hand and the tree, the arm and the tree, and the body and the tree could not be destroyed; for the hand and so forth are inactive [in that specific action], and the action of the finger has a different locus [from them]. If an action, even when having a different locus, were capable of destroying a contact, then it would follow that all contacts would be destroyed simultaneously by any action produced anywhere.

If you ask what the solution is in your own view regarding this, [we reply]: it is because we accept that the disjunction between the hand and the tree, produced by the disjunction between the finger and the tree, is the destroyer of the conjunction between the hand and the tree. As for what the Omniscient One (Sarvajña) has stated—that "the destruction of the conjunction between the hand and the tree may be caused by the action of the finger itself, even though it is in a different locus; and there is no over-extension [of this principle], because we accept that only a conjunction within a series of substratum and superstratum is destructible by an action in a different locus"—that too is not tenable. This is because experience shows that in all cases, it is only a contradictory cause in the same locus that acts as a destroyer; and in the absence of a subverting argument, it is improper to abandon that established rule.

Sound and disjunction are both effects of disjunction; among these, we accept that disjunction is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of sound. For when a bamboo is being split, and while one part is held down by the foot and another part is being pulled upward, we do not perceive any non-inherent cause for the sound produced there other than the disjunction between the bamboo part and space. Nor, in the case of the whistling of a bamboo being burnt and splitting by a forest fire, do we perceive any non-inherent cause for the sound other than disjunction.

And from the distinction between causes and non-causes, we infer the distinction between effects and non-effects; otherwise, how could it be that when there is a mutual separation between two fingers produced by their respective actions, even though the conjunctions between those fingers and the tree have not yet been destroyed, the conjunctions between the hands and the tree and so forth are nonetheless destroyed? For it has been stated that in such a case, it is precisely a succession of separations born of separation (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*) that destroys each respective conjunction.

However, there is no consensus regarding the disjunction between cause and non-cause following the disjunction of two causes, because it is possible for that action produced in one bamboo leaf to generate a disjunction from space and other locations just as it generates a disjunction from the other leaf; for we observe that by an action produced in a finger, a disjunction occurs from as many points of contact as it previously occupied, and likewise by an action produced in a lotus petal.

Nor do disjunctions originate from spaces such as that of ether, like the disjunction between the ends of two leaves. We maintain that even if a single action were to initiate a hundred disjunctions—provided those disjunctions are not contrary to the conjunctions that originate the substance—that action would produce disjunctions contrary to the conjunctions that originate the substance, but not disjunctions that are not contrary to the conjunctions that originate the substance; and furthermore, that which is not contrary to the conjunctions that originate the substance cannot be contrary to the conjunctions that originate the substance.

If it is asked, "Whence is this [known]?"—it is because the diversity of causes is necessary due to the diversity of effects. Now, one might object: "The diversity of actions is indeed necessary; thus, let one action produce a disjunction that is opposed to the conjunction initiating a substance, as in the case of a blooming lotus bud, while another action produces both [types of disjunctions]: that which is opposed to the conjunction initiating a substance and that which is not opposed."

Not so; for the contradiction between effects is indeed the basis for postulating a diversity in their causes. And that contradiction consists in one [effect] being the counter-opposite of the conjunction that initiates a substance, while the other is not its counter-opposite; thus, it is appropriate to postulate a corresponding diversity as well.

Now, this action residing in the leaf produces merely the disjunction of the two halves; that disjunction, in turn, initiates a further disjunction from the subsequent space-points (such as ether) which is not the counter-agent to the conjunction that originated the substance. Since that [subsequent disjunction] would result in the action being subject to the production of another disjunction independently [of other factors], it requires a time characterized by the destruction of the substance.

But surely, even at that time, action itself should produce that [subsequent disjunction], since it belongs to the past; for the time for action to produce a disjunction is immediately after its own origination. [Objection: If this were so, then once another disjunction has been produced by the [initial] disjunction, the action would not produce a conjunction with another location either. [Reply: No, because action is not yet past with respect to the production of conjunction; otherwise, the action would never perish, since it is destroyed solely by the subsequent conjunction.

This disjunction (vibhāga) is destroyed by subsequent conjunction (uttarasaṃyoga) and lasts for three moments; in some cases, it is destroyed by the destruction of its substratum (āśrayanāśa). For example: when there is action (karma) in a part (aṃśu) of a thread (tantu), immediately thereafter there is a disjunction from two parts; at that same time, there is action in another part of the thread. Then, by the disjunction of the two parts, there is the destruction of the conjunction that originated the thread; and by the action of the [other] thread-part, there is a disjunction. Then, due to the destruction of the conjunction that originates the substance, there is the destruction of the thread; and from that destruction, there follows the destruction of the disjunction produced by the action of the other thread-part.

[Objection: In that case, there would be no destruction of the action produced in another part of the thread, because of the absence of a cause for its destruction; for an action depends upon time [to be destroyed] by means of a subsequent conjunction. [Reply: But even then, let the action produce that [subsequent conjunction]; since it belongs to a past time, it would be destroyed upon producing the disjunction, and once the disjunction is destroyed, there is no subsequent conjunction. [Objection: No, for just as the disjunction of the thread in the state of perishing was produced by the action arisen in the thread, so too must a disjunction of its part (the *aṃśu*) be produced.

That [action] is also indeed the destroyer of the originating conjunction; thus, by the disjunction of the thread from its parts, there arises the disjunction of the thread from space, and by that, the subsequent conjunction, and by that, the destruction of the action. Alternatively, when an action occurs in a thread at a certain time, at that very time an action also occurs in its parts; and that action, while in the state of being destroyed, simultaneously initiates disjunctions from the locations of the thread, its own parts, space, and so forth, because all these disjunctions are not opposed to the originating conjunction. And thus, from the disjunction of the part (the cause) and space (the non-cause), [the disjunction of the whole from space arises].
The destruction of the action inherent in the yarn occurs through the conjunction that arises immediately after the disjunction produced between the effect—the yarn—and the non-effect—such as space.

In some cases, it occurs through two [factors], as follows: when there is a conjunction between a thread (*tantu*) and *vīraṇa* grass, there is simultaneously action in a part of the thread and action in the *vīraṇa*. By the action of the thread-part, there is disjunction from another part; by that [disjunction], there is the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the thread. By the action of the *vīraṇa*, there is disjunction between the thread and the *vīraṇa*, as well as the destruction of the conjunction between the thread and the *vīraṇa*. Following the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the thread, there is the destruction of the thread; following the destruction of the conjunction between the thread and the *vīraṇa*, [there is the destruction of the *vīraṇa*].
The conjunction of the vīraṇa grass with another location results in the destruction of that disjunction by means of those two [conjunctions] which cause the destruction of the substratum. || 10 ||
Now, one might object: "Let there be conjunction even in conjunction, and disjunction even in disjunction. To prevent this undesirable consequence, he says:
"The absence of conjunction and disjunction in conjunction and disjunction is explained by [the same reasoning as] minuteness and magnitude. (11)
Just as minuteness and magnitude do not possess minuteness and magnitude, so too conjunction and disjunction do not possess conjunction and disjunction. || 11 ||
Actions [are inferred] from actions, qualities from qualities, and [the existence of] atomicity and magnitude [is inferred] from atomicity and magnitude. || 12 ||
And the second sutra has been explained by me. || 12 ||
Now, one might ask: why is there no conjunction between two substances that stand in the relation of part and whole? To this he says:

because of the absence of separate existence (*yutasiddhi*), conjunction and disjunction do not exist between cause and effect. Separate existence means either existing independently of one another or residing in different substrates; the meaning is that such [separate existence] is absent in the case of the part and the whole. || 13 ||

Now, as an incidental digression, another section is introduced to establish that the relationship between word and meaning is conventional (*sāṅketika*). In this regard, he states the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*):
"Because it is a quality (*guṇatvāt*). (14)

The word "conjunction" (saṃyoga) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Thus, the meaning is: how could there be a conjunction—which is a quality—of a word, which is itself a quality, with an object such as a jar? || 14 ||

Furthermore, in some cases the object of perception is characterized by color, taste, and so forth; therefore, conjunction with it is not possible, because qualities are not admitted to exist within other qualities. Thus he says:
"The quality also is perceived. (15)

The word "also" (*api*) implies that a quality (*guṇa*) is likewise an object [of sound]. The meaning is that a quality such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth is the object of sound, but there is no relationship of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between them. Alternatively, the meaning is that even a quality is manifested or expressed by sound, and therefore the relationship of sound with it is not conjunction. (15) Furthermore, he states that for some substance (*dravya*), such as space (*ākāśa*), there is no conjunction produced by the action of one of the two, nor is there one produced by the action of both; this is because sound itself is devoid of motion (*niṣkriya*). He says: [The verse continues: naivānyatarakarmajo na caivobhayakarmajaḥ / saṃyogaḥ kāraṇaṃ śabde vibhāgastathaiva ca // 16 // There is no conjunction produced by the action of one [factor], nor indeed is there one produced by the action of both, which is the cause of sound; and the same applies to disjunction (*vibhāga*). (16) This means that the conjunction of the drum and the stick, or the conjunction of the hand and the drum, is not the cause of the sound. Nor is the conjunction of the drum and the ether (*ākāśa*) the cause of the sound, because ether is inactive (*niṣkriya*). Likewise, the disjunction of the drum and the stick, or the disjunction of the hand and the drum, is not the cause of the sound. Nor is the disjunction of the drum and the ether the cause of the sound, because ether is inactive. Therefore, since neither conjunction nor disjunction is the cause of sound, sound must arise from something else. What then is its cause? It is the *saṃyogaja-saṃyoga* (conjunction born of conjunction). That is to say, when the conjunction of the drum and the stick occurs, a conjunction is produced in the drum and the ether; from this conjunction of the drum and the ether, the sound arises. Similarly, when the conjunction of the hand and the drum occurs, a conjunction is produced in the drum and the ether; from this conjunction of the drum and the ether, the sound arises. Thus, the conjunction of the drum and the ether is the cause of the sound. This is what is meant by saying that the conjunction born of conjunction is the cause of sound. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the same applies to disjunction": just as conjunction is not the cause of sound, disjunction is also not the cause. For instance, when the drum and the stick are separated, or when the hand and the drum are separated, the resulting disjunction does not produce the sound. Nor does the disjunction of the drum and the ether produce the sound, because ether is inactive. Therefore, just as conjunction is not the cause, disjunction is also not the cause. Consequently, since neither conjunction nor disjunction is the cause, sound must arise from something else. What then is its cause? It is the *vibhāgaja-vibhāga* (disjunction born of disjunction). That is to say, when the drum and the stick are separated, a disjunction is produced in the drum and the ether; from this disjunction of the drum and the ether, the sound arises. Similarly, when the hand and the drum are separated, a disjunction is produced in the drum and the ether; from this disjunction of the drum and the ether, the sound arises. Thus, the disjunction of the drum and the ether is the cause of the sound. This is what is meant by saying that the disjunction born of disjunction is the cause of sound. Regarding the phrase "nor indeed is there one produced by the action of both": this refers to the case where two objects, such as two pieces of cotton wool, move toward each other and collide. In that case, a conjunction produced by the action of both is not the cause of the sound. Why? Because the conjunction of two substances that possess parts (*sāvayava*) is not the cause of sound. If it were, then when two hands clap together, the sound produced would be greater than when a single hand claps against a wall. However, in reality, the sound produced when two hands clap together is not greater than when a single hand claps against a wall. Therefore, the conjunction of two substances that possess parts is not the cause of sound. Consequently, the conjunction produced by the action of both is also not the cause of sound. This is what is meant by saying "nor indeed is there one produced by the action of both. Regarding the phrase "there is no conjunction produced by the action of one": this refers to the case where a substance possessing parts, such as a drum, is struck by a substance possessing parts, such as a stick. In that case, the conjunction produced by the action of the stick alone is not the cause of the sound. Why? Because the conjunction of two substances that possess parts is not the cause of sound. If it were, then when a single stick strikes a single drum, the sound produced would be greater than when many sticks strike many drums. However, in reality, the sound produced when a single stick strikes a single drum is not greater than when many sticks strike many drums. Therefore, the conjunction of two substances that possess parts is not the cause of sound. Consequently, the conjunction produced by the action of one is also not the cause of sound. This is what is meant by saying "there is no conjunction produced by the action of one. Regarding the phrase "nor is the conjunction of the drum and the ether the cause of the sound": this means that the conjunction of the drum and the ether is not the cause of the sound. Why? Because ether is inactive (*niṣkriya*). If the conjunction of the drum and the ether were the cause of the sound, then when a drum is struck by a stick, the sound would arise at the very moment of the conjunction of the drum and the ether. However, in reality, the sound arises after the conjunction of the drum and the stick has occurred. Therefore, the conjunction of the drum and the ether is not the cause of the sound. This is what is meant by saying "nor is the conjunction of the drum and the ether the cause of the sound. Regarding the phrase "because ether is inactive": this means that ether is devoid of motion. If ether were active, then the conjunction of the drum and the ether might be the cause of the sound. However, since ether is inactive, the conjunction of the drum and the ether cannot be the cause of the sound. This is what is meant by saying "because ether is inactive. Regarding the phrase "the same applies to disjunction": this means that just as conjunction is not the cause of sound, disjunction is also not the cause. For instance, when the drum and the stick are separated, or when the hand and the drum are separated, the resulting disjunction does not produce the sound. Nor does the disjunction of the drum and the ether produce the sound, because ether is inactive. Therefore, just as conjunction is not the cause, disjunction is also not the cause. Consequently, since neither conjunction nor disjunction is the cause, sound must arise from something else. What then is its cause? It is the *vibhāgaja-vibhāga*. That is to say, when the drum and the stick are separated, a disjunction is produced in the drum and the ether; from this disjunction of the drum and the ether, the sound arises. Similarly, when the hand and the drum are separated, a disjunction is produced in the drum and the ether; from this disjunction of the drum and the ether, the sound arises. Thus, the disjunction of the drum and the ether is the cause of the sound. This is what is meant by saying that the disjunction born of disjunction is the cause of sound. However, in reality, the sound produced when two hands are separated is not greater than when a single hand is separated from a wall. Because it is devoid of activity. || 16 ||
The phrase "of a certain word" implies "and of a certain object," as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 16 ||
He states another objection regarding the relationship: "Because of the usage [of the words] 'when it is absent, it does not exist'. (17)

The meaning is that even when jars, cloths, and so forth are non-existent—as seen in such linguistic usages as "there is no jar in the house," "there is no cloth," "the letter *u* has not been heard before," "the cloth was," or "the cloth will be"—the word [denoting them] has neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*) with that non-existent jar and so on. This is the intended sense. || 17 ||
What follows from this? To this he says: "The word and its meaning are unrelated. (18)
If there is no conjunction between word and object, then it follows that this means word and object are indeed without any relation.

Now, one might ask: why could there not be one of the two relations, namely conjunction or inherence? To this he says: "Because [the word] is neither conjoined with the staff nor inherent in the particular. (19)

There are two types of cognition: "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*) and "an elephant is a *kuñjara*. Of these, the first arises from conjunction (*saṃyoga*), while the second arises from inherence (*samavāya*). The cognition [of "elephant"] is dependent on inherence because the specific part, the trunk (*hasta*), is inherent in the elephant; for one who possesses a trunk by way of being its inherent substrate (*samavāyin*) is an "elephant. This is due to the particularity (*viśeṣa*).

The state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) belongs to the particularities (*viśeṣa*) alone through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), such as in the case of hands and so forth, but not even to threads and the like; for there is no cognition such as "the cloth possesses threads" where the part functions as a qualifier. Likewise, there is no cognition such as "the object possesses the word 'jar'. Thus, the point is that between the word and the object there is neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*). || 19 ||
Now, if there is neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*) between word and meaning, then by what relation does a word convey a specific meaning? To this, he says:
"The cognition of meaning from a word is based on convention (*sāmayika*). (20)

Regarding the term *sāmayika*: *samaya* is the convention (*saṅketa*) of the Lord, taking the form: "From this word, this meaning is to be understood. Whatever word has been conventionally established by the Blessed Lord for a particular meaning, that word conveys that meaning. Thus, the very will of the Lord is the relationship between word and meaning; that [will] is the *samaya*, and [the relationship] is dependent upon it—this is the sense. For example, whatever medicinal herb is crushed by the tips of the fangs of a mongoose destroys all snake venom.

And that convention is sometimes grasped through linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). For example, when an employer says, "Bring a jar," an onlooker child infers the knowledge of the person being employed as he brings the object with a neck and a bulbous body: "This activity of his is produced by knowledge, because it is an activity, like my own activity. And that knowledge is produced by this sentence, because it occurs immediately after it; thus, through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*), the child acquires proficiency regarding objects such as jars and cloths, concluding: "This object with a neck and a bulbous body, which is the object of this knowledge, is denoted by the word 'jar'."

In some cases, it arises directly from the words of a reliable person (*āptavākya*), as in: "This object, possessing a shell-like neck, is denoted by the word 'jar' (*ghaṭa*). In some cases, it arises from analogy (*upamāna*), such as: "A *gavaya* is similar to a cow," "As is a bean (*mudga*), so is the *mudgaparṇī* plant," or "As is a black gram (*māṣa*), so is the *māṣaparṇī* plant"—these being examples of analogy based on similarity (*sādharmyopamāna*). In some cases, it arises even from a statement of censure (*nindā*), as for instance, upon hearing the censuring words: "The camel is superior [in size], with very long lips, a long neck, eating hard thorns, and the lowest of animals," one perceives an animal of that kind and acquires the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that "this is a camel."

In some cases, it occurs through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a well-known term, as for example, upon hearing the sentence, "The honey-bee drinks nectar in the interior of a blossomed lotus," there arises [the cognition]: "This is that which is denoted by the word 'honey-bee,' because it is the agent of drinking nectar in the interior of a blossomed lotus"; or likewise, "The *pika* sings sweetly in the mango tree."

This [cognition] is either inference or verbal testimony itself, serving as the means of acquisition (vyutpādaka) through the power of co-referentiality with well-known words; or it is a specific type of analogy (upamāna), because of the application (*upanaya*) of the common property of being a honey-drinker to other individual entities such as bees.
The followers of Bhaṭṭa (Tautātikas) hold that the convention (*samaya*) resides in the universal (*jāti*) alone, since the individual is presented merely by implication (*ākṣepa*).

The Prābhākaras maintain that there is a capacity (*śakti*) for both the universal and the individual, but while the capacity regarding the universal must be known, the capacity regarding the individual is effective simply by its existence in its own nature (*svarūpasat*).

The elders maintain that the referent of a word (*padārtha*) consists of the individual, the configuration, and the genus (*vyaktyākṛtijātayaḥ*), and that this is precisely the power (*śakti*) [of the word]. This is the case for words such as "cow" (*gav-ādi*). However, regarding words denoting qualities, actions, and so forth, it has been explained in detail in the *Mayūkha* that their referents consist only of the genus and the individual. (20)

Now, having reached the turn of the enumeration, [the author] states both *paratva* (remoteness) and *aparatva* (nearness) in a single passage for the sake of clarity of the student's intellect and for the sake of conciseness, since they are the causes of mutually connected worldly transactions:
"That which is remote and that which is near [are established] by means of two things situated in the same direction and at the same time, which are respectively distant and proximate. (21)

"Far and near" (*paramaparam*) is an expression where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is emphasized; "is produced" (*utpadyate*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Alternatively, "far and near" refers to the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*); here too, "is" (*iti*) is to be supplied. "In the same direction" (*ekadikkau*) means those two [objects] which have a single direction; the meaning is "by means of two masses (*piṇḍa*) situated in the same direction. Even objects occupying the same location are in the same direction, yet priority and posteriority (*paratvāparatve*) are neither produced nor conventionally designated by them; therefore, it is said "by means of those that are proximate and remote" (*sannikṛṣṭaviprakṛṣṭābhyām*).

Proximity (*sannikarṣa*) is the smallness of the conjunction with what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyogālpatva*), while remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) is its abundance; the meaning is "by means of those two. By this, the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) has been stated. However, the conjunction between space and the object is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). For instance, in the case of a person facing east, priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparātva*) arise in respect to two objects situated in the east, depending on the greater number of conjunctions with what is conjoined in one object and the smaller number of such conjunctions in the other. (The non-inherent cause has thus been stated.)

Regarding the phrase "by means of the near and the distant": by means of the object (*viṣaya*), he indicates the cognition (*pratyaya*) which possesses that object. Thus, it is stated that relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Priority and posteriority arise only between two things situated in the same direction; therefore, they do not arise everywhere. Relative cognition arises for only a single observer; therefore, they do not arise in every case. Due to the restriction of relative cognition, they do not arise at all times.

Since the two [qualities] produced by the power of their causes are established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayatva*); for otherwise, they would neither arise nor be perceived. Indeed, if there were mutual dependence, both would fail to arise and remain unperceived; yet "remoteness" (*paratva*) and "proximity" (*aparatva*) are perceived, and their perception cannot occur without their arising.

"By two [factors] belonging to the same time"—this is said with reference to temporal priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*). In this context, "by two belonging to the same time" means: those two bodies, such as that of a youth and that of an elder, which possess one and the same time, namely the present, are "belonging to the same time"; it is by these two that [priority and posteriority are produced]. Proximity (*sannikarṣa*) consists in having a birth separated by fewer vibrations of the sun.

In this case as well, by means of the object (*viṣaya*), one indicates the cognition of the possessor of the quality (*viṣayin*); therefore, the two bodies—the young and the old—are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*), while the conjunction of time with the body is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). The cognition that [the one] was born separated by fewer solar revolutions is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) for "remoteness" (*aparatva*), and the cognition that [the other] was born separated by more solar revolutions is the instrumental cause for "nearness" (*paratva*). Furthermore, these qualities of nearness and remoteness arise even between two bodies situated in indefinite directions and locations.

In that regard, the destruction of spatial priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) occurs in seven ways. However, their production occurs simultaneously; otherwise, there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). [The seven ways are: from the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*); from the destruction of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); from the destruction of the substance (*dravya*), which is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); from the destruction of both the efficient and non-inherent causes; from the destruction of both the efficient and inherent causes; from the destruction of both the inherent and non-inherent causes; and from the destruction of the efficient cause, the non-inherent cause, and the inherent cause.
