In that case, the production of "remoteness" (paratva) occurs first from the destruction of the relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi); then follows the cognition of the generality of remoteness; thereafter comes the destruction of the relative cognition; and from its destruction, the destruction of remoteness occurs at the time of the cognition of the substance qualified by remoteness. All this is to be inferred in the same manner as the destruction of duality (dvitva).

Also from the destruction of the non-inherent cause (*upamāyikāraṇa*): for instance, at the very moment the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises, there is motion (*karma*) in the object (*piṇḍa*) which is the substratum of "remoteness" (*paratva*). Then, at the very moment the production of "remoteness" occurs, there is disjunction (*vibhāga*) between the direction (*dik*) and the object. Then, when there is the cognition of the generality (*sāmānyajñāna*) of "remoteness," there is the destruction of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between the direction and the object. Subsequently, from the cognition of the generality, there is the destruction of the relative cognition; and simultaneously with the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the object, there is the destruction of both "remoteness" and "nearness" (*aparatva*).

In that case, since the destruction of the cognition of relative distance (*apekṣābuddhi*) occurs simultaneously with the destruction of "remoteness" (*paratva*), it cannot be its cause of destruction. Now, one might object: "If qualities were destroyed even by the destruction of their non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), then there would be great confusion—for instance, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) would be destroyed by the destruction of the contact between the self and the mind. This is not so; for "remoteness" is pervaded by spatial distance, and when the substratum of "remoteness" moves elsewhere, that distance ceases to exist, making the cessation of "remoteness" necessary.

And since there is no other cause of destruction at that time, it is by the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*) that the destruction of conjunction itself is postulated as the cause of destruction. No such cause is postulated for mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth, because their effects—such as memory and pleasure—are observed even after a long interval. This is merely an illustration; distance (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) are also destroyed by the destruction of the conjunction with the limiting object (*avadhi*) and the observer (*draṣṭṛ*), for the underlying logic is the same.

In some cases, the destruction of "remoteness" (paratva) occurs even from the destruction of its inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa). To illustrate: when, by an action produced in a constituent part of the body, there is a disjunction from another part, at that very moment the relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) arises; from that disjunction follows the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the body, and the production of remoteness; in the subsequent moment, from the destruction of the conjunction comes the destruction of the substance, while the cognition of the generality (sāmānyajñāna) of remoteness arises; and from the destruction of the substance comes the destruction of remoteness and the destruction of the relative cognition due to the cognition of the generality. Thus, because these events are simultaneous, the destruction of remoteness does not result from the destruction of the relative cognition.

In some cases, the destruction of "priority" (paratva) results from both the destruction of the substance and the destruction of the relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi). For example: first, there is the production of action in a part of the aggregate and the production of the relative cognition; then, the disjunction from another part and the production of priority; then, the destruction of the originative conjunction and the cognition of the universal (sāmānyajñāna); then, the destruction of the substance and the destruction of the relative cognition; and finally, the destruction of that priority.

In some cases, the destruction of "remoteness" (paratva) occurs through the destruction of both the substance and its conjunction; for example: when there is a disjunction of the parts of the substance, at that very moment there arises the action of the whole (piṇḍa-karma) and the relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi). Immediately thereafter, there arise the destruction of the conjunction of the parts, the disjunction of the whole from the direction [of space], and the production of "remoteness. Then follow the non-destruction of the substance and the destruction of the conjunction of the whole with the direction, as well as the cognition of the generality (sāmānyabuddhi) of "remoteness. Subsequently, through the destruction of the substance and the destruction of the conjunction of the whole with the direction, there is the destruction of "remoteness," and through the cognition of the generality, there is the destruction of the relative cognition.

In some cases, the destruction of "remoteness" (paratva) results from both the destruction of conjunction and the destruction of the relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi). For example: [first] the production of remoteness and the motion of the object; [then] the cognition of the universal and the disjunction; [next] the destruction of the relative cognition and the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the object; and finally, the destruction of remoteness.

In some cases, destruction results from the destruction of the inherent cause (*samavāyin*), the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyin*), and the efficient cause (*nimitta*). For example: the production of priority (*paratva*), the disjunction of the parts of the body, and the motion of the body occur simultaneously; immediately thereafter, the cognition of the generality of priority, the destruction of the conjunction of the parts, and the disjunction of the body from space occur; and immediately after that, from the simultaneous occurrence of the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), the destruction of the substance, and the destruction of the conjunction of the body with space, there follows the destruction of spatial priority or posteriority (*aparatva*).

However, for temporal priority and posteriority produced by time (*kāla*), there is no destruction [of the qualities] due to the destruction of their non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Just as for spatial [priority and posteriority], the destruction of proximity (*sannikarṣa*) and remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) occurs upon the destruction of the conjunction between space and the substance, it is not so for the temporal ones. Regarding those two [temporal ones], three positions should be inferred as before: [destruction] from the destruction of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), from the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), and from both. || 21 ||
He states the distinction regarding temporal priority and posteriority: "From the priority of the cause and from the posteriority of the cause. (22)

Time is the cause of remoteness (*paratva*) and nearness (*aparatva*). Regarding these two, remoteness and nearness, [the text] has figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) stated "conjunction with time which is the non-inherent cause of remoteness" and "conjunction with time which is the non-inherent cause of nearness"; otherwise, there would be the fault of non-connection (*ananvaya*), for remoteness and nearness are certainly not produced by remoteness and nearness themselves. Therefore, by figurative indication, the meanings of the words "remoteness" and "nearness" are the conjunctions with time that produce them. || 22 ||
Now, one might ask: "Why should there not be remoteness even in that which is remote, and proximity even in that which is proximate?
To this, he says: "The absence of remoteness and proximity in [the qualities of] remoteness and proximity has been explained by [the absence of] smallness and largeness. (23)
Actions [are purified] by actions. || 24 ||
Qualities are [known] by their groups. || 25 ||
These sūtras have already been explained previously; they are not explained here. || 23–25 ||

It has been stated that properties such as priority and posteriority reside only in corporeal substances, while knowledge, pleasure, and so forth reside in the self. In this regard, following the student's desire to know what exactly inherence (*samavāya*) is, the author sets aside *buddhi*—even though it was due for its turn in the order of enumeration—and instead states the investigation of inherence:
"That from which [the cognition] 'this is here' arises with respect to cause and effect is inherence. (26)

The phrase "of cause and effect" is an illustration; it should also be understood as referring to "that which is not cause and effect. As it is stated in the treatise titled *Padārthapraveśaka*: "Inherent relation (*samavāya*) is that connection between things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relation of the supported and the support, which is the cause of the cognition 'it is here'."

The non-existence of two unrelated things is *ayutasiddhi* (inseparable inherence). Just as the cognitions "curd in this bowl" and "jujube fruits in this bowl" arise, so too do the cognitions "the cloth is in these threads," "the mat is in these *vīraṇa* grasses," "qualities and actions are in this substance," "cowness is in this cow," "knowledge is in this self," and "sound is in this ether" arise; these cannot arise without a relation. Therefore, it is inferred that some relation exists.

Nor is this [inherence] merely conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because the causes of its production—such as the action of one of two things and so forth—are absent; because it does not terminate in disjunction (*vibhāga*); because the related entities are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*); because it is to be inferred only by virtue of having a fixed substratum; and because it is imperceptible, unitary, and eternal. Now, if inherence is one, then there arises the undesirable consequence of confusion (*saṅkara*) among categories such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) and the like, since the inherence of "actionness" (*karmatva*) and so forth would be possible in a substance. This is not so, for there is no confusion precisely because of the restriction regarding the container and the contained (*ādhārādheya-niyama*).

Although the very same inherence that constitutes substantiality (dravyatva) also constitutes quality-ness (guṇatva), action-ness (karmatva), and so forth, nevertheless, substance is not the substratum for these [qualities and actions], because they are not perceived there. Substantiality is perceived only in substances, quality-ness only in qualities, and action-ness only in actions, and nowhere else; this restriction is established precisely through the observation of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). Just as, despite the existence of a particular conjunction between a bowl and curd, the bowl alone is the substratum and not the curd—such being the restriction regarding the relationship of locus and located (āśrayāśrayibhāva)—so it is here as well.

In this case as well, the restriction will be established precisely through the distinction between the power of the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the power of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*); for it is not the case that by means of a substance (*dravya*), action-ness (*karmatva*) and so forth are manifested in the same way that substance-ness (*dravyatva*) is. As it has been said:
"Consciousness alone, the blessed one, is our refuge in the apprehension of reality."

For there is no contrary cognition regarding the nature of being a substratum; indeed, it does not occur that "substance is the action," nor does it occur that "the threads are in the cloth. By this [principle], even though color inheres in air, the status of being a substratum in the expression "color in air" is not cognized as belonging to the air. Therefore, the inherent power of its own nature (*svabhāva-śakti*) alone is the regulator in all cases. And this [substratumhood] is eternal, because it is without cause.

For there is a rule that the production of entities occurs from an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), while the efficient and non-inherent causes follow it; likewise, whatever may be the inherent cause of inherence itself, would that be through another inherence or through that very same inherence? Not the first, because it would lead to an infinite regress. Nor the second, for it is not possible for that very same inherence to be inherent in itself, as that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

If it is asked how there can be the cognition "the inherence of the cloth in the threads" and "the inherence of color in the cloth," [the answer is] that it is by way of the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*), because if another inherence were admitted, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. If it is then argued, "In that case, the cognition 'here is the color of the cloth' would also occur through the relation of essential identity alone; what is the need for inherence?"—we say no, because in that instance there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against the existence of an additional relation.

If it is argued that in this case as well—namely, in the instance "there is an absence of a jar on this ground"—there must be either inherence (*samavāya*) or some other relation, we say no; for that [absence] is established by the relation of essential nature (*svarūpa-sambandha*) alone. Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of a jar—which are eternal and inherent in multiple loci—would become universals (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), being an effect inherent [in its substrate], would follow as being perishable; and antecedent absence (*prāgabhāva*), being an unproduced entity inherent [in its substrate], would follow as being imperishable. Nor is "being an entity" (*bhāvatva*) the determining factor here, because "being an entity" is precisely what is to be proven.
The Bhaṭṭas maintain that even in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), there exists another relation called "qualificative relation" (*vaiśiṣṭya*).

In that regard, if there were only one single qualificative relation for all individual instances of non-existence, then it would follow that even where a jar is present, there would be the cognition of the non-existence of a jar; for the presence of the qualificative relation of the non-existence of a cloth would necessarily entail the presence of the qualificative relation of the non-existence of a jar. If it is argued that the jar itself is the preventer of the cognition of the non-existence of a jar in that location, [we reply] no, because by virtue of the relation of qualificative inherence (*vaiśiṣṭya-sambandha*), the absence of the preventer itself would still exist there.

Nor is it the case that the very nature of the substratum is such that the manifestation of the absence of a jar does not occur therein, for the absence of the jar is perceived in that very place immediately after the jar has been removed. If it is argued: "In your view as well, why is there no cognition of possessing color immediately after the destruction of color, given that inherence (*samavāya*) is eternal and unitary?", [we reply: this is explained by the fact that such a cognition does not arise precisely because the color has been destroyed. Let us leave it at that, for the critique of inherence has already been released by the rays of direct perception (*pratyakṣamayūkha*). || 26 ||
Establishing its distinction from the five categories beginning with substance, he says:
"The negation of [the properties of] substantiality and quality has been explained by means of existence (bhāva). (27)

Existence (*bhāva*) means being (*sattā*). Just as being is not identical with substance (*dravya*) and the rest because it is cognized by a distinct cognition, so too inherence (*samavāya*) is distinct from substance and the rest for that very same reason. The mention of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) is illustrative; "action-ness" (*karmatva*) and the others should also be understood in this way. (27)
It establishes oneness—by way of its true nature. || 28 ||

The word "explained" (*vyākhyātam*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Its reality (*tattvam*), that is, its oneness (*ekatvam*), is explained by way of its existence (*bhāvena*, *sattayā*). Just as a single existence (*sattā*) is the cause for the application of the cognition of "being" (*sad-buddhi*) everywhere, so too inherence (*samavāya*) is one and the same, being the cause for the application of the cognition of "inherence" (*samaveta-buddhi*) everywhere. This is because there is no distinction in its own marks (*svaliṅga*) and because there is an absence of specific marks (*viśeṣaliṅga*); for we do not perceive any specific mark or differentiating characteristic of inherence by which we might admit its plurality (*nānātva*).

For this very reason, it is eternal; for even when there is a difference in place, time, and so forth, it is impossible for that which is non-different [from its relata] to be non-eternal, just as existence (*sattā*) itself is not. Now, an objection may be raised: "If this inherence (*samavāya*) is merely a relation, then there would be a separation between the threads and the cloth, or between the cloth and its color. This is not so, because separation is untenable due to the absence of separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*). Indeed, there is no such thing as the existence of color and the colored object, or of a part and the whole, while they remain unconnected, such that a separation could occur. If it is argued that "separate establishment itself is what is being posited," we say no, because such a possibility is sublated by the fact that it is never experienced in that way.

The Prābhākaras maintain that inherence (*samavāya*) is manifold and non-eternal. But that is untenable; for there is no such cognition as "the inherence of color has perished," whereas there is the cognition "color has perished. The Naiyāyikas hold that inherence is perceptible. That too is untenable; for inherence is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), because, while being distinct from the self, it is an entity that does not inhere [in another], like the mind or like time and so forth. (28)
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the seventh chapter in the *Śāṅkara Vaiśeṣikasūtropaskāra*.

This seventh chapter is now complete. The deviation from the [original] order was due to the desire to satisfy the curiosity of the students; now, he resorts to the order of the enumeration [of categories]. Among these, the examination of cognition (*buddhi*) is the subject matter of the eighth chapter. Cognition was previously mentioned for the purpose of establishing the self (*ātman*); reminding [the reader] of that, he says:
Knowledge regarding substances has been explained. || 1 ||

Regarding the phrase "in the substances" (*dravyeṣu*), the author indicates the third chapter by means of its subject matter (*viṣaya*). The meaning is that cognition (*jñāna*) has been explained by these two sūtras: "The well-known [nature] of the sense organs and their objects is the cause for [inferring] something other than the sense organs and their objects," and "That which is produced from the contact of the self, the sense organs, and the objects is [cognition] distinct [from them]. In that regard, the mention of synonyms—namely, "intellect" (*buddhi*), "apprehension" (*upalabdhi*), "cognition" (*jñāna*), and "notion" (*pratyaya*)—is intended to refute the Sāṅkhya position regarding the definition of intellect in their own system (*samānatantre*).

For the Sāṅkhya school indeed determines the distinct meanings of terms such as *buddhi* (intellect) and so forth. To explain: "Prakṛti is the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; and it is one and only one. The *puruṣas* (spirits), however, are fundamentally diverse; they are immutable, eternal, non-transforming, and have the nature of eternal consciousness. They are like the lame because they do not undergo transformation, while Prakṛti is like the blind because she is insentient."

When Prakṛti develops a desire for the enjoyment of objects and a longing to perceive the distinction between Prakṛti and Puruṣa, it then undergoes transformation under the influence of its proximity to Puruṣa. Its first transformation is the intellect (*buddhi*), which is a specific internal organ. The intellect itself is the Great One (*mahat*); as it has been said: "From Prakṛti arises the Mahat."

And that intellect (*buddhi*) is stainless like a mirror; its transformation into the form of an object—such as the forms "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth"—through the channel of the external senses, is called "cognition" (*vṛtti*). When this cognition, residing within the translucent intellect, is not distinguished from the conscious *puruṣa*, there arises a specific kind of conceit, "I know," and that itself is "apprehension" (*upalabdhi*).

A "cognition" (*pratyaya*) is that specific transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*) itself, which takes the form of pleasure, pain, and so forth, arising solely through the channel of the sense organs from contact with objects such as garlands and sandalwood paste. For this very reason, all things—knowledge, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*)—are merely specific transformations of the intellect; existing in *prakṛti* itself in a subtle state, they manifest and disappear due to differences in their conditions.

"But the person (puruṣa), like a polished leaf, reflects [the object] in the intellect (buddhi) without being attached"—this which they maintain is refuted by the following argument, indicated by the citation of a synonymous term as a proof. For instance: if the word *buddhi* is derived in the instrumental sense (*karaṇavyutpatti*) as "that by which one cognizes," then it ultimately amounts to nothing other than the mind (*manas*). And the mind is not perceptible; however, the intellect (*buddhi*), on the other hand, is indeed known through perception, as in the experience "I am cognizing."

Furthermore, cognition and the like are not properties of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), because they are established as being properties of the agent alone; for there occurs the manifestation [of these states] in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "I-ness," as in: "I know," "I perceive," and "I apprehend. If it is argued that this is merely a conceit (*abhimāna*), we reply that there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) of their reality.

If it is argued that the soul’s (*puruṣa*) state of being an immovable substrate (*kūṭasthatva*), which consists in its not being a receptacle for adventitious qualities (*āgantuka-dharma*), is itself the subverting argument [against the existence of such qualities], we say no; for even if it were a receptacle for adventitious qualities, its eternity (*nityatva*) is still possible. Indeed, the substratum of qualities (*dharmin*) and the qualities themselves (*dharma*) are not one and the same reality, such that the production and destruction of the qualities would necessarily entail the production and destruction of the substratum. Thus, he who experiences volition (*cetayate*) is the very same who perceives, knows, apprehends, and ascertains; therefore, the postulation of a separate entity [distinct from consciousness] is not tenable. This is the general direction [of the argument]. || 1 ||

And that knowledge is of two kinds: *vidyā* (valid cognition) and *avidyā* (invalid cognition). *Vidyā* is fourfold, characterized as perceptual, inferential, memorial, and scriptural (*ārṣa*). *Avidyā* is also fourfold, characterized as doubt, error, dream, and non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*). Among these, that which is inferential is not born of the senses; why is this so? He says: "In that regard, the self and the mind are imperceptible" (Sūtra 2).

Here, "self" (*ātman*) refers either to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) or to one's own self (*svātman*). Regarding one's own self, it is stated that it is not perceptible because it is obscured by occasional mental cognitions of the form "I," such as "I am fair," "I am thin," or "I have long arms. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), there is the inclusion of other substances such as space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), direction (*diś*), air (*vāyu*), and atoms (*paramāṇu*).

That which arises from the senses (*indriyajam*) is also twofold: pertaining to the omniscient and pertaining to the non-omniscient. That pertaining to the omniscient is the knowledge of the multitude of various objects through the proximity characterized by *yogaja-dharma*; for instance, atoms [are established] because they are knowable (*prameyatva*), nameable (*abhidheyatva*), and existent (*sattva*).

If it is argued that this is not so because of the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), since magnitude (*mahattva*) is a cause for perception yet atoms are not large, and since possession of color (*rūpavattva*) is a cause for visual perception yet the directions (*diś*) and so forth are not colored—then we say no. For that [perception] is possible through the mind alone when assisted by the merit born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*), or through the eyes and other senses when aided by that same merit. Indeed, the merit born of yoga possesses an inconceivable power; it does not require any other auxiliary, unlike [the argument] "this person is not an expert in Mīmāṃsā because he is a human being like me," which is unconvincing due to its lack of a subverting tarka against the contrary case.
Furthermore, non-omniscient perception is of two kinds: conceptual (*savikalpaka*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

Kīrti, Diṅnāga, and others maintain that conceptual cognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For instance, such cognition has an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression; however, no connection between an object and a verbal expression—that is, a name—is possible by virtue of which a cognition could be colored by a name such as "jar" or "cloth."

Furthermore, a connection between an existing particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and that which is non-existent is impossible, nor is that which is non-existent an object of the senses. Therefore, sensory observation (*ālocana*) is produced by the sense organ, and through the power of that observation, conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) arises; as it functions toward that object, it is called "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).

But this is untenable; for it would follow that [the cognition] has an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression and yet is produced by sense-object contact and thus constitutes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—this is a case of "doubtful negative concomitance" (*sandigdhavyatirekitva*). Furthermore, the qualification by a name is indeed possible in visual cognition, because, as in the case of "fragrant sandalwood," there is the possibility of "presented perception" (*upanītabhāna*).

Alternatively, the specific connection with a name does not appear in perceptual cognition; rather, there is merely the recollection of the name. It is only when recollected that the name serves to differentiate the object, just as the recollection of the counter-positive functions in the cognition of an absence (*abhāva*). Furthermore, since universals (*jāti*) and other categories have already been established as real entities, even determinate perception (*savikalpaka*) is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it arises from the contact of the sense organ with its object. If it is asked, "But since indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) neither initiates linguistic usage nor is itself an object of linguistic usage, what is the proof for its existence?", the answer is: determinate perception itself [serves as the proof].

For that [cognition] is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), and it does not arise without the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*); for it has been established that in the case of a qualified cognition, the causes are the cognition of the qualifier, the sensory contact with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and the non-apprehension of the non-connection between those two. || 2 ||
In order to clarify where knowledge arises, how it arises, and what its causes are, he says:
"In the exposition of knowledge, the procedure for the accomplishment of knowledge has been stated. (3)

Regarding that which is to be designated by another cognition—namely, what its mode is, what its object is, and what its property is—when the designation of that cognition must be made, the "method of accomplishment" (niṣpattividhi), the "method of origination" (utpattividhi), or the "mode of origination" (utpattiprakāra) of the cognition is stated; this is the meaning of "it is said. This is because the suffix *kta* is prescribed in the sense of an initial action (*ādikarman*). || 3 ||
He states what the method of accomplishment is like:
"Among those qualities that are proximate in their sequence, substance is the cause for the accomplishment of knowledge. (4)

Regarding the cognition that arises with respect to qualities such as color and so forth, and actions such as upward throwing and so forth, the substance is the cause; since both of these are apprehended only as residing in a suitable substance, it is the suitability of the substance alone that is the governing factor there. Furthermore, their contact is necessarily constituted by the substance, because they are apprehended through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*).

Although the scent of the unsuitable parts of the campaka flower and the camphor particles attached to it is perceived, nevertheless, in that case, the substance itself—which serves as the constituent of the contact—is what is required, even if it is unsuitable [for direct perception]. Although the suitability of a substance is not the governing factor in the perception of sound, nevertheless, since the sound is perceived as inhering in that very [substance], that [substance] alone is the governing factor. If it is asked, "Why is the postulation of an unseen contact made?", the answer is no; because knowledge is produced, for a cause must necessarily be postulated on the basis of its effect—this is the sense.
Furthermore, he states the method for the accomplishment of knowledge:
"Because there is an absence of generalities and particulars within generalities and particulars, knowledge arises from that very [absence]. (5)

Existence (*sattā*) is the universal; its particulars are substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*). Likewise, the particulars of these universals are earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth, form-ness (*rūpatva*) and so forth, and throwing upwards-ness (*utkṣepaṇatva*) and so forth.

In that regard, for universals residing in substances, there arises cognition through all the sense organs from that very same suitable substrate and from its basis, namely, conjunction-inherence (*saṃyukta-samavāya*); likewise, for universals residing in qualities and actions, there arises cognition through all the sense organs from that very same suitable substrate and from their respective bases, namely, conjunction-inherence-inherence (*saṃyukta-samaveta-samavāya*) and inherence-inherence (*samaveta-samavāya*). Furthermore, in the case of the universal "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*), [cognition occurs] through conjunction-inherence-inherence; and in the case of "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*), "oneness" (*ekatva*), and so forth, it occurs through inherence-inherence.

Cognition through all the sense organs arises from existence (*sattā*) due to inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), inherence in what is inherent in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), and inherence in what is inherent (*samavetasamavāya*). As for quality (*guṇatva*), neither inherence in what is conjoined nor mere inherence constitutes the immediate causal contact (*pratyāsatti*). Now, an objection is raised: the restriction [implied by the word] "only" (*avadhāraṇa*)—that it arises "only" from the contact with its own substratum—is untenable; for since there indeed exist further universals and particulars within universals and particulars such as "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*), the contact with those must also be a cause. To this he replies: "Because of the absence of further universals and particulars."

For universals and particulars do not reside within other universals and particulars, as that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress. Their mutual distinction is perceived through their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), or else through the convergence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) characterized by existing in all cows while not existing in non-cows. The same applies to "pot-ness" and so forth. || 5 ||

Now, one might object: "Just as there is no cognition independent [of other factors] regarding universals and particulars because of the absence of further universals and particulars therein, why should it not be the case that cognition regarding substances, qualities, and actions is likewise independent? To this he replies:
"In the case of substances, qualities, and actions, [cognition] depends upon universals and particulars. (6)

The subject under discussion is that "knowledge arises. First of all, there exists a cognition characterized by substanceness (*dravyatva*), qualityness (*guṇatva*), and actionness (*karmatva*) with respect to substances, qualities, and actions. And since a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) arises from the sensory contact between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and the sense organ, the requirement of the generalities (*sāmānya*) and their particulars (*viśeṣa*) is necessary therein. For indeed, there occurs the qualified cognition: "This is a substance," "This is a quality," and "This is an action"—this is the intended meaning. || 6 ||
Is it then the case that even with respect to a substance, cognition depends solely on the general and the particular? To this he says:
"With respect to a substance, [cognition] depends on substance, quality, and action. (7)

The phrase "knowledge arises" is the subject under discussion. An example of such knowledge is: "A white bell-topped cow is walking. In this case, the substance (dravya) is the bell as the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa), "white" is the quality (guṇa), and "is walking" is the action (karma). Thus, the meaning is that there can be no cognition of a qualified object without first apprehending its qualifiers, nor can there be such cognition without a relation to the qualifiers; therefore, there is a dependence upon substance, quality, and action. || 7 ||
In that case, does this dependence on quality and action apply even to qualities and actions themselves? No, he says:
"Because there is an absence of quality and action within qualities and actions, there is no dependence on quality and action [in their case]. (8)

The word "knowledge" (jñāna) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Since there is no cognition of a quality-possessor with respect to a quality, nor a cognition of an action-possessor with respect to actions, there is no dependence on qualities or actions for the cognition directed toward them. The sense is that there is no quality in a quality, nor an action in actions, such that it could appear therein as a qualifier. || 8 ||

Now, raising the objection as to how there can be no dependence on quality and action when quality and action manifest themselves in the cognition of quality and the cognition of action, he begins another section:
"From the whiteness inherent [in the object] and from the cognition of whiteness, there arises the cognition of the white [object]; these two stand in the relation of cause and effect. (9)

By the expression "of that which inheres" (samavāyin), he states the causality of the relation; and thus, since there is no inherence of a quality in a quality and no inherence of an action in an action, there is no requirement for those [qualities or actions] in the cognition of them as such; however, they certainly exist as qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa) or as qualificands (viśeṣya).

And thus, it has been stated that in the cognition "the conch is white" and so forth, the inherence of whiteness, the quality of whiteness, and the cognition of the qualifier "whiteness" function as causes; likewise, the relation of the qualifier, the qualifier itself, and the cognition of that qualifier are the causes for the valid perceptual cognition of the qualified object. By this, everything previously stated is established. || 9 ||

[Objection: Just as in the case of "the one possessing a bell" (*ghaṇṭāvān*), the cognition of a substance is dependent upon [another] substance, so too in cases such as "this is a pillar" (*ayaṃ stambhaḥ*) or "this is a jar" (*ayaṃ kumbhaḥ*), the cognition of a substance is the cause for a cognition that has a substance as its qualifier; and if this were so, there would never be a cognition of a substance at the very outset. To this, he says:
"In the case of substances, [cognitions] are not mutually causal. (10)

The word "cognitions" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Even though the cognition of a jar occurs at a time subsequent to the cognition of a pillar, it is not the effect of the cognition of the pillar, because the pillar cannot function as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the jar. || 10 ||
Now, an objection is raised: "A sequence is observed among cognitions such as those of a jar and a cloth, and a sequence is necessarily constituted by a causal relationship. To this, he says:

"The sequence of cognitions such as those of a jar and a cloth arises from the non-simultaneity of their causes and from the sequence of those causes; it does not arise from a relationship of cause and effect [between the cognitions themselves]. (11)

The sequence of cognitions such as those of a jar or a cloth is dependent upon the sequence of their causes; it is not dependent upon a causal relationship [in the sense of one cognition being the cause of another]. To the question of how that sequence of causes itself arises, he says: "Because of the non-simultaneity of causes. The simultaneity of cognitions has been refuted; therefore, there can be no simultaneity even for the various causes of those cognitions. For if there were simultaneity of causes, then simultaneity of effects would also follow; and in that case, the principle that "the non-arising of simultaneous cognitions is the mark of the mind" (*manas*) would be largely undermined. This is the intended meaning. || 11 ||
Thus ends the first daily lesson of the eighth chapter in the *Śrī-Śāṅkara-Vaiśeṣika-Sūtropaskāra*.

In the second daily lesson of the eighth chapter, having described the method of production for perceptual cognition— both determinate (*savikalpaka*) and indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*)— the author now states a portion [of the system] in order to describe the perception of a qualified object as possessing a further qualification (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya-pratyakṣa*).
"This feeding was performed by you"—this [statement] depends upon cognition. (1)

First, with respect to a proximate object, the cognition "this" arises; and with respect to a remote object, the cognition "that" arises. With reference to the cognition that "this [agent] is independent in the action," there arises the cognition of agency colored by the notion of "by you. With reference to the cognition that [the object] is the domain of causal operation, there arises the cognition of "object" (karman) as in "it has been done. With reference to the cognition that "this one is the agent in the act of eating and this one is the instigator," there arises the command "feed him. With reference to the cognition that "this is the domain of the activity of the one to be directed and the director," there arises the cognition "him. In this manner, other cases as well should be inferred as being dependent upon cognition. || 1 ||
He states that this [causal relation] is indeed to be determined through positive and negative concomitance:
"Because [the effect] exists when [the cause] is perceived, and because it does not exist when [the cause] is not perceived. (2)

When this [object] is proximate to the cognition "this," when it is remote yet ascended upon the intellect as the object of the cognition "that," when it is the agent proximate to the cognition "by you," when it is the object of action (karman) in the cognition "done," when both the one to be enjoined and the enjoiner are the objects of the cognition "let him feed," and when the operation of both is the object of the cognition "him"—only when it is thus proximate does such a cognition arise. However, regarding objects that are not perceived, these cognitions do not manifest;
the meaning is that this is indeed to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). || 2 ||
Now he begins another section:
"The term 'object' (artha) refers to substances, qualities, and actions. (3)

The status of being an *artha* (object/purpose) for these substances, qualities, and actions has been stated by various rules; therefore, among those three, the convention of the Vaiśeṣikas is that they constitute an *artha*, because all three are presented by the word *artha*. This was stated by the teacher Praśastadeva: "And the state of being denotable by the word *artha* belongs to the three. (3)
He introduces another section: "The fivefold nature [of the body] with respect to substances has been refuted. (4)

The phrase "in the substances" (*dravyeṣu*) indicates the section defining the category of substance (*dravyapadārtha*). By the sūtra beginning with "of those that are perceptible and imperceptible" (*pratyakṣāpratyakṣāṇām*), the fivefold nature—that is, the nature consisting of the five elements—of the body and so forth has been prohibited and refuted. Just as the body does not have a manifold material cause (*nānāprakṛtikatva*), so it is for the sense organs such as the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*) which will be discussed hereafter. The point is that by this, their capacity to grasp specific, restricted qualities (*pratiniyataguṇagrāhakatva*) is established. || 4 ||
He states the purpose for which this was begun:
"Because of its abundance and because it possesses odor, earth is the primary cause in the cognition of odor. (5)

The term *gandhajñāna* means that by which odor (*gandha*) is known; this refers to the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*). In that [sense], earth (*pṛthivī*)—meaning the earth-element as the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*)—is the source. Why is this so? To this he says: "Because it possesses odor. For it has been stated that that which possesses odor cannot be produced from that which is odorless. And the fact that [the sense of smell] possesses odor is established because of the rule that external sense organs possess qualities belonging to the same class as their objects.

If that is so, then since there is no difference in their being composed of earth (*pārthivatva*), why is there this restriction—that the other parts of the body do not manifest odor (*gandha-vyañjakatva*) while the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*) alone does? To this he says: "Because of abundance" (*bhūyastvāt*). Abundance consists precisely in being composed of earthly parts that are not overwhelmed by parts of other substances. And this technical sense of "abundance" is also accepted in the sister system (*samānatantre*). || 5 ||
He extends this [principle] to the other sense organs as well:
"In the same way, water, fire, and air [are the objects of the tongue, eye, and skin], because there is no distinction in their tastes, forms, and touches. (Sūtra 6)

The phrase "the nature" (prakṛti) is understood to apply to the sense organs of taste, sight, and touch. Therefore, by respective order, water and the other elements are the respective natures of the tongue and the rest, because they grasp their own specific objects. In this rule as well, the principle of necessity (bhūyastva) alone is the governing factor. Furthermore, it has been stated that the proof for the tongue and the other senses possessing taste and so forth is precisely the rule that they possess specific qualities belonging to the same class as their objects of perception. Thus, the auditory organ (śrotra) is simply a portion of space delimited by the ear-cavity, which is assisted by a particular unseen merit (adṛṣṭa). || 6 ||
Thus ends the second Āhnika of the eighth Adhyāya in the *Śrī-Śaṅkara-Vaiśeṣika-Sūtropaskāra*.
And this eighth Adhyāya is completed.

Following the definition of ordinary perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa*) produced by the two types of contact—conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*)—he now states the ninth Adhyāya, which aims to explain ordinary perception produced by other types of proximity (*pratyāsatti*).
Because of the absence of activity, qualities, and designation, [the effect] is non-existent prior [to its production]. //1//

The word "effect" (*kāryam*) is to be supplied [as the subject]. "Prior" means prior to the production of the effect; the meaning is that the effect—such as a jar or a cloth—is non-existent [prior to its production] and is the counter-positive (*pratiyogī*) of the absence of its own producer at that time. The reason for this is: "due to the absence of action, quality, and designation."

If the effect, such as a jar, were existent even at that time [prior to its production], then it would be designated by way of possessing action and possessing qualities; just as when a jar has been produced, it is designated in such ways as "the jar stands," "the jar moves," or "this jar is seen to possess color. However, no such designation exists prior to its production. Therefore, it is understood that it was non-existent at that time.

And while the *vīraṇa* grass is being arranged, while the threads are being joined, while the clay is mounted on the wheel, and while the activities of the potter and others are proceeding, there arises for everyone in the world a perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣapratīti*) such as "here there will be a mat," "a cloth," or "a jar," because it occurs immediately after the opening of the eyes. Nor does the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) consisting of either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*) suffice here; therefore, the proximity of being a qualifier related to the sense organ (*indriyasambaddhaviśeṣaṇatā*) is the governing factor in this case.

Now, one might object that there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*): the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) exists when there is the cognition [of the relation], and the cognition [of the relation] exists when there is the status of being a qualifier. This is not so; for the status of being a qualifier is simply the very nature of those two [the qualifier and the qualified] which is capable of generating a cognition of their connection. And that [nature] exists even prior to the cognition. As it is stated in the *Nyāyavārttika*: "The relation of qualifier and qualified exists in the case of inherence (*samavāya*) and in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*)."

Furthermore, this antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) is the producer of its counter-positive (pratiyogin). For when a jar has been produced, that very same jar cannot be produced at that very same moment; even if other causes are present, the deficiency in the causal complex must be traced to the deficiency of its own antecedent non-existence. If it is argued that the jar itself acts as an obstacle to the production of that [same] jar, then its status as a cause must necessarily be admitted by virtue of being the absence of an obstacle.

If it is objected: "If the jar itself is its non-existence, then when the jar is destroyed, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of its re-emergence," we say no. This is because the destruction of the jar is also opposed to it; for indeed, while one contradictory entity exists, another contradictory entity cannot appear. Nor is there a spatial opposition between these two such that they might coexist at the same time, as is the case with "cowness" and "horseness. What then? Their opposition is temporal; and thus, how could they possibly exist simultaneously? || 1 ||
He states that another type of non-existence is established by the force of cognition:
"existent and non-existent" (sadasat) || 2 ||

Just as the non-existence of an effect prior to the operation of its cause is established by both perception and inference, so too, immediately after the operation of a destroyer such as a mallet, the very same effect—such as a jar—is established by perception and inference itself as being "non-existent now," despite having existed [previously]. For there occurs the cognition: "The jar is destroyed," or "The letter *ga*, previously heard, does not exist now," and so forth; this is the intended meaning. || 2 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that it is the jar itself, in a particular state, that brings about the conventional usage of "destruction," and that there is no destruction of the jar other than the jar? To this, he says:
"[Destruction is] a different entity, because of the absence of activity, qualities, and designation for that which is non-existent. (3)

The word "existent" (sat) is the remainder of the sūtra. "Existent" is an entity distinct from the non-existent (asat). Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of the absence of action, quality, and designation. For even at the time of its destruction, a jar does not exist [in the same way]; there are no such designations as "the jar exists," "now the jar has color," or "bring the jar. Therefore, because of this difference in nature, the existent is an entity distinct from the non-existent. || 3 ||
Having established antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), he speaks in order to establish mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*):

"Where a jar or the like, though actually existent, is treated as non-existent, there the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*) is perceived. For indeed, there occurs the cognition: 'The horse is non-existent as a cow,' 'the cow is non-existent as a horse,' 'the cloth is non-existent as a jar,' 'the cloth is not a jar,' 'the cow is not a horse,' 'the horse is not a cow,' and so forth. Thus, in this case, the cow is possessed of the mutual non-existence of the horse, and the jar is possessed of the mutual non-existence of the cloth; it is mutual non-existence itself—another name for the absence of identity—that appears."

In this case, identity (*tādātmya*) is the delimiting property of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, this absence is co-locatable with its counter-correlate; for there occurs the cognition, "The pot is not the floor. And it is eternal, because identity between a pot and a cloth is never possible. (4)
Now he states the fourth non-existence, called absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva): "And whatever else is other than that which is non-existent, that too is non-existent. (5)

Therefore, that which is non-existent (asat) other than the three types of non-existence previously mentioned is absolute non-existence (*atyantāsattva*). In both instances, the term "non-existent" (*asat*) is a designation where the abstract quality (*bhāva*) is the primary referent. Among these, one "non-existent" is the subject (*uddeśya*) and the other "non-existent" is the predicate (*vidheya*). Thus, the final meaning is established as follows: that non-existence which is distinct from the three aforementioned types of non-existence is absolute non-existence.

In that regard, antecedent non-existence has a subsequent limit (the point of production), while destruction has a prior limit (the point of cessation). Mutual non-existence is co-located with its counter-positive, whereas absolute non-existence possesses characteristics distinct from all three; therefore, this is a fourth kind of non-existence. || 5 ||
Now he begins another section; therein, first regarding destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), he states the causal complex for its perception:
"It is non-existent, because there is no perception of it as having come into being, due to the memory of its prior existence, just like the perception of a contradictory object. (6)

By the phrase "asat" (non-existent), he refers to knowledge in the form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, there exists a perceptual cognition such as: "the jar is non-existent," "the jar has perished," or "now the jar is destroyed. In this regard, the example is "like the direct perception of a contradictory [object]. Just as there is a clear direct perception of a contradictory object such as a jar, so too is there one of its destruction. He states the reason for this: "because of the absence of direct perception of that which has occurred. This means because there is no direct perception of a jar or the like that has already arisen and then perished.

By this, he states "non-apprehension of the capable" (*yogyānupalabdhi*). In that regard, this reasoning (*tarka*) acts as an auxiliary: "If a jar were present here, it would be seen, just like the ground; yet it is not seen; therefore, it does not exist. He states another auxiliary: "from the memory of what has occurred" (*bhūtasmṛteḥ*). This refers to the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), such as the jar; thus, the "recollection of the counter-positive" is expressed. (6)

Extending the argument regarding the perceptibility of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) to prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), he says: "Likewise, because there is the perception of existence within non-existence. (Sūtra 7)

Although this term "non-existence" (abhāva) is general in application, by virtue of the context it refers specifically to prior non-existence (prāgabhāva). Just as there is perceptual knowledge regarding destruction (pradhvaṃsa), so too is there regarding prior non-existence. Why? Because existence is perceptible. Since an existing thing—such as a jar or a mat—is perceptible, that is, since it is made an object of perception through direct perception, [its prior non-existence is likewise perceived].

Alternatively, the meaning is that it is because the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the entity (*bhāva*), and the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) are perceptible, that is, they possess the requisite fitness (*yogyatva*). This is because, in the apprehension of a relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*), both the fitness of the locus and the fitness of the counter-positive are necessary conditions. By the word "and" (*ca*), the author combines the recollection of the counter-positive and the logical reasoning (*tarka*) already mentioned. Thus, even for a beginningless antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and an endless destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsa*), there is perceptibility provided there is merely the absence of specific qualifications [obstructing perception]. (7)
He states that mutual non-existence is perceptible: "By this, the non-existence of a jar, the non-existence of a cow, and the non-existence of a property are explained. (8)

By the phrase "by this," he extends the previously mentioned arguments regarding the recollection of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and the perception of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). The non-perception of what is perceptible (*yogyānupalambha*) is the same in all cases. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate what has been stated. By stating that even for a supersensible (*atīndriya*) property such as demerit (*adharma*), its mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) is perceptible in a locus such as pleasure or cognition, he demonstrates that in the apprehension of mutual absence, the perceptibility of the counter-correlate is not the determining factor; rather, the mere perceptibility of the locus is the determining factor.

Otherwise, how could the mutual absence of a *piśāca* in a pillar be apprehended by the thought "the pillar is not a *piśāca*"? For the non-apprehension of a *piśāca* as having the nature of the pillar is what apprehends that mutual absence; and since that non-apprehension is opposed to the existence of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), it would be impossible for there to be non-apprehension if the identity of the *piśāca* were present in the pillar.

If it is argued: "In this case, identity with a *piśāca* is not the counter-positive; what then? It is the *piśāca* itself. And since that [identity], even while residing in the pillar, is not perceived—just like gravity—the non-perception of that [identity] does not contradict the existence of the counter-positive," we say no. For, just as the non-perception of the counter-positive, the non-perception of the delimiting property of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) is also a cause for the apprehension of absence.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the apprehension of mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) is dependent upon the apprehension of counter-positiveness (pratiyogitva), and since counter-positiveness consists in being of the nature of the absence of mutual absence, the apprehension of mutual absence is itself dependent upon the apprehension of mutual absence? [Reply: No, for it has been stated that the factor governing that apprehension is simply a property known as not residing in the locus (adhikaraṇa), which serves as the delimiting condition (avacchedaka) of counter-positiveness. 8.

Now he states the perceptibility of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*): The cognition "this which existed [formerly] does not exist now" takes destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) as its object; it does not manifest the state of having previously existed (*bhūtatva*), but rather this perceptual cognition, which manifests only "this does not exist," takes absolute non-existence as its object. The term "not having existed" (*abhūta*) indicates that [destruction] has production and cessation as its objects; the fact that [absolute non-existence] is not a different entity is intended for that same purpose, just as one says "earth-ness does not exist in water" or "water-ness does not exist in earth."

For if earth-ness were present in a composite substance consisting of water, it would be perceived; yet it is not perceived. Therefore, one should see that here too there is the employment of reasoning (*tarka*) to conclude that it does not exist. And thus, when a thing will never exist at any time in a certain locus and has never existed there at any time, the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of that thing in that locus is to be understood. Furthermore, regarding things past and future, the cognition "it is not there" in that locus has as its objective support respectively the posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) and the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
For this very reason, this [absolute non-existence] is designated as being "absolute" and "pertaining to all three times. (9)

Now, one might object: "The absence of a jar in the house is not an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*), because a jar may exist there at some time; nor is it prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), since those two reside only in their own inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); nor is it an absolute absence itself characterized by production and destruction, because that would involve a contradiction—being both absolute and subject to production and destruction; nor is this simply a fourth kind of relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*), as that would undermine the threefold classification. To this, he says: "In the statement 'there is no jar in the house,' there is a negation of the house's relation to an existing jar. (10)

The relation of a jar with a house is conjunction (*saṃyoga*); its negation is [non-existence]. If that [conjunction] never occurs at any time with respect to the jar, then it is absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). If it will occur, it is antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); if it has occurred, it is destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).

If you argue that there must be a cognition such as "the contact with the jar does not exist in the house," what is the meaning of the statement "there must be a cognition"? If the intended meaning is that there must be a cognition having that [non-existence] as its object, then we accept this as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). If, however, it means a cognition that explicitly mentions that [non-existence], then the mention of the locus "in the house" itself results in the mention of the relation; for the nature of being a substratum (*ādhāratva*) consists precisely in the form of a relation between a property and its locus. So, does the jar actually exist there?

What is the meaning of "it exists" in that case—is it that [the jar] is inherent (*samaveta*) or conjoined (*saṃyukta*) there? Not the first, because a jar inherent there is absent. Not the second, because conjunction has been negated. If it is argued that, in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that jars and the like are purely positive (*kevalānvayi*), since any other conjunction or inherence with them is negated everywhere—this is not so, because the negation of both of those is itself the nature of the negation of the jar.

Is the pot and its conjunction one and the same reality, such that the negation of the pot’s conjunction would entail the negation of the pot? Or is the pot and the inherence of its conjunction one and the same reality, such that the affirmation of that [inherence] would constitute the affirmation of the pot? For it is not the case that wherever those two are negated, the pot is also present there, which would allow for its status as a purely positive (kevalānvayi) entity; rather, the negation of whatever is affirmed is indeed its negation.

Alternatively, the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of the jar in the house exists precisely by virtue of its being its inherent locus (*samavāyitva*), and that very absence is the object of the cognition "the jar does not exist in the house," just as [the absence] exists in the potsherd by virtue of [the jar’s] being its conjunct locus (*saṃyogitva*). If this were so, one might argue that the jar would be non-existent because it is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute absence that is purely positive (*kevalānvayin*); [the author replies: this would indeed be the case if [the jar] were non-existent everywhere by virtue of both being a conjunct locus and an inherent locus. This is the sense. || 10 ||
He begins another section:
"The perception of the self arises from a specific conjunction of the self and the mind within the self. (1.11)

The word "knowledge arises" is to be understood as the ellipsis. There are two kinds of yogis: those whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are concentrated, who are designated as "united" (*yukta*); and those whose internal organs are not concentrated, who are designated as "disunited" (*viyukta*). Among them, the "united" are those who, having fixed their minds with devotion upon the object to be directly realized, possess profound meditation (*nididhyāsana*); in them, knowledge arises regarding the self (*ātman*), the individual self (*svātman*), and the supreme self (*paramātman*). This is what is meant by "direct perception of the self."

The self (*ātman*) is "directly perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*), meaning that knowledge in which the self is the object of direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*). Although even people like us possess knowledge of the self at times, it is said to be "as if non-existent" because it is obscured by ignorance (*avidyā*). The phrase "from a specific contact between the self and the mind" means that this specific contact between the self and the mind is aided by merit (*dharma*) born of yoga (*yogaja*); [the knowledge arises] from that. || 11 ||
If it is asked: "How can there be omniscience for those whose knowledge is restricted to the self alone?", he says:

"Knowledge arises"—this follows from the context. The word "thus" (*tathā*) means by the mind alone, as assisted by *dharma* born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*). Regarding the four other substances—atoms, mind, air, space, direction, and time—the term "substance" (*dravya*) includes their qualities, motions, and universals; the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) includes the category of inherence (*samavāya*), even though it is perceived by direct perception; and the term "gravity," "elasticity," and so forth, includes those residing in the self, such as the effort that is the source of life, indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), mental impressions (*bhāvanā*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and the like—all being gathered through this causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Because the assistance provided by the dharma born of yoga is equal [in all cases], otherwise omniscience could not have been stated. || 12 ||
Having described the direct knowledge of those who are "joined" (yukta), he now speaks of those who are "disjoined" (viyukta):
"And of those whose internal organs are not concentrated, whose meditations have been withdrawn. (13)

"Those whose internal organs are not concentrated" (*asamāhitāntaḥkaraṇāḥ*) is explained by the term "those who have withdrawn their meditative absorption" (*upasaṃhṛtasamādhayaḥ*). Alternatively, to the question "In what way are their internal organs not concentrated?", he says: "those who have withdrawn their meditative absorption. Those by whom meditative absorption—consisting of *nididhyāsana* (repeated contemplation)—has been withdrawn, that is, set aside or abandoned, are so described.

For, by the power of their meditative absorption (*samādhi*), they attained the perfections of the body such as *aṇimā* and others characterized by transformative powers, as well as the perfections of the senses such as hearing from afar; and having gained full confidence even in their absorption, and having realized through the scriptures—such as "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released, then he shall be merged"—that there was no further duty remaining, they perceived that only worldly enjoyment remained to be performed, and thus [took birth] in various places, such as the continents and sub-continents, in various successive births.

Thinking, "As long as we enjoy the fruits of previously accumulated karma—whether in the form of horses, elephants, birds, serpents, and so forth, or even for as long as it may last, and whether through the state of gods, sages, or humans—we shall surely reach the stage that is free from all danger," those whose sensory powers are augmented by the force of dharma born of yoga perceive everything that is hidden or remote as if it were directly before their eyes. || 13 ||

Now, one might object: "In those [qualities and actions], there can be no mental cognition because the mind lacks independence regarding external objects; nor can it be produced by the external sense organs, since those [senses] grasp only objects that are in contact and present, and because they depend respectively on the emergence of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, as well as on light and other such conditions. Anticipating this objection, the author states—establishing the proximity [of the senses] with respect to certain categories—"From inherence in that [substance], [there is perception] of qualities and actions" (VS 4.1.14).

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "perceptual knowledge arises. If the material sense organs depend upon contact, then [knowledge] arises with respect to atoms, ether, space, and time through the inherence in that which is conjoined with one's own mind; and with respect to other substances, through the conjunction of the minds of various scholars who have been summoned for the purpose of experiencing a plurality of bodies, and through the inherence in that which is conjoined with them, knowledge of the qualities and so forth of those respective substances is produced. This has been stated in accordance with the ease of logical demonstration.

In reality, it is only the quality (*dharma*) born of yoga that constitutes the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) between the external sense organs and the mind; for by that alone all logical inconsistencies are pacified. The drinking of the ocean and the creation of the Daṇḍaka forest serve as the illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). || 14 ||
[The opponent asks: Is there [a capacity]? He says: No—because [the capacity] inheres in the self, it belongs to the qualities of the self. (15)

The subject under discussion is that direct perceptual knowledge arises for yogins. However, regarding qualities such as cognition (buddhi) and others which are inherent in the self, direct perceptual knowledge arises precisely through the relation of inherence-in-the-conjoined (saṃyuktasamavāya), just as it does for people like us; thus, in that case, there is no dependence on any other type of sensory contact. In this context, direct perception—whether worldly or transcendental—is knowledge produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object, which is non-erroneous, or else it is born from the object itself. The definition "direct perception is knowledge characterized by immediacy" applies commonly to both the worldly and the transcendental. || 15 ||
Thus ends the first daily lesson of the ninth chapter in the *Śāṅkara-Vaiśeṣika-Sūtropaskāra*.
The Second Daily Lesson of the Ninth Chapter.

In this manner, in the preceding daily lesson, perception belonging to yogis and perception belonging to non-yogis have been examined with respect to their causes, their essential nature, and their definitions. Regarding the two-fold division of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) into perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*laiṅgika*), he now begins the examination of the inferential.
"This is the effect of that," "this is the cause of that," "conjoined," "contradictory," and "inherent"—such is inference based on signs (lingika). || 1 ||

"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the subject under discussion. "Inferential" (*laiṅgika*) refers to that which is born from a mark (*liṅga*); a mark is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*). Pervasion has been explained therein: when there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that would oppose the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) [a certain property] in a particular locus, that locus is the "subject" (*pakṣa*) with respect to that [property]. Such a means of valid cognition consists of either a prover (*sādhaka*) or a sublater (*bādhaka*); for only that which possesses the absence of both is a subject. Indeed, when a prover or a sublater exists, no one can have doubt or the desire to prove [the matter]. For this very reason, the ancients held that the subject is a locus whose property to be proved (*sādhyadharma*) is doubted, or a locus whose property to be proved is desired to be proven.

Jīvanātha Miśra maintains that the *pakṣa* (the subject) is that locus where there is an absence of a means of knowledge that prevents the arising of a doubt which is to be removed by the determination of the existence of the probandum (*sādhya*) as something yet to be produced. Some others hold that the *pakṣa* is that locus where there is an absence of a proving means (*sādhakamāna*), conjoined with the absence of a desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*). According to this latter view, however, the status of being a *pakṣa* exists even in cases of sublation (*bādhasthala*). This should be examined in the *Anumānamayūkha*. Thus, it is said that the property (*dharma*) of this *pakṣa* is the *liṅga* (the logical mark). And the *liṅga* is that which, whether perceived, inferred, or heard, generates a cognition in the form of direct experience; that [cognition] is *laiṅgika* (inferential). As it has been said:

"That which is connected with the object of inference (*anumeya*), which is well-known (*prasiddha*) in what possesses that [object], and which is absolutely absent where that is absent—that is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) which brings about inference. By this, it is shown that the inferential mark (*liṅga*) alone is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of inferential cognition (*anumiti*), and not the "consideration" (*parāmarśa*) of it; for the latter, being devoid of an operation (*nirvyāpāra*), cannot be an instrument, whereas the former (the mark) has precisely that [consideration] as its operation. If it is asked, "How can there be inference in cases where smoke and so forth are past or future?", the answer is no, because the object of proof (*sādhya*) is also inferred there even when it is past or future, since the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) resides in that very [mark].

If it is asked: "How can there be inference where the pastness, futureness, or presentness of the smoke and so forth is not ascertained?"—the answer is: "Not at all, because in that case the probandum (*sādhya*) is also subject to doubt. If it is further asked: "In a case where existence is ascertained on the preceding and succeeding days, but there is doubt on the middle day, how can there be inference?"—the answer is: "Because by means of the smoke and so forth delimited by that specific day, one infers the fire and so forth delimited by that same day; for it is precisely in this way that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is determined to be the cause [of inference]."

If it is asked how there can be an inference from the delusion that there is smoke when there is merely a mass of dust, [the answer is: because only that which is known as being pervaded (vyāpta) possesses the status of a logical mark (liṅga), and because the nature of the inference corresponds to the validity or invalidity of that cognition; otherwise, even for you, how could the "subsequent reflection" (parāmarśa) serve as the instrument (karaṇa) in that case?

If it is asked how, in cases where the inferential mark (*liṅga*) is beyond the senses, the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection) can be its operation since it is not produced by it, [the answer is: because the status of being an operation is included therein as a "spontaneous means" (*kṣaimika-sādhanatā*), which consists in being that which ensures the existence of [the effect]; otherwise, the status of being an operation for *samavāya* (inherence) or for hearing and so forth would be untenable. The inference of fire and so forth from smoke, light, and so forth is based on an effect as the inferential mark (*kāryaliṅga*).

Inference from a cause is as follows: for example, the inference of sound from the specific contact of a drumstick with a drum by a deaf person; or the inference of merit, heaven, and so forth, from the performance of sacrifices, ritual bathing, and the like according to rule by a righteous person; or the inference of rain from the performance of the Kārīrī sacrifice and other rites according to rule; or the inference of the emergence of water from the digging of a stream full of water; or the inference of an increase in a river from seeing rain upstream.

And this single relationship, characterized as the relation between cause and effect, has been stated in two ways: the inference of the sense organ of touch from the perception of the body, which is its conjoined (saṃyogin) substrate; the inference of a mongoose hidden behind a thicket from the perception of its adversary, the hissing snake; and the inference of fire, which is its inherent (samavāyin) substrate, from the heat of water. || 1 ||

But surely, this enumeration is not all-inclusive; for it does not include the inference of the rise of the ocean tide from the rising of the moon, of the clarity of water from the rising of Agastya, of the rising of the moon from the blooming of night-lotuses, of the setting of one set of fourteen constellations from the rising of another set of fourteen constellations, nor of color from taste, or of a specific taste from a specific color. To this he replies:
"The relation between cause and effect of this [inference] arises from a part. (2)

The sole determinant here is simply the relation "this belongs to that": namely, for this probans such as smoke, this is the probandum such as fire; or else, for this [probandum] such as fire, this is the pervaded (vyāpya) such as smoke. Thus, the mere apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) is the essential factor, and not even the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth. Now, if it is asked whether, according to the previous sūtra, the enumeration [of specific relations] is therefore not the essential factor, he replies: "the relation of cause and effect. By this, he indicates that other types of relations are also implied.

And in the word "sambandha" (relation), there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the relatum; thus, "sambandha" means the presentation of a relation. To the question "From what does that presentation arise?", he says: "from a part," that is, from a single portion, namely the example alone—the ablative case is used here with the elision of the suffix *lyap*. Therefore, the meaning is that in this system as well as in systems such as Sāṅkhya, the presentation of relations—such as the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth—occurs by following the example.

Thus, being possessed of an essential relation (*svābhāvikasambandha*) constitutes the state of being the pervaded (*vyāpyatva*). Essentiality (*svābhāvikatva*), moreover, consists in being without a limiting adjunct (*anaupādhikatva*). This absence of an adjunct is to be understood as follows: in the case of certain perceptible factors, it is known through the certainty that they do not pervade the probandum (*sādhya*), or through the certainty that they do not pervade the probans (*sādhana*). Regarding supersensible factors established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), some may pervade both [the probandum and the probans], some may pervade neither, some may pervade the probans alone, or some may pervade the probandum alone.

In that regard, it should be determined that [the alleged upādhi] is not an upādhi because it pervades the probans (*sādhana*) in the first case, because it does not pervade the probandum (*sādhya*) in the second case, and likewise because it pervades the probans in the fourth case as well. Regarding the third case too, one should apply the following reasoning: since it is impossible for a pervader to be a pervader of that alone, how could the other [the non-pervader] be a pervader of that alone? Thus, its status as a non-upādhi is to be ascertained through such considerations as the equality of logical necessity (*tulyayogakṣema*).
