Since even the demoness of doubt that "some condition (upādhi) might exist here" does not invade any practical usage involving affirmation or negation, it is not to be accepted; thus, the possibility of ascertaining the absence of a condition exists. The definition of a condition and the definition of pervasion have already been stated.

That inference is of two kinds: for oneself (*svārtha*) and for others (*parārtha*). Among these, inference for oneself arises from one's own contemplation of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Inference for others arises from the knowledge of the pervasion and the property of the subject produced by a formal argument (*nyāya*) uttered by another. A formal argument (*nyāya*) is a statement that generates a verbal cognition which, in turn, produces the third consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*). Its members (*avayava*) are five. Therein, the state of being a member (*avayavatva*) consists in being a statement that generates a verbal cognition which generates a verbal cognition that prompts the third consideration of the mark. And those statements are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*).

In this context, the *pratijñā* (proposition) is a sentence that is a member of a formal argument (*nyāya*) which generates a verbal cognition whose object is neither less nor more than that of the intended inference. The *hetu* (reason) is a member of a formal argument ending in the ablative case, pertaining to the probans under consideration. The *udāharaṇa* (example), however, is a member of a formal argument that demonstrates the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between the probandum and the probans under consideration. And the *upanaya* (application) is a member of a formal argument that demonstrates the presence of the reason—qualified by that invariable concomitance—in the subject (*pakṣa*).

The conclusion (*nigamana*), however, is that member of the syllogism (*nyāyāvayava*) which establishes the connection of the subject with the probandum under discussion. Thus, the syllogism proceeds as follows: "The word 'sound' is impermanent because it is produced; whatever is produced is impermanent; and this [sound] possesses the property of being produced, which is pervaded by impermanence; therefore, it is impermanent. These very members—proposition (*pratijñā*), application (*upadeśa*), illustration (*nidarśana*), synthesis (*anusandhāna*), and conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*)—are the Vaiśeṣikas' names for these members, derived from their literal meanings. Furthermore, the manner in which debate (*vāda*), disputation (*jalpa*), and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*) proceed, as well as the definitions of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), should be sought in the *Vādivinoda*. 2.
He begins another section to include other means of valid cognition within inference:
"By this, verbal testimony is explained. (3)

That which is accepted by the Naiyāyikas and others as verbal cognition (*śābda*)—defined as knowledge produced by words—is also explained by this [same principle] as being inferential (*laiṅgika*), that is, originating from a logical mark (*liṅga*). Just as inferential cognition depends upon the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), so too does verbal cognition. For instance: "These word-meanings possess a mutual connection, because they are recalled by [words] possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, like the collection of word-meanings in the phrase 'Bring the cow' (*gām abhyāja*)."

For in that case, a collection of words possessing expectancy and other such factors, having grasped the fact that the mutual connection of word-meanings is pervaded by the state of being connected, infers that state of being connected; what need is there for a word to serve as an additional, postulated means of valid cognition?

If it is argued that this is not inference because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of an untrustworthy statement such as "there are five fruits on the riverbank," we say no; for [the definition] is qualified by the phrase "spoken by a trustworthy person" (*āptoktatva*). For "trustworthiness" (*āptatva*) consists in possessing a knowledge of the true meaning of the sentence in question, and not merely being non-deceptive. If it is further argued that this [trustworthiness] is difficult to ascertain prior to the comprehension of the sentence's meaning, we say no; for even those who maintain the intrinsic validity of verbal testimony (*śabdaprāmāṇyavādin*) accept that "being spoken by a trustworthy person"—which excludes deviant words—must be apprehended [as a condition].

There is a dependence on those [means of knowledge] for the sake of grasping their validity; however, verbal cognition is established even without that grasping. For you, however, such a grasping of the mark (*liṅga*) is necessary—namely, that it be qualified by being spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatva*). If it is argued that this is not so because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is qualified by being spoken by a reliable person, we say no, because it is possible to grasp it in a general way, as "this person is not mistaken in this matter."

If it is argued that "here" (atrātra) ultimately results in "in the connection under discussion," and thus its apprehension was previously impossible, we say no; for through the power of context, co-utterance, and so forth, it is possible to ascertain the speaker's reliability in a general sense, thereby making the ascertainment of the logical mark (liṅga) possible. Even if there is occasional sublation in such cases—as in the case of steam and the like, where inference proceeds by taking it for smoke—this does not invalidate the process.

Is it to be proved that these word-meanings are indeed already combined (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), or that they are merely capable of being combined (*sambhāvitasaṃsarga*)? Not the first, because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of what is spoken by an unreliable person (*anāpta*). Nor the second, because even if mere compatibility (*yogyatā*) is established, there would be no firm engagement (*niṣkampapravṛtti*) due to the lack of certainty regarding the combination; furthermore, since compatibility is already known as a qualification of the reason (*hetu*), what is the use of inference? If this is argued, we say no, because it is precisely the necessity (*niyama*) itself that is to be proved. Moreover, as it has been stated, there is no deviation because the reason is qualified by the fact of being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*).

Now, one might object: "Expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) is the prior absence of the cognition of a relation to be produced in the hearer; and since that [absence] is a cause by its very existence (*svarūpasan*), once that [absence] is known, the cognition of the relation already exists, rendering inference useless. This is not so. For we do not define expectancy as merely the prior absence of the cognition of a relation. What then? It is that [absence] qualified by the non-invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) implied by and indicated by those [words] which have been recalled. Thus, expectancy is known precisely from the knowledge of the qualifying factor (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*).

If it is argued that there should be expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) only for those [words] [that are semantically related], we say no; for then in the case of "The buffalo is grazing on the bank of the river with pure water," there would result the cognition of a syntactic relation (*anvaya*), since an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) exists between the river and its bank. Furthermore, in the case of "A blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*), although there is no inseparable connection between the blue color and the lotus, an inseparable connection is possible between the substance and the quality implied by them. Alternatively, expectancy is simply the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) regarding the objects recalled by the words, or the non-termination of the denotative function (*abhidhāna*). Even so, the knowledge of that [expectancy] is necessary, because—unlike a deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—it is a factor useful for the cognition [of meaning] when the cause is being known, just like pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Therefore, let semantic competency (*yogyatā*) be defined as either the absence of certainty regarding the lack of concomitance (*ananvaya*), or the absence of subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), or its observation in similar instances (*sajātīya-darśana*), or else as the state of being the qualificand of a valid cognition that the relation with one word-meaning is not the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in the other word-meaning; the knowledge of this is necessary. Furthermore, the knowledge of proximity (*āsatti*)—in the form of an uninterrupted recollection—is also a requisite factor. And since the specific nature of the relation is determined solely by the specificities of the related terms, there is no possibility of establishing an unintended particularity.

Alternatively, the establishment of the specific [relation] intended as the delimiting factor of the cognition occurs through the following inference: "These words are preceded by a cognition of the connection between the meanings they recall, because they constitute a collection of words possessing expectancy, semantic competency, and contiguity, like the collection of words 'gām abhyāja'.

As for the thesis that "these words possess the connection of the meanings they recall," that should be disregarded, because the possession of a connection between word-meanings by the words themselves is contradicted. Nor is the "possession of connection" by words simply their status as indicators of a connection by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*), since, being unestablished prior to the inference, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be grasped.

Some assert that gesture (*ceṣṭā*) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To this it is replied: gesture is of two kinds—conventional (*kṛtasamayā*) and non-conventional (*akṛtasamayā*). Among these, the conventional gesture merely causes one to remember a word residing in the intention (*abhiprāya*), but it does not produce a cognition of the connection (*saṃsarga*) itself, just like a written letter. In that case, the word itself, as it has ascended to the level of memory, is the means of valid cognition; and the status of the word as an inferential mark (*liṅga*) has already been stated. Furthermore, the remembrance of the word is not an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) of the gesture, because the meaning of a word is understood even in the absence of a gesture. If it were indeed an operation, it would follow that a gesture must invariably be present.

[Objection: But if this is so, how can the linguistic usage of one who is mute and deaf depend upon gestures? For he lacks the apprehension of the convention (*samaya*) regarding them. [Reply: No, because it must be considered how even with respect to an object, cognition arises from his gestures, since he likewise lacks the apprehension of the connection (*saṅgati*) with the object. As for his linguistic usage, however, it is possible due to the apprehension of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), just as in the case of an elephant or a horse; through the striking of the whip or the goad, proficiency in various usages is established.

However, that which is not based on a convention (*akṛtasamayā*) but follows from a specific action (*kṛtyānvayinī*) prompts the person being directed (*prayojya*) by causing them to remember the intention of the director (*prayojaka*); it does not, however, produce any valid cognition (*pramā*) anywhere. For example, when one has heard the command "you must go upon the sound of the conch," one sets out as soon as the conch is blown; or when it is agreed that "whenever I raise my index finger, you must strike him," one strikes him at that time—but in neither case does one cognize anything [as a new object of knowledge].

However, that which follows from an informative [act] (*jñapti*) and for which no convention has been established is, for example: "By raising ten fingers, you must understand that the number ten, or the number of seals (*mudrā*), or the number of ancient coins (*purāṇa*), is meant by you"—this is predominant in its agent (*kāraka*). "Upon seeing the contraction of the hand, you must come"—this is predominant in its action (*kriyā*).

Thus, by this gesture, only the individual word-meanings (padārthas) are independently reminded, but their mutual relation (parasparam-anvaya) is not made known; for, unlike the case of case-endings such as the agentive or objective which express that relation, there is an absence here of any fixed constituent parts of the gesture capable of expressing it. If it is asked, "In the absence of a cognition of the relation, how can activity or cessation [of activity] arise from a gesture?", understand that it arises from either doubt or apprehension. Therefore, even gesture is not a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). || 3 ||
Now, one might object: "How can sound (śabda) be a logical mark (liṅga), since sound, by its very nature as an indicator (apadeśa), is distinct from a logical mark? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The reason (hetu), the indicator (apadeśa), the logical mark (liṅga), the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), and the instrument (karaṇa) are synonymous. (4)

That by which an object is pointed out or expressed is called *apadeśa*, which is synonymous with "word" (*śabda*). And this [word] is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as a synonym for "reason" (*hetu*) or "mark" (*liṅga*). The meaning is that it is an instrument of knowledge by way of being a mark. Likewise, the word "instrument" (*karaṇa*) also applies specifically to the mark (*liṅga*) as the instrument for inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika-jñāna*). There are two ways in which an instrument functions: some function through dependence on sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*), while others function through the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). But since a word has neither contact with its object nor invariable concomitance with it, how could it cause the object to be known?

If it is argued that [the word] conveys [the meaning] through convention (*saṅketa*), [we reply: for convention indeed pertains to the individual word-meanings (*padārtha*), but not to their relation (*saṃsarga*). If it is argued that there is convention even with respect to that [relation], we say no; because since that [relation] is of many kinds, it is impossible for it to be the object of convention. If it is argued that the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) also appears by the very power of the convention regarding the word-meanings, we say no; because if one thing were presented through a convention concerning another, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that there is a restriction based on the fact that the relation is one that is recalled by the words, then, by the force of such a restriction, it is precisely inference (*anumāna*) that gains its opportunity.

Since even a convention (saṅketa) is nothing more than a mere wish, it would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga). If it is argued that the will of God (īśvarecchā) does not lead to such over-extension, we say no; for even in the absence of His will, the bank and so forth are presented by words such as "Gaṅgā. Enough, then, with this audacity toward the Naiyāyikas! || 4 ||

To demonstrate that even comparison (*upamāna*) and other means of knowledge accepted by others—which function by the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—are included within inferential cognition (*laiṅgika*) alone, he says:
"Because it depends upon the cognition that 'this belongs to that'. (Sūtra 5)

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "of comparison (upamāna), presumption (arthāpatti), probability (sambhava), and non-existence (abhāva). The meaning is: because of that state of being dependent upon those [means of knowledge], namely, the state of being dependent on that [cognition] for which a cognition of the form "this is the pervaded of that pervader" is required as its producer. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with a word ending in the suffix *kta*, according to the rule for the class beginning with *āhitāgni*; or it may be derived from the class beginning with *tāraka*.

In this context, analogy (*upamāna*) is indeed nothing other than inference by means of verbal testimony. For instance, when a forest-dweller is asked by an urbanite who desires to know, "What is a *gavaya* like?", he replies, "A *gavaya* is similar to a cow. Therein, by the force of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), one determines immediately upon hearing the sentence of transfer (*atideśavākya*) that "that which is similar to a cow is denoted by the word *gavaya*. Having gone to the forest and perceived such an individual, however, one then recognizes it, thinking, "This is what is denoted by the word *gavaya*."

If it is asked, "Since the property of being a *gavaya* (*gavayatva*) was not known as the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) at the time of hearing the analogical statement, how can there be a determination of the name?", [the answer is] that its cognition is possible through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). If it is asked, "How can there be secondary signification when there is no syntactic inconsistency (*anvayānupapatti*) in the sentence 'A *gavaya* is similar to a cow'? [the answer is] that there is indeed an inconsistency of intention (*tātparyānupapatti*). For it is not improper to point out the similarity to a cow—though it is a composite entity—as the basis for application to one who is seeking to learn the meaning; rather, the intention of this [statement] lies in a specific, non-composite genus (*akhaṇḍajāti*), and thus secondary signification is possible.

Alternatively, the word "gavaya" denotes the gavaya because it is used by the learned for that purpose when no other mode of application (vṛtti) is possible; for when a word is used by the learned for something in the absence of any other mode of application, it denotes that thing, just as the word "go" denotes a cow—it is through such inference alone that one determines the name "gavaya. Furthermore, the reasoning (*tarka*) which you claim to be an auxiliary to comparison (*upamāna*) would be better situated within inference, where its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is already established; what is the use of comparison, whose status as a means of valid cognition must still be postulated? A detailed discussion on this point is to be sought in the *Anumānamayūkha*.

Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also nothing but inference (*anumāna*). To explain: the cognition of an unperceived fact—such as the existence outside of the living Caitra, which is determined by a stronger means of knowledge through his absence from the house—necessitates the postulation of his existence outside. In that case, the realization of existence outside is dependent upon the ascertainment of the relationship of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between the fact to be established and its establishing factor; for there occurs either the knowledge that the presence of a living person in the house is invariably concomitant with existence outside, or the knowledge that the absence from the house of a living person is otherwise inexplicable (*anupapanna*) without existence outside.

In that regard, in the first case there is only positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*), whereas in the last case there is only the apprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*). If it is argued that "concomitance exists, but its apprehension is not required here," [the reply is] no, because without the apprehension of concomitance, there would be no room for fallacious presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti-ābhāsa*); for by means of a concomitance that is real in its own nature, there would be the postulation of only that which is the actual subsumer (*upapādaka*). This is the general direction. It should be understood that presumptive testimony based on doubt and that based on contradiction are included within inference (*anumāna*).

For even contradiction (*virodha*), characterized by the rule of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), is constituted by pervasion (*vyāpti*). Presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) is also an inference from an inferred [fact] (*anumitānumāna*): by the sentence "Devadatta is fat and does not eat during the day," fatness is inferred; and by that fatness, eating at night is inferred—[the reasoning being]: "Devadatta eats at night, because if he were not eating during the day, his fatness would be impossible."

Probability (*sambhava*) is also nothing but inference (*anumāna*). For its illustration is as follows: "A *droṇa* is possible in a *khārī*; an *āḍhaka* is possible in a *droṇa*; a hundred is possible in a thousand," and so forth. In this regard, this *khārī* possesses a *droṇa* because it is composed of it; whatever is composed of something possesses that thing, just as a jar possesses parts. Other cases should be understood in the same way. As for such instances as "learning is possible in a Brāhmaṇa" or "heroism is possible in a Kṣatriya," these are not valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at all, because they do not provide certainty.

Non-existence (*abhāva*) is also not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the inference of the absence of a cause from the absence of its effect is included within inference itself, as it is rooted in pervasion (*vyāpti*), just like the inference of a cause from an effect.

However, in the system of Bhaṭṭa, the means of cognition that apprehends non-existence regarding the ground and so forth is called "non-apprehension" (*anupalambha*). This is included in perception in some cases and in inference in others, since non-existence is grasped by the eye and other senses themselves. Nor is the sense organ exhausted merely by apprehending the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), for its operation continues until the apprehension of the non-existence is complete.

*Itihya* is a traditional narrative whose original speaker is unknown, consisting of a succession of reports. The collection of particles *iti ha* refers to past events; the state of being such is *aitihya*. If that [tradition] does not have a sublated object, then it is inference due to the inclusion of words [within its structure]. For instance, "There is a Yakṣa in this banyan tree," or "Gaurī is in the Madhūka tree"—if these were spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*), then they are like the aforementioned [inference]. If they were not spoken by a reliable person, then they are not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, it is established that there are only two means of valid cognition: perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). || 5 ||
Having explained inference (*laiṅgika*), he now begins another section:
"Memory [arises] from a specific conjunction of the self and the mind, and from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). (6)

The word "arises" (*utpadyate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. A specific conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*), namely the proximity of an intention (*praṇidhāna*) and so forth, serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*); from this, memory—a particular kind of knowledge—arises in the self, which is its inherent substrate (*samavāyin*). He states the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) with the words "from the latent impression" (*saṃskārāt*). By the word "and" (*ca*), the prior experience and its operation are conjoined. This [memory] conforms to the truth or untruth of the original experience, just as one who has fled after perceiving a rope as a snake remembers it exactly as such.

Nor does memory arise continuously, because it is dependent upon the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). As stated by the venerable Praśastadeva: "Memory, which has past objects as its domain and is the cause of subsequent cognition, recollection, desire, and aversion, arises from a specific conjunction of the self and the mind that depends on the observation of a sign, desire, recollection, and so forth, as well as from an impression produced by intense practice, interest, or repeated experience regarding what has been seen, heard, or perceived."

The knowledge of the ṛṣis (*ārṣajñāna*) has not been separately defined by Sūtrakṛt, as it is included within the category of yogic perception (*yogipratyakṣa*). However, it is described in the section titled *Padārthapradeśa* as follows: "The intuitive knowledge (*prātibhajñāna*) which arises for the ṛṣis—the authors of the sacred scriptures (*āmnāya*)—regarding objects beyond the senses, such as dharma and so forth, whether past, future, or present, and whether recorded in texts or not, due to the contact of the self and the mind and through a specific merit (*dharmaviśeṣa*), that is *ārṣa*."
And this [intuition] sometimes occurs even for worldly people, as in: "The girl says, 'My brother will come tomorrow; my heart tells me so. || 6 ||

Thus, having explained the fourfold knowledge (vidyā), it is now appropriate to explain ignorance (avidyā). Among these, doubt (saṃśaya) and error (viparyaya) have already been defined previously by way of context; he now speaks in order to define dream (svapna):
"Likewise, dream [is a form of avidyā]. (7)

The meaning is that just as memory arises from a particular conjunction of the self and the mind as well as from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), so too does dream-cognition arise. Dream-cognition is that mental experience which occurs through the gateway of the senses for one whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased and whose mind has dissolved.

And that [dream-cognition] is of three kinds. First, some arises from the intensity of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*): when one who is lustful or angry sleeps while intensely contemplating a certain object, there arises in that state a cognition in the form of a direct perception, such as "this is the battle between Karṇa and Arjuna," produced by the force of impressions generated from hearing the *Purāṇas* and other texts. Second, some arises from a disorder of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), namely wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*). Among these, due to a disorder of wind, one sees such things as traveling through the sky, wandering the earth, or fleeing in fear of tigers and other predators.

By the power of the accumulation of the *pitta* humor, one perceives the entry into fire, the embrace of flames, the blazing of golden mountains, the flashing of lightning bolts, the burning of the quarters of the sky, and so forth. However, due to the predominance of the *śleṣman* humor, one perceives the crossing of the ocean, immersion in rivers, the falling of torrential rain, silver mountains, and the like.

Furthermore, by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), there arises in one whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) has been purified through the practice of *siddhi* a cognition regarding things experienced in this life or experienced in another life. Among these, that which indicates auspiciousness arises from merit (*dharma*) and has as its objects riding an elephant, climbing a mountain, obtaining an umbrella, eating milk-rice (*pāyasa*), beholding a king, and so forth. However, from demerit (*adharma*), dream-cognition arises having as its objects anointing with oil, falling into a blind well, riding a camel, sinking in mud, witnessing one's own marriage, and so forth.
In this context, the causality belongs only to the three combined; this distinction should be understood by relying on their relationship as subordinate and principal factors. || 7 ||

Now, one might object: "In the midst of a dream, there arises a cognition that takes the form of a memory of an object experienced within that very dream; in that case, the state of being a dream does not apply [to that cognition], because a dream consists of direct experience. Therefore, for what reason does such a cognition arise?
To this, he says: "The final stage of the dream" (svapnāntika). || 8 ||

The word "so" (*tathā*) is carried over from the preceding sūtra. Therefore, the meaning is that just as a dream [occurs] due to a particular conjunction of the self and the mind and due to a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), so too does the state immediately following a dream (*svapnāntika*). The only difference is this: dream-cognition arises from an impression produced by a previous experience, whereas the state immediately following a dream arises solely from an impression produced by an experience occurring at that very time. As it was stated by the teacher Praśastadeva: "It is simply memory, arising from the recollection of past cognitions."
Thus it has been said by the authors of the *Vṛtti*: "Dream-cognition is not something other than recollection, because its purpose is the manifestation of an object previously experienced.

Some maintain that whatever cognition within a dream possesses the status of valid knowledge (*pramā*) is "dream-final" (*svapnāntika*), such as [the thought] while lying on a bed, "I am lying down," and so forth. (8)
He combines the causes for dreaming and the end of dreaming:
"And from dharma. (9)
The particle "ca" has the sense of a collective conjunction (adharmasamuccaya). This has already been explained. || 9 ||
Now, with reference to the alternative explanation, he says: "Ignorance [arises] from the defect of the sense organs and from the defect of mental impressions. (10)

Although the term *avidyā* (ignorance) expresses a general state, it here refers specifically to error (*viparyaya*), because doubt, dreaming, and non-determination have already been mentioned [in the preceding verses]. In this context, "defect of the sense-organ" (*indriyadoṣa*) refers to the impairment caused by the dominance of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and so forth. "Defect of the mental impression" (*saṃskāradoṣa*) refers to its association with the non-perception of specific features (*viśeṣādarśana*); for false cognition arises dependent upon that [association]. || 10 ||

He states the general definition of ignorance (*avidyā*): the indeclinable word *tat*, which has the same meaning as a pronoun, refers back to ignorance. That ignorance is defective knowledge—that is, erroneous knowledge, the cognition of something as what it is not; it is delimited by a qualifier residing in a different locus, meaning it possesses a qualifier that does not reside in the substantive (*viśeṣya*). Furthermore, "defect" (*doṣa*) includes the state of a cognition being non-ascertaining (*aniścaya-rūpatva*). By this, even when one alternative exists, doubt is indeed defective because its nature is non-determinative. Thus, this [definition] encompasses all four types: doubt, error, dream, and non-apprehension (*anadhyavasāya*). || 11 ||
Knowledge is not defiled. || 12 ||

The term "knowledge" (jñāna) is understood to carry over [from the previous definition]. That which is non-defective—meaning that which is produced by non-defective sense organs—is either the experience of something as it actually exists in a particular locus, or an experience whose qualifier (prakāra) is co-located with its qualificand (viśeṣya), or an experience whose qualifier does not reside in its qualificand; this is the meaning of "valid knowledge" (vidyā). And that [valid knowledge] is of only two kinds: perceptual (ādhyakṣa) and inferential (laiṅgika). || 12 ||

[Objection: But surely even the knowledge of a seer (ārṣa) has only a qualifier that is in the same locus [as its object], and that is not produced by the sense organs because its object is not in contact [with them]. Nor is it inferential, because it arises without the consideration of a logical mark (liṅga). Thus, this instrument [of knowledge] turns out to be a third means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). To this, he says:
"The knowledge of a seer and the vision of the perfected ones arise from merits (dharma). (1.24)

The knowledge of the sages (ṛṣis), such as Gālava and others, concerning the past and the future, is called *ārṣa* (sagely). Furthermore, the knowledge of perfected beings (*siddhas*) regarding objects that are hidden or remote—attained through mantras, medicinal herbs, pills, collyrium, and so forth—and the vision of those who have attained supernatural powers (*siddhis*), both arise from *dharma*s as a direct perception of reality. The author of the *Vṛtti* maintains that these two are distinct from yogic perception. *Ārṣa* knowledge is indeed the fourth type of cognition; it belongs to both sages and ordinary people.

And that is indeed mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), produced either by the mind assisted by creative imagination (*utprekṣā*) or by a logical mark (*liṅga*) such as the observation of a necessary rule (*niyama-sandarśana*). In this case, the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti-dhī*) depends solely on impressions (*saṃskāra*) from a previous birth, just like the grasping of the pervasion between the drinking of breast milk and its being a means to a desired end.

The Praśastācāryas, however, maintain that the vision of the Siddhas is not a distinct type of knowledge. For instance, if it is said that the Siddhas possess a perception of objects that are hidden or remote, arising from the power of accomplishments such as magical pills (*guṭikā*) or collyrium (*añjana*), then it is simply *pratyakṣa* (perception). But if it depends on signs (*nimitta*) such as the movements of the planets and constellations belonging to the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms, then it is purely *laiṅgika* (inferential), because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is determined through the observation of concomitance (*sahacāra*). || 13 ||
Thus ends the second Āhnika of the ninth chapter in the *Śrī-Śāṅkara-Vaiśeṣika-sūtra-upaskāra*.

This ninth chapter is completed. The subject matter of the tenth chapter is the demonstration of the distinctions among the qualities of the self (*ātmaguṇa*) based on their causes. In that regard, since pleasure (*sukha*) is not mentioned in Gautama’s sūtra defining the categories of objects of knowledge—which states: "The self, body, sense organs, objects, intellect, mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation are the objects of knowledge"—the author first states the distinction between pleasure and pain in order to dispel the misconception that pleasure is non-different from pain.
Pleasure and pain are distinct entities because they have different causes—desirable and undesirable respectively—and because they are mutually contradictory. || 1 ||

The mutual state of pleasure and pain as being distinct entities—that is, their difference or heterogeneity—is what is meant. Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of the distinction between the causes of the desired and the undesired. The "desired" is that which is sought after, such as garlands, sandalwood, women, and so forth; the "undesired" is that which is not sought after, such as gadflies, mosquitoes, thorns, and so forth. Because of the distinction—that is, the difference—between such causes, and because the heterogeneity of the effect necessarily depends upon the heterogeneity of the cause.

He states another means of differentiation: due to contradiction, characterized by non-coexistence; for there is no simultaneous experience of pleasure and pain within a single self. By the word "and" (ca), he adds a further differentiator based on their difference in effects. To explain: favor, attachment, clarity of the eyes, and so forth are the effects of pleasure, while dejection, a darkened face, and so forth are the effects of pain; thus, they are also distinct from one another on that account.

This has been stated by the teacher Praśasta: "Pleasure, characterized as favor (anugraha), arises when desired objects such as garlands and the like are present; it is produced from the contact of the self and the mind, depending on merit (dharma) and other factors, following the cognition that 'this is desirable,' and it is that which generates favor, attachment, and joy in the eyes and so forth. This [pleasure] arises from memory regarding past objects such as garlands and sandalwood paste, and from conceptualization (saṅkalpa) regarding future ones.

Furthermore, in the *Gautamīya-sūtra*, it is stated that even for one who contemplates pleasure as suffering for the sake of detachment, detachment may arise; this [contemplation] is for that purpose. || 1 ||
"Now, let it be granted that pleasure and pain are distinct from one another; yet they might both be non-different from cognition, as in the case of memory and direct experience. To this, he says:
"Furthermore, the absence of the distinction between doubt and certainty is the reason [for their being] different types of cognition. (2)

The meaning is that if pleasure and pain were distinct from cognition—that is, if they were different from cognition—the absence of being included within doubt (*saṃśaya*) and certainty (*nirṇaya*) serves as the logical reason (*hetu*) or mark (*liṅga*). This is the sense: if pleasure or pain were cognition, would it be of the nature of doubt or of the nature of certainty? Not the first, because it does not present two alternative possibilities (*koṭi*). Nor the second, because it does not present even one possibility. Thus, by the sublation of all specific instances, there follows the sublation of the general category.

For there are only two specific qualities of cognition: doubtfulness and certainty. Since both of these are sublated in the case of pleasure and pain, the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*) itself is also sublated therein. By the word "and" (*ca*), he includes the sublation by direct experience (*anubhava*). There is a mental experience of pleasure and pain in the form "I am happy" or "I am miserable," but there is no experience in the form "I know," "I doubt," or "I ascertain. || 2 ||
He states another point of distinction:
"The accomplishment of those two [is known] through perception and inference. (3)

The accomplishment or production of those two—doubt and certainty—arises from perception and from the logical mark (*liṅga*). Pleasure or pain is neither produced by the causal complex of perception nor produced by the logical mark. For pleasure is of four kinds: that which pertains to sense-objects (*vaiṣayika*), that which is mental or imaginary (*mānorathika*), that which is based on conceit (*ābhimānika*), and that which is habitual (*ābhyāsika*). Among these, three do not arise at all from sensory contact.

If it is argued that, in the first instance, there must be cognition because it arises from the contact of a sense-organ with its object, we say no; for a single component of a causal complex does not necessarily produce a result of the same genus. Otherwise, since space and time are common to all things, it would follow that every effect belongs to a single genus. Furthermore, would the pleasure arising from the contact of a sense-organ with its object be non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) or conceptual (*savikalpaka*)? It cannot be the first, because it would then follow that it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Nor can it be the second, because both [the sense-organ and the object] lack the nature of apprehending the relationship between a substantive and its qualifier.

Furthermore, because pleasure and pain must necessarily be experienced, if cognition itself were necessarily experienced, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Regarding "inferential" (*laiṅgika*), it is simply that which arises from a mark (*liṅga*), just like [the cognition] concerning sense objects. However, the authors of the *Vṛtti* explain that the production of those two—cognition and pleasure—is explained by the explanations of perceptual and inferential cognition; they explain that while perceptual cognition is born of the senses and inferential cognition is born of a mark, pleasure and so forth are not of such a nature. || 3 ||
He states that pleasure and the like differ from inferential knowledge based on a difference in their mode of appearance: "It was," and so forth. (4)

The word *iti* denotes a mode [of cognition]. The word *api* serves to include other modes, such as "will be. Thus, in inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika-jñāna*)—such as "there was fire on the mountain" or "there will be fire on the mountain"—modes such as past and so forth are observed; however, pleasure or pain arising in such a manner is not perceived. || 4 ||
He adds another reason for the distinction:
"And because, even when [the cause] exists, the effect is not observed" (sūtra 5).

Since pleasure or pain is not observed when there is contact between the sense-faculties and their objects, even though there is the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), and so forth, pleasure or pain is neither mere perception nor mere inference. This is the meaning: it has already been stated that pleasure and pain do not constitute general cognition (*jñānasāmānya*).

Is this specific cognition (jñānaviśeṣa) direct perception (pratyakṣajñāna) or of the nature of inference (anumiti)? It cannot be the first, because in the direct perception of garlands, sandalwood, and so forth—which arises from the contact of the sense organs with their objects—there is no experience of the quality of pleasure (sukhatva). Nor can it be the second, because in the inference of sandalwood or the inference of fire, there is no experience of pleasure or pain; therefore, that specific cognition [of pleasure] does not exist either. || 5 ||
He states another distinguishing feature:
"Because it is observed in other inherent causes of a single object" (sūtra 6).

The phrase "of pleasure and pain" is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the object]. With respect to pleasure, the uncommon causes inherent in the same substrate (*ekārthasamaveta*) are: merit (*dharma*), attachment to pleasure, desire for the cause of pleasure, the effort to acquire it, and the cognition of garlands, sandalwood, and so forth. With respect to pain, however, they are: demerit (*adharma*) and the cognition of undesirable things such as thorns and the like. The meaning is that [pleasure and pain] are observed to have these causes which are inherent in the same substrate. As for cognition, however, non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition does not at all require an uncommon cause inherent in the same substrate.

Conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), however, requires the knowledge of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*); that, moreover, is another cause which is not of a different genus (*svavijātīya*) from itself. As for the contact with the mind (*manaḥsaṃyoga*), it is not intended [as a specific cause] because it is common to all cognitions. Although recollection (*smṛti*) requires the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) as its specific cause, nevertheless, since that distinction is already established even if it were not explicitly stated, the investigation of difference proceeds by taking perception (*anubhava*) as the basis. Although inferential cognition (*laiṅgika*) depends on the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the recollection of pervasion, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), and so forth, the word "another" (*antara*) itself excludes those.

Therefore, this is the meaning established by the proof: pleasure and pain are distinct from experience (anubhava), because they are produced by uncommon causes that reside in the same locus as themselves and belong to their own class, just like memory and like the first instance of sound.

Now, if pleasure and pain were distinct from cognition due to a difference in their causes, and if pain were distinct from pleasure—just as a pillar is distinct from a jar—because their respective causes (such as atoms, dyads, or red semen and ovum) are different, then [the opponent might argue] that there is no distinction between them. To this, he says:
"In one part," meaning in a single body, [there is a distinction] because of the specific differences in the head, back, belly, and vital organs. (7)

"One part" (*ekadeśa*) means a limb. "In one" (*ekasmin*) means in the body. "Head" is one part; likewise the belly, the back, the vital points (*marmāṇi*), the sinews (*snāyu*), and so forth. Their "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) refers to their specific nature (*vaijātya*); from those distinctions [arises] their distinction as causes.

In that case, the difference [in species] arises precisely from the difference in the causes; for the genus of the inherent cause of the head is not the same as that of the belly, the back, and so forth. Just as there is a difference in species between cloth and a jar due to the difference in their material causes—such as threads and potsherds—so too is such a difference possible here. Furthermore, even threads and potsherds differ in species from fibers and shards respectively. Thus, one should investigate this at every stage. Even though atoms are common [to all effects], it is the difference in their respective material causes that serves as the determinant of difference everywhere.
However, as for substantiality (*dravyatva*), its homogeneity with the material cause does not entail heterogeneity; such is the general direction [of the argument]. (7)
Thus ends the first daily lesson of the tenth chapter in the *Vaiśeṣikasūtropaskāra* by the venerable Śaṅkara.
In the second daily lesson of the tenth chapter, he now begins the detailed analysis of the three types of causes as an incidental discussion:
"The cause [is defined] with respect to a substance because of its inherence in the effect. (1)

The cognition "this is the inherent cause" and the corresponding linguistic usage should be understood as applying to substance alone. Why is this so? He says: "Because of the inherence of effects. For it is in that [substance] alone that the effects—namely, substances, qualities, and actions—inhere. (1)
Is it then the case that substances possess only the status of being inherent causes? To this he says:
"Or from conjunction. (2)

Just as threads are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) in the production of a cloth, so too is the conjunction of the shuttle and the threads an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), because it is also a cause of the cloth; thus, by way of that conjunction, both the shuttle and the thread are instrumental causes of the cloth. The word "and" (*vā*) is used in a conjunctive sense. This is because, although the thread is the inherent cause with respect to the conjunction of the shuttle and the thread, it is an instrumental cause with respect to the cloth by way of that [conjunction]. || 2 ||
He states what kind of causality exists in respect to action:
"Actions [arise] from inherence in their cause. (3)

The word "non-inherent causes" (*asamavāyikāraṇāni*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. And the state of being a non-inherent cause is the causality of a cause that is inherent in the same effect as that which stands in a causal relation [with the effect]. This [causality] arises either from inherence in the same object as the effect (*kāryaikārthasamavāya*) or from inherence in the same object as the cause (*kāraṇaikārthasamavāya*). Regarding these, the Vaiśeṣika technical terminology is that the former is "light" (*laghu*) and the latter is "heavy" (*mahatī*). In this context, by what kind of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) do actions (*karma*) serve as non-inherent causes for conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), and impression (*saṃskāra*)? To this he says: "Because of inherence in the cause" (*kāraṇe samavāyāt*).

The meaning is that [action] is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of conjunction and so forth because it inheres in their inherent cause; thus, by means of the simpler proximity characterized as inherence in the same object as the effect, action serves as the non-inherent cause for conjunction and the like. || 3 ||

In response to the inquiry as to what kind of causality exists for qualities such as color (*rūpa*), which reside in parts, with respect to the qualities and so forth of the whole (*avayavin*), he says: "Likewise, [color is a cause] also through inherence in the same object as its cause" (VS 4.1.12).

"Color" (rūpa) indicates color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, weight, fluidity, and so forth. The word "likewise" (tathā) extends [the property of] being a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa). Regarding the phrase "due to inherence in the same object as the cause" (kāraṇaikārthasamavāyāt): the inherent cause of the color and other qualities of a composite whole is that composite whole itself; through inherence in the same object as that, by way of a great proximity, it initiates the color and other qualities of the composite whole. This is to be understood everywhere as follows: for example, the color and other qualities of the potsherds initiate the color and other qualities in the jar. By the word "and" (ca), [the author] also includes their status as occasional efficient causes (nimitta) in certain instances. || 4 ||
He states the close proximity of conjunction—which serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*)—at the commencement of a substance:
"Conjunction [is the cause] of the cloth because of its inherence in the causes" (5).

The meaning is that conjunction (*saṃyoga*), by virtue of its inherence in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), is also a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to an effect such as a cloth, through the proximity characterized by "inherence in the same object as the effect" (*kāryaikārthasamavāya*). According to some, the word "cloth" (*paṭa*) also includes the case of inherence in the same object as the cause of the effect-substance (*kāryadravyakāraṇaikārthasamavāya*). || 5 ||
He states that conjunction is sometimes a cause through a great proximity: "And because of inherence in the cause of the cause" (6).

The conjunction called "accumulation" (pracaya), which resides in the parts of a tuft of cotton, initiates largeness in the tuft of cotton; in this case, the meaning is that the proximity [of the cause] consists in its inherence in the same object as the effect. || 6 ||
Having thus defined causality as determined by inherence, he begins another section to define efficient causality:
"From conjunction with that which inheres [in the cause], the specific quality of fire [is produced]. (VS 7.1.9)

Heat is the specific, unique quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of fire; through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), it is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) for qualities produced by cooking (*pākaja*). This is also an illustration: all [entities] are efficient causes with respect to cognition (*jñāna*). Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression (*bhāvanā*) are exclusively efficient causes. This detailed exposition should be understood as intended to demonstrate the perception of pleasure and the other [qualities]. || 7 ||
Now, in order to strengthen the authority of the sacred tradition (āmnāya), he states once again the very point already mentioned:
"The application of those things that have been observed and whose purposes are observed, in the absence of [those] observed [purposes], leads to prosperity. (8)

Regarding actions that are seen—that is, those perceived through valid means of knowledge such as sacrifice, giving, bathing, and so forth—whose visible purpose has been taught: for instance, in such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" and "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," the fruit is expressed in grammatical coordination with the injunction itself; in some cases it is conveyed by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), as in "For one who studies these nights, streams of ghee and streams of honey flow for his ancestors"; and in some cases it is obtained through implication (*aupādānika*), as follows:

In such cases as "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," the [result] is not mentioned in conjunction with an injunction (*vidhi*), nor is it established by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); therefore, it is "derived from implication" (*aupādānika*)—that is, it must be postulated. This is because heaven alone, being inherently beautiful, must be postulated as the fruit. Furthermore, since these actions perish very quickly, their status as causes for a fruit that occurs after a long time would otherwise be untenable; for this very reason, their performance—that is, their execution—is for the sake of *apūrva*, which leads to prosperity (*abhyudaya*). This is the meaning.

[Objection: "Granted that this would be so if the authority of the Śruti were established, but that itself is difficult to attain. For you do not accept the authority of the Śruti on the grounds of its being eternally faultless—as the Mīmāṃsakas do—since you admit it to be of human origin (pauruṣeya). And because errors, negligence, and a desire to deceive are possible in a person, [the author] says: 'In the absence of observed [faults]' (dṛṣṭābhāve). This means: provided there is an absence of those defects of a person, such as error, negligence, and a desire to deceive, which are observed in other persons like ourselves."

Since the Supreme Person (puruṣadhaureya), who is inferred either as the creator of the earth or as the speaker of the Vedas, is presented as being free from defects, his words cannot be devoid of meaning, nor can they have a contrary meaning, nor can they have a purposeless meaning. For it is only through the defects of the elements, the senses, and the mind—namely, error, negligence, and lack of proficiency in the instruments [of cognition]—that impurities of speech are possible. Such impurities are not possible in the case of the Lord's speech; as it has been said:
"A speaker might speak untruth because he is seized by passion, ignorance, and so forth."
If those [qualities] do not exist in the Lord, how could he speak otherwise? Thus [it is said]. (8)

But surely, there is disagreement precisely regarding the point that the Veda was composed by that Lord; therefore, he says: "The authority of the sacred tradition [Āmnāya] is due to His word" (Sūtra 9).

Thus, at the conclusion of the treatise: by his word—that is, by the word of that Lord (Īśvara), through his composition—the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the *āmnāya*, the Veda, is established. For it has been proven that the Vedas are indeed of human origin because they consist of sentences; yet, persons such as ourselves cannot possibly be the speakers of those [Vedas] divided into thousands of recensions (*śākhās*), because their subject matter transcends the senses, and persons such as ourselves do not perceive objects beyond the senses.

Furthermore, the Vedas are the words of a trustworthy person (*āptokta*) because they are accepted by the great multitude (*mahājanaparigṛhītatvāt*). That which is not the word of a trustworthy person is not accepted by the great multitude; since this [Veda] is accepted by the great multitude, it is therefore the word of a trustworthy person. Being the composition of an independent person constitutes "being the word of a trustworthy person. And "being accepted by the great multitude" consists in its purpose being practiced by persons belonging to all philosophical systems (*sarvadarśanāntaḥpātipuruṣa*). It has been stated that the occasional absence of results is due to defects in the action, the agent, or the means.

If it is argued that this is not so because there is no recollection of an author, we say no; for the existence of an author has already been established. Furthermore, its being composed by such an author is proven precisely because it was composed by an independent person; indeed, as has been stated, independence in the composition of the Veda with its thousands of branches is not possible for people like us. Moreover, since valid cognition (*pramā*) is produced by excellence (*guṇa*), it is necessary that even Vedic valid cognition be produced by excellence.

And in that case, the quality to be stated is the speaker’s knowledge of the true meaning of the sentence; and such a speaker exists only in the Veda, who possesses direct perception of objects such as heaven and the unseen force (*apūrva*), and such a person is none other than God—thus it is well said. || 9 ||
The illustrious Śaṅkara, son of Bhavānī and son of Bhavanātha, devoted to the worship of Bhava,
has composed this commentary on the Kaṇāda-sūtras.
Although this work is not a source of praise for others and may even be fit for ridicule,
it must nevertheless be attended by thousands of disciples with the same reverence shown to a teacher.
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the tenth chapter in the *Śāṅkara-Vaiśeṣika-sūtropaskāra*. And this tenth chapter is completed.
And this treatise is also completed.
